Germany’s Merz cancels trip to UN in New York as pressure mounts at home
Friedrich Merz opts to remain in Berlin following far-right AfD gains and ahead of crucial regional votes
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has cancelled a trip to the UN General Assembly next week as he faces mounting pressure at home during a string of difficult state elections.
A government official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they couldn’t publicly discuss a trip that hadn’t been announced officially, said Wednesday that Merz won’t travel to New York as originally planned because “his presence is required in Berlin”. Merz had been expected to speak at the General Assembly next Wednesday.
There was no word on why his presence in Germany was required. But speculation has mounted that Merz’s job is in danger following a stinging defeat for his centre-right party by the far-right Alternative for Germany party in an election on September 6 in the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt.
That damaged the already unpopular chancellor’s authority as he tries to push through reforms to Germany’s sluggish economy.

The President of the European Commission detailed how the EU will tackle climate change-induced impacts.
Ursula von der Leyen says this summer of extreme heat was a "mere of preview" of the high temperatures to come.
The President of the European Commission did not mince her words when she listed the many places around Europe that experienced extreme weather this summer leading, she said, to 35,000 excess deaths.
In a moving moment, she introduced the family of a firefighter who died fighting flames. The parliament gave a prolonged standing ovation in honour of the fallen hero.
She called the the repeated heatwaves "a summer of truth" in the annual State of the Union speech, in which policy and plans for the year ahead are laid out.
She said mitigation, adaptation and preparedness must lie at the heart of Europe's approach to tackling extreme weather.
"We will present a new framework for climate resilience next month. We will identify 100 of the most vulnerable territories in Europe. And we will assess the risks — and at which level they should be managed," the Commission chief recalled as 660,000 hectares were burnt to the ground and roughly 12 million tonnes of crops were lost.
Von der Leyen also announced a new Climate Insurance Alliance.
"Today, only around 25 per cent of catastrophe losses in Europe are covered by private insurance. This means that, far too often, national budgets become the insurer of last resort.
We need to take action to close this gap," the Commission chief told MEPs in Strasbourg.

State of emergency declared in Russian Arctic village after 200-ton diesel spill reaches the sea
Authorities have declared a regional state of emergency in Taymyr after a diesel fuel spill in the settlement of Syndassko, the Krasnoyarsk Krai government reported.
The spill occurred on the morning of September 15, when a diesel fuel storage tank was damaged in Syndassko, on the shore of Khatanga Bay. Law enforcement sources in the region told the Russian state news agency TASS that a storm caused the accident, with rising water levels in Khatanga Bay flooding and damaging the tank on the coastline.
Between 170 and 200 tons of diesel fuel leaked from the tank, according to various estimates, and reached the bay, the region’s Emergency Situations Ministry reported.
Local authorities said there is no threat to residents’ life or health, and that the petroleum products have not entered the body of water from which Syndassko residents draw their water.
The tank belongs to Taymyr Alliance Trading (TAT), a Khatanga-based company that supplies electricity to several settlements. Investigators have opened a criminal case over violations of environmental protection rules governing the operation of industrial facilities, sources who spoke to TASS said.
Taymyr’s head, Alexey Chlenov, said “no obvious signs of environmental damage have been found.” He added that Syndassko’s power supply has not been disrupted, with fuel in reserve tanks expected to last 10 days.
Syndassko, one of Russia’s northernmost settlements, is home to about 500 people.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Japanese and US lawmakers agreed that bolstering deterrence against China is key to preventing a Taiwan conflict during a meeting in Washington, on Tuesday.
Liberal Democratic Party lawmakers Hirofumi Takinami, Miyamoto Kazuhiro, and Suzuki Daichi met with Senator Thomas Tillis, co-chair of the Senate Taiwan Caucus, and Representative Ami Bera, co-chair of the Congressional Taiwan Caucus, according to a press release from Bera’s office.
The Japanese lawmakers are members of the House of Councillors Taiwan Friendship Group.
"We were able to share the understanding that a crisis involving Taiwan is indeed a crisis for Japan and a crisis for the Japan-US alliance," Takinami told reporters after the meeting, according to Jiji Press. The US lawmakers expressed support for Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s remarks in November that suggest Japan may intervene militarily if China decides to seize Taiwan by force.
Speaking to the Diet, Takaichi said, “If battleships are used and a naval blockade involves the use of force, I believe that would, by any measure, constitute a situation that could be deemed a threat to Japan’s survival.”
Last Wednesday, Kitamura Haruo, a member of the House of Councilors from the Conservative Party of Japan, pledged to promote legislation based on the US’ Taiwan Relations Act and Taiwan Travel Act.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense’s 2026 white paper reiterated its assessment that China represents the nation’s “unprecedented and greatest strategic challenge.” It also warned that Beijing has ramped up military activities around Taiwan in recent years and is attempting to normalize such activities while strengthening its military capabilities.

Aleees to set up battery materials plant in Tainan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:53:38 UTC
16:53:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Advanced Lithium Electrochemistry Co. plans to set up a production facility in Tainan to fulfill growing orders for cathode materials used in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, CTEE reported Wednesday.
LFP batteries are known for their stable structure and high safety and are widely used in electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and power systems. The cathode is a key battery component that affects safety and performance, according to Anue and Hoyu Resources Technology.
Aleees plans to lease an existing factory in Tainan and install new equipment to make LFP precursor materials, which are used to produce LFP cathodes. The company has signed a pricing agreement with a North American customer to manufacture and supply the materials.
The agreement covers 20 years of shipments starting July 1, 2027. Trial production at the Tainan plant is scheduled to begin in January next year, with shipments expected to start in July.
Aleees has not disclosed the customer's identity due to a confidentiality agreement. Supply chain sources said the order is related to the expanding use of energy storage systems and electric vehicles in North America.
The Tainan plant is expected to play a key role in Aleees' restructuring as battery supply chains move to reduce reliance on China. The company is one of the few LFP cathode material manufacturers outside China with patents covering LFP composition, structure, and manufacturing processes.
The facility is initially planned to have an annual production capacity of 25,000 to 50,000 metric tons of precursors, with the figure potentially rising to 100,000 tons as orders increase. Aleees expects the North American agreement to begin contributing to revenue in mid-2027, with its contribution potentially increasing in 2028.

Taiwan labor groups urge unified penalties for minimum wage violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:52:45 UTC
16:52:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Labor groups have called on the government to standardize penalties for employers who pay below the minimum wage, saying inconsistent local rules weaken enforcement, CNA reported Wednesday.
The Taiwan Labor Front said fine standards vary among local governments and industrial parks overseen by the Ministry of Economic Affairs. It said the differences could reduce the effectiveness of the Minimum Wage Act.
Taiwan Labor Front Secretary-General Yang Shu-wei (楊書瑋) said enforcement varies widely across the country. Under current guidelines for economics ministry industrial parks, he said an employer could commit more than 50 violations before receiving the maximum fine.
Yang said similar differences exist among Taiwan’s six special municipalities. Tainan and several counties have yet to establish specific fine guidelines for minimum wage or Labor Standards Act violations.
Taipei Confederation of Trade Unions Deputy Chair Wang Yen-chieh (王燕杰) said authorities recorded 153 minimum wage violations nationwide last year. Under the fine standards used in economics ministry industrial parks, only a small number of repeat offenders would have received the maximum penalty, per Rti.
Labor groups said consistent enforcement is especially important for younger workers, who often have less bargaining power and may fear losing their jobs if they report violations.
Taiwan Alliance for Advancement of Youth Rights and Welfare Secretary-General Chang Yu-chia (張祐嘉) cited a 2024 labor ministry survey showing 59% of workers aged 15 to 29 did not state an expected salary when applying for jobs, per UDN.
Among young workers who received pay raises, 23.5% said minimum wage increases were one factor. Chang said the findings showed the minimum wage remains an important safeguard for workers with limited bargaining power.
The Taiwan Labor Front urged the labor ministry to work with local governments and the economics ministry to create a nationwide penalty standard. It proposed imposing the maximum fine after an employer commits five or more violations, per Nownews.
The group also urged financial regulators to review sustainability reports filed by listed companies. It said companies that violate minimum wage rules but fail to disclose the cases should be publicly identified, per CTS News.
The labor ministry said it has asked local authorities to follow common penalty principles under the Labor Standards Act when handling minimum wage cases. It has proposed formally adding the Minimum Wage Act to the guidelines, and local labor authorities have agreed to follow the revised standards once the changes are completed, per Tai Sounds.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) criticized the legislature Tuesday for failing to forward the 2026 budget to the Cabinet after it completed its third reading in August.
Cho said that while the Cabinet is still waiting for the legislature, important work remains to be done, per NOWNews. Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) added that the delayed implementation of the 2026 budget could have a knock-on effect on a supplementary budget proposal submitted to the legislature Sept. 3, per Liberty Times.
Lee said the supplementary budget includes increases in welfare benefits and bonuses for civil servants, teachers, and military personnel, benefiting roughly 3.9 million people. Lee explained that a delay in forwarding the 2026 budget could affect benefits for millions of people, as well as the NT$145.7 billion (US$4.58 billion) allocated to strengthen Taiwan’s defense capabilities.
KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) rejected the characterization of the situation as a delay, noting that the deadline for forwarding the budget was set for Sept. 29 during a previous caucus negotiation, per UP Media. However, DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) argued that the legislature has taken too long to complete the administrative work, per CNA. He said it was reasonable for the public to question the legislature’s efficiency after a month had passed without the budget being forwarded.
Chuang reiterated his criticism Wednesday, saying the outcome of caucus negotiations should not prevent Cho from commenting on the issue, per Newtalk. He said roughly NT$224 billion in spending could not proceed because the 2026 budget had not yet taken effect.
The legislature responded that it would hand over the 2026 budget, which consists of seven volumes, to the Cabinet before the end of the week, per CNA. It reiterated that Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) announced during caucus negotiations on Aug. 26 that the deadline would be set for Sept. 29 to allow sufficient time for personnel to organize the large number of bills passed in August.

Marine Corps tests new robot boat to hunt underwater mines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:52:02 UTC
16:52:02 KST

- U.S. Marine Corps explosive ordnance disposal teams tested a new Unmanned Surface Vessel at Camp Pendleton in late August as part of the LEON hazard-clearing system.
- The Marine Corps expects to begin fielding the USV to EOD companies in fiscal year 2027, with the rest of LEON following within two years.
Marine Corps explosive ordnance disposal teams tested a new unmanned boat at Camp Pendleton in late August, part of an effort to clear mines and other explosive hazards from coastal waters without putting divers directly in harm’s way. The Explosive Hazard Defeat Team, working under Program Manager Combat Support Systems, ran the Unmanned Surface Vessel through two weeks of trials off the Southern California coast.
The boat is a commercial unmanned surface vessel fitted with sonar, forward-looking infrared cameras, and both line-of-sight and acoustic communications gear. It can drive itself along programmed routes.
It is the fourth piece of a five-part system the Marine Corps calls Littoral Explosive Ordnance Neutralization, or LEON. The full system also includes a remotely operated vehicle, diver equipment, an unmanned underwater vehicle, and an amphibious unmanned ground vehicle, each meant to extend how far Marine explosive ordnance disposal technicians can operate from a hazard before they have to approach it directly.
“The USV is a key part of the LEON System of Systems (SOS). While it provides a search capability, it will primarily enable the other LEON systems to conduct operations below the surface, locating and identifying potential hazards, then relaying that information to the surface for real time updates. The LEON SOS will enable maneuver by identifying safe routes for transit within the littorals,” said Capt. Timothy Guinan, project officer, Explosive Hazard Defeat Team.
The boat’s main job is to scan for hazards and serve as a communications relay, called a Mobile Gateway Buoy, linking the underwater and shallow-water parts of the LEON system to command elements on shore or afloat. It can run missions for up to 14 hours at a stretch, according to Guinan, covering large stretches of coastline with little more than a small crew monitoring it from a distance.
“Unmanned systems allow operations to continue without fatigue. These systems can be launched and left to conduct a mission for upwards of 14 hours covering large areas of the littorals, while it requires minimal manpower to monitor the system,” Guinan said.
Marines from 7th Engineer Support Battalion’s explosive ordnance disposal company took part in the testing, known formally as a Field User Evaluation. That gave fleet Marines, rather than engineers alone, a chance to run the system through waypoint navigation, target deployment, and location verification before offering feedback to the program office.
The teams started in calm water, learning the controls and setting up mock mine targets, then moved into a wider-area search through varying sea conditions off the Pacific coast.
“The events were very successful. Everyone was communicating well. The platform itself was running well, had long endurance and gave us good results to refine and further develop the capability,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Alfredo Andrade, officer in charge, Explosive Ordnance Disposal Company, 7th Engineer Support Battalion.
Andrade said the push toward unmanned maritime systems reflects a broader goal within the EOD community: reducing how often Marines have to physically approach a suspected explosive hazard, and cutting the strain that repeated deployments put on a limited pool of trained technicians.
“Some of the conflicts that we are engaged in take a toll on the force, and surging in new forces is costly. It turns into a logistical problem. To preserve the safety and the health of the forces…the USV and the [LEON] program exist to ensure that we have readily available combat power,” Andrade said.
The Marine Corps expects to begin fielding the USV to explosive ordnance disposal companies in fiscal year 2027, with the rest of the LEON family of systems set to follow over the two years after that.

At least eleven Palestinians, including five children, were killed and 14 others injured on Wednesday after a residential building damaged during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza collapsed in southwestern Gaza City, according to the official Palestinian news agency WAFA.
The six-storey building collapsed onto its residents and tents sheltering displaced Palestinians nearby, leaving dozens of people trapped beneath the rubble, WAFA reported, citing rescue teams.
Residents said more than 60 people, most of them displaced Palestinians, had been staying in the building, which had suffered damage and developed cracks following Israeli bombardment.
Rescue efforts hampered by equipment shortages
Rescue teams began working early on Wednesday to search for survivors and recover those trapped beneath the rubble, but faced a severe shortage of heavy machinery and other equipment, according to WAFA.
The collapse adds to the growing number of Palestinian casualties reported since a ceasefire took effect in October 2025.
Gaza’s health ministry said 1,375 Palestinians have been killed and 4,686 injured in Israeli attacks since the ceasefire began.
The ministry said the Palestinian death toll from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023, has reached nearly 74,000, with more than 174,000 people injured.

English village votes to ‘secede’ from Britain over asylum centre

- Residents oppose plans to house over 1,200 asylum seekers at a disused military site, citing lack of local government engagement and community concerns.
- The government plans to end using hotels for migrants by 2029, shifting to military bases, while emphasising safety and addressing a national asylum backlog.
AI generated
LONDON – An English village of around 350 people announced on Sept 16 that a vast majority of residents had voted yes in an “independence referendum” to protest against plans to house over 1,200 migrants in a nearby facility.
Piddington in central England, 25km from the university city of Oxford, has grabbed headlines with its tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote.
The village’s parish council announced on Sept 16 that with 312 ballots counted, 285 had voted to secede from Britain over plans to house asylum seekers in a nearby disused military site, in a symbolic vote with no real legal basis.
Residents were handed a ballot paper with the statement: “I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination.”
“I think what this result shows is that Piddington campaigners have done an incredible job to highlight their concerns about the proposed asylum centre,” the leader of Oxfordshire county council, Tim Bearder, told the BBC.
He accused the government of proposing the plan “without engaging with local people”.
But Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told Sky News she would “gently say to the people of Piddington that we inherited a massive asylum backlog” and it is unacceptable for the whole burden to “fall on poorer communities”.
Around Britain, regular protests have been staged in towns and villages against the housing of asylum seekers in hotels and other facilities.
The Piddington referendum was a play on the British comedy film Passport To Pimlico.
In the 1949 classic, a small group of Londoners discover treasure and declare independence making them exempt from post-war rationing and other bureaucratic restrictions.
“What we’re doing is a very British thing – we’re voting,” the local parish council chair Tim McNally said ahead of the result.
“Because this is a really important topic... not just in this region, (but) across the whole of the United Kingdom. We’re just ground zero,” he said.
According to government information, the proposed centre would be used for a minimum of 10 years to house single adult male asylum seekers.
The “safety and security” of the migrants, staff at the base and the local community would be “of the utmost importance”, it said.
The Labour Party, in power since July 2024, is phasing out the use of hotels as migrant accommodation, a policy it inherited from the previous Conservative government.
It has vowed to completely end their use by the end of this Parliament, due in 2029, turning instead to ex-military bases. AFP

Who decides what comes next in Gaza?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:49:56 UTC
16:49:56 KST

Share & more
Amid the ongoing Israeli genocide that has destroyed entire neighbourhoods, displaced the vast majority of the population, and left Palestinians in the Gaza Strip facing a multitude of humanitarian crises, US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace has been attempting to lay the foundation for a system that will govern the enclave for years to come.
As Gaza’s future is being planned from the outside, something that should go without saying apparently needs to be said: No plan can be legitimate or sustainable without people in Gaza having a real say in the decisions that will shape their lives.
For nearly three years, we in Gaza have been living among destroyed homes and worn out tents. Our families have been scattered; our friends, neighbours, and loved ones have been injured and killed; and Israeli attacks and restrictions have long since caused the collapse of the basic services needed to sustain life.
The plans and promises being put forward for our future by those outside the enclave often seem entirely disconnected from this reality. Nearly a year after last October’s so-called ceasefire, they have also not been reflected in real actions. On the ground, we have yet to see any meaningful change.
The Board of Peace has established a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG). An International Stabilisation Force (ISF), consisting of soldiers from various countries, is also supposed to deploy to oversee security in the enclave.
No plan can be legitimate or sustainable without people in Gaza having a real say in the decisions that will shape their lives.
The NCAG is made up of Palestinians from Gaza, which seemingly sets it apart from the various redevelopment plans being proposed entirely by outsiders. People in Gaza have had no say in selecting its members, but we are clinging to hope that they can do something to improve our lives.
We have been subjected to such brutality and have been made so desperate that many would be willing to welcome anyone who can ease their suffering and bring back some sense of normal life. The names and backgrounds of the NCAG’s members are less important to us. Ultimately, we will judge it based on whether it is actually able to make a difference.
Something similar can be said for the ISF: If an international force means the Israeli military withdraws and people no longer have to live with the constant fear of bombing, incursions, or being displaced again, many would naturally see it as a chance for a safer life.
With Israeli leaders who have overseen the devastation in Gaza, including Ben-Gvir and Katz, once again openly speaking about expelling Palestinians from the Strip, it remains to be seen whether any of the Board of Peace’s redevelopment plans will be implemented or whether the ISF will ever deploy.
For now, Israel is still blocking members of the NCAG from entering Gaza and any kind of reconstruction from moving forward. But there are plenty of examples already of the disastrous results that occur when hostile and outside powers attempt to impose “solutions” on Palestinians in Gaza that serve their interests rather than those of the people who actually live here.
The case of UNRWA
One sign that the Board of Peace is not interested in consulting or representing the perspectives of Palestinians in Gaza in its plans for the future is the position it has taken on UNRWA, the UN’s agency for Palestine refugees.
On 1 July, the Board of Peace said in a social media post that “UNRWA has no place in the new Gaza”. This isn’t merely an issue of replacing one institution with another.
UNRWA is not something that is distant from our lives. The agency was established in 1949 in the aftermath of the Nakba, when hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were displaced from their homes. For more than seven decades, it has provided education, healthcare, and aid and development services to Palestinian refugees in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria.
The talk of excluding UNRWA from Gaza’s future also carries greater significance than the question of who will provide these services.
More than 65% of Gaza’s population are refugees registered with UNRWA who were displaced from their homes in 1948 or their descendents. For us in Gaza, UNRWA has never been just a blue logo on bags of flour. Its presence extends into the details of daily life that generations of Palestinians have known – a school children attend, a medical clinic families turn to, a lifeline refugees depend on when their options run out.
We have our own criticisms of UNRWA, but critiquing an agency is very different from wanting it to disappear. The talk of excluding UNRWA from Gaza’s future also carries greater significance than the question of who will provide these services.
UNRWA’s continued existence reflects the fact that the Palestinian refugee question remains unresolved, and Israel has long sought to dismantle the agency as a way of burying this question.
That is why, for many of us, talk of ending UNRWA’s role or replacing the agency carries a political meaning that goes far beyond the logistics of who distributes food or runs a school. It raises questions about the fate of Palestinian refugees themselves, their rights, and how their cause might be redefined without them being genuine participants in that discussion.
A dangerous precedent
The Board of Peace’s vow to exclude UNRWA from Gaza’s future is not the first time Palestinians in the enclave have been presented with an alternative to an existing system without having a meaningful role in designing it.
At the end of May last year, the US- and Israeli-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) began distributing food through militarised distribution sites that bypassed the UN and humanitarian organisations that have worked in Gaza for decades, including UNRWA.
The GHF was presented as a solution to the widespread starvation faced by Gaza’s population at the time, ignoring the fact that the same authorities offering the “solution” had created the starvation crisis to begin with.
The results were sadly predictable: In just over three months, 1,172 people were killed by the Israeli military and armed security contractors in the vicinity of GHF sites, and the world’s foremost authority on hunger officially declared that a famine was taking place.
These numbers aren’t just statistics in UN reports. I was one of the Palestinians forced to go to GHF sites in search of food for my starved family. I remember leaving before dawn on multiple occasions with my friend Ahmed for the distribution sites. Each time, I knew I might not come back.
When I hear talk today about new systems and institutions being designed for us, I can’t see them as just administrative arrangements on paper. I have experienced what an “alternative” can mean when it is not designed around people’s safety, dignity, and needs.
On one of our attempts, we ran with crowds of people towards the food amid gunfire, with Israeli tanks nearby, and snipers positioned around the area. I made it back to my family that day, but Ahmed was shot in the head and taken to the hospital in critical condition.
When I returned to our tent, my family did not ask what food I had brought back. It was enough for them that I had returned alive. Ahmed survived, but he is still in a difficult condition.
This is why, when I hear talk today about new systems and institutions being designed for us, I can’t see them as just administrative arrangements on paper. I have experienced what an “alternative” can mean when it is not designed around people’s safety, dignity, and needs.
In Gaza, the question at the aid sites was much simpler and harsher than all the discussions about how efficient the distribution system was: Would you return to your family with food, or would you not return at all?
Living with the consequences
People in Gaza do not necessarily reject every new institution or every attempt to find new arrangements for governance, security, and reconstruction after the war. The need for an administration that can restore basic services, provide security, and rebuild Gaza is clearer to those living here than to anyone else.
We live with the destroyed homes, lack of basic services, insecurity, and absence of reconstruction every day. For us, the needs are immediate, not just abstract questions. But the GHF experience showed why it is not enough to present Palestinians with a new system and expect us to blindly trust that the people designing it have our best interests in mind.
Gaza is not an administrative problem to be solved. It is a society of more than two million Palestinians. When the meetings are over, the plans are signed, and the delegations leave, we are the ones who will remain here to live with the consequences of the decisions others are making for us.
That is why a sustainable future for Gaza cannot be built through institutions and political plans designed and implemented by outsiders. If the decisions being made today will shape our lives for years and even decades to come, then the conversation must begin with the people who will live with their consequences: what we want, what we need, and what kind of future we want to build for ourselves. Gaza’s future cannot be drawn for Palestinians without them.

U.S. Army spends $18M turning cavalry regiment into tank brigade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:47:29 UTC
16:47:29 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Akima Facilities Operations $18 million to repair and refit equipment for a cavalry regiment converting into a heavy brigade combat team.
- Army Contracting Command expects the work to be completed by Oct. 18, 2027, with locations and funding set individually for each order.
The U.S. Army is spending $18 million to repair and refit equipment as one of its cavalry regiments transforms into a heavy brigade combat team, trading in lighter reconnaissance vehicles for the tanks and armored fighting vehicles that define the Army’s most heavily armed formations. Army Contracting Command awarded the contract modification to Akima Facilities Operations, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The switch from a cavalry regiment to a heavy brigade combat team is not a simple relabeling. A cavalry regiment is built for scouting and screening, using wheeled and lightly armored vehicles to find the enemy and report back. A heavy brigade combat team is a different animal entirely, organized around M1 Abrams tanks and M2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicles, designed to fight through resistance rather than avoid it. Moving a unit from one structure to the other means overhauling much of what it owns, from vehicles to support equipment, so it matches the new formation’s requirements.
That overhaul work is what this contract pays for. In Army contracting language, it is called induction and repair, a process in which vehicles and equipment are brought in, inspected, and either fixed or refurbished so they are ready for use under the unit’s new configuration. Some of what comes in may already belong to the Army and simply needs reconditioning. Other items may need more extensive rebuilding before they can be issued to soldiers.
The modification, worth $17,927,838, adds funding to an existing contract, W52P1J-20-F-0137, rather than creating a new one. Only one company submitted a bid for the work, and the Army awarded it to that sole bidder, a detail the contract announcement discloses but does not explain further.
The Department of War did not identify which cavalry regiment is undergoing the conversion, nor did it say where the repair work will take place. That is not unusual for a contract structured this way. Locations and funding will be worked out separately for each order placed under the agreement, rather than fixed in advance, and the current phase of work is expected to be finished by Oct. 18, 2027, giving the Army roughly a year to complete it.
Akima Facilities Operations is based in Herndon, Virginia, and is part of Akima, a group of companies that holds a range of federal contracts covering logistics, facilities support, and equipment maintenance work for the U.S. government. The company’s role here fits that broader business line: keeping military hardware serviceable rather than manufacturing it.
What remains unclear is the scale of the work. The Army did not disclose how many vehicles or pieces of equipment the induction and repair effort will cover, nor did it release the total value of the underlying contract beyond this modification. Army Contracting Command, which manages the agreement from its headquarters at Rock Island, Illinois, has not said whether additional modifications are expected as the conversion moves forward.

Lebanese in Israeli-occupied south fear bleak future once UN peacekeepers withdraw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:43:00 UTC
16:43:00 KST

Lebanese in Israeli-occupied south fear bleak future once UN peacekeepers withdraw
RMEICH, Lebanon, Sept 16 - Kicking up a column of dust, the United Nations peacekeeping vehicles were the only cars on the road as they passed bombed-out buildings on their way to Christian towns deep in southern Lebanon's Israeli-occupied zone.
More than six months of Israeli bombardment and demolition, triggered by a Hezbollah rocket attack in early March, have left villages abandoned and residents forcibly displaced across swathes of land. Shrubs encroach on minarets and rusting metal gates mark where homes once stood.
Entry from the rest of Lebanon is controlled from newly established Israeli checkpoints. Beyond one, Israeli Merkava tanks were stationed halfway along the desolate road.
Reuters reporters embedded with French peacekeepers from U.N. force UNIFIL for rare access to the area and to Rmeich, one of three predominantly Christian towns whose residents stayed put as Israel's military established a self-declared "security zone" in southern Lebanon.
Since Israel seized the zone, UNIFIL troops have been escorting convoys of food and other goods to the Christian towns. But nearly five decades after it was established, the U.N. force's mandate will conclude at the end of the year — leaving residents of Rmeich fearful that their link with the rest of Lebanon will be severed.
"What's going to happen to us? What's going to happen to these shop owners and these merchants? If they want to bring goods from Beirut here, how are those goods going to arrive?" said George Ibrahim, a 45-year-old schoolteacher from Rmeich, where roughly 6,000 people still live.
It is the largest concentration of people in the Israeli-occupied zone, where Israeli bombing has destroyed predominantly Shi'ite Muslim villages from which Hezbollah, an Iran-backed Lebanese armed group, has historically drawn support.
"We consider ourselves to be living in a large prison, isolated," Ibrahim told Reuters. "Without UNIFIL, I don't know what the future is."
GOODS IN CHRISTIAN TOWN START TO RUN LOW
In response to a request for comment, an Israeli military official said they did not consider UNIFIL's role vital to humanitarian efforts and that Israel was working "to make things easier for the population".
UNIFIL was established in 1978, days after Israel invaded southern Lebanon in response to attacks by Palestinian militants. Initially set up for six months to confirm Israel's withdrawal, its mandate was repeatedly renewed, including after Israeli troops eventually withdrew in 2000.
Following a month-long war in 2006 between Israel and Hezbollah, its role was expanded to monitoring a new ceasefire across the Lebanese-Israeli border and ensuring humanitarian access for civilians.
It set up a hotline to defuse tension between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, which formally remained at war, and helped a U.N. cartographer in Lebanon map out the Blue Line, the de facto border between the two countries after 2000.
More than 300 peacekeepers have been killed in Lebanon, including seven in this year's war, which has killed more than 4,300 people in Lebanon and left 300,000 still displaced.
The force has become part of the landscape. Near Rmeich's church, boys playing football asked peacekeepers if they could jump inside their vehicles.
"Civilians need support from UNIFIL, and that's what we are providing," said Captain Julien, who heads a French reconnaissance company within UNIFIL, and asked to withhold his last name in line with security guidelines.
"What will happen after? I don't know, but I hope that we find another way for the civilians to get through the Israeli lines and to live peacefully," he said, adding that a security escort was needed to cross the many Israeli checkpoints in the occupied zone.
Last week, convoys of aid and goods carried by local traders and destined for Rmeich were canceled at the 11th hour without an established reason, including the one Reuters was meant to accompany.
Though UNIFIL made at least two trips into the Israeli zone, they did not escort supplies, and residents in Rmeich said stocks of fresh produce and fuel were beginning to run low.
Fruit and vegetable shops in the town center were closed. Others carried only non-perishables on half-filled shelves. A young man with a falafel shop used the last of his tomatoes for a sandwich, as booms from Israeli military activity elsewhere in the south echoed through Rmeich.
The Israeli military official said Israel was in the "security zone" to clear the area of Hezbollah, and did not want to stay in the long term or intend to establish permanent bases.
CONFLICT MONITORING ROLE
More than half of UNIFIL's nearly 50 bases now lie within Israeli-occupied territory, including its headquarters at Naqoura, only accessible by crossing two Israeli military checkpoints.
If no extension is granted, UNIFIL will begin gradually closing its bases starting January 1, with more than 7,500 peacekeepers from nearly 50 countries leaving and handing positions to Lebanese troops.
As Israeli strikes on the south intensified, bases there became safe havens for Lebanese contractors providing services for them. Several told Reuters that UNIFIL's withdrawal would leave them jobless and homeless.
With access to southern Lebanon restricted by Israel's occupation, people close to the mission warn that the mission's departure could also put an end to the "world's eyes and ears" in the south.
During periods of war across the Blue Line, UNIFIL has monitored exchanges of fire and violations of international law.
"UNIFIL are the custodians of the Blue Line," a senior U.N. official told Reuters on condition of anonymity. "They have documents spanning decades, including minutes of meetings, cartographic works, measurements — there are questions about what happens to those records and to the Blue Line at such a sensitive time."
This year, the force facilitated access to Israeli-occupied parts of southern Lebanon for U.N. staff investigating possible war crimes. Such access will likely become extremely rare, if not impossible, without a U.N. presence, two people familiar with the mission said.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on UNIFIL's looming withdrawal and Israel's view of the Blue Line.
SCRAMBLE TO EXTEND MISSION
After U.S.-brokered talks, Lebanon and Israel agreed in June to a plan that would see Israeli troops gradually withdraw as Lebanese troops disarm Hezbollah and take control of southern Lebanon. But Hezbollah has refused to disarm in full while Israeli troops occupy Lebanese territory, and the plan has stalled.
Now, a last-minute scramble is underway to keep UNIFIL troops in Lebanon past the end of this year. Two-thirds of Lebanon's parliament signed a petition last month to extend its mandate and Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said an extension was Lebanon's "first choice."
Diplomats privately describe an extension as unlikely. In June, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres outlined several options for a uniformed U.N. presence in Lebanon but the Security Council has yet to take action.
"We have a plan for withdrawal, and this will involve handing back positions to the Lebanese Armed Forces," said UNIFIL spokesperson Kandice Ardiel.
"Of course, we will be looking at these in great detail given the situation at the time. We can't speculate what the situation will be then, but the bottom line is we will have to hand these positions back."
The U.S. and Israel last year both welcomed the U.N. Security Council's decision to only renew UNIFIL's mandate one final time. Israel said a gradual withdrawal was the "correct decision" after UNIFIL had failed to prevent Hezbollah's military build-up in south Lebanon.
As the mission readies to draw down, residents of Rmeich see their prospects as bleak.
Najib Amil, a Catholic priest in the town who remembers when UNIFIL troops first deployed nearly 50 years ago, said that with their connection to the rest of the country increasingly shaky, locals feared being seen as "collaborators" by other Lebanese.
"Will Israel leave us here or kick us out? And if they let us stay, how are we going to be? Administratively, will we be with (Israel), or with Lebanon?" he said. REUTERS

EU's von der Leyen calls for pacing frontier AI models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:41:56 UTC
16:41:56 KST

In her State of the Union address, von der Leyen called for pacing the development of frontier AI models due to their disruptive potential, pledging closer safety cooperation with Canada, the UK and other like-minded countries.
The EU will support industry efforts to slow the development of more disruptive AI technologies and will collaborate with partners such as Canada and the UK on AI safety, the Commission chief said on Wednesday.
In her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hailed AI's potential to benefit humanity, provided its risks and opportunities are properly balanced.
She singled out the growing risks posed by so-called frontier AI models, those pushing the boundaries of the technology.
"As the frontier models become more capable, these risks have come sharper into focus. Models being developed will allow hacking on a level we never thought possible. And they will soon be in the hands of adversaries who see the world very differently to us," she said.
The Commission President referred to recent incidents in which AI agents escaped their testing environments and independently hacked other systems, as occurred in the OpenAI-Hugging Face breach in July.
"CEOs of the most advanced companies tell us that it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models. To pace the frontier. If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too," von der Leyen continued.
The EU already has one of the world's most comprehensive laws on artificial intelligence, the AI Act, which gives the Commission oversight of risk-mitigation measures for the most advanced models.
"We will step up together with our like-minded partners like Canada, the UK and others. We want to team up on model evaluation, verification, early-warning, AI security and much more," she added.
The Commission chief also announced she will convene a discussion with leading AI labs on how public authorities can support industry efforts to pace the frontier of this disruptive technology.

Iran war has cost the US more than $38 billion so far, says Congressional Budget Office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:40:45 UTC
16:40:45 KST

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office reports that up to $3 billion more is being spent on the war each month, depending on the intensity of fighting.
The US had spent more than $38 billion (€33 billion) on its war with Iran by the beginning of August, according to the country's Congressional Budget Office (CBO).
The estimate covers costs incurred by the US Department of Defence from the start of the conflict on 28 February to 1 August, just over five months later.
The Defence Department did not provide information to the CBO for its assessment, which instead relied on government databases and publicly available reports. The CBO said its estimates were therefore subject to “considerable uncertainty”.
Nevertheless, the figure broadly aligns with an estimate given by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in July, when he said the war had cost $37.5 billion.
The largest proportion of the cost is reportedly the $21.7 billion that has been spent on replacing munitions.
The CBO also warned about the depletion of missile-defence interceptors. It estimates the US has probably used between half and two-thirds of its inventory of those weapons since June 2025, leaving stocks depleted for several years.
On Monday, a Pentagon inspector general report warned that the US-led military campaign against Iran, known as Operation Epic Fury, had resulted in “strategic inventory shortfalls”.
The CBO also warned that the conflict is having a wider impact on the US economy, largely because disruption to oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea has pushed up energy costs.
The estimate was prepared in response to a request for information from Representative Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget committee.
Boyle criticised the amount spent: “this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs.”
“Donald Trump and Republicans have spent years telling Americans that we cannot afford to help families here at home,” Boyle said in a statement, "but apparently they can find tens of billions of dollars, and potentially much more, for a reckless war that is leaving Americans to pay the price.”
In June, the White House requested an additional $87.6 billion (€76 billion) in supplemental funding, much of it for the war effort. Congress has not approved the request.

(China Economic Roundtable) China steps up efforts to protect rights, interests of new employment groups
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
15:40:37 CST
16:40:37 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China has adopted a slew of measures to strengthen the protection of rights and interests of new employment groups as they have become an increasingly vital force in the country's job market, an expert said at the latest episode of China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency.
New forms of employment refer to jobs emerging with the rise of internet platforms, such as food delivery couriers, ride-hailing drivers, online marketers, livestreamers and online domestic workers, said Huang Kun, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Labor and Social Security.
Chinese authorities attach great significance to protecting the rights and interests of these workers and have made marked headway in this regard, according to Huang.
As the new job groups rely on internet platforms for their work, authorities have stepped up efforts to regulate algorithm rules of platform operators that may infringe on workers' lawful rights, according to Huang.
Special campaigns have been launched to tackle these issues. Major platform companies are being pushed to thoroughly check and fix problems, improve their labor rules, and make their algorithms fairer.
In April, the general offices of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council made public a guideline on enhancing services for new employment groups. The document calls on internet platforms to regulate algorithms, improve transparency, and protect workers' rights to be informed about, participate in and choose algorithm-related rules.
It also requires platforms to hear views from trade unions and worker representatives when adjusting rules on order allocation, pricing and delivery-time estimates.
In terms of optimizing insurance services, China has expanded a pilot occupational injury insurance program for nationwide new employment groups starting July 1 this year. Under this program, more workers will receive occupational injury protection, Huang said.
Launched in July 2022, the program covered major platform companies in delivery, ride-hailing and intra-city freight, ensuring that insurance premiums cover per order.
As China is mulling a comprehensive regulation document on protecting the rights and interests of workers in new forms of employment, Huang called for establishing a reporting system for platform firms on their employment practices, strengthening cross-regional and cross-industry supervision, and supporting trade unions in serving these workers.
Oversight and regulation should be further strengthened to safeguard the workers' basic rights, including the rights to fair pay, rest, information and participation, Huang said, also calling for strengthening vocational and skills training programs for these workers and further improving their working and living conditions by beefing up public services. ■

Iran war cost hits $38bn, forecast to rise $3bn a month: CBO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:40:35 UTC
16:40:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month: CBO
The six-month-old-and-counting US-Israeli war on Iran has cost $38 billion so far and that amount is projected to rise by $3 billion a month, Congress' nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ways to end the conflict and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz.
The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5% in the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office accounting, which totaled expenses through 1 August.
The mounting costs have strained US munitions stockpiles and driven up energy prices, raising concerns about the country's ability to respond to other potential conflicts and adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.
The cost was close to the $37.5 billion that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reported at a Senate hearing on 21 July.
The budget office said the majority of the costs stem from the rapid drawdown of munitions, estimating that it could take five years to replenish US stockpiles. Reuters reported in August that the US had used "virtually all" of its long-range precision missiles during the war.
The Department of Defense did not cooperate with congressional financial auditors, CBO reported.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly described President Donald Trump's attacks on Iran as "decisive action" to prevent Tehran from harming US personnel or interests. She said in a statement that the US military has "more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and beyond.”
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell disputed the report's findings of munitions shortages and said, "We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing."
The cost inquiry was conducted at the request of the top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania.
“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded," Boyle said in a statement.
"Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs."
The report did not include costs of recent strikes on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on US military installations in the region. It also did not factor in the borrowing expenses associated with financing the war, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.
Impact on US readiness
The CBO accounting found the war could have sprawling consequences for the US defense posture and the domestic economy.
The deficit in critical munitions, including missile interceptors, risks hampering the Pentagon's response in the event of another major conflict, such as potential hostilities involving China and Taiwan, CBO said.
At the July hearing in the Senate, Hegseth pleaded for nearly $90 billion in emergency funding to restock munitions supplies.
“Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” Hegseth said.
The Pentagon’s inspector general reported this week that Iran had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings on US bases in the Middle East as well as aircraft including fighter jets, refueling planes and drones.
It put the war cost through June 19 at $33.4 billion, saying the amount included about $184 million in damages to US diplomatic facilities from Iranian strikes.
Energy shocks caused by attacks in the Strait of Hormuz—the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil traveled before the war—and on energy facilities in neighboring Gulf countries have sharply increased prices for consumers and global producers.
The rising cost of the war also threatens to weigh on deteriorating US fiscal health. The nation's total public debt surpassed $40 trillion in August.
Trump regularly contrasts the Iran war with the illegal US invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan that followed the 11 September 2001 attacks.
The eight-year US war in Iraq, which involved more than 100,000 ground troops at its peak, cost $2 trillion, Reuters reported. The two-decade-long US conflict in Afghanistan, which also involved more than 100,000 troops at its most intense, cost $2.3 trillion, according to Brown University's Costs of War project.

BEIJING, September 16. /TASS/. Russia and China are actively developing their comprehensive partnership and strategic cooperation in all areas, including in the military field, Russian Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilyova said at the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum, an international security and defense conference.

"These approaches are reflected in Russia’s proposals for a new Eurasian security architecture and are supported by many states, including members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO)," Tsivilyova stressed. The SCO operates on the basis of openness, non-interference, equality, and mutual respect', in line with 'the principles of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, mutual consultations, respect for cultural diversity and a commitment to joint development.'"
The deputy defense minister also noted that a multipolar world order would help create conditions for a new system of international law, including in promising fields that determine the future of humanity. "As an example, I would like to cite an agreement proposed by China to establish the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which was signed on July 16, 2026, in Shanghai by 29 states, including Russia. The document provides a basis for international regulation in this sensitive area," Tsivilyova said.

TIANJIN, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Airbus on Wednesday delivered the first aircraft assembled at its new Final Assembly Line (FAL) for A320 family aircraft in the northern Chinese port city of Tianjin, the second of its kind in both China and Asia.
The delivery represents a major milestone in Airbus' industrial footprint expansion in China and across its global industrial system, the company said.
China Eastern Airlines took delivery of the A320neo aircraft. Currently operating the largest Airbus fleet in the Chinese mainland, the airline in 1985 took delivery of an A310, China's first Airbus aircraft.
"The delivery underscores Airbus' long-term commitment to our Chinese partners and our confidence in the continuous growth of China's civil aviation market," said Philippe Mhun, Executive Vice President Programmes and Services of the Commercial Aircraft business at Airbus.
He Xiaoqun, vice president of China Eastern Airlines, said the two companies have worked together for more than four decades, with their cooperation expanding from aircraft acquisition to areas including operational support, maintenance engineering and technical services.
Mhun added that the second FAL in China, which was put into operation last October, is a critical facilitator for the company's global A320 Family ramp-up trajectory toward a production rate of 75 aircraft per month, and provides the necessary flexibility and capacity to meet strong market demand.
Since the inauguration of the first FAL in Tianjin in 2008, Airbus' first commercial aircraft assembly line outside Europe, the facility has assembled and delivered over 800 A320 Family aircraft. Chinese airlines now operate over 2,300 Airbus aircraft, about one-third assembled and delivered in Tianjin.
China, the country with the largest air-travel population, is Airbus' largest single-country market for civil aircraft. Airbus said its fleet share in China has risen from about 20 percent in 2008 to more than 50 percent today.
According to Airbus' latest Global Market Forecast, China's demand for new passenger aircraft is expected to reach 8,830 units over the next two decades, accounting for more than 20 percent of the estimated global total of 42,060 units.
"Looking ahead, we will continue to enhance our industrial footprint in China, underscoring our unwavering trust and deep-rooted cooperation with our Chinese partners," said Erik Buschmann, chief operating officer of Airbus China.
He added that the first delivery from the new assembly line stands as a "vivid testament to the long-term partnership, mutual achievement, and shared success between China and Europe." ■

Imports jumped 28 percent from a year earlier to 11.15 trillion yen, the Finance Ministry said in a preliminary report. Meanwhile, exports grew 19.3 percent year on year to 10.05 trillion yen, lifted by overseas demand for semiconductors and automobiles. ■

Harri Tiido: Big money's big worries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:40:00 UTC
16:40:00 KST

Harri Tiido: Big money's big worries
In Harri Tiido's commentary series, the grand plans of the ultra rich are under review this time. The truly rich decide for themselves where and what to build so they do not have to mix with the rest of the crowd, Tiido notes.
Every person has their own worries. And the ultra rich have extreme worries, because so much has been accumulated and they cannot let it all disappear. Not to mention the extraordinarily valuable life of the ultra rich themselves. Until now, many have worried that some part of their wealth might end up benefiting all sorts of people, meaning the less wealthy or, God forbid, the poor. Hence the pathological tendency of many rich people to hire tax experts and lawyers to reduce the portion of their income that goes to taxes, meaning society's general needs. But I will not dwell on that this time.
To begin, a few words about how great wealth brings great influence, technological as well as political. For several figures, the state has become a constraint they wish to escape. Why should members of parliament decide how business may be conducted, whether artificial intelligence should be limited, and so on. Several ideas have emerged for creating independent territories where full individual sovereignty, meaning the sovereignty of the rich person, would apply.
So far the idea has moved forward with difficulty. One well‑known project was California Forever. It became public in 2023 when investors bought so much land that U.S. security services suspected a possible Chinese connection. Part of the land was near Travis Air Force Base. In fact, the plan was to build a city from scratch for about 400,000 residents. And the new settlement was supposed to be a place to test new forms of governance, because how long can you endure this democracy.
The project fell apart a year later when local residents caught on and understood what it would mean for local agriculture and the river delta ecosystem. The effort stalled, although the project leader has reportedly not given up and is trying to turn the acquired land into a center for shipbuilding, the arms industry, and technology.
This project was only a foretaste. In Donald Trump's administration, there are said to be several figures trying to create similar autonomous cities, for example in San Francisco's Presidio and in an old naval air station. Plans for creating similar cities have also been mentioned in the context of Greenland and the Gaza Strip. Perhaps this sheds new light on the interests of Trump's circle.
Regarding other plans, there has been talk of Palantir and Paypal cofounder Peter Thiel and other tech billionaires planning to establish ocean‑based communities and entire countries where their own laws and rules would apply.
Looking toward the future with concern, the ultra rich have in mind the need to secure one reliable refuge.
Doomsday thinking and the need to give it a real‑estate form have created, in addition to the ultra rich's plans, an entire industry offering bunker services. A home underground bunker can reportedly be built behind the house for a few tens of thousands of dollars. The upper end of the price scale is limited only by imagination.
For the truly rich who want to enjoy familiar comforts even after doomsday, several potential refuges have been created. These safe places are built with durability in mind to ensure security and self‑sufficiency in case of natural disasters, nuclear attacks, pandemics, and other global catastrophes.
For example, Elysium in New Zealand with luxurious living quarters, a spa, and gourmet food. In France there is a place called Citadel, in Japan the high‑tech Quantum Ark, in Kansas the Survival Condo in a former missile base, in the Czech Republic the underground Oppidum, in Switzerland Quantum Underground, and in Germany's mountains Vivos Europa One. In addition, there are chains like Orsos Islands, which represent a doomsday refuge on water, and the global underground shelter network Terra Vivos. And so on.
The truly rich decide for themselves where and what to build so they do not have to mix with the rest of the crowd. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg is building a massive complex on Hawaii's Kauai island reportedly costing more than 400 million dollars. Of that, the underground bunker alone costs 100 million. Peter Thiel once bought land in New Zealand for the same purpose, but local authorities blocked his plans. New Zealand still seems to be a popular future refuge among billionaires.
A large share of Silicon Valley billionaires are said to have already acquired some kind of refuge, as have several other well‑known figures. Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison bought, for example, 98 percent of Lanai island in Hawaii in 2012. Something similar is said to exist for Bill Gates, Oprah Winfrey, Richard Branson, and Google cofounder Larry Page.
Elon Musk, for example, does not intend to remain on Earth and aims for space, meaning Mars. With a possible stop on the Moon, but that is said to be too close to Earth.
An interesting project is underway in Argentina. The idea is that if nuclear war were to break out in the northern hemisphere, then the southern hemisphere, more precisely the part of South America south of the Tropic of Capricorn, should be protected from nuclear radiation flows. I cannot comment on this claim, but in any case the region has begun to attract the ultra wealthy.
Peter Thiel bought a property in Buenos Aires in April for 16 million dollars. His argument about the need for a strategic refuge in the southern hemisphere is also the basis for the project in Mendoza by Martin Varsavsky, who belongs to the Silicon Valley elite.
Varsavsky founded the company Campo Wamani and acquired a land area equal to five times the size of Buenos Aires. A completely independent living environment is planned there, where electricity is produced with solar panels, water is obtained from mountain springs, and there is also an airfield. In addition, a data center will be built there, into which large language models are planned to be loaded so that in case of catastrophe tech billionaires would have access to digital capabilities even if the global server system no longer functions.
Varsavsky initially promoted the project as a refuge for tech magnates in case of a third world war, but when the matter became more widely known through the Financial Times, he began to describe it as a simple resort.
Humanity, in their view, is expendable; only the survival of the best, meaning themselves, matters. Artificial intelligence will help them manage even without the rest of the people.
--

U.S. Air Force pays $148M to keep 1960s jet engine flying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:39:22 UTC
16:39:22 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Collins Engine Nozzles two sole-source contracts worth a combined $148.3 million for J85 engine fuel-system parts.
- The J85 turbojet powers the U.S. Air Force's T-38 Talon trainer, and the contracts run through 2029 and 2032 respectively.
The U.S. Air Force is paying close to $148.3 million to keep an engine that has powered its supersonic jet trainer since the 1960s running. The Defense Logistics Agency awarded Collins Engine Nozzles two contracts for fuel-system parts on the J85 turbojet, the engine that powers the T-38 Talon, according to Department of War contract announcements.
The J85 controls fuel delivery in the engine’s combustion chamber through nozzles and spray bars, components that wear out and need periodic replacement to keep the engine running safely and efficiently. Both parts are being bought fresh under these contracts.
The larger deal, worth $77,967,014, covers a one-time purchase of fuel injection nozzles, with work running until Jan. 31, 2032. The second contract, worth up to $70,290,396, covers main spray bars over a three-year ordering period that ends Sept. 14, 2029. Because that second contract is structured as indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity, the Air Force will place individual orders against it as parts are actually needed, rather than buying a fixed batch upfront.
General Electric originally built the J85 as a lightweight turbojet, and it has powered the T-38 Talon, the aircraft the Air Force uses to train fighter and bomber pilots, for more than 60 years. Variants also flew on the Northrop F-5, an aircraft some U.S. squadrons still use to simulate enemy fighters in training.
The Defense Logistics Agency did not put either contract up for competitive bidding. It cited 10 U.S. Code 3204 as justification for going sole-source, the law that allows agencies to skip competition when only one company can reasonably supply the part. Collins Engine Nozzles, based in West Des Moines, Iowa, has built fuel-system hardware for the J85 for years, which is typically why an agency treats a supplier as the only realistic source.
The Department of War did not say how many nozzles or spray bars are covered, or which T-38 or F-5 units will get the parts first.

U.S. Marine helicopters getting upgrade to share battlefield data faster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:32:52 UTC
16:32:52 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Northrop Grumman a $34.4 million contract modification to build additional Link 16 data-link kits for Marine Corps UH-1Y and AH-1Z helicopters.
- The kits let helicopter crews share targeting and positioning data automatically with other aircraft and ships instead of relying on voice radio, with delivery expected by March 2027.
Marine Corps attack and utility helicopters are getting more secure links to share battlefield data with other aircraft, ships, and ground units. The U.S. Navy awarded Northrop Grumman a $34.4 million contract modification to build additional Link 16 kits for the UH-1Y Venom and AH-1Z Viper helicopters, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
Link 16 is the encrypted network the U.S. military and its allies use to pass targeting data, aircraft positions, and other tactical information automatically between aircraft, warships, and ground troops. Without it, crews rely on voice radio to relay the same information, a slower and less precise method. Adding Link 16 to the Venom and Viper lets Marine helicopter crews see and share that data the same way fighter jets, destroyers, and other Link 16-equipped units already do.
The new order covers 8 kits for the UH-1Y and 9 for the AH-1Z, the hardware that physically integrates the radio into each airframe. It also includes 17 additional B-Kits, the shared radio and processing units that can be installed across both helicopter types, plus spare parts and technical support.
The contract itself is not new. Naval Air Systems Command, which manages Navy and Marine Corps aircraft programs from Patuxent River, Maryland, is increasing the ceiling on an existing agreement rather than opening a new one. That means no money changes hands yet. The Navy will pay Northrop Grumman only as it places individual orders against this higher ceiling, a standard practice for the type of contract involved. The work was not put out for competitive bidding, since it extends a contract Northrop Grumman already holds.
Naval Air Systems Command expects the additional kits to be delivered by March 2027. The Department of War did not say how many Venom and Viper helicopters across the Marine Corps fleet still need the upgrade, or how much the full contract could ultimately be worth once all potential orders are counted.

Antarctic ozone hole expands above average in early September: EU climate agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:30:51 UTC
16:30:51 KST

Melike Pala
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The Antarctic ozone hole expanded rapidly in early September, reaching an estimated 25 million square kilometers (9.6 million square miles), about 5 million square kilometers (1.8 million square miles) above the average for the period, according to the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.
The service said Wednesday that the ozone hole had developed at a typical rate since the second half of August, consistent with patterns observed over the past 46 years.
However, its area grew sharply during the first half of September, with forecasts indicating that it could expand further in mid-September.
Copernicus attributed the rapid development to a sudden drop in minimum temperatures at about 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) above the South Pole, where temperatures can allow the formation of polar stratospheric clouds.
These clouds contribute to chemical ozone destruction by activating halogens in the presence of sunlight during the Southern Hemisphere's spring, generally between August and November.
Despite the rapid increase in area, other indicators monitored by the service, including the minimum ozone column value within the defined ozone-hole area and the ozone mass deficit, remained close to historical average levels.
The ozone layer protects life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation by absorbing much of it.
Human-made emissions have caused significant thinning of the layer over the past several decades, increasing exposure to ultraviolet radiation.
The Antarctic ozone hole is particularly pronounced because the region's stable polar vortex and stratospheric winds help maintain the cold conditions associated with ozone depletion.
The ozone hole typically forms over Antarctica during the Southern Hemisphere's spring and gradually changes as atmospheric conditions evolve.
The largest Antarctic ozone hole on record took place in 2006, covering 29.6 million square kilometers (11.4 million square miles), according to Copernicus.

Top AI execs met with federal ministers as copyright proposal leaked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:29:56 UTC
16:29:56 KST

Top AI execs meet with Albanese ministers as leaked copyright reforms spark political blow-up
Senior executives from OpenAI and Anthropic were meeting with federal ministers just as its proposals to rewrite copyright law for AI leaked to the public, sparking fury from creatives and critics across the political spectrum.
The Albanese government has been trying to thread the needle of enticing major AI companies to grow their investment in Australia, while also addressing concerns about the risk and harms associated with the AI boom.
AI companies have said Australia's copyright regime is a sticking point over plans to invest here. They fear their unauthorised use of copyrighted material to create — or "train" — their AI models is breaking the law.
Earlier this week, senior ministers met with senior US executives of the two top AI companies, Anthropic's special international envoy, Jeffrey Bleich, and OpenAI's vice president of global policy, Ann O'Leary, amid their push for an Australian expansion.
Confidential AI copyright consultations leaked
After ruling out a broad exemption for AI companies to train their models on copyrighted materials in Australia late last year, the ABC revealed yesterday the government held secret consultations earlier this month that would pave the way for AI companies to train their models in Australia.
Under one option, AI companies could gain permission after striking a minimum number of deals with rights holders, without paying other creators whose work they used.
The other option would require companies to either pay to a new central body that would distribute money to rights holders, or to separate organisations representing various groups of creators, like the music or writing industry.
Both options would give creators the right to opt-out, reversing the existing onus for companies to seek permission to use copyright material, and would come with other protections and requirements on its use.
A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland told the ABC on Tuesday the government was consulting creators, media organisations and AI companies about options intended to give creators control and fair payment.
OpenAI also confirmed on Tuesday it was participating in the consultations and said it was committed to working constructively with the government, creators and industry.
In a submission to the government's AI inquiry released today, OpenAI explicitly stated that Australia's copyright settings were a factor in its plans to grow its Australian presence.
"Copyright policy is part of that investment environment," OpenAI said.
Creatives and political opponents hammer government for proposals
Musician Holly Rankin, who performs as Jack River, criticised the proposals for shifting the burden of protecting copyright onto individuals.
Ms Rankin accused the government of breaking promises that creators would retain control over their work, and questioned why attracting investment should require concessions from them, if the proposals were put through.
"They also say they're very capable of doing everything. It seems everything except for licensing content correctly," Ms Rankin said.
Advocacy group Save Our Arts called on the government to rule out a change that would make AI training opt-out, rather than opt-in.
"The starting point should be simple: if somebody wants to commercially exploit an Australian creator's work, they should seek permission from the person who owns the rights," campaign director David Latham said.
The Coalition accused the government of departing from its assurances to creators, while saying it wanted Australia to attract leading technology companies.
In a joint statement on Tuesday, shadow attorney-general Michaelia Cash and communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson called for the government to release the full consultation material and rule out allowing AI training on copyright material without consent.
"But you do not attract investment by simply giving away Australians' intellectual property," Senator Cash said.
She said AI companies should negotiate deals with rights holders under existing copyright law, which she argued should be enforced rather than weakened.
Greens arts spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said the government should protect creators' ability to decide how their work was used and receive payment for it.
"If AI companies want to use Australian content, they need to pay for it just like everyone else," she said in a statement on Wednesday.
