Crimes against the Estonian state plea deal: Defendant faces 7 years in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:31:00 UTC
15:31:00 KST

Crimes against the Estonian state plea deal: Defendant faces 7 years in prison
A plea agreement was struck on day one of the trial of a pro-Kremlin propagandist charged with activities harmful to Estonia's national security.
Oleg Bessedin's hearing began on Tuesday at the first-tier Harju County Court. He has been in custody since his arrest last November, and faces seven years in prison under the terms of the plea agreement.
Lead State Prosecutor Taavi Pern told ERR's Russian-language portal that, following negotiations with the defendant and his lawyer, the Prosecutor's Office agreed to resolve the criminal case via a plea agreement provided Bessedin serves seven years of actual prison time and the court confiscates more than €73,000 in assets obtained via the crimes.
Those crimes are primarily acting against Estonia's national security. "According to the evidence, Oleg Bessedin, in cooperation with Russian state institutions and their representatives, has consistently participated in influence activities directed against Estonia. The aim has been to spread propaganda and disinformation in order to divide Estonia's population and sway people into supporting Russia's political choices," Pern said.
According to the indictment, Bessedin also disseminated narratives which Russia has used to justify attacks on neighboring states, amplifying them in such a way as to give those involved in Russia's political decision-making the impression that these represented the overall views of Estonia's Russian-speaking population; he also benefited materially from these activities.
"According to the evidence, Oleg Bessedin has directly harmed Estonia's security, and earned criminal proceeds in doing so," Pern said. "Therefore, Oleg Bessedin's crimes against the state must be followed by a severe and effective punishment. The prosecutor's condition for resolving the criminal case through a plea agreement was a lengthy actual prison sentence and the confiscation of proceeds obtained through the crimes."
Bessedin's lawyer, Dmitri Školjar, said that after two preliminary hearings, Tuesday's hearing began via ordinary proceedings, and an agreement was reached during the day. "We met, discussed it all day and resolved the disputed issues. Ultimately we signed a plea agreement and submitted it to the court today, asking for the proceedings to continue under a plea agreement," Školjar said.
He added that the court only received the materials on Tuesday, and still needs to review them, meaning it will make a decision on the agreement on Monday, September 28.
Sentences to run concurrently to 7 years' real prison time
Under the agreement, Bessedin will be sentenced to seven years in prison, comprising two years and nine months for violating sanctions and six and a half years for activities against the state. The agreement provides for the sentences to run concurrently, with the more severe sentence partially absorbing the lesser one, resulting in a total sentence of seven years.
The sentence will also take into account the time Bessedin has spent in custody since last November. He will be eligible to apply for release on parole after two and a half years.
The court also granted the defense lawyer's request to lift additional restrictions on his client. Bessedin has been held in solitary confinement, and according to his lawyer, his isolation from other detainees should now end, which will also allow him to communicate with his family.
The charge sheet states that from May 2022 at the latest, Bessedin actively participated in influence activities conducted for the benefit and in the interests of Russia and, in the course of these activities, was in contact with various Russian institutions, officials and individuals involved in Russian influence operations.
According to these charges, by taking part in these influence activities, he committed non-violent acts directed against Estonia's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Additionally, prosecutors have charged him with distributing sanctioned Russian television shows and content in Estonia via television and social media channels under his control, as well as making sanctioned content available to other channels. The purpose of the international sanctions imposed on Russia is to prevent the spread of Russian propaganda and disinformation and to curb Russia's capacity for aggression.

Lietuvos bankas: Economy will grow steadily, while inflation will begin to ease next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:30:12 UTC
15:30:12 KST

The Lithuanian economy will continue to grow this year, but households will feel the impact of rising prices more acutely as energy costs increase. Average annual inflation is projected to exceed 5% before moderating next year. The latest projections by Lietuvos bankas indicate that wage growth will outpace inflation throughout the projection horizon, supporting further increases in households‘ purchasing power.
‘Higher energy costs this year have once again highlighted how quickly external shocks can affect everyday life. Nevertheless, the Lithuanian economy is proving resilient, supported by growing exports, investment financed through EU funds, and increased defence spending. It is also important that the surge in energy prices does not translate into long-term inflation. As energy price pressures ease, inflation is expected to moderate significantly next year,’ says Gediminas Šimkus, Chair of the Board of Lietuvos bankas.
Lietuvos bankas projects the economy to grow by 2.7% this year, 2.4% in 2027 and 3.1% in 2028. Compared to June, the growth projection for next year has been revised up by 0.4 percentage points, while that for 2028 has been revised down by 0.2 percentage points.
The revisions largely reflect the impact of the second-pillar pension reform, which has been more limited than previously expected. Individuals are taking time to spend the withdrawn funds. By August, €3.5 billion had been transferred to account holders. Lietuvos bankas estimates that around €0.6 billion had been spent on consumption by the end of June. Some of the withdrawn money may still be spent later but this is unlikely to provide a significant additional boost to the domestic demand in the near future. Consequently, this year and next year, economic growth will be more moderate than previously projected.
Exports will contribute more to economic growth this year and next year, supported by stronger demand from Lithuania’s trading partners. Investment trends also remain favourable on the back of EU-funded projects and rising defence spending.
Lietuvos bankas projects domestic consumption to go up by 3% this year and 1% in 2027. Real exports are expected to increase by 4.8% and 3.6%, respectively, while investment is projected to rise by 8.2% and 5.7%.
Tensions and uncertainty in the Middle East have led to a surge in energy prices, which spilled over to other prices, particularly transport services. The overall rise in prices has been tempered by a slower increase in food prices. Average annual inflation is expected to be 5.1% this year, although it may exceed 6% in some months.
In the coming years, inflation is expected to decline steadily and, by the end of the projection horizon, to return to a level typical of an economy converging towards Western living standards. This will be primarily driven by declining energy prices, slower wage growth and weaker impact of taxes. Average annual inflation is expected to be 3.1% in 2027 and 2.6% in 2028.
The labour market situation remains favourable for employees. Wage growth is supported by strong demand for labour but the scope for further increases in employment will be increasingly constrained by the declining working-age population and weaker migration flows.
Unemployment is expected to stand at 6.7% this year and fall to 6.6% in 2027. Average wages are expected to rise by 9.4% this year and 7.6% next year.

The US Department of Defense Inspector General has reported that the war with Iran has caused a munitions shortage and a “bottleneck” in replenishing stockpiles—contradicting statements by US President Donald Trump, who regularly denies the existence of supply issues, the BBC reports.
Trump has previously claimed that US munitions reserves are virtually unlimited and that anyone saying otherwise is spreading fake news. However, the independent watchdog reported that between February and June, the US expended munitions worth over 22 billion dollars, resulting in a shortage of strategic equipment. When asked about the watchdog’s report, the White House responded that there is more than enough ammunition.
The report provides the first independent insight into typically classified information regarding US weapons stockpiles.
Previous estimates had already painted a grim picture. During the conflict, US forces expended large quantities of ammunition for long-range systems, as well as vast numbers of missiles and air-defense munitions, to repel Iranian strikes. In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) concluded that stockpiles of ammunition for certain missile interception systems—such as Patriot and THAAD—had been significantly depleted, with inventories in some cases cut by as much as half.
The Inspector General’s report does not disclose the exact quantity of remaining weaponry;
however, it indicates that equipment is running low and reveals bottlenecks in the ammunition replenishment supply chain. The report adds that the Department of Defense is working to accelerate procurement processes and production capacity to address the ammunition shortage.
The White House has rejected the watchdog’s assessment; on the 15th of September, spokesperson Anna Kelly stated that the United States possesses more than enough ammunition to achieve all its strategic objectives—and then some. Trump and other US administration officials have also sought to portray reports of weapons shortages as a betrayal of the country.
In a post on X on the 4th of August, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth dismissed reports of weapons shortages as false. Meanwhile, in a lengthy post on Truth Social on the 3rd of September, Trump emphasized that the US holds virtually unlimited stockpiles of weapons and continues to build up its inventory to prepare for any contingency. When the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran, Trump stated that the conflict would be over within a few weeks. In September, he said that the war in Iran would end after the midterm elections scheduled for the 3rd of November.
Polls show that the war in Iran is highly unpopular among Americans. A survey conducted in early September indicates that only 23% of Americans (and just half of Republican voters) believe the US is in a better position regarding Iran than it was at the start of the war.

The 39-year believes that the saga will only end one of two ways -- when “the Russian regime is toppled” or the Russians succeed in killing him, he said.
Thumann is an outspoken supporter of Ukraine’s war against President Vladimir Putin and a supplier of attack drones to Kyiv. Authorities first warned him last December that he could be in danger, he said.
Soon after, “I was explicitly told that the threat comes from Russia and that a murder attempt on me is planned,” he said.
His life has been turned upside down by being forced to go underground, although he still manages to oversee his company’s work.
“I’m more or less completely isolated from the outside world,” he said, adding that communication with family was “sporadic” and “only digital”.
Contacted by AFP, the interior ministry of the southern state of Bavaria -- where Donaustahl is based -- said it was aware of the case but declined to comment further, noting that it was under investigation by federal prosecutors.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 15, 2026
- Perpetrators ‘will pay’ -
Defence firms across Europe appear to be increasingly in Russia’s crosshairs as Western security services say Moscow is stepping up a campaign of sabotage across the continent, a charge Russia denies.
Last week firebombs were hurled outside a defence tech firm and near a drone maker in the Bavarian city of Munich, an arms industry hub. Two Bulgarian nationals were arrested.
While no one has yet been blamed, the incident came days after Germany said Russia was responsible for an attempted attack using an explosive-laden drone at an airport in the eastern city of Leipzig, a key transport hub for military goods.
Thumann is also not the first defence executive believed to have become a target. In 2024 the United States foiled an alleged Russian plot to assassinate the boss of Rheinmetall, Germany’s biggest defence group, CNN reported at the time.
Following the Leipzig incident, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last month Germany was increasingly “in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers”, and warned that perpetrators of such acts “will pay”.
The term “hybrid attack” is used to refer to acts ranging from drone activities to sabotage and cyberattacks, which fall short of full-blown military assaults.
Russia has dismissed Berlin’s accusation that it targeted Leipzig airport, and routinely rejects claims it is behind other incidents.
Thumann believes that “drone companies and every defence company in Europe, not only in Germany... are in danger”.
“Every EU country is a target -- and every defence company is a target -- of Russian aggression,” he added.
Two so-called “low-level agents” have so far been arrested in connection with the plot against Thumann, though he believes the danger remains.
Berlin accuses Russian intelligence of recruiting low-level, or disposable, agents, often through social media, to carry out “hybrid attacks”, usually with little training and for relatively small sums.
- ‘In a real war’ -
While Donaustahl is a relatively small player in German defence, Thumann styles himself as a “disruptor” seeking to shake up a cumbersome industry which has been too slow to respond to the rapidly changing face of modern warfare.
He is an advocate of producing drones more cheaply and en masse -- which is what he believes placed him in Russia’s crosshairs.
“The Russians aren’t afraid of 10,000 drones produced by a large company,” he said.
“They are afraid of a million drones developed by a small firm and manufactured by many companies across Europe.”
Donaustahl’s products include strike drones and warheads for interceptor drones -- UAVs that aim to counter attacks from other hostile drones.
The firm develops and sells the products, but outsources the large-scale production to larger partners.
For Thumann, it is high time that the German government confronts the reality that it is engaged in a conflict with Russia.
“In my view we are already in a real war,” he said.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov echoed the language earlier this month, saying that Berlin’s counter-measures to the Leipzig incident -- closing a Russian consulate and a cultural centre -- indicated the “start of a real war”.
The Donaustahl boss urged politicians to accept that a conflict had already begun, and to “act decisively and not just engage in symbolic politics, but really do things that clearly set boundaries for Russia”.

Europe faces winter gas risks as storage lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:28:30 UTC
15:28:30 KST

Europe is approaching winter with low gas stocks as disruptions to liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies from the Gulf push up prices and slow efforts to replenish reserves.
EU storage facilities were about 68 percent full on Sept. 14, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Qatar has largely suspended LNG shipments amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
“Europe is prepared for a normal winter, but it is not well insulated against a severe one,” Erisa Pasko, lead European gas analyst at Energy Aspects, told Anadolu Agency.
The consultancy expects European storage to reach 69 percent of capacity by the end of October, leaving stocks near a 14-year low heading into winter. Inventories could fall to 16 percent by the end of March even under normal weather conditions.
Energy Aspects does not expect Europe to run out of gas, but says prices must remain high enough to curb demand and attract LNG cargoes. Pasko also warned that gas becomes harder to withdraw quickly as storage levels decline.
Germany is the most exposed major market, she said. Its storage was 55.8 percent full on Sept. 14, compared with 52.5 percent in the Netherlands.
The European Commission said on Sept. 3 there was no immediate threat to gas supplies. It cited more diverse supply sources, greater LNG import capacity and lower demand as reasons the EU was better prepared than in 2021-22.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,511,530 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022

Russia has lost around 1,511,530 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Sept. 16.
The figure includes 1,530 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,345 tanks, 25,339 armored combat vehicles, 149,557 vehicles and fuel tanks, 49,820 artillery systems, 2,132 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,642 air defense systems, 442 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,630 unmanned ground systems, 519,069 aerial drones, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

EU digital wallet: 24 of 27 members will miss the deadline

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:25:37 UTC
15:25:37 KST

The EU has set a December 24, 2026, deadline for every EU country to launch a digital ID wallet; only three have delivered so far. Watch the video!
The EU is asking countries to offer at least one certified digital wallet by the end of 2024. Before the deadline, EU-funded pilot projects with 350 organisations issued over 1,500 digital credentials and completed more than 8,000 cross-border transactions.
The free wallet can hold national IDs, driving licences, diplomas, health insurance, and bank details. It uses three safeguards: selective disclosure, unlikability, and issuer-blindness. Using the wallet is optional, and paper documents are still valid.
The rollout is uneven across countries. Italy leads with almost 8 million monthly users. Germany plans to launch in January 2027, while the Netherlands postponed its rollout to late 2027 after a pilot had only 57 users. Bulgaria is still working on legislation.
Businesses must accept the wallet by December 24, 2027, but banks need to comply earlier, starting in July 2027, because of anti-money-laundering rules. The digital rights group EDRi has raised concerns about draft rules that would require facial recognition and reduce privacy protections.

Germans who opted for alternative civilian service once went to help vulnerable people in countries devastated by the Nazis, including Russia and Belarus. Then Moscow started a new war in Europe.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:24:27 UTC
15:24:27 KST

Germans who opted for alternative civilian service once went to help vulnerable people in countries devastated by the Nazis, including Russia and Belarus. Then Moscow started a new war in Europe.
From 1990 through the 2000s, Germans traveled to Russia and several other countries to perform alternative civilian service. German women came too, but as volunteers. They worked in hospitals, residential facilities for people with mental and neurological disabilities, and other care homes, and helped older people in their homes. One motivation was to atone for their ancestors’ guilt during World War II, seek reconciliation with the peoples who had suffered under Nazi Germany, and do something useful for them. Meduza spoke with volunteers from those years and the organizers behind the initiative.
In the mid-1980s, pacifist organizations took Germany’s alternative civilian service program abroad
After World War II, West Germany had no armed forces of its own. It did not begin establishing them until the mid-1950s, and a military service law was adopted in 1956. At the same time, West Germany’s constitution enshrined the right to refuse military service on grounds of conscience and perform alternative civilian service instead. This service had to benefit society in some way and was performed in hospitals, nursing homes, and other social care institutions.
An army began taking shape in East Germany at around the same time. But unarmed service was not permitted until 1964. Men who refused to bear arms on religious or other grounds could then serve in construction units known as construction battalions. This was not a civilian alternative in the West German sense: members of the construction battalions remained military personnel and wore uniforms, but were not issued weapons. They could be assigned to build defense installations and other military facilities.
For many years, proving one’s pacifist convictions in West Germany was extremely difficult. The process became easier in the 1980s, and officials realized that people seeking alternative civilian service could provide cheap labor. The number of people entering alternative civilian service rose sharply. Eventually, Sergey Krivenko, a board member of the International Memorial Association, told Meduza, German pacifist organizations secured permission for participants to perform this service abroad.
One of these organizations was Action Reconciliation Service for Peace (ASF). Founded in the late 1950s, it later helped men perform alternative civilian service abroad in countries that had suffered under Nazi aggression. ASF also recruited men and women seeking volunteer experience for projects abroad.
“ASF and other organizations began looking for local groups that could arrange this kind of volunteer work,” Sergey Krivenko said. “In other words, it wasn’t done through the government but through NGOs [nonprofit organizations]. In the early 1990s, a special center called Compassion was established within Moscow Memorial to help former victims of political repression. Those were hard times, with everything falling apart. Social services were only just being established. Most of the work was like this: older people lived alone and needed someone to clean, cook, and go shopping for them. The idea came up to bring in volunteers from [ASF and other organizations] to do this work. And it worked.”
The German initiatives also established contacts with other NGOs, churches, and residential institutions, sending volunteers to work with them.
In her book “Nestrashny mir” (“A World Without Fear”), special education teacher Maria Berkovich says that at the children’s home near St. Petersburg where she began volunteering in the 2000s, all volunteers were called Germans because there had never been any others:
The first German volunteers came to the children’s home more than 10 years ago. Ever since then, they have come every year and stayed for a year; when their term ends, new volunteers replace them. The organization also has ties to a German school for occupational therapists, so every year two or three of the school’s graduates come to the children’s home for six months to work with the children… Tanya, Sveta, and I became the first Russian volunteers at this children’s home.
The director of a St. Petersburg foundation that helped children and adults in residential institutions told anthropologist Anna Klepikova that when volunteers began working at the children’s home, few staff members saw any point in it. Klepikova quotes her in the book “Naverno, ya durak” (“I Must Be an Idiot”):
Most people thought we were wasting our time on nonsense. They told me point-blank, ‘Sure, you can tell the Germans whatever you want to get money out of them, but you and I understand that these children don’t need anything, right? And that they can’t develop, right?’ I think that if it hadn’t been a German organization, it simply wouldn’t have happened, because Russians who suddenly started working with children like these would have been seen as idiots. That’s all there is to it.
Hundreds of volunteers came to Russia — most of them without knowing Russian
The German volunteers who spoke with Meduza said the organizations that sent them paid for their trips. The program was funded not by the government but through donations collected by civic organizations. These funds could be used to rent shared apartments for volunteers and cover food, transportation, and other basic expenses.
Sergey Krivenko said Germans worked in at least Moscow, St. Petersburg, Volgograd, and Perm in Russia, as well as Minsk in Belarus. Their numbers were not especially large: Moscow, for example, might have hosted 10–20 volunteers a year. In all, hundreds of young people from Germany spent time in Russia and Belarus over the years.
Sergey Krivenko gave Meduza his overall impression of the German volunteers he met in the late 1990s and the 2000s:
They were incredibly interesting young men and women. [Some of them] were part of the volunteer ”social year” program. But of course they were young and wanted to have fun. After all, this kind of work was a chance to travel somewhere for free, and an adventure too. They also had strong ideological motivation: we’re doing a good thing, helping people. […] Sometimes we met some very interesting characters. One, for example, was the grandson of an SS general. He made a conscious decision to go to Russia to repay his family’s debt, as he saw it.
The volunteers studied the language while they worked. Many of Meduza’s interviewees said they were supposed to take a two-week intensive Russian course in Germany before leaving. Some spoke positively about the course; others did not. Either way, they had to overcome the language barrier once they arrived.
“They came without knowing Russian,” Sergey Krivenko said. “And within the first three months, through their contact with victims of political repression… they began to speak and understand it reasonably well. It was amazing.”
Young men doing alternative civilian service came to Russia from the early 1990s through the late 2000s. Germany abolished compulsory military service in 2011 and shifted to a professional army, reducing the number of German citizens working in social care institutions. Even so, volunteers continued coming to post-Soviet countries to do charitable work.
‘I have so many memories that usually shock people’
“If you have no connection to Russia, you don’t pay attention to what the media reports about it,” one German volunteer said in an interview with the charity Perspektivy. “Of course, I had a general picture in my head: freezing winters, Red Square, Moscow, St. Basil’s Cathedral, a samovar. All the usual clichés. Growing up in East Germany, I encountered the ‘big brother’ from the Soviet Union in kindergarten and at school, but even so, I had no idea what Russia was really like. I even bought a kettle back then and brought it to Russia because I didn’t know whether I’d be able to buy one there.”
Sofia came to Russia in the early 1990s. She told Meduza that her work had been arranged through a Moscow church:
A priest met us and arranged for us to stay in his nephew’s apartment. It had three rooms: the nephew lived there, and the five of us got the other two rooms. Four boys and me. We had fun, but I got away from them pretty quickly. I was from East Germany, and they were from West Germany. We could communicate easily, but they were too Western for me. And I realized I wouldn’t learn Russian if I stayed with them.”
With help from the Orthodox community, Sofia then found a home with a local family. The host church also arranged volunteer placements for her and the other young people. They mostly helped older people in their homes:
I had to buy groceries, and I learned to make porridge. Cleaning too. It was very nice. I met some remarkable people. One was a former Russian teacher who would sit with me and teach me the language. There was also a former cosmonaut who told me how he had been made to stand on his head for long periods and how they had conducted some kind of terrible experiments on him.
Volunteers could also help at one of Moscow’s residential institutions in their free time if they wished. Sofia said about 50 children of all ages lived there, from infants to teenagers approaching adulthood. Because the facility was understaffed, some of the children were often tied to their beds. “It was a very sad sight,” Sofia said. “The home had children with severe illnesses, as well as orphans who acted as caregivers for the sick children. I tried to teach them English and German. I was just a volunteer — I saw what needed doing, and I did it.”
Another volunteer, Matteo, performed his alternative service in Minsk through ASF in the mid-2000s. He said he became interested in Russian while still in school, thanks to a Ukrainian friend of his father’s. Alternative service in the former Soviet Union therefore seemed like an appealing option. Matteo was assigned to a children’s residential institution in the Minsk neighborhood of Navinki. He also spent some time helping adults at a residential facility for people with mental and neurological disabilities in the city’s Drazhnya neighborhood. Matteo said:
I still remember the stench in the hallways [at the institution in Navinki]. I have so many memories that usually shock people, yet by the end of the conversation, you’re left feeling that the person you’re talking to still hasn’t really understood. Because they never lived in that system.
There was one very withdrawn autistic boy who usually stood in a corner and sometimes hit himself. By the end of the year, I could communicate with him and was the only person who could calm him down. I was proud of that at the time. But at the end of the year, I told him I was leaving. He hit me and himself very hard. When I came back for a couple of days six months later, he was just as withdrawn as ever. Who knows whether that means it was all for nothing. Or maybe it wasn’t…”
Matteo also told Meduza about the institution in Drazhnya:
For me, Drazhnya was darker than Navinki. The building was bigger, and I usually stayed in the first two rooms on the ground floor. Four young women with cerebral palsy lived there; they had previously been at the institution in Navinki. Farther down, in the shadows of the hallway, there were beds and wheelchairs with people in them, amid moans and a stench. And there was a television mounted on the ceiling, with two or three orderlies sitting around it. I only found the courage a couple of times to ask someone from the hallway to go for a walk outside. I usually preferred the comfort and familiarity of those first two rooms.
Matteo said that he and the women who lived in the first two rooms would usually go for walks, talk, drink tea, smoke, go shopping, dye their hair, and listen to music. “We had a friendly relationship, but naturally, it wasn’t entirely equal,” Matteo said. “Unlike in Navinki, they had their own lockers and even cellphones. They often called to ask when we were coming back. Sometimes they messaged so often that it got annoying.”
Anthropologist Anna Klepikova’s book “Naverno, ya durak” (“I Must Be an Idiot”) includes a foundation director’s account of how difficult it was to find volunteers for an adult residential institution in St. Petersburg: “Volunteers fainted, and we had to send the German volunteers home because they couldn’t handle working in the adult institution.” According to the director, volunteers found it easy to imagine themselves in the adult residents’ place and picture themselves living in the same “utterly inhuman conditions.”
“We spent three years fighting just to get the residents spoons, for example,” the foundation director said. “There were no spoons, and they lapped food out of bowls like dogs. And the smells — when we first arrived at the residential facility for people with mental and neurological disabilities, it was absolutely horrifying. People lay there all day, wet and covered in filth, in pain that no one paid any attention to.”
Like Matteo, a volunteer named Emma worked in Minsk, though she came in the 2010s. She decided to volunteer immediately after finishing school, before enrolling at a university. Emma’s mother was a historian, and Emma said Germany’s history had mattered to her since childhood:
When you realize that you’re German, what that may mean to other people, what grievances they may have — entirely justified grievances… It was important to me to do this work.
Our hosts in Minsk had lists of former prisoners of concentration camps and other Nazi camps, including elderly women who had been forced to work in Germany. We visited them to help. We went shopping and cleaned for them. But they were always fussing over us and feeding us. It was very nice.
I also worked at a center for children with various kinds of cancer. We just played with them, made things out of clay, and drew pictures. I remember spending a lot of time with one girl who was seven or eight years old and lived in isolation in a separate room. You couldn’t simply walk in to see her. You needed a mask and shoe covers. I played with her so her mother could get some rest.
‘Our volunteer service was in the cause of peace. And now there was a new war’
The institutions’ overall atmosphere did not strike the volunteers who spoke with Meduza as “a horror movie with no escape.”
Although conditions in the social care institutions were difficult, Sofia said the people around her were very curious during her time there, and it was easy to become part of the local community. Everyone was intrigued: “Some Germans have come here to volunteer.” People wanted to support the young volunteers who had come to help.
One volunteer told the charity Perspektivy that he ate nothing but bread and butter for his first few weeks: “Back then, every store still had those separate departments, and without knowing Russian, it was almost impossible to buy anything. It took some time, but human relationships are always what matters most. And because our relationships with people were good, I felt comfortable and quickly got used to everything. We were a good team, and people took good care of us.”
Meduza’s interviewees said they made many local friends and stayed in touch with them for years. As a result, after volunteering, Sofia, Emma, and Matteo all returned more than once to Moscow, Minsk, and other cities in the former Soviet Union.
In early 2022, Emma flew to Russia as an exchange student studying medicine. Her program lasted around six months, so she was in Moscow when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine:
Our earlier volunteer service was in the cause of peace. We felt guilty, and it took decades before we were able to come as volunteers to countries that had suffered during World War II. And now there was a new war.
If I had known in advance, I wouldn’t have gone at all. Everything became clear only on February 21–22. I’ll never forget those days. I don’t think the other German exchange students felt the way I did, because they hadn’t had my experience or grappled with the subject of war the way I had. And I couldn’t find the words [to explain it all to them]. In those circumstances, with all that propaganda, and especially as a German, a “daughter of fascists,” it wasn’t easy.
Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Emma volunteered at Moscow’s Sakharov Center in her free time until her exchange program ended in the summer of 2022.

Spain sets out 2030 sustainable tourism strategy – with residents a ‘core’ focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:22:07 UTC
15:22:07 KST

With 100 million international visitors expected this year, and ongoing concerns about overtourism, Spain is putting people and sustainability at the centre of its countrywide policy.
Spain is on course to welcome 100 million international visitors this year, but amid concerns over mass tourism, the country is rethinking how it manages continued growth.
In a presentation at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, Carlos Ruiz González, director of the Spanish Tourist Office for the Gulf region at Turespaña, outlined how Spain’s Tourism 2030 plan will put people and sustainability at the centre of its next phase of growth – with residents and lesser-visited destinations a key focus.
Developed in consultation with more than 200 tourism experts, businesses, government bodies and other organisations, the plan recognises that destinations across Spain face very different challenges. These range from mature coastal resorts and heavily visited cities such as Barcelona to rural and inland areas looking to attract more tourists.
Spain, the world’s second-most visited country, welcomed 96.8 million international tourists in 2025, while tourism accounts for 12.6% of the country’s GDP and supports around three million jobs.
Visitor numbers are continuing to rise in 2026, but the government is increasingly looking beyond arrivals as it considers how to manage growth and reduce pressure on destinations facing overcrowding.
“For the last few years, our government has been thinking about what we should do to manage this success,” Ruiz González said. “We have some destinations that are dying of success, I would say. Well, we have a big country, a diverse country.
“So, the government of Spain decided this has to be a full government policy, a country policy, and not just tourism. All the ministries, all the sectors in Spain are aligned.”
How does Spain plan to make tourism more sustainable?
Devised with a three-phase roadmap, which will be delivered through a series of two-year action plans, Spain Tourism 2030 is a government-wide policy covering economic, social and environmental sustainability.
According to Ruiz González, the main challenges range from climate change and employment to housing pressures, overcrowding and regional depopulation.
Recognised as a “core audience”, but “not a side effect of it”, residents are one of five groups at the centre of the new strategy, alongside destinations, businesses, tourism workers, and visitors.
“We want the residents also to be part of the system,” Ruiz González said. “Tourists go where people live, so people need to keep living and be able to afford to buy a house or buy an apartment or just walk in and out without problems.”
Part of the strategy will focus on spreading visitors more widely across Spain, while encouraging slower trips and longer stays.
Where should tourists go to in Spain?
While Spain is not looking to discourage tourists from its most popular destinations, Turespaña wants travellers to explore rural and lesser-visited parts of the country.
“Some destinations don't need much promotion – they are very well known,” Ruiz González said. “Basically, we want people to go more inland in Spain. We also want people to travel slow, to stay as long as possible.”
For travellers interested in nature and hiking, he highlighted the Pyrenees and Picos de Europa, as well as the Sierra de Guadarrama mountain range, a national park within easy reach of the capital, Madrid.
Ruiz González also highlighted the historic cities and smaller towns of Castilla, while Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network is helping make destinations beyond the established tourism hotspots easier to reach.
“We want all our destinations to be part of the solution,” he said.

====================================================================================================

NAZA lays bare Israel’s public diplomacy failures as global narratives take hold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:16:20 UTC
15:16:20 KST

Israel’s representation abroad has often been described as another front in the country’s conflicts, yet its public diplomacy operation has repeatedly struggled to keep pace in recent years. The battle for global public opinion has often appeared disorganized, a problem reflected not only in the fallout surrounding NAZA. 
For long periods, no single figure was in charge of Israel’s public diplomacy effort, the system did not operate with a unified line, and responses to controversies sweeping through the international media often arrived only after a narrative had already taken hold.
Since the outbreak of the war following the October 7 massacre, Israel has faced an intense battle over international perceptions. Yet for extended periods, there was no single figure leading the country’s public diplomacy operation, while serious allegations against Israel were sometimes left unanswered or addressed only after they had already spread widely.
The position of head of the National Public Diplomacy Directorate remained vacant for nearly two years. Only in April 2026 did the government approve the appointment of former Israeli ambassador to Britain Tzipi Hotovely. In July, Doron Spielman was appointed the directorate’s international spokesperson, a position that had not previously existed in that form.
The ministry was dismantled, public diplomacy left without a clear address
The story of Israel’s public diplomacy apparatus began before the war. At the start of 2023, a separate Public Diplomacy Ministry was established for Likud lawmaker Galit Distel Atbaryan, alongside the National Public Diplomacy Directorate already operating within the Prime Minister’s Office. The directorate itself had no permanent chief until August that year, when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu chose Moshe “Moshik” Aviv for the post and the Cabinet approved the appointment days later.
The Public Diplomacy Ministry headed by Distel Atbaryan quickly ran into difficulties. She complained repeatedly that it lacked authority and even basic equipment, saying at one point that she was uploading videos from her spokesman’s phone because the ministry lacked the resources it needed and was forced to improvise. In the hours after the October 7 massacre, she said she wanted to engage in public diplomacy but did not know what she was permitted to say under military censorship rules.
With the outbreak of the war, then-IDF spokesman Rear Adm. Daniel Hagari became one of the most prominent Israeli figures communicating with audiences at home and abroad. Through frequent briefings and material released by the military, including battlefield footage and intelligence, Hagari provided updates on IDF operations and presented Israel’s account of the circumstances that led to the war and its military objectives.
But changes to the structure of Israel’s public diplomacy operation began almost immediately. On October 13, 2023, Distel Atbaryan announced her resignation after responsibility for Israel’s international public diplomacy efforts was transferred to the Diaspora Affairs Ministry alongside the Foreign Ministry’s existing work, and her ministry was subsequently dismantled.
Explaining her decision at the time, Distel Atbaryan said: “There is already a highly capable minister responsible for national resilience, there is the Home Front Command, and there are civilian organizations doing sacred work. And if I am being honest, I can no longer find any justification for this duplication of authority. Running a government ministry is expensive, and the people of Israel need every shekel.”
She added: “When I see the Public Diplomacy Ministry stripped of the powers it was originally given, I have no choice but to honestly admit that every day it continues operating from this point on constitutes a waste of public funds. Under the current circumstances, this ministry cannot make a significant contribution to the country, and the good of the country is more important to me than anything else. For all these reasons, I have decided to resign as public diplomacy minister.”
About 10 days later, on October 22, the government approved the ministry’s closure and transferred its 23.8 million shekel budget to the Tekuma Authority, established to rehabilitate Gaza border communities devastated in the October 7 attack. Twenty-nine positions from the ministry were also transferred to the rehabilitation authority.
Foreign-language spokespeople instead of a structured system
As the government tried to reorganize the operation, the Prime Minister’s Office recruited three spokespeople for the foreign media on October 24: Mark Regev, a former Israeli ambassador to Britain who had previously served as Netanyahu’s foreign-media spokesman; journalist Tal Heinrich; and British-born Eylon Levy, an Oxford and Cambridge graduate who became one of Israel’s most recognizable English-language voices online.
But difficulties persisted inside the government system. On November 14, 2023, a Knesset hearing addressed the suspension of funding for the Foreign Ministry’s overseas public diplomacy efforts. Zeev Elkin, then chairman of the Knesset subcommittee dealing with foreign policy and public diplomacy, said it was “unthinkable that in the middle of a war, the Foreign Ministry’s ongoing public diplomacy operation is shut down because of a lack of funding.” A Finance Ministry representative said money had been allocated but had not yet received final approval.
In December, the Knesset Finance Committee discussed increased funding for the Settlement Ministry and the National Public Diplomacy Directorate in the Prime Minister’s Office. A Finance Ministry representative said the directorate would receive an additional 40 million shekels. The discussion also included a monthly cost of 200,000 shekels for operating a television studio under Yossi Shelley, as well as 15 million shekels for a hostage administration that had yet to be established at the time.
On March 31, 2024, Eylon Levy announced the end of his tenure as an English-language government spokesman. He had been suspended several weeks earlier after posting on X in response to then-British Foreign Secretary David Cameron. The post prompted a complaint from Britain and a request for clarification over whether Levy’s remarks represented the Israeli government’s position. It was not the only controversy during his tenure; Ynet also reported that he had auditioned for Israel’s Dancing with the Stars after the war began.
Two months later, in May 2024, Aviv resigned as head of the National Public Diplomacy Directorate after roughly 10 months in the role. He had entered the job shortly before the war after previously overseeing state ceremonies and public diplomacy programs, and had not previously headed Israel’s national communications operation. His departure left the directorate without a permanent chief for an extended period.
Only on April 26, 2026, after nearly two years without a permanent head, did the government unanimously approve Netanyahu’s decision to appoint Hotovely to lead the National Public Diplomacy Directorate in the Prime Minister’s Office. Hotovely had previously served as settlement affairs minister, diaspora affairs minister, deputy foreign minister and Israel’s ambassador to Britain. She entered the post on May 5.
On July 1, Doron Spielman, 53, was appointed international spokesperson for the National Public Diplomacy Directorate. Formally, the position sits within the Prime Minister’s Office communications structure. Spielman had previously served as an IDF reserve spokesman to the foreign media with the rank of major during the war.
No clear communications line
The question, however, is not only who leads the National Public Diplomacy Directorate, but who sets Israel’s communications line in real time. Within the security establishment, no single figure has consistently filled the role of a dominant public communicator in recent years. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, who took office during the war, rarely appears in the media or addresses the public regularly in Hebrew or English. IDF spokesman Brig. Gen. Effie Defrin has also maintained a lower public profile than Hagari did during the early stages of the war.
More significantly, the gap between the speed at which events unfold and the pace of the Israeli response has been evident in several major controversies during the war, including the death of Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, the killing of World Central Kitchen aid workers and investigations alleging disproportionate use of force by Israel.
In early 2024, six-year-old Hind Rajab became one of the most recognizable symbols of civilian suffering in Gaza. For days, her fate was unknown after she spoke by telephone with rescue workers and pleaded with them to reach the vehicle in which she was trapped. During the call, she said: “They’re shooting at us. There’s a tank in front of me.” Her body was later found in the car, along with members of her family. The bodies of two Palestinian Red Crescent paramedics dispatched to rescue her were found nearby.
The story received extensive coverage from international media outlets, including the BBC, The New York Times, international news agencies and Britain’s Guardian, which led its report on the discovery of her body with words from her call with rescuers: “I’m so scared.”
Israel’s initial response included the assertion that Israeli forces had not been present near the vehicle at the relevant time. The case was later subjected to further military review. In August 2026, the IDF acknowledged that Israeli troops had fired on the vehicle carrying Rajab and her family and ordered a criminal investigation over alleged failures surrounding the coordination of the Palestinian Red Crescent ambulance sent to rescue her.
From a public diplomacy perspective, however, the damage had already been done. The emotional impact of the recordings of the child, combined with the gap between the initial Israeli account and later findings, made it harder for Israel to present a consistent and credible message in real time.
Another major incident occurred on April 1, 2024, when seven World Central Kitchen aid workers were killed in central Gaza after an Israeli drone struck their convoy. The dead included citizens of Australia, Britain and Poland, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen and a Palestinian employee.
The strike triggered an international uproar. Images of the damaged vehicles, together with the fact that the victims were humanitarian workers and citizens of countries friendly to Israel, prompted harsh condemnation from Western leaders and heavy diplomatic pressure. Then-U.S. President Joe Biden demanded that Israel take action following the incident.
A year later, another example emerged of the gap between the pace of reporting and the Israeli response. In June 2025, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera, citing Palestinian sources, reported dozens of dead and wounded near a U.S.-backed aid distribution center in Rafah amid allegations that Israeli troops had opened fire. Within hours, the claims had appeared across major international media outlets.
The IDF initially said it was “unaware of casualties caused by IDF fire inside the aid distribution compound” and that the matter was being examined. The Gaza Humanitarian Foundation said at the time that there had been no shooting at the center or in its immediate vicinity. But by then, the initial reports had already spread.
The BBC reported deaths from tank fire near the aid distribution center, Sky News also reported fatalities and Reuters reported the Palestinian allegations while noting at the time that Israel had not yet responded. Israeli statements and security-camera footage later released by GHF, which showed no unusual incident inside the distribution site itself during the period shown, came only after the allegations had already received extensive global exposure.
With no dominant Israeli voice responding immediately, former prime minister Naftali Bennett attacked the government’s handling of the episode.
“Israel has no public diplomacy. The operation is not being managed,” Bennett wrote on X. “The global media is charging at Israel with a huge lie about a ‘massacre’ that did not happen. This is one of the government’s biggest failures in this war. The result is a diplomatic collapse and a dangerous embargo. The importance of public diplomacy cannot be overstated. The failure is simply chilling.”
In another case, in May 2025, images from Gaza showing nine children from the family of Dr. Alaa al-Najjar, a pediatrician at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, also became a major element of international coverage. Images of the dead children appeared repeatedly on television and news websites around the world. As the Palestinian account received broad exposure, no prominent official Israeli spokesman appeared in the immediate aftermath to provide a counterweight or explain Israel’s position.
The latest example is the controversy surrounding NAZA, the film by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, which won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival and raises serious allegations about Israel’s conduct during the war in Gaza. Once again, critics argue, the Israeli response came late. According to Ynet’s reporting, the Israeli Embassy in Italy warned officials about the Venice screening a month in advance but was unable to prevent it. Israeli officials failed to obtain a copy beforehand and learned the full details of its content only after it was screened.
The film is based on testimony from 24 anonymous Israeli soldiers and military intelligence personnel and makes serious allegations concerning Israeli targeting policy in Gaza. One of its most sensitive claims is testimony that, in one case, approval was allegedly given for a strike in which as many as 500 people could have been killed, an allegation that featured prominently in international coverage of NAZA. 
The IDF has categorically rejected the claim, saying: “The IDF has never planned, approved or carried out a strike in which approximately 500 civilians, or any number approaching that figure, were expected to be killed.” Israeli officials have also stressed that no independently verifiable evidence has been presented for the claim and that the anonymous source’s identity, role and knowledge of the alleged incident cannot be independently assessed. The film won the Special Jury Prize in Venice on September 12 and has since become the focus of a fierce debate in Israel and abroad.
The domestic criticism of the film and its creators then became an international story in its own right. French newspaper Le Monde framed the controversy around the contrast between the film’s reception overseas and the reaction in Israel, highlighting accusations of “treason” directed at the filmmakers. The Guardian, which was involved in producing the documentary, issued a statement saying it was “deeply concerned” by what it described as an authoritarian response to NAZA in Israel.

dark metal roof shapes community canteen beside mountain stream in china
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:15:17 UTC
15:15:17 KST

engawa-like edge connects the canteen with the landscape
Nestled deep within the Wuling Mountain National Nature Reserve in Chengde, Hebei, the Aranya Wuling Mountain resort community sits quietly in its natural surroundings. Life here unfolds along mountain springs; layers of vegetation and clear streams form a natural barrier that gives the area a tranquil, secluded atmosphere, away from the noise of the outside world. The Shan Canteen, designed by LLLab. architects, is a community building for everyday dining and public leisure, located on a grassy slope beside the stream. The site is higher to the north and lower to the south, with water views to the west and a landscaped garden to the east. The building sits low to the ground, its dark grey metal roof softly reflecting the sky and blending quietly into the environment. The hip-and-gable roof gives the building a clean silhouette from every angle. Its deep eaves extend continuously around the perimeter, creating an engawa, a semi-open space that mediates between the interior and the outdoors. Here visitors can pause to enjoy the view, feel the breeze, and listen to the sound of the stream.
Natural wood and diffused light create a calm dining space
Inside the canteen, horizontal long windows bring the outdoor landscape into the interior, making the natural scenery a backdrop for dining. The downward-sloping eaves block the summer sun while directing the gaze toward the water features. The dining area has 108 seats. Between it and the food court counters, a skylight covered with washi paper filters sunlight into soft, diffused light, adding a gentle ambiance to the space. The interior uses natural wood veneers, with ceilings and walls clad in a wood finish. The warmth of the wood stands in quiet contrast to the cool greens and blues of the outdoors. The clean, LLLab. studio’s contemporary design works with the natural setting, offering guests a comfortable, home-like dining experience while the mountain landscape remains present throughout.
low roof being as close as possible to the ground to protect the tranquillity of the surrounding nature
a hidden feeling for the guests behind the trees

architectural language stays in very concise manner to slow down the experience
engawa experience along the green lawn looking to the riverside
roof lines emphasizing the natural skyline from the mountain
simple directionality of architectural space smoothens the ambience
framed view and directional ceiling paneling lines bring the views to the nature outside
roof and space with symmetry extending to the further back end of the kitchen, completing the imagined space

Defense agency rejects Datasel talks as EU funding period ends

Defense agency rejects Datasel talks as EU funding period ends
The State Defense Investment Centre (RKIK) has rejected a proposal by arms firm Datasel to resolve an ongoing dispute through a joint working group, noting the financing period for the contracts has expired.
Datasel, an Italian company acquired in 2024 by Indian-owned Neco Defense Munitions, signed four contracts with RKIK to supply artillery ammunition for Ukraine using EU European Peace Facility (EPF) funding. However, disputes over delayed, substandard deliveries led the RKIK to terminate and pursue legal action.
Revelations Estonia had paid up to €70 million in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine that were never delivered led to the resignation of Hanno Pevkur as defense minister.
Datasel this week sent a letter to the government, members of the Riigikogu and the RKIK proposing a joint working group to resolve disagreements and confirming its readiness to complete deliveries. The company said it has the resources and supply chain to fulfill its contractual obligations.
"It is not too late to resolve the disagreements," lawyer Veiko Viisileht, acting for Datasel, told "Aktuaalne kaamera". "Datasel is ready to sit down with the RKIK at the same table and resolve all disagreements."
RKIK gave a blunt response, however, with its lawyer Maria Pihlak noting the contracts had been financed through the European Peace Facility, but the period for using that funding has now ended.
"Simply put, this means that the RKIK does not have the budgetary resources today to accept the remaining ammunition that has allegedly been produced or is being produced in the future," Pihlak said. "Negotiations like these will not lead anywhere, anymore. We have an ongoing lawsuit, we have an ongoing arbitration dispute, and we will continue to defend our rights in these proceedings."
The two sides also disagree over the termination of the contracts. "These contracts were terminated because they repeatedly violated deadlines," Pihlak noted. Viisileht countered that whether the contracts were validly terminated "is a contentious issue both in court and in arbitration."
SDE MP Raimond Kaljulaid, a member of the Riigikogu National Defence Committee, said Datasel's latest appeal had not served to boost the company's credibility either, pointing to the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) investigation into the use of EPF funds by Estonia.
"What has changed is that news has come that this company is also being investigated very seriously at the European level," Kaljulaid said. "My first reaction was that maybe this has given them some idea that whatever it takes, let's try to fulfill our contractual obligations now so that we can somehow get this issue off the ground."
Datasel is being represented on the Estonian side by law firm LINKLaw and the PR company Powerhouse.
In 2024, the RKIK signed four contracts with Datasel, an Italian firm acquired by Indian-owned Neco Defense Munitions, paying roughly €70 million up front. Deliveries were however reported as being delayed or substandard, leading RKIK to terminate and pursue legal action. Datasel denies any wrongdoing.
The National Audit Office (Riigikontroll) had flagged the same inventory problems a year earlier, and the Ministry of Defense promised to fix them, but it did not. The same audit also found €59.8 million in prepayments to Datasel for munitions for Ukraine, none of which actually arrived in Ukraine. The EPPO is investigating that.
Hanno Pevkur (Reform) resigned as defense minister on September 2, taking political but not personal responsibility for the saga. His replacement has been named as Martin Herem, former Estonian Defense Forces commander and a retired general.

Saudi Aramco declined to comment.

Separate ship-tracking data from Kpler showed four such tankers, capable of carrying a combined eight million barrels, loading at Ras Tanura on Wednesday.
The increase comes as other Gulf producers offer more crude for loading outside the Strait of Hormuz after securing vessels to shuttle supplies through the waterway, often with their tracking signals switched off.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, has relied on its East-West pipeline to divert crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu since the war with Iran severely curtailed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The kingdom shut the pipeline on Friday after it was damaged in drone attacks, sending global oil benchmarks to multi-month highs.
At least one Asian buyer with cargoes scheduled for loading this month said Aramco had notified it that shipments from Yanbu would be delayed and rescheduled. The notice did not specify the length of the delay.
Saudi Arabia has also informed European customers that some crude cargoes scheduled for loading in September will be cancelled, while shipments from Yanbu have been suspended, trading and shipping sources said.

Ukraine war drives European demand for bigger, cheaper missile arsenals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:12:54 UTC
15:12:54 KST

Ukraine war drives European demand for bigger, cheaper missile arsenals
Sept 16 - European militaries are increasingly exploring cheaper missiles and interceptors after conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East exposed the limits of small inventories of high-end weapons.
Along Europe's eastern flank, Russia's daily drone and missile attacks on Ukraine have highlighted a lesson often overlooked in peacetime procurement planning: modern conflicts can consume weapons faster than many countries can replace them.
"If you think you have enough cruise missiles in your inventory, you probably don't," said Douglas Barrie of the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
Analysts say Europe's defence sector spent years focused on small production runs of sophisticated weapons rather than wartime-scale manufacturing, leaving governments now racing to seek lower-cost systems that can be fielded in greater numbers alongside advanced weapons from companies such as Lockheed Martin, MBDA and Rheinmetall.
Industry executives say the challenge is no longer missile design but building the manufacturing capacity needed to sustain a modern conflict.
"Big wars are fought with numbers, not wonder weapons," said Stockholm International Peace Research Institute researcher Markus Schiller.
A new generation of defence startups says it can help meet the demand by developing cheaper missiles and interceptors designed for large-scale production.
The Netherlands in June ordered 700 Ruta Block 2 cruise missiles from European startup Destinus for Ukraine in a €250 million ($288 million) deal, while Britain's Ministry of Defence awarded initial Skyhammer interceptor contracts to Cambridge Aerospace.
"Given how the battlefield has evolved since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, developing low-cost but effective weapons systems is important," the Estonian Defence Forces told Reuters.
THE ARITHMETIC OF MODERN WAR
Ukraine has already built a layered response, downing many of the thousands of long-range drones Russia launches each month with mounted machine guns, interceptor drones and electronic warfare to preserve more advanced interceptors for higher-end threats.
Steven Barrett, chief executive of Cambridge Aerospace, said Russia could launch up to 900 Shahed-type drones in a single night. Attempting to defeat them with traditional interceptors, as the U.S. has at times done in the Middle East, "would cost billions of dollars per night ... which is just impossible for any of our allies to sustain," he said.
Andreas Bappert, chief technology officer of missile company Frankenburg, said future systems must reduce the cost of a successful interception from as much as €20 million to around €1 million to €2 million.
Ukrainian startup Fire Point says it aims to build a ballistic-missile interceptor for less than €1 million, roughly one-quarter to one-sixth the cost of a U.S.-made Patriot air-defence interceptor.
Lockheed Martin this year unveiled a lower-cost Patriot missile. But even at less than half the cost of a Patriot PAC-3, it would remain above startup targets and is not expected to enter production until 2028.
Unlike the PAC-3, which is designed to defeat ballistic missiles and advanced aircraft, many of the emerging low-cost systems are focused primarily on drones, cruise missiles or other lower-end threats. Industry executives and analysts say they are intended to complement rather than replace high-end air-defence systems.
CAN EUROPE BUILD ENOUGH?
Investors are increasingly backing emerging missile makers as they seek to scale production. Cambridge Aerospace raised $300 million last month to expand production, while Destinus is pursuing additional funding ahead of a planned IPO.
"The challenge for Europe is not that the technology does not exist," Destinus founder Mikhail Kokorich told Reuters. "The bigger challenge is industrial capacity, or the ability to produce, qualify and replenish systems on the scale required by modern conflicts."
Cambridge Aerospace is investing heavily to secure rocket motors and other critical components while incorporating commercial technologies such as automotive radar chips.
Fire Point uses a network of manufacturing partners, while Destinus has plugged into Rheinmetall's industrial base through a joint venture announced earlier this year.
Cambridge Aerospace aims to produce 2,500 interceptors a month by the end of the first quarter next year, while Frankenburg is targeting output of up to 100 missiles a day and 1,500 missiles in 2026.
Industry executives say scaling production depends not only on funding but also on securing components, obtaining approvals and expanding manufacturing processes.
Fire Point hopes to demonstrate a successful ballistic-missile interception by mid-2027, compressing what Chief Executive Iryna Terekh said would otherwise be a decades-long process into a few years.
Frankenburg Chief Executive Kusti Salm said manufacturing capacity itself could become a deterrent if adversaries concluded Europe could rapidly replace missiles consumed in combat.
"If the enemy knows that we can produce en masse ... the equation tells him, I'm not going to reach my objectives," he told Reuters. REUTERS

France would back Dutch veteran Knot to lead ECB, wants chief economist job in return, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:10:00 UTC
15:10:00 KST

France would back Dutch veteran Knot to lead ECB, wants chief economist job in return, sources say
PARIS/FRANKFURT - France would back Dutchman Klaas Knot to succeed Christine Lagarde as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) - provided the powerful post of ECB chief economist went to a French candidate, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters.
The informal proposal has the support of French President Emmanuel Macron, the sources said. But it would be likely to face stiff resistance from Germany, setting the stage for high-stakes political haggling among the euro zone’s political and economic heavyweights.
Macron’s office did not immediately return a request for comment, while Knot declined to comment. The Dutch Finance ministry was not immediately available for comment.
The ECB declined to comment.
The succession race has gained momentum in recent weeks amid speculation that Lagarde and fellow executive board member Isabel Schnabel might both step down before their terms expire in late 2027, hastening a reshuffle at the top of the ECB.
The ECB president and five other members of the executive board are appointed by consensus among leaders of the currency bloc’s 21 countries, with the three largest economies – Germany, France and Italy – holding de facto permanent representation.
An early exit by Lagarde, who is French, and Germany’s Schnabel would accelerate decisions due to be made next year and create the conditions for a broad deal to fill their roles and that of chief economist Philip Lane, whose term expires in May.
France backs Knot over de Cos
Under the plan, Knot – who led the Dutch central bank from 2011 to 2025 – would take the presidency with France’s blessing, the sources said, speaking on condition of anonymity because such negotiations are private and the proposal remains informal.
Knot is viewed by market participants as a pragmatist, naturally inclined toward tighter monetary policy but flexible enough to shift course as economic data dictates.
“He is a hawk, but in a smart way,” a French official said of Knot.
Former Bank of Spain governor Pablo Hernandez de Cos, who was regarded as a swing voter on the rate-setting governing council, is seen as Knot’s primary rival.
However, because de Cos hails from southern Europe, his appointment would almost certainly entail one of the euro zone’s “frugal” northern countries taking the chief economist role to preserve the balance of power.
Competition for the chief economist role
In return for backing Knot, France wants the role of chief economist – picked by the ECB president from among the executive board’s members – for itself, the sources said.
They identified Banque de France deputy governor Agnes Benassy-Quere and Laurence Boone, former chief economist at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and a junior Europe minister in a previous Macron government, as names on Paris’ shortlist.
Helene Rey, currently at the Bank for International Settlements, is another name that has been floated by Paris, the sources said.
Appointing any of them would go some way to preserving the gender balance on the ECB’s board, where Lagarde and Schnabel are currently the only women.
The manoeuvre risks immediate pushback from Berlin, however. 
While the proposal would leave Germany with Schnabel’s vacated seat and her market operations portfolio, officials there are also eyeing the chief economist role, widely considered the board’s second most influential post.
France’s mounting debt woes have made Paris keener than ever to keep a firm hand on the levers of euro zone monetary policy. Less indebted and more economically orthodox Germany meanwhile remains wary of any softening of the ECB’s commitment to price stability.
Lagarde has said she will stay till 2027
Lagarde has publicly signalled an interest in advocating for European integration ahead of next year’s presidential election in France, where eurosceptic far-right leader Marine Le Pen is polling strongly.
Stepping down before the election in May would guarantee Macron a decisive say in picking Lagarde’s successor before he leaves office.
Lagarde has stopped short of shutting down talk of an early departure, simply saying: “You are not going to see the back of me before 2027.” 
Media reports have frequently linked her to the leadership of the World Economic Forum.
Schnabel has not commented on a report by Germany’s Handelsblatt that she is in discussions about a senior role at the International Monetary Fund.
Lagarde’s eight-year mandate formally concludes at the end of October 2027, with Schnabel’s term ending two months later. REUTERS

US burns through dozens of missile interceptors in single Iranian attack on Jordan: Report
Unknown

2026-09-16

Busra Nur Cakmak
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The US military used as many as 70 Patriot interceptors and more than a dozen THAAD anti-missile interceptors to counter a recent Iranian ballistic missile attack on Jordan, highlighting growing pressure on American air defense stocks, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday.
US forces fired between 60 and 70 Patriot interceptors against an attack involving about 20 ballistic missiles, while more than a dozen Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors were also launched, the newspaper reported, citing US and regional officials familiar with the matter.
The number of interceptors expended was roughly equivalent to what US forces have used during an entire week at other points in the conflict, according to the report.
Iran reportedly used warheads that separated into multiple projectiles as they approached their targets, complicating efforts to intercept them.
The defenses did not stop all incoming threats, with Iran striking fighter jets and other aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, though no US personnel were killed in the latest attack, the Journal said.
Iranian attacks have become increasingly complex during the conflict, employing different missile types, trajectories, maneuvers and warheads in attempts to penetrate US defenses, officials told the newspaper.
US Central Command declined to comment on the report, while the Pentagon rejected suggestions that American munitions were depleted.
“Reports suggesting that the United States’ munitions are depleted are completely false,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said, adding that the US military remains capable of responding to threats.
President Donald Trump also said Monday that the US maintains large stocks of interceptors and is increasing production.
The Defense Department's inspector general, however, said in a report this week that the conflict “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
By mid-July, the US had used about 1,700 Patriot interceptors and more than 200 THAAD interceptors during the conflict, according to officials cited by the Journal. US Navy ships had additionally fired about 150 Standard Missile interceptors against Iranian missiles and drones.
Lockheed Martin, which manufactures Patriot interceptors, produced 620 in 2025 and is seeking to increase annual production to roughly 2,000, according to the report.
US officials have also expressed concerns that the transfer of large quantities of munitions to the Middle East could affect Washington's ability to respond to potential threats elsewhere, including in Europe and the Indo-Pacific.
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command, separately told CBS' “60 Minutes” this week that he was not concerned about interceptor shortages and that US forces were prepared for any contingency.
The pressure on interceptor inventories has also prompted Gulf states to seek additional air defense munitions after months of Iranian missile and drone attacks, while affecting the availability of systems for Ukraine's defense against Russian strikes, according to the Journal.
