Denmark is set for a week of changing autumn weather, with periods of rain, sunshine and mild temperatures, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI.
Monday began cool, particularly in central Jutland, where temperatures fell to between 6 and 8 degrees.
“The temperature is down to 6-8 degrees, so if you are going out cycling, you can clearly feel that autumn has arrived,” DMI duty meteorologist Jesper Eriksen told Ritzau.
The rest of Monday is expected to remain dry, with a mix of sunshine and clouds. Temperatures will reach between 15 and 18 degrees, with light to moderate winds from the west.
### Tuesday to be warmest day
Tuesday is expected to be the warmest day of the week.
Winds will turn to the south, bringing slightly warmer air over Denmark and pushing temperatures to between 17 and 21 degrees.
There will be periods of sunshine, although some rain is possible, particularly in Jutland.
More rain is expected to reach Jutland later Tuesday afternoon before moving east during the evening and overnight.
Wednesday will bring some sunshine but also showers.
Temperatures are expected to fall back to between 15 and 18 degrees, while winds will turn west again.
Thursday and Friday are expected to bring periods of rain and showers, with temperatures remaining between 15 and 18 degrees.
Winds from the west and southwest are also expected to strengthen gradually toward the end of the week.
Eriksen said the week would not be particularly cold despite the unsettled weather.
“In the week as a whole, you will not need the really warm clothes, but in periods you will need rainwear and rubber boots,” he said.
It remains unclear whether September will bring another spell of warmer weather later in the month.
“We will have to see what happens, whether the last spasms with some warmth arrive. It is not decided yet,” Eriksen said.
More than half of the Danish schools that were selected for the latest Pisa survey declined to participate. In total, 398 schools were drawn for the survey. Of those, 215 chose not to participate, writes Kristeligt Dagblad.
When a selected school chooses to decline, a reserve school could step in. In advance, two reserve schools had been designated for each of the drawn schools.
Therefore, a total of 283 schools ended up participating in the survey. However, this is significantly fewer than in 2022, when 347 schools participated.
According to Kristeligt Dagblad, the number also remains below the OECD’s “technical minimum requirement”.
According to Monika Klingsbjerg-Besrechel, chief consultant at Statistics Denmark, which was responsible for the practical part of the survey, the many declines have not affected the quality of the survey.
“Fortunately, we reached a higher response rate, but despite that, we were unfortunately still below the minimum requirement from the OECD. If we had not had the reserve schools, we really would have been in serious trouble,” she says to Kristeligt Dagblad.
She points out that it was subsequently investigated whether the many declines had affected the result.

Lukas Graham withdraws from Ed Sheeran’s tour over Macklemore controversy

2026-09-16
04:39:45 UTC
13:39:45 KST

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

Kravchenko relinquished personal protection after suspicion against NABU director entered in register – UP
Ruslan Kravchenko, who was dismissed as prosecutor general by presidential decree on 15 September, relinquished his personal protection two hours after information about a notice of suspicion against Semen Kryvonos, Director of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), was entered in the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations.
Source: Mykhailo Tkach's article (English translation coming soon)
Quote: "The prosecutor general's statement announcing that he was temporarily dispensing with personal state protection is dated 01:00 on 14 September – approximately two hours after information regarding the notice of suspicion against the NABU director was entered in the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations."
Details: The article suggests this may indicate that Kravchenko already understood at that point that he was leaving the country not as part of a routine official trip, since having state protection would have made it considerably easier to establish the prosecutor general's whereabouts.
Kravchenko crossed the border through the Shehyni border crossing at 02:30, three hours after the notice of suspicion was issued and an hour and a half after he dispensed with State Security Administration protection. This may indicate that he took both steps while already being near the border.
Kravchenko's wife left the country a day earlier, on 12 September, crossing the border into Moldova and later travelling to neighbouring Romania.
"It is also important to note that information that Kravchenko was planning to leave the country had been circulating in the highest government offices several days before his departure," the article says.
Previously: On 15 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree dismissing Ruslan Kravchenko as prosecutor general.
Background:
- Kravchenko submitted his resignation as prosecutor general amid an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) into the alleged "protection" of scam call centres.
- On 14 September, Kravchenko said he had signed a notice of suspicion against NABU director Semen Kryvonos and accused NABU and SAPO of seizing materials from criminal proceedings against employees of the anti-corruption agencies in the course of searches conducted as part of Operation Carthage.
- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in law enforcement, Kravchenko left Ukraine in an official car on the night of 13-14 September. Kravchenko said in a statement that he had left to go on an official trip.
- According to an order by the prosecutor general dated 13 September, a copy of which was seen by Ukrainska Pravda, Kravchenko left for Paris for five days "to take part in PACE hearings on Ukrainian children". However, he was not listed among the speakers on the event agenda.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appealed to parliament to support Kravchenko's dismissal as prosecutor general.
- Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk reported that parliament had received a motion from President Zelenskyy seeking Kravchenko's dismissal. The Verkhovna Rada Committee on Law Enforcement approved the motion.

EU should strengthen intelligence sharing to counter Russian hybrid attacks — Kallas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
03:57:00 UTC
12:57:00 KST

EU should strengthen intelligence sharing to counter Russian hybrid attacks — Kallas
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas made the statement during a European Parliament debate in Strasbourg on Russia's hybrid warfare, Ukrinform's correspondent reports.
Kallas said that Russia adapted its methods depending on the country, manipulating the information space and interfering in elections in some countries while carrying out physical attacks in others. She said these attacks targeted military infrastructure, public transport, and critical facilities. She stressed that joint intelligence efforts needed to cover the full range of Russia's hybrid warfare tools and said that intelligence sharing was therefore vital. Kallas urged EU member states to do more and make the best possible use of the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre (INTCEN).
She stressed that Moscow would no longer be able to hide behind ambiguity. According to Kallas, Russia had long used ambiguity as a weapon, but clearly identifying the source of attacks would make it harder for Russia to conceal its involvement and would help European citizens recognize and understand the patterns behind such attacks. She said that Germany's investigation, attribution, and transparent public communication following the attack in Leipzig had therefore been particularly important. She also noted that in July, EU countries had jointly exposed what they described as FSB cyber aggression in Europe, adding that such efforts needed to be carried out systematically.
Kallas also urged Europeans not to give in to what she described as attempts by the Kremlin to intimidate them. She said that Putin's hybrid attacks were intended to intimidate European societies, paralyze them, and make them hesitate, which she argued was precisely what he wanted. She stressed that fear should not dictate Europe's choices and called for concrete action and a confident response to such attacks.
The statement came amid a series of hybrid incidents in Europe over the previous 48 hours, as Russia engaged in new provocations. A Russian frigate fired signal flares toward a Danish helicopter, NATO fighter jets shot down a Russian drone in Lithuanian airspace, another hostile UAV was recovered from a body of water in Poland, and a passenger train came under attack near the Ukrainian-Polish border. In addition, an investigation into suspected sabotage attempts and attacks on logistics hubs and critical infrastructure is ongoing in Germany.
As Ukrinform previously reported, according to media reports, the European Union is discussing strengthening its intelligence centre and data sharing between member states.

Nyadol Nyuon responds to criticism over 'no white culture' remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
03:09:04 UTC
12:09:04 KST

IN BRIEF
- The lawyer says race and culture should not be conflated, arguing there is no single "white culture".
- Nyuon previously began returning her OAM as part of what she called her "slow and certain" departure from Australia.
Lawyer and human rights advocate Nyadol Nyuon has defended her claim that there is "no white culture" after remarks she made turning a televised debate drew criticism.
Nyuon appeared on the ABC's National Forum on migration on Monday, where she rejected the idea Australia was historically monocultural and said she had "no intention of assimilating".
But she stressed that did not mean rejecting Australia, its laws or the country she says she "deeply" loves.
She argued that describing Australia as an "Anglo-Celtic culture" risked creating the impression there was a single "white culture" migrants were expected to adopt.
"There is Italian culture, there is French culture, there is Argentinian culture, but there is not this notion of sort of a white culture that is being threatened," Nyuon told the forum.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The discussion came amid a broader national debate about migration, multiculturalism and what it means to be Australian.
Following criticism of her remarks, Nyuon expanded on the argument in a social media post on her LinkedIn account.
'No white culture'
"Apparently, saying there is no white culture has offended some people," she wrote on Tuesday.
"There is no white culture as there is no black culture."
Nyuon argued that race and culture should not be treated as interchangeable, pointing to the cultural differences that exist between people who may otherwise be grouped together according to skin colour.
"Black is a colour, not a culture. There are Black people. There is Ethiopian culture," she wrote.
Nyuon also defended her argument that Australia had never been monocultural, pointing to the hundreds of First Nations that existed before colonisation as well as the long histories of Chinese migrants and Afghan cameleers in Australia.
A debate over belonging
During the forum, former deputy prime minister John Anderson argued there were legitimate concerns among Australians about social cohesion and whether some groups respected Australian culture and values.
Anderson described those values as including individual dignity, equality before the law and the separation of the secular and sacred.
Nyuon acknowledged Australians had a right to be concerned about threats to social cohesion but challenged the way the issue was being framed.
She argued the migration debate could become a proxy for conversations about race and questioned why a person's appearance should influence perceptions of their belonging.
"Whenever we attempt to speak about how our belonging can look like, you meet such resistance, and the majority of the time that resistance comes from how you look," she said on Monday.
'I love this country'
Nyuon also spoke about her complicated relationship with Australia and her previously announced intention to begin the process of renouncing her Australian citizenship.
The lawyer, who was born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia after her family fled the Sudanese civil war, came to Australia as a teenager.
In April, Nyuon revealed she had written to the governor-general's office to begin returning the Medal of the Order of Australia she was awarded in 2022 for "service to human rights and refugee women".
"This is the first step in my slow and certain process of leaving Australia and releasing my connections to this country," she wrote at the time.
Nyuon said she remained "so grateful" to Australia and would "always be indebted to it", but linked her decision to her experiences with Victoria University and WorkSafe Victoria.
Nyuon resigned from Victoria University in 2025, after overseeing an $800,000 WorkSafe Victoria project aimed at preventing workplace gendered violence, which was plagued by delays, strained relationships and resourcing issues.
An independent evaluator later found instability and mismanagement meant it could not properly assess the program's success.
Speaking on National Forum, she said she loved Australia but was conscious that political circumstances could affect whether she and her children felt they could remain.
"Many migrants deeply, deeply love this country. I love this country," she said.
In her subsequent LinkedIn post, Nyuon maintained her comments about culture were not intended as an insult.

During Question Time on Tuesday, Anthony Albanese said he had not known about the posts and labelled them "completely unacceptable".
But Credlin questioned the idea that Labor was not aware of his posts on social media.
"They were all out there on his social media feed and I don't for a minute believe that this was missed when he was vetted for his job as a Labor staffer," she said.
"It is my view that someone saw these comments and thought they could get away with them.
"Giving a cosy job to the PM's best mate was worth it."
Senator Dowling confirmed on Tuesday he had stood down Mr Muldoon.
"After being alerted to abhorrent tweets from my staffer, I've decided to not continue with his casual contract," Senator Dowling said.
"Everyone in public life has a responsibility to do better when it comes to political discourse. The words used were unacceptable at any time."
Removed from Australia Day Ambassador duties
In Question Time on Wednesday, Mr Albanese was asked about Mr Muldoon's role as an Australia Day Ambassador.
"I'm advised he's been an ambassador since 2014," Mr Albanese said, adding he was not an ambassador this year.
The ABC understands Mr Muldoon was part of a NSW-based Australia Day Council program and was not selected to be an ambassador for any local government area in 2026, but was waitlisted.
Assistant minister to the prime minister Patrick Gorman said he became aware of the issue on Wednesday morning.
"I asked the National Australia Day Council CEO to engage with the New South Wales Australia Day Council to remove Mr Muldoon from any ambassador duties," Mr Gorman said in a statement.
Mr Albanese also said he had no involvement in the hiring of Mr Muldoon as a Labor advisor.
Play School star turned political actor
An internal party figure during Kevin Rudd's prime ministership and a repeat guest on ABC shows including The Drum and Play School, Mr Muldoon had largely faded from political consciousness until Senator Dowling's hiring of him in July was noted by Politico on Monday.
News Corp subsequently reported a series of offensive social media posts, including one in which he made derogatory comments about Jewish people.
Mr Muldoon has a long association with the Labor Party and penned a children's book with Mr Rudd in 2010.
Both Mr Muldoon and Mr Rudd have been contacted for comment.
Mr Muldoon was a host on ABC's Play School program for several years, and also appeared in a number of dramas aired on the public broadcaster, including Goolagong, Bay of Fires and Rake.
He was a regular contributor on The Drum, a political program that ran on the ABC between 2010 and 2023.
There were about 70 people invited to the prime minister's wedding at the Lodge last year.
Senator Price said Mr Muldoon's attendance at the wedding proved he was "not just an ordinary Labor staffer".
"He is best mates with the prime minister, even attending his wedding," she said.
"Muldoon's comments show just what kind of people the prime minister surrounds himself with."

 Physicalism is, in slogan form, the thesis that everything is physical. The thesis is usually intended as a metaphysical thesis, parallel to the thesis attributed to the ancient Greek philosopher Thales, that everything is water, or the idealism of the 18th Century philosopher Berkeley, that everything is mental. The general idea is that the nature of the actual world (i.e. the universe and everything in it) conforms to a certain condition, the condition of being physical. The hole in the ozone layer is healing, but extreme weather may be slowing progress down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
02:35:18 UTC
11:35:18 KST

The hole in the Earth’s ozone layer is significantly smaller than it’s been in recent history, but it is still far from fully healed, according to the World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO’s) latest annual checkup.
The hole in the ozone layer, a protective region of the atmosphere that begins roughly nine miles above Earth’s surface, was discovered in the 1980s. Studies attributed its presence to human-made chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which destroyed ozone molecules. The layer plays a vital role in absorbing the sun’s ultraviolet radiation, which can cause diseases such as skin cancer. Repairing it became a matter of international priority, with nations signing on to the Montreal Protocol on Substances That Deplete the Ozone Layer, an international treaty banning CFCs, in 1987. Since then, for scientists and activists, the recovery of the ozone layer has stood as a victory, showing that we can act to prevent human-caused damage to our planet.
In the latest edition of the WMO’s Ozone and UV bulletin, the organization finds that the hole is “significantly” smaller than its average size between 1990 and 2020. Still, University of California, Los Angeles, professor Suzanne Paulson cautions against overoptimism. The hole has been healing at a slower rate than scientists had predicted it might, she says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“It does go up and down every year, so any one year doesn’t really tell you a whole lot,” she says, referring to seasonal fluctuations in the size of the ozone hole. “It certainly hasn’t gotten worse in recent years, but for the most part, we haven’t really seen major improvements.”
This is the second year in a row that the WMO has detected positive change in the ozone hole, but there are still some warning signs highlighted in the report. The amount of ozone in the atmosphere can fluctuate through the year, and October is typically the month in which there is the least ozone. In 2025 ozone hit a low in September, however.
“While we have seen its area increase rapidly in early September this year, other indicators remain close to historical averages,” said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmospheric Monitoring Service (CAMS), in a statement. “These findings highlight the importance of monitoring the complicated interaction between human-made disturbances and natural factors. CAMS provides the high-quality data, forecasts and analyses needed to understand the state of the ozone layer and track its long-term recovery.”
The report also notes that the level of ozone was below average across a large area that extended from Greenland and Europe into Central Asia, Japan and the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia. The report attributed the anomaly to a strong Arctic winter vortex in January and February 2025.
That’s the kind of extreme weather that is becoming more frequent because of climate changes, Paulson says. Further anomalies in the ozone layer could become more common as global warming intensifies, she says.
“Climate change creates more extreme weather, so I think that that is part of a slowly increasing trend,” she says.

322 ceramic tiles translate electromagnetic fields into textured switchstation facade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
02:10:00 UTC
11:10:00 KST

3d printed ceramic wall adorns electrical substation facade
Powerwall by Studio RAP forms a 40-sqm ceramic3D printed artwork within the facade of a new 150 kV switchstation in Beverwijk, the Netherlands. Designed by Powerhouse Company for energy infrastructure operator TenneT, the building responds to the redevelopment of the area around the Bazaar, where technical infrastructure and large-scale commerce are giving way to a neighbourhood with housing, workspaces, public space, and a renewed connection to the waterfront. The switchstation is conceived as part of this changing urban context, combining its technical requirements with an architectural treatment that addresses its scale and presence along the street. Powerwall is integrated into the brick facade as a large-scale relief inspired by the invisible electromagnetic fields generated by the electrical equipment inside the building.
The switchstation is organised into two complementary volumes. A taller brick volume contains the primary electrical installation, while a lower metal volume accommodates secondary functions. Deep brick piers introduce rhythm and depth to the main facade, while sculptural metal lamellas wrap around the lower volume and visually connect the two parts. Their gently undulating profiles create changing patterns of shadow across the facade. Together with the 3D printed ceramic artwork, these elements give the infrastructure a more layered architectural presence within the developing neighborhood.
all images by Studio Pim Top
322 tiles translate electromagnetic fields into ceramic relief
Powerwall translates the movement of electromagnetic fields into a continuous ceramic landscape of lines, folds, and changing depths. Using computational design, design practice Studio RAP developed 322 unique 3D printed ceramic tiles that combine to form an 8-by-5-meter relief. Each tile was produced in Studio RAP’s Rotterdam workshop using in-house robotic clay printing. The process allows variations in form, texture, and depth across the individual components, which are assembled into a continuous surface on the brick facade. After firing, the tiles were finished with a translucent turquoise glaze. The glaze settles into the grooves and recessed areas of the relief, emphasising its three-dimensional surface. As sunlight moves across the facade, the changing illumination alters the appearance of the ceramic surface, bringing different lines, folds, and depths into view throughout the day. The scale and placement of Powerwall make the artwork visible from a distance, while its variations in texture and relief become more apparent at closer range.
Powerwall forms a 40-sqm ceramic artwork within the switchstation facade
Brick, metal and ceramic shape the switchstation facade
The architectural composition by architectural group Powerhouse Company combines the substantial brick volume with the lighter metal enclosure and the textured ceramic relief. Deep brick piers give the main volume a vertical rhythm, while the metal lamellas introduce a more fluid profile around the lower section. Their undulating surfaces produce shadows that change according to the position of the sun. Powerwall adds another layer to this material composition. Its turquoise ceramic surface contrasts with the brickwork while remaining integrated into the building envelope. The combination of computational design and robotic clay printing allows the artwork to occupy a substantial section of the facade without repeating a single tile. The result places an energy facility within the visual and spatial context of the surrounding neighborhood. As switchstations and transformer stations become increasingly present within urban areas, the project explores how infrastructure can accommodate operational requirements while also responding to its architectural surroundings.
Powerwall is integrated into the brick facade as a continuous relief
digital ceramic fabrication meets energy infrastructure
Powerwall forms part of Studio RAP’s wider approach to digital craftsmanship in architecture. From its Rotterdam workshop, the studio develops ceramic facades, ornaments, and architectural artworks using computational design and in-house robotic 3D clay printing. Powerhouse Company, founded in 2005, is an international architecture practice with studios in Rotterdam, Munich, Oslo, and Nairobi. Its work includes adaptive reuse, residential developments, interiors, private villas, and public buildings. For Switchstation Beverwijk, Powerhouse Company worked with Studio RAP to integrate a digitally fabricated ceramic artwork into an essential piece of energy infrastructure. Completed in 2026, the project combines a functioning switchstation with a facade that responds to the building’s technical purpose through material, geometry, and changing light.

Under normal circumstances, the formal margin of error for a sample of this size (with a 0.95 confidence level and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) would not exceed 4.1% for figures close to 50%, 3.5% for figures close to 25%, 2.5% for figures close to 10%, and 1.8% for figures close to 5%.
Under wartime conditions, in addition to the formal margin of error indicated above, there is also a certain degree of systematic bias.

When Timber Isn't the Right Material: Rethinking Material Selection for High-Performance Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

The relationship between humans and wood has endured since the Greco-Roman era, when a variety of techniques were developed to maximize its unique properties and characteristics. Beyond its warmth, texture, and natural appeal, wood has proven its ability to meet a wide range of technical requirements while adapting to diverse environmental and geographic conditions, maintenance demands, and fire-resistance standards. In response to the evolving needs of the built environment, interior and exterior finish materials that replicate the appearance of wood have emerged as viable alternatives. Among them, Wood Finish Aluminum offers a durable, high-performance solution for long-lasting projects, providing a textured wood-look appearance while maintaining minimal environmental impact.
Working with solid wood at both small and large scales presents challenges related to high humidity, coastal environments, wildfire-prone regions, heavily trafficked public spaces, and maintenance requirements, all of which can limit its suitability for certain applications. To preserve the visual qualities of wood while meeting these demands, architects specify materials such as Sculptform's Wood Finish Aluminum, which provides the appearance of wood while addressing project-specific performance, durability, and environmental requirements.
As an example, the Daldy Street Workplace Development uses wood-look Aluminum Click-on Battens to create a cohesive architectural language throughout the atrium and interior fit-outs. The scale of the project required a system capable of maintaining consistency without compromising construction efficiency. By aligning multiple stakeholders, the processes of system design, documentation, manufacturing, and delivery were coordinated to support the project's execution. The result was a workplace that demonstrates how design intent can be realized through thoughtful system selection and precise coordination.
Building a Dialogue With the Outdoors
However, every project presents its own unique design challenges and opportunities. Designed by Nomad Design and built by McClure Homes Design Build (MHDB), Desert Temple House embraces a warm, natural wood aesthetic that blends with its surroundings while delivering the durability and low maintenance essential for Southern California's climate. Its American Oak Wood Finish Aluminum Screens were selected to harmonize with the desert landscape, echoing its sandy tones and organic forms while extending seamlessly into the interior.
The project sought to balance resident privacy with a stronger connection between indoor and outdoor environments, creating a visual dialogue with the surrounding landscape. To support this design intent, the Click-on Screens system was developed to provide greater design flexibility and a consistent aesthetic. Panels were installed using both back- and end-mount methods, allowing for a seamless integration across the façade. In addition, the system's modular design simplified installation, while factory-spaced clips ensured precise alignment and consistency throughout the exterior envelope.
 "The aluminum Click-on Screens, particularly the wood textures, are unparalleled on the market. The ability to use natural timber and aluminum battens interchangeably, with a near-perfect match in wood species and grain, provides a level of design flexibility and aesthetic cohesion that we have not found elsewhere." —Andrew McClure, Nomad Design
Compared to other wood-look alternatives, such as powder-coated finishes, wrapped aluminum offers superior resistance to UV-related fading while providing a textured finish and maintaining a low environmental impact. To demonstrate this performance, Sculptform conducted a series of weathering tests that compared the color stability of its Wood Finish Aluminum with other wood-effect products. Color fading was measured after accelerated weather testing, evaluating changes in both the wrapped wood-grain finish and a comparable powder-coated wood-effect product. Demonstrating durability and long-term stability under demanding conditions, the wood-finish coating has been tested against key performance criteria aligned with AAMA 2605 standards, which evaluate how surfaces perform under accelerated environmental exposure. These tests assess resistance to UV radiation, moisture, salt spray, chemicals, and abrasion, helping ensure long-term performance in challenging climates. In addition to outstanding color retention and fade resistance, the finish provides enhanced protection against surface degradation and environmental wear.
From decorative interior and exterior wall and ceiling cladding to projects requiring a fire rating, this Wood Finish Aluminum achieves its weather and abrasion resistance through the application of a specialized cross-linked topcoat. The polyolefin film is manufactured in Japan using electron beam curing technology and bonded to the aluminum panels through a wrapping process. A reactive polyurethane (PUR) hot-melt adhesive provides enhanced resistance to moisture and temperature fluctuations. Furthermore, Hoffman scratch test results indicate that the exterior polyolefin film exhibits little to no visible marking after rigorous testing, outperforming other olefin-based films.
The finishes are free of PVC, toluene, and xylene, and their manufacturing and packaging processes produce low volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions. The wood-look finish complies with the California Department of Public Health's Standard Method for the Testing and Evaluation of Volatile Organic Chemical Emissions from Indoor Sources Using Environmental Chambers, Version 1.2 (2017).
Creating a Design Language Based on Technique
Wood Finish Aluminum addresses challenges associated with fire code compliance and long-term maintenance while preserving the visual appeal of wood. Easy to install through a Click-on System and available in a variety of finishes, the aluminum substrate used in the battens satisfies the non-combustibility requirements of AS 1530.1, ASTM E136, and ISO 1182 (the international standard for non-combustibility testing of homogeneous materials). The applied wood-look finish is separately assessed to Group 1 in Australia, per NCC 2022 Volume One Specification 7 Clause S7C4 (determined in accordance with AS 5637.1:2015 and full-scale room testing to AS ISO 9705:2003), and Group Number 1-S in New Zealand, per NZBC Verification Method C/VM2 Appendix A (based on ISO 9705:1993 full-scale testing, supported by small-scale cone calorimeter screening to ISO 5660/AS 3837). The finish also carries a Class A rating under ASTM E84, together meeting fire safety requirements for most exterior applications. Although fire-resistance classifications vary by region, evaluating factors such as flame spread, flammability, and heat and smoke release remains an important consideration when specifying materials in architectural design. These performance criteria add another layer of complexity to the selection process, helping ensure that materials meet both aesthetic and safety requirements.
Designed by Bates Smart in collaboration with local firm KCCT, the Australian Embassy in Washington, D.C., demonstrates a contemporary approach by replicating the appearance of blackbutt wood while satisfying Class A fire safety requirements. The building features a large glass atrium and expansive public gathering space, where acoustic performance was a key design consideration to reduce sound transmission between the embassy's meeting rooms. To meet these requirements, L-shaped Click-on Battens were fabricated from aluminum with an acoustic backing and finished with a wood veneer. The veneer was custom-produced with microperforations across its surface to act like a sponge, enhancing sound absorption. In fact, each batten required a carefully calibrated pattern of perforations to achieve optimal acoustic performance.
From its visual appeal to long-term cost savings and design flexibility, Wood Finish Aluminum is engineered to maintain its appearance and performance over time reproducing the character, texture, and look of natural wood through a warm, tactile wood-grain embossing. Although the finish incorporates a repeating pattern, it is designed to minimize noticeable repetition and distinctive grain characteristics. This effect is further reduced through an installation method that mixes and randomizes roll positions, creating a more varied and natural appearance across the surface.
In terms of maintenance, surface dirt, dust, stains, and other debris can affect the appearance of the battens, making periodic inspections and cleaning recommended. In coastal environments, for example, routine maintenance helps remove salt buildup and other visible deposits, preserving the finish over time. Designed by Woods Bagot for Lowe Living, Hampton Hill is a residential development that introduces the warmth of wood to reinforce its coastal identity. Rather than using traditional wood soffits, the project uses Sculptform's Click-on Cladding in a Gray Eucalyptus Wood Finish with a Shadowline profile. This solution delivers the visual texture of wood while meeting the site's performance requirements, including exposure to wind, rain, and coastal conditions. Wood Finish soffits soften the building's architectural language and visually connect with the landscaping spilling over the balconies.
When defining a project's material palette, cladding plays a vital role in shaping its architectural language. Regardless of the design aesthetic or style, material choices can strengthen a building's relationship with its surroundings, create seamless transitions between indoor and outdoor spaces, and integrate technical solutions tailored to the specific needs of each project. Through careful coordination of materials, building systems, and trades, thoughtfully designed products such as Sculptform's Wood Finish Aluminum cladding offer architects new possibilities for creating enduring designs without sacrificing the warmth and natural beauty of wood.

Renshaw reveals secret behind milestone ODI century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
01:28:59 UTC
10:28:59 KST

The ODI ton was his first for Australia across any format since his only Test century in 2017, when he opened the batting against Pakistan at the SCG.
He recently returned to the Test arena, after a three-year absence, and again opened the batting in Australia's innings victory over Bangladesh in Mackay last month.
But he played down the batting order in his nine ODI matches prior to Harare.
Renshaw said avoiding the pressure of opening the batting helped him score his century.
"Higher up the order I [get] a bit giddy,'' Renshaw said.
"For me, my tempo when I come in the middle overs is just trying to hit the gaps, hit where the fielders aren't.
"With spin being a very big factor in that middle period … I see it as my strength. I really understood my role. It made it really simple for me."
Renshaw was named in Australia's Test squad for the upcoming series against South Africa.
Australia will face the Proteas in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).
The next ODI against Zimbabwe will be played on Friday in Harare.

An experience occurred. It happened. I also acknowledge that it happened to me, but I refuse to think about it in that way. Doing so would make it too intimate, and I don’t want that because the experience was not a good one.
In fact, it was positively horrible. It showed me something about the world that I didn’t want to know. But even worse than that, it showed me something about myself that I didn’t want to know. I didn’t want to know it because knowing is inescapable. Now I have to do something with this new knowledge.
I have to do something with it because I cannot bear to have it floating around untethered in my mind. I want to have a reason for it. I want to be able to explain it, because explaining it means I can confine it to one part of my reality, a part that can never fully encompass me. And that means I won’t have to think about it any more.

Tony Burke set to unveil Labor's new migration plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
00:36:01 UTC
09:36:01 KST

In Brief
- Labor has previously proposed reducing net overseas migration and set a target of 225,000 arrivals a year by 2027-28.
- Burke was initially scheduled to unveil the policy last month but it was pushed back.
Labor is expected to unveil its long-awaited migration policy, with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke set to outline the plan at the National Press Club on Thursday.
The policy was initially due to be unveiled by Burke at a National Press Club address in August. However, the speech was cancelled at the last minute after the government failed to secure cabinet agreement on the best approach.
Since then, Labor has maintained it was still finalising its plans.
The announcement is expected to detail how Labor will reduce net overseas migration from about 300,000 in 2025 to 245,000 in 2026/27 and 225,000 per year thereafter.
It comes as migration has emerged as a key political battleground, with pressure mounting on Labor to release its strategy.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has repeatedly declined to provide further details, refusing to set a timeframe for migration announcements and saying they would be made at "appropriate times".
What could Labor be planning?
Labor has previously proposed reducing net overseas migration and set an annual target of 225,000 by 2027-28.
Burke has already flagged plans to make more changes to the visa system to curb net overseas migration, with the government officially confirming in August that it would slow the processing of working holiday visa applications.
The horticulture and tourism sectors have been calling for certainty, raising fears that a backlog of working holiday visas could mean there aren't enough workers for regional businesses in the summer months.
Labor is also expected to tighten rules for international students and their families and further restrict some visitor visas.
Potential changes could prevent international students from switching courses to extend their stay, increase scrutiny of onshore visa applications, limit the number of family members attached to student visas, and restrict transfers from higher education into vocational education and training programs.
Some tourist visas are also expected to be reduced from 12 months to six months.
The Albanese government has already confirmed that Australia's annual humanitarian intake of 20,000 places will not be reduced.
Burke has previously argued migration plans should be considered alongside housing supply, saying in June: "If you go at migration the wrong way, then you can actually make the housing situation worse."
Political pressure builds
Negotiations between the government and the Coalition over migration settings have stalled over the last week, with the Opposition pushing for deeper cuts to net overseas migration and stronger powers around deportation.
But both parties have criticised One Nation's plan revealed on Monday saying it would "shock" the economy and devastate the construction, health and aged care sectors.
One Nation proposed cutting temporary migration by more than 750,000 places over three years, arguing Australia's migration system requires a major "reset".
Under the policy, international students, recent graduates and their family members would be hit hardest, with migration places in those categories reduced by almost 470,000 over three years.
Burke has told SBS News he tried to find a path for bipartisan agreement with the Opposition.
"I had hoped that the Opposition would work constructively to make sure the immigration minister of the day had additional powers to be able to regulate net overseas migration," he said on Wednesday.
"At the moment, they haven't agreed to measures which they claim to support.
"I would much rather have more targeted levers available."
Independent ACT senator David Pocock took aim at Labor on Wednesday morning, saying current conversations about migration were "unproductive" and had to factor in what the country needed over the next 10 years.
"The big thing I would love to see is a plan," he told ABC's Radio National.
"There's this constant talk about numbers, about classes of visas, rather than actually having the conversation as a country — what is our 10-year plan for migration?"
It was those "hard conversations" that were paramount to Australia's migration debate, he argued.
"To me, that’s how you solve this issue ... rather than having this ridiculous fight over a number that raises all sorts of concerns for aged care, for healthcare, for farmers who are relying on backpackers."
"It just seems so unproductive."
The Coalition is yet to release its migration policy, but has hinted that its plan will tie migration figures to the amount of new homes built, which is currently tracking around 173,000 per year.
Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he was looking forward to seeing the detail of Labor's plan but was "deeply sceptical about Labor's ability to deliver, because for four years they've failed to deliver".
"As for our own policy, we are close to releasing it, but we're actually going to do the work to get it right because we are not the government," he told reporters in Canberra.
"We are seeking to be the government after the next election and we're not going to put out a half-baked policy like One Nation has that hasn't even been costed, the budgetary impacts of which they have no idea."
— With additional reporting by Anna Henderson, Jack Revell, and the Australian Associated Press.

UN considers storing aid for Ukraine in underground facilities after warehouse strikes

The expenses had not been included in the organization’s $2.3 billion humanitarian aid budget for 2026, the coordinator explained.
Schmale noted that the United Nations is investing in equipment to protect its personnel, including additional armored vehicles and drone detection devices.
In addition, the organization is considering requests from the Ukrainian side to install mobile shelters against drones on streets and near bus stops amid the growing number of civilian casualties, the UN Humanitarian Coordinator in Ukraine said.

Early puberty is linked to higher anxiety risk in girls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
00:00:14 UTC
09:00:14 KST

An analysis of the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) data found that an earlier start and a faster tempo of puberty in girls were associated with a higher risk of an anxiety disorder diagnosis and social anxiety disorder symptoms. On the other hand, a later start to puberty and a slower tempo were associated with a lower risk of social anxiety symptoms compared with girls who developed at an average rate. The paper was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
Puberty is a major developmental transition in which young people undergo rapid physical, hormonal, emotional, and social changes. The age at which puberty begins, known as pubertal timing, varies considerably between individuals. In recent decades, it has been gradually decreasing in many Western populations. Puberty also differs in tempo, meaning the speed at which these developmental changes progress once they have begun.
Both timing and tempo may influence how adolescents adapt psychologically to this period of change. Earlier pubertal development has been repeatedly linked to a greater risk of anxiety in girls, although the evidence is less clear for boys. Social anxiety disorder has been linked to puberty particularly often because it first emerges during adolescence in many cases. This disorder involves an intense fear of being judged, embarrassed, or negatively evaluated by others.
Also, entering puberty earlier may expose young people to heightened social expectations and self-consciousness before their emotional coping abilities have fully developed. Likewise, a faster pubertal tempo may leave less time to adjust to the biological and social changes that accompany adolescence.
Study author Anne Marie Ladehoff Thomsen and her colleagues note that previous research on the potential influence of pubertal tempo on anxiety has mostly been conducted on small samples, assessed only one aspect of puberty, or combined boys and girls, in spite of their differences in hormonal and other developmental aspects. They conducted a study in which they investigated the associations between pubertal timing and tempo with anxiety disorders, and social anxiety disorder in particular. These authors hypothesized that earlier and faster pubertal development would be associated with a higher risk of anxiety, but more so in girls than in boys.
To overcome the shortcomings of previous studies, they analyzed data from a large population-based study: the Puberty Cohort of the Danish National Birth Cohort. From 1996 to 2002, Danish-speaking pregnant women were invited to participate in the study at their first antenatal visit with a general practitioner. Approximately 50% of general practitioners in Denmark participated, enrolling around 92,000 women with their unborn children. This represented a 60% participation rate among eligible women and corresponded to 30% of all children born in Denmark during this period.
The participating women were interviewed about their health and health-related behaviors in four consecutive telephone interviews around gestational weeks 17 and 32, as well as 6 and 18 months after they gave birth. Questionnaires were also mailed to them when their children were 7 and 11 years old. When their children were 18 years old, the young adults received a digital invitation to complete another questionnaire, asking for information on their mental health, family relations, social relations, and health behaviors. In total, 49,963 young adults participated in this data collection.
The Puberty Cohort consisted of single-birth children (excluding twins and multiples) born between 2000 and 2003 to mothers who participated in the first telephone interview during pregnancy. Ultimately, this involved 15,818 children who completed at least one web-based questionnaire on their current pubertal development, starting from 11.5 years of age and then every six months throughout puberty. Of these children, 8,123 were girls.
Of the group, 13,208 completed at least two pubertal development questionnaires, allowing researchers to calculate their pubertal development tempo and explore the relationship between their physical development and mental health diagnoses registered in the Danish National Patient Register. Additionally, a smaller subset of participants completed mental health questionnaires when they were 18 years old, allowing the study authors to calculate associations between pubertal development and self-reported mental health characteristics.
The results showed that children with earlier pubertal development, particularly girls, tended to have parents with lower socioeconomic status who were less likely to live together when the children were 7 years of age. Their mothers tended to have their menarche (their first menstrual period) at an earlier age compared with their peers and were more likely to have experienced a psychiatric disorder during the first trimester of pregnancy. These children were also more often bullied at 7 years of age compared with children with average pubertal timing. Adolescents with later puberty tended to show the opposite pattern.
By 19 years of age, 4% of girls had an anxiety disorder diagnosis. Eight percent had contact with a private practice psychologist or psychiatrist, and 4% had redeemed prescribed psychotropic medications (drugs that affect the mind, emotions, and behavior, such as antidepressants and anti-anxiety medications). In boys, 1.5% had an anxiety disorder diagnosis by this age, 3.5% had contact with private practice psychologists or psychiatrists, and 1.4% had redeemed psychotropic medications.
In girls, an earlier start and faster tempo of pubertal development were associated with a higher risk of any anxiety disorder diagnosis and self-reported social anxiety disorder symptoms, as well as a higher likelihood of seeking psychological or psychiatric treatment and being prescribed psychotropic medications. More specifically, for each year earlier that breast development began, the odds of an anxiety disorder diagnosis were 26% higher. Each year of earlier pubic hair development was associated with 49% higher odds of self-reported social anxiety disorder symptoms compared with the average. On the other hand, later pubertal development was associated with a lower risk of anxiety and social anxiety symptoms.
Findings in boys were inconsistent, and no firm links between pubertal timing and anxiety disorder risk could be established.
“If earlier and faster puberty increases the risks of an anxiety disorder diagnosis and SAD [social anxiety disorder] symptoms, targeted interventions are warranted for girls with early/fast puberty and sub-clinical anxiety. Findings for boys need further exploration,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the links between pubertal development and mental health. However, it should be noted that the design of this study does not allow any definitive causal inferences to be derived from the results.
The paper, “Pubertal timing and tempo and anxiety symptoms, disorders and treatments in Danish adolescents: A population-based follow-up study,” was authored by Anne Marie Ladehoff Thomsen, Andreas Ernst, Katrine Strandberg-Larsen, Charlotte Ulrikka Rask, Anne Gaml-Sørensen, Pernille Jul Clemmensen, Thea Emily Benson, Nis Brix, Onyebuchi A. Arah, and Cecilia Høst Ramlau-Hansen.

Another Russian general killed in war against Ukraine
Media reports have suggested that Major General Anton Grunis, Commander of the Russian Armed Forces' 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade, was killed in the war against Ukraine shortly after reporting to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on the "capture" of Kostiantynivka.
Source: Russian propaganda agency Anna News, citing a source in the 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade; Suvorovskoe Bratstvo, the Telegram channel of the Suvorov military school alumni community; Russian media outlet Astra
Details: The exact circumstances, date and location of the Russian general's death have not yet been disclosed.
On 28 August, the Russian Defence Ministry reported that Defence Minister Andrei Belousov had honoured Grunis with Russia's highest state decoration, presenting him with the Gold Star of the Hero of the Russian Federation "for courage and heroism displayed in the performance of his military duty".
The unit commanded by the general took a direct part in the fighting for the city of Kostiantynivka in Donetsk Oblast, which Russian forces have been trying to capture since October 2025.
As early as July, the Russian General Staff and Grunis personally reported to Putin that the city had supposedly been fully occupied. A spokesperson for Ukraine's General Staff denied these claims.
According to publicly available information, Grunis graduated from the Kazan Suvorov Military School in 1996, before turning 17. He took part in the wars in Chechnya and against Georgia.
In 2021, the general retired from active service but returned to the Russian armed forces after the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Under his command, Russian forces were active on the Bakhmut and Kostiantynivka fronts.
The 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade (military unit No. 40318), commanded by Grunis, was formed in 2014 from illegal armed formations of the so-called "Luhansk People's Republic", a Moscow-backed terrorist organisation. It included, among others, the Prizrak terrorist group.
After these formations were integrated into the regular Russian armed forces, the brigade became part of the 2nd Army Corps. It was later incorporated into the newly formed 3rd Guards Combined Arms Army of Russia's Southern Military District.

Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
00:37:09 BST
08:37:09 KST

Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump
- Published
"Wouldn't it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" asked Finland's President Alexander Stubb this summer.
The question was rather tongue-in-cheek. US President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state - causing deep offence amongst many Canadians.
Finland is one of the EU's 27 member states and a close ally of Canada as a fellow Arctic nation. Teasing tones aside, President Stubb put his finger squarely on the pulse of deepening EU-Canadian relations. "Canada is more Europe-minded than most Europeans!" is a smiling retort you often hear in Brussels at the moment.
On Sunday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU.
The catalyst for this very public, ardent new love-in is Donald Trump. Just the other day, the US president posted a map of North America on his Truth Social site, including Canada and Greenland - a territory that's part of EU country Denmark - all overlaid with the US flag.
- Carney eyes 'unique alliance' with EU as trade war with US intensifies 
  - Published2 days ago
- Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map 
  - Published8 September
Trade negotiations between the US and Canada broke down late last month. European countries, which have been hit by their own Trump tariffs, have privately watched the spat play out with a mixture of interest and, for many, admiration.
While the EU, led by the European Commission, simply accepted new blanket Trump tariffs without fighting back, Carney has prominently stood up to the US president, swiftly imposing counter-tariffs on the United States.
When it comes to courting the EU, Canada appears to some to be even keener than one of the bloc's closest neighbours.
"Canada right now seems more interested than the UK to get as close to Brussels as possible, as a non member state" says Mark Lowen, director of the European Council of Foreign Relations think tank. "It's remarkable."
Canada, but not the UK, successfully joined the European Union's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence fund earlier this year. The UK remained on the sidelines following a row over costs and political tensions. A summit designed to reset and improve EU-UK relations has just been delayed - again - over cross-Channel differences.
By contrast this week, Carney is invited as a special guest to the European Commission President's annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France on Wednesday. Carney will hold a speech in the European Parliament there on Thursday, a day after President von der Leyen outlines the EU's political and policy priorities.
Officials on both sides insist this is more than just "blah blah politics", as one EU diplomat put it to me. He was speaking on condition of anonymity so as to be able to discuss the subject freely. Carney and von der Leyen are both expected to mention plans to forge closer ties. "As close as you can get without (Canada) actually becoming an EU member," the diplomat told me.
'Trump effect' prompts efforts to diversify - but are they achievable?
In the corridors of Brussels, there's whispered talk of constructing a "special association agreement" with Canada.
The unofficial aim for both sides, I'm told, is to reduce reliance on Washington in several key areas:
- Digital and tech developments, in which the US and China dominate
- Energy: Canada is rich in liquified natural gas (LNG) the EU needs since it cut back its energy dependency on Russia
- Raw materials and critical minerals: Canada has them in abundance
- Trade and defence procurement: Canada has been on a "buy European" spree of late, purchasing German attack submarines, for example, and airborne early-warning planes from Sweden's Saab. Its view appears to be: why reward the US by buying American equipment after being slapped with trade tariffs amounting to 50% in some sectors?
A Nanos opinion poll from April suggests more than four in five Canadians favour strengthening ties with the EU.
Close to three in five support Canada actually joining the bloc, though Article 49 of the EU Constitution would appear to make that impossible. Without wanting to seem facetious, the European Union is not (yet) the Eurovision Song Contest, in which indisputably non-European Israel and Australia have - controversially - been allowed to compete.
Back to trade: ties between Canada and the EU are far from novel. The EU is already Canada's second-largest trading partner - albeit far behind the US, which buys about 70% of Canadian exports.
The far-reaching Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) trade deal was agreed just under a decade ago and has been provisionally implemented, eliminating 99% of tariffs on Canadian goods exports.
Privately, European officials admit this renewed high-level courtship between Ottawa and Brussels has everything to do with the actions of Trump's second term in office.
The US president is by now infamous amongst US allies for what they view as his unpredictability and his penchant to use trade or security ties as leverage.
There's a growing sense in Europe - which has, since World War Two, looked to the US as its closest ally abroad - and in Canada, whose economy has been intertwined with the US for decades, that neither can any longer fully rely on Washington. They believe it's time to diversify.
"The Canadian government is committed to trade diversification, doubling non-US trades in the next 10 years, and doing more with the European Union will be very key to achieving that target," Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association (CEUTIA) told the BBC.
An even tighter Canadian-EU alliance, covering far more sectors than trade alone, would continue a recent trend of both parties to form new association agreements around the world. In Canada's case, this includes a sectoral deal with China, which raised international eyebrows earlier this year.
EU insiders put all of this down to the "Trump effect".
- Carney gambles on the world's biggest investors betting on Canada 
  - Published1 day ago
- The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts 
  - Published31 August
- What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans 
  - Published6 days ago
But decoupling from the US altogether would seem unrealistic - for both Canada and the EU.
The US is the EU's largest overall trading partner, if you take goods and services together.
Canada and the US have the largest bilateral trading relationship in the world, valued at nearly US$900bn (£668bn) last year. This dwarfs the $130bn of total EU-Canada bilateral trade during the same timeframe.
The vast majority of Canadian exports head to the US.
So, Ottawa could sign new trade agreements, but replacing customers and supply chains built around America's massive market would be a tall order.
This week, I hear, Carney and von der Leyen will vociferously defend a global system of rules-based trade.
"This is not about trying to keep the past alive. We need to forge a new rules-based future in trade and beyond. With or without Washington," diplomats tell me.
There's an EU-Canada summit scheduled for the end of next month. After that, working groups are expected to start the less-than-sexy task of tackling the legal and technical details in the different areas in which the EU and Canada now hope to establish closer ties.
So are EU and Canada really becoming BFFs?
A huge turning point for Europe in its attitude towards Washington came early this year when Trump refused to rule out taking Greenland from fellow Nato power, Denmark, by force.
Around that time, Carney - who's also the former governor of the Bank of England - gave a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, calling on middle-sized countries to stick together against economic coercion by global super-powers. Europe sat up and took notice.
Why then, you might ask, haven't Europe's leaders been more outspoken in their support for the Canadian prime minister during the current escalation in trade tensions with the US? Carney has been defiant, declaring that Canada was "at war" with the US over trade.
He swiftly imposed counter-tariffs on the US in the name of "sovereignty".
Paolo Gentiloni, a former EU economy commissioner and former Italian premier, commented on social media: "Here is a speech I would like to hear in Europe."
Yet - in public - Europe's leaders have remained cautiously quiet.
Though not, it seems, out of any lack of support for Mark Carney.
A number of Europe's leaders, like Finland's president - but also French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, herself once a true Trump fan - are involved in behind-the-scene chats with Carney about deepening relations, I'm told.
But - and it's a big but - no leading European politician wants to stick his or her neck out for Carney in public right now and risk having voters at home blame them for possibly incurring the wrath of - and fresh punitive tariffs from - the US president.
Over the coming months, every large country in the EU holds key elections. Germany's took place just over a week ago. France chooses a new president in April and early May. Italy, Spain and Poland have yet to set a date for their parliamentary elections.
When it comes to applauding Carney right now, Europe's leaders are hiding behind the EU institutions.
Under EU rules, the European Commission deals with trade on behalf of the member states. The EU Commission and EU parliament presidents invited Carney to Strasbourg this week.
But some officials I speak to in Brussels warn that Carney should also wake up and smell the European coffee.
Brussels may feel warmly towards Canada, and believe Ottawa shares many of the same values and priorities, but there are still loud EU voices, like France, that prefer to prevent non-member countries from getting too favourable a deal.
That's despite pressure on the EU to show more flexibility when it comes to accommodating allies, considering the turbulent times we live in.
It's a conundrum the UK faces too.
Carney flies to Liverpool later this week, after leaving the European Parliament, for his first face-to-face meeting with new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.
As well as discussing UK-Canada ties, who knows - might the two men end up debating ways to best woo the EU, too?

Gas stations in Kyiv region to gain access to Defense Forces’ air situation awareness system
According to Ukrinform, Timur Tkachenko, head of the regional state administration, announced this on Telegram.
Pursuant to a decision by the Kyiv Regional Defense Council and under the coordination of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, gas stations in the region will gain access to a special digital air situation awareness system, which is used by the Defense Forces. AI data centre provider could become one of Australia's biggest stock floats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
23:18:58 UTC
08:18:58 KST

AI data centre provider Firmus courting investors ahead of IPO on Australian Securities Exchange
In short:
AI data centre company Firmus Technologies is intending to raise up to $7 billion in an initial public offering next month.
The company aims to have seven AI data centres across Australia, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia within the next 24 months.
What's next?
A Firmus spokesperson declined to comment on the likely size of the capital raising, or how much of the company might be sold.
AI data centre developer Firmus Technologies is courting investors in Asia and Australia ahead of a widely expected multi-billion-dollar share market float next month.
The company has been making headlines over its expansions and resulting community concerns, as well as through its partnerships.
Last week Firmus announced it had signed a multi-year deal with OpenAI for two new AI factory sites in Malaysia.
At the same time, the company has been growing its presence in northern Tasmania with three data centre projects and a flurry of sports sponsorships, including with the Tasmania Devils AFL team.
One AI data centre is currently under construction in Launceston, where its parent company is headquartered, and another near George Town has council approval while a site at Wesley Vale is still awaiting approval.
Plans are also underway for projects in South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, Western Australia and the ACT.
Firmus already has significant operations in Singapore, and over the next 24 months, it says it hopes to have seven AI data centres across four countries.
This narrative of aggressive expansion will stoke interest in its expected float on the Australian share market next month.
Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in an initial public offering (IPO), which could value the company at more than $50 billion, depending on what proportion of the company is sold.
If that pans out, it could make Firmus the second-largest float in Australian history, after the federal government raised $14 billion by selling a third of Telstra three decades ago, valuing the entire company at $42 billion.
Based on its share price yesterday, Telstra had a market value of $53 billion.
An important caveat for many of the figures being touted in the financial press for Firmus's float is that they are based on conjecture and hype.
The company's public offer document, the prospectus that potential investors will review, has yet to be lodged with the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).
The valuation reports are based partly on an invitation for a "roadshow" in Asian and Australian capitals sent out to potential investors by investment banks handling the float for Firmus.
The roadshow will help determine how much demand there is for stock, based on forecast earnings.
A spokesperson for Firmus declined to comment on the likely size of the capital raising, or how much of the company might be sold, which will depend on the demand.
'Mum and dad investors' also likely for IPO, expert says
Sam Baker, private wealth adviser at Shadforth Financial Group, told the ABC it was widely known Firmus had been looking to debut this year on the ASX.
"It now appears as if the company is fronting investors both in Asia, and soon to be Australia, as a preamble to looking to do an initial public offering of up to $7 billion," Mr Baker said.
"They're telling the story of the business, providing details, which will largely be provided in any prospectus for the initial public offering.
"But it's about sort of gauging interest as to what or whether investors would be interested and at what price they would be potentially prepared to pay for any shares in an initial public offering."
Mr Baker said investors in Australia and overseas would likely be interested.
"In an initial public offering, they tend to have cornerstone or institutional investors, but I would expect a raising of this size will also be looking to attract retail, or mum and dad, investors," he said.
Mr Baker said while IPOs could be used for the founders to "cash out", it seemed Firmus was raising funds to support the rollout of its AI data centres across Australia and South-East Asia.
From Bitcoin to AI
Firmus's most advanced project is at St Leonards in Launceston, and it has approval for another at Long Reach, near George Town, in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone.
The company is seeking approval for another at Wesley Vale in Tasmania's north-west.
Firmus has struggled to gain a social licence in Tasmania, but Mr Baker did not believe that would necessarily impact the IPO.
"Broader institutional investors are mainly focused on getting a return," he said.
"Whether or not there is some resistance across the retail shareholders, that will remain to be seen."
Firmus began as a bitcoin miner in 2019, subsequently pivoting to data centre development.
Its co-CEO Oliver Curtis was sentenced to two years' jail in 2016 for conspiring to commit insider trading.
The trial heard how he shared in $1.4 million of illegal profits from insider trading using confidential information between May 2007 and June 2008.
In October 2025, Mr Curtis was asked about his reflections on the ordeal and whether Tasmanians could trust Firmus.
"The experience of the past presents an opportunity for the future," he told ABC Radio Hobart at the time.
"It's all about resilience, it's all about how you get back on the horse, and it's all about basically making sure that you are completing what you believe you need to complete.
"For me, this is about more than an individual; this is about a company.
"I'm so fortunate we have a hugely amazing, talented team around us — and that's the story."

EU considers tougher visa restrictions for Russians — Kallas
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said this during an address to the European Parliament, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
Kallas stressed that EU sanctions had already cost the Russian economy EUR 1 trillion and said that the EU was finalizing what she described as the largest-ever list of individual and corporate restrictions. She added that the EU was also systematically dismantling Russia's shadow fleet, with EU naval operations taking the initiative in inspecting suspicious vessels. According to Kallas, the EU's diplomatic efforts around the world had resulted in fewer countries allowing the tankers to sail under their flags, and hundreds of vessels had already been stripped of their flags as a result.
Speaking about diplomatic pressure and restrictions on the movement of Russian citizens, the EU's foreign policy chief said that further decisive action was needed.
Kallas said that the EU had already reduced Russia's diplomatic presence in the bloc, introduced new requirements for movement within the Schengen Area, and limited the staff of Russia's mission to the EU to 40 people. She noted that member states were taking similar measures and pointed out that Hungary had recently expelled 10 Russian diplomats. However, she said there was still potential to do more, including further tightening controls on the movement of Russian diplomats within the Schengen Area, banning visas for Russian former combatants, and reviewing the issuance of tourist visas to Russian citizens. Kallas emphasized that the EU needed to reduce the number of people who could potentially carry out attacks on European territory.
As Ukrinform reported, the EU has stepped up measures aimed at countering Russian sabotage networks and expelling Russian diplomatic mission personnel who have used diplomatic cover for malicious activities.
In particular, Hungary's expulsion of 10 Russian diplomats was one of the latest steps aimed at neutralizing this threat. At the same time, Brussels is discussing the need for a complete entry ban on Russian military personnel and veterans of Russia's military aggression against Ukraine, as well as closing channels used to circumvent oil sanctions.

Turkey arrests dozens in crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists
- Published
Turkish police have arrested dozens of people as part of the government's recent crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists and venues.
The protesters were detained as they gathered on Tuesday outside Istanbul's main courthouse.
They were calling for the release of another group of LGBTQ+ activists, who were arrested over the weekend in a series of raids on gay bars and at the homes of activists.
The Turkish government has detained members of the LGBTQ+ community and activists as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe", which the government says has been designed to protect family values.
At Tuesday's protest, people chanted "Long live the struggle for freedom!" and called for the detained activists to be released, news agency AFP reported. Police made several arrests after some demonstrators unfurled a banner reading "Being LGBTQ is not a crime".
"What we are seeing now is deeply disturbing," one protestor told AFP.
Rights groups have described a widening campaign against the LGBTQ+ community. Over the past week the authorities raided association offices, blocked websites and made arrests across multiple provinces.
The government has also blocked or restricted access to the social media accounts and websites of dozens of LGBT, media and rights organisations, according to a post from the NGO Human Rights Watch.
Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has described LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.
The Commissioner for Human Rights at the Council of Europe, Michael O'Flaherty, has raised concerns about the arrests.
"I am concerned by reports of a series arrests, raids and the blocking of websites and social media accounts targeting LGBTI civil society and human rights defenders across Turkey," he said.
O'Flaherty's statement said that Turkey's Minister of Justice had said the operation was being conducted against 162 individuals, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces under the coordination of several Chief Public Prosecutors' Offices.
