As Russia closes in on Sloviansk, this taxi driver keeps working
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:18:12 UTC
01:18:12 KST

As Russia closes in on Sloviansk, this taxi driver keeps working
Oleksandr behind the wheel of his work car, in Sloviansk, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 17, 2026. (Lisa Bukreyeva / The Kyiv Independent)
SLOVIANSK, Donetsk Oblast — From a brick-walled garage that barely fits the blue car parked inside, Oleksandr Richak carefully backs his taxi cab out onto the narrow street.
The 42-year-old usually starts work around 8 a.m., once the early-morning rush hour of deadly Russian drone activity in the eastern front-line city subsides.
As he briefly parks the car outside a damaged one-story house, his wife, Nataliia, walks over and hands him a bottle of lemon-flavored water. Her worried eyes follow Richak as he drives off, watching until he disappears from view.
"Before it was fine, but now with the FPV (first-person view) drones hitting so many cars…" she says, unable to finish the sentence.
"Whenever I hear (a loud explosion), I immediately call him."
As Russian troops gradually advance toward Sloviansk, the security situation in what was once a relatively safe haven in the eastern Donbas region has significantly worsened this year. Now only around 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Russian troops, an intensifying barrage of glide bombs and FPV attacks is gradually destroying the city.
Many Sloviansk residents are now doing something that until recently, they had never contemplated — fleeing.
Every day brings more reminders of the potential cost of staying. Richak drives past new ruins, and the number of shops, cafes, and restaurants still opening their doors each morning is dwindling.
"Every night, something gets hit," Richak says, driving past a series of destroyed and damaged buildings.
Richak drives for five minutes before arriving at the eerily empty Sloviansk central bus station. Alongside a few other remaining Sloviansk taxi drivers, he waits for bookings, lighting up a cigarette and opening the OnTaxi app on his phone.
Another taxi arrives at the bus station, driven by 54-year-old Ruslan Kuzmenko. The two men greet each other on the station square.
Suddenly, they're interrupted by the unmistakable buzzing of an FPV drone.
"It is an interceptor drone," Kuzmenko says calmly, just seconds before a loud explosion blasts out from the direction of a nearby market.
"Turns out it's not," he says.
"It hits, and someone is just unlucky."
Richak and Nataliia both studied in Sloviansk when they were younger, and in 2006, after completing 18 months in the military, he returned to the city. Nataliia and their one-year-old daughter followed a year later. They added a son to the family in 2013 and bought their first home in 2018.
"There was such life here," he says fondly.
Before the full-scale war broke out in 2022, Richak drove a truck, delivering cakes and pastries from the local confectionery factory Valensiya all across the country. The war forced a change of career, and four years ago he swapped the truck for a taxi to supplement his main job as a gas repair worker.
His first booking comes in, and he jumps in the cab to pick up a 40-year-old soldier named Yurii, who needs to view a potential new apartment as its current tenant has decided to leave Sloviansk.
During the drive over, Yurii, who asked to disclose his first name only as his family still lives in Russian-occupied territories, mentions he is originally from the now-occupied town of Velyka Novosilka in Donetsk Oblast.
Richak's face lights up at the mention of a place he frequently visited for work before the war. They share memories of the town and discover they both know the same woman from there. Richak remembers her from the police academy.
"What a small world!" Yurii says, laughing as he hands cash to Richak and leaves the taxi.
read also
Up until 2014, Richak worked in the police for 10 years. In a country strained by corruption, in need of Western reforms, and still under the strong influence of the Kremlin, he hoped he could make a small but positive contribution to his homeland.
The rest of his roughly 25-man police unit had other ideas. When Russia invaded Donbas in 2014 and its proxy troops occupied Sloviansk, all but two of them defected in what he believes was a prearranged plan.
"We were placed on alert, but I learned that my entire unit had gone over to the side of the (Russian proxy forces), including the commander," he says.
Richak was not surprised — he had heard their views during the 2013-2014 Euromaidan Revolution, and knew how they felt about Ukraine moving closer to Europe and away from Russia.
A week into the occupation, he walked out of the city to escape.
Pro-Russian sentiment persists among some Sloviansk residents, typically from the older generation who grew up in the Soviet Union. Even to this day, under constant Russian bombardment, there are occasionally clients who support Russian President Vladimir Putin, and blame President Volodymyr Zelensky for Moscow's war.
Richak says he encounters someone like this about once a month. Often, they will rant during the drive, insist that he speaks Russian, and, when he refuses, slam the door in anger when they leave.
His response as they exit his taxi is the same one he gives to everyone.
"Have a nice day."
Richak's second booking buzzes his phone into life. Fifty-nine-year-old retiree Lyudmila Hurkina rarely leaves her house these days. Her husband suffered a stroke in May, is bedridden, and she tries to leave him on his own as little as possible.
But she can't avoid errands like buying food or picking up his medicine, and a taxi allows her to get back home as quickly as possible.
She already knows what it's like to flee, forced to leave the city of Horlivka when it fell to Russian proxy forces in 2014. If she has to do it again, she doesn't know how she will afford it — two weeks of her husband's medicine costs UAH 3,000 (about $67), nearly the full amount of her pension.
"I might have to leave again and start all over," she says as they arrive at the hospital.
"But now I am 59. I don't know whether I can start over in a new place and build up a life."
The stories that are shared in taxis in Sloviansk are often understandably heavy, centered on survival in a city Russia seems determined to destroy.
Richak says he often feels like a therapist, listening to people's problems and giving them advice when he can. But it can also work the other way, with Richak hearing useful information about the situation in the city.
"We drive on the road, and there is the feeling of having known them for 10 years," Richak says.
A regular working day in Sloviansk will see Richak take around 15 bookings. He tries to wrap up and be home by 8 p.m., before the 9 p.m. curfew and the inevitable increase in Russian drones as night falls.
On a typical day, he'll take in around UAH 3,000 ($70), but after taxi app commission and expenses like fuel, he takes home around half.
His main job as a gas repair worker is no less dangerous than driving a taxi around a city constantly in the sights of Russian glide bombs and drones.
On 24-hour standby, he and his team rush to repair gas pipelines damaged in Russian attacks. The threat of double-tap strikes, a deliberate tactic Russia uses to target emergency workers, is ever-present.
On Aug. 19, a Russian Molniya drone exploded three meters away from him as he responded to a call. Though his team survived and he escaped with a concussion, the experience further heightened his anxiety.
"Next time it might hit me directly," he says. "These are weapons that can take life away from you at any moment."
Another booking comes in — three generations of one family, a grandmother, her daughter, and her granddaughter.
Seven-year-old Aliya is on her way to perform a song in church alongside some of the other remaining children in Sloviansk.
"The Russians stole their childhood."
"The children act as though they are okay, but it is still stressful for them," 52-year-old grandmother Oksana Mykhalchyk says.
"The Russians stole their childhood," Aliya's mother, Khrystyna, adds.
As the family exits the taxi, the sounds of air defense fire echo across the city. Richak parks his car under a tree in the courtyard of a residential building to wait out the danger.
After a while, he returns to the bus station. "There are very few taxi drivers today," he says.
Richak knows that as Russia further encroaches on the city, there will be less and less work for him. The once-bustling streets were packed with entertainment venues and hosted a Christmas market he recalls with fondness.
Despite growing up in Kharkiv Oblast, Sloviansk has always been his second home; he used to visit the city during school breaks and stay at his aunt's. Coming from a village, Richak saw Sloviansk as a big city, and he watched it grow as he built a family of his own.
He feels certain that Russia will reduce Sloviansk to rubble before the urban fighting begins, much like other cities in the Donbas.
"I don't think there is another scenario," Richak says. "We are mentally preparing for a time when we are not going to return to the city."
Shortly after spending the day with Richak, his wife and daughter left Sloviansk, joining their son in Kharkiv Oblast.
After his shifts, Richak has to return each day to an empty home — he can only leave Sloviansk if the gas service relocates him elsewhere.
Richak tries to distract himself from thoughts of fear with his work, talking to people and staying busy.
"You still think about it constantly anyway," Richak says. "Every day, it never leaves you."
All the taxi passengers interviewed in August for this story later told the Kyiv Independent they had since decided to leave Sloviansk due to near-misses amid ever-intensifying Russian drone and glide bomb attacks.
Richak remains, mentally adjusting to each passing day and the ever-present possibility of death.
"It hits, and someone is just unlucky," Richak says. "That is how we live."

But meeting local residents, such as Oleksandr, and hearing their stories of resilience reminded me why Donbas holds a special place in my heart. Russian forces attack Dnipropetrovsk region more than ten times, two injured

Researchers launch global tracking project to measure the daily mental health impacts of cannabis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:00:05 UTC
01:00:05 KST

A new global research initiative aims to track the real-time habits and health outcomes of both recreational and medicinal cannabis users over a two-year period. The project will map how local laws, individual mindsets, and daily routines shape the positive and negative effects of cannabis on the brain. The study protocol was recently published in Comprehensive Psychiatry.
As cannabis laws relax around the world, usage is rising. Many people consume the plant recreationally, but a growing number of individuals use it for medical reasons. Pain management and mental health symptom relief are common motivations for medicinal use. The actual effectiveness of cannabis for mental health remains a subject of intense debate among researchers. Some individuals report substantial benefits, noting that the drug eases their anxiety and stabilizes their mood. Others experience adverse reactions, including worsened depression, heightened paranoia, and the onset of cannabis use disorder.
Researchers want to understand why these outcomes vary so wildly from person to person. Part of the explanation likely involves the specific chemical makeup of the products being consumed. Cannabis contains different compounds, most notably tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, which produces the psychoactive high, and cannabidiol, or CBD, which does not. High doses of THC are generally linked to a greater risk of adverse mental health effects. At the same time, preexisting psychiatric conditions and biological vulnerabilities play a role in how a person reacts to the drug.
Past research on cannabis often viewed the drug through a narrow lens, focusing heavily on either its potential harms or its supposed benefits. Funding sources and disciplinary boundaries frequently restricted the scope of these investigations. The existing literature also tends to overlook the environmental and cultural contexts in which people consume the drug. The social stigma attached to cannabis, local law enforcement practices, and community norms can all influence an individual’s psychological relationship with the substance. Additionally, most medicinal users purchase and consume cannabis without any formal medical supervision, making their habits difficult to track in clinical settings.
To build a more complete picture of modern cannabis consumption, a team of scientists launched the “Blowing Minds” project. Nora de Bode, a researcher at Erasmus University Rotterdam in the Netherlands, is the lead author of the study protocol. She collaborated with Erasmus University colleagues Emese Kroon, Jia Hua Hsieh, and Janna Cousijn.
The research team plans to recruit 1,800 participants between the ages of 18 and 65. To qualify, individuals must consume cannabis at least four times a week. The study compares people who use the drug recreationally with those who use it medicinally. Because the researchers want to measure the impact of different legal environments, they are recruiting subjects from a variety of regions. The initial rollout includes participants from the Netherlands, the United States, Canada, and Brazil, with plans to expand into parts of Asia and Africa.
The study takes place entirely online. Participants begin by completing an extensive series of baseline questionnaires. They report their preferred methods of consumption, such as smoking or vaping, and estimate the potency of the products they buy. They also answer questions about their physical health, sleep quality, and history of psychological trauma or mental illness. The surveys ask participants to reflect on how their friends, family, and local government view cannabis, which helps the researchers quantify the social pressure surrounding each user.
After finishing the surveys, the participants complete a battery of digital cognitive tests. These assessments measure memory, processing speed, general intelligence, and emotional perception. One specific test tracks how easily a participant’s attention is captured by images related to cannabis, which can serve as an indicator of addictive behavior.
Once the baseline measurements are established, the subjects begin a 14-day intensive tracking period using a mobile application. This technique, known as the experience sampling method, allows researchers to observe behavior in a natural setting rather than a laboratory. Every morning, the app asks the participants how well they slept and whether they used any substances the day before. Throughout the day, the app sends five random notifications. When prompted, the participants have one hour to log their current mood, stress levels, and cannabis cravings. They rate their feelings of happiness, anxiety, loneliness, and physical pain on a sliding scale.
In addition to the random prompts, the participants are instructed to open the app right before they consume cannabis. They log their intention to use the drug and record their immediate emotional state. By capturing mood and craving data right before consumption and comparing it to the random check-ins throughout the day, the researchers can see what emotional triggers prompt a person to use. They can also track how the drug alters the user’s mood in the hours that follow.
The project extends far beyond the initial two-week tracking period. The researchers will contact the participants again one and two years after their baseline assessments. The subjects will retake the digital cognitive tests and fill out the mental health questionnaires a second and third time. This longitudinal approach allows the team to map out long-term trajectories. They hope to identify whether certain habits, such as relying on highly potent products to cope with negative emotions, consistently lead to cognitive decline or worsening mental health over a multi-year period.
Running a remote, multi-year study presents distinct logistical challenges. Because the participants are paid for their time, the online format is vulnerable to fraudulent responses. People might try to enter the study multiple times or use automated software to complete the surveys. The researchers employ digital security measures to flag suspicious activity, manually check for contradictory demographic answers, and verify regional locations using internet routing data.
The daily tracking period also requires a high level of commitment from the participants. Being interrupted by phone notifications five times a day for two weeks can cause fatigue, leading some individuals to skip questions or provide rushed answers. In any multi-year study, a portion of the participants will inevitably drop out before the final follow-up. The research team uses statistical models designed to handle missing data to account for these dropouts.
By making their digital materials and anonymized data available to other scientists, the research team hopes to standardize how cannabis habits are measured globally. Sharing this framework will allow other laboratories to replicate the study in different countries or among specific age groups.
The study, “Blowing minds: A cross-cultural, longitudinal investigation to unravel the highs and lows of recreational and medicinal cannabis users,” was authored by Nora de Bode, Emese Kroon, Jia Hua Hsieh, and Janna Cousijn.

Russia’s “Domestic” Sniper Ammo Turns Out to Be Packed With US and Finnish Components
Unknown

00:57:06 KST

- Category

Russia’s “Domestic” Sniper Ammo Turns Out to Be Packed With US and Finnish Components
A Russian weapons manufacturer supplying the military with sniper rifles has begun producing ammunition using US-made and Finnish components, including precision bullets and cartridge cases.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Insider on September 14, Russian arms manufacturer Promtekhnologiya, which produces weapons and ammunition under the ORSIS brand, has supplied Russian forces with factory-assembled sniper cartridges containing components made by US companies Hornady and Peterson, as well as Finland’s Lapua.
The findings indicate a shift from earlier cases in which Russian troops were documented using complete imported cartridges or ammunition assembled outside regular factory production. Promtekhnologiya is now reportedly receiving enough foreign components to incorporate them into ammunition manufactured at its own facilities.
The Insider reported that Russian snipers received .308 Winchester ammunition for ORSIS rifles assembled with Peterson cartridge cases and 178-grain Hornady BTHP Match/OTM bullets, weighing 11.53 grams each.
Where US components were in short supply, Promtekhnologiya reportedly turned to Lapua Scenar bullets manufactured in Finland. Those cartridges were assembled with Russian-made Irbis 570 powder and cases marked ORSIS.
Testing cited by The Insider showed the ammunition producing groups of around 0.5 MOA at 300 meters, equivalent to a spread of roughly 4.5 centimeters.
The latest findings build on an earlier investigation by The Insider, which found that more than 10 million bullets manufactured in NATO countries entered Russia between March 2022 and February 2024. Among them were precision projectiles in calibers such as .338 Lapua Magnum and .375 CheyTac, commonly used for long-range shooting.
The Insider also identified indications that some American components reached Russia through European countries. In June 2022, Russian company IF Tetis registered a batch of Hornady bullets whose testing documentation had been issued by Finland’s Lapua Test Shooting Lab.
Earlier, Ukraine’s military intelligence identified 5,816 foreign-made components in 202 Russian weapons systems, including missiles, drones, and armored vehicles, highlighting Moscow’s continued reliance on foreign technology despite international sanctions.

a spiral of timber beams and steel frames tiny 40-sqm tokyo home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:55:32 UTC
00:55:32 KST

Tato Architects / Yo Shimada builds House in Musashi-Koyama
House in Musashi-koyama by Tato Architects / Yo Shimada is a home for a family of four on a flag-shaped lot measuring less than 40 sqm in a dense residential district of Tokyo. Facing a large park to the north, the site was created by dividing a plot in two where a single, relatively small house had previously stood. Its limited dimensions presented a familiar challenge in Tokyo: how to accommodate a family home on increasingly subdivided urban land.
The initial approach was to stack two full floors within the site’s permitted 60 percent building coverage, placing shared spaces such as the living room on one level and bedrooms and other private rooms on the other. This arrangement, however, would have resulted in compact floor plans with limited flexibility for everyday activities, including finding space for a dining table. Instead, the architects divided the floor into four sections and arranged them in a spiral. The resulting skip-floor configuration creates a sequence of interconnected levels, allowing sightlines to extend both upward and downward through the house. While dividing the available floor area into smaller sections could have made the rooms feel more confined, the visual connections between levels give the interior a greater sense of continuity and spatial depth. The entrance is positioned at the mezzanine, reached by a stair running along the narrow access strip of the flag-shaped lot. From this level, the sequence of floors winds upward towards the roof terrace, while the stair descending from the mezzanine leads to the lower level, where the individual rooms are arranged.
all images by Shinkenchiku-sha
spiral arrangement addresses the limits of the tiny urban plot
The compact dimensions of the house also informed its structural system. With people and architecture positioned in close proximity, conventional timber framing could have become visually dominant within the small interior. Instead, the skip floors are supported by 30-millimeter-thick laminated veneer lumber (LVL) beams connected with slender steel members no thicker than a handrail. The structural elements remain close to the scale of furniture, allowing the spiral floor arrangement to occupy a volume measuring approximately 3.6 by 6 meters and 7.2 meters high without introducing a heavy structural presence. The system creates the four interconnected floor sections within the permitted building volume while maintaining visual connections across the levels.
A series of openings is added to the maximum permitted building volume to bring daylight and views into the interior. Each opening responds to a specific orientation or domestic function. A clerestory faces south, while a bay window projects towards the park to the north and creates a place to sit close to the exterior view. In the kitchen, another bay window combines daylight with storage. A skylight above the narrow access strip brings light into the house while providing an upward view, and the entrance makes full use of the limited space available within the flag-shaped site. These elements work as extensions of the main volume, creating additional points of contact between the interior, the surrounding neighbourhood, and the sky. Their arrangement can be compared to a plant growing within dense vegetation, with its leaves extending into the available gaps.
The multiple changes in level introduce a different pattern of movement and occupation from a conventional two-storey house. Instead of separating the home into two complete horizontal layers, the spiral sequence distributes domestic functions across several interconnected levels. The completed house demonstrates how this arrangement can create a greater sense of spaciousness within a footprint of less than 40 square meters. By combining skip floors, a furniture-scale structural system, and a series of carefully positioned openings, House in Musashi-koyama explores how a compact urban home can accommodate a family of four while responding to the increasingly limited dimensions of residential plots in Tokyo.

Belarus is holding military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania from Sept. 15-18, the Belarusian Defense Ministry said on Sept. 15.
The Belarusian Defense Ministry described the drills as "defensive" and said they are aimed at improving the military's ability to "protect the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
The exercise is focused on preparing troops to conduct a "strategic military operation," including securing the border, countering alleged sabotage and reconnaissance groups, and combating drones and light aircraft.
Exercises are being held at the Gozhsky training ground in Grodno Oblast, around 6 kilometers (4 miles) from the Lithuanian border, as well as at the Brestsky and Ruzhansky training grounds, roughly 15 and 60 kilometers (9 and 37 miles) from the Polish border.
Belarus has a history of tensions with its NATO neighbors, including Poland and Lithuania. Minsk has previously been accused of using hybrid tactics against the two countries, including facilitating the arrival of migrants from the Middle East and Africa to its borders with the EU, which triggered a major migration crisis.
Belarus also allowed Russian forces to use its territory as a staging ground for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The exercises also come amid a buildup of military infrastructure along the Belarus-Ukraine border, leading Kyiv to warn that Moscow may be planning to draw its closest ally deeper into the full-scale war.
"The threat of a reopened northern front is intended to stretch Ukrainian forces, pulling units from their current positions along the front line," Michael Kofman, a senior fellow at the D.C.-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told the Kyiv Independent.
Units of Russia's 101st Missile Brigade, which is equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile system, are deployed in Belarus, Ukraine's military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said in an interview published on Sept. 7.
Belarus is also building new railway infrastructure in the country's southern Gomel Oblast that will be capable of receiving military trains carrying personnel and heavy equipment, the Belarusian Railway Workers' Community reported on Aug. 24.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on May 15 that Ukraine had recorded fresh contacts between Moscow and Minsk aimed at convincing Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko to "join new acts of aggression."
Russia was considering using Belarusian territory to attack neighboring NATO member states, according to Zelensky.
Zelensky said on May 21 that Ukraine was prepared to take "preventive" measures against Russia and Belarus in response to potential military threats along its northern border.
Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko denied that Belarus intends to enter the war, saying in an interview published on June 15 that the country poses no military threat to Ukraine. Lukashenko added that Belarus would only become involved if it were attacked.

Smelling chocolate helped men complete more reps without feeling more tired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:03:54 UTC
00:03:54 KST

Smelling chocolate helped men complete more reps without feeling more tired
A whiff of chocolate may be enough to give workouts an unexpected boost.
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Simply smelling chocolate helped men complete more leg extension repetitions without making the workout feel harder, with dark chocolate producing the strongest effect. The researchers think familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation by making the brain anticipate eating.
- Share:
A tough leg day may have an unexpectedly simple boost: the smell of chocolate. According to a new study published in Frontiers in Physiology, exposure to chocolate aromas before and during resistance exercise helped participants complete more repetitions without making the workout feel more difficult.
"Exposing moderately trained men to chocolate odors right before and between sets of resistance exercise significantly increased their overall training volume without increasing their perceived exertion," said senior author Dr. Mohamed Nashrudin bin Naharudin, an assistant professor at the Faculty of Sports and Exercise Science at the University of Malaya. "Seeing a substantial increase in repetitions without the athletes feeling like they were exerting themselves any harder is a fascinating psychobiological outcome."
Testing Chocolate Scents During Exercise
The study included 23 healthy men in their early to mid-20s who were moderately trained. Researchers separated them into three groups and exposed each group to one of three samples: liquified dark chocolate containing 90% cocoa, liquified milk chocolate containing 60% cocoa, or water as a control.
"We know olfaction is powerfully wired into the brain's appetite and emotion networks, but surprisingly, no study has systematically looked at the three-way interaction between smell, appetite, and actual resistance exercise capacity," said Nashrudin Naharudin.
Before exercising, the participants had gone without food for at least 10 hours. They then performed leg extensions, an exercise in which a person sits and straightens the lower legs against resistance to lift a weight.
Researchers measured leg extension performance both before and during the training session. Before exercising, participants also rated their hunger, fullness, desire to eat, and intention to eat in the near future. While completing their sets, researchers measured hunger and desire to eat after each 30-second exposure to one of the scent samples.
Dark and Milk Chocolate Produced Different Effects
The two chocolate aromas influenced appetite in notably different ways.
Compared with both the water control and milk chocolate conditions, smelling dark chocolate was consistently associated with lower hunger, less desire and intention to eat, and greater feelings of fullness before exercise. The dark chocolate aroma therefore appeared to reduce appetite mainly by decreasing hunger and increasing perceived fullness.
Milk chocolate had a different effect. Participants rated its smell as more pleasant than either dark chocolate or water, but the aroma did not significantly change their hunger or appetite.
The effects were not limited to appetite. Chocolate aromas also appeared to influence how much exercise the participants could complete.
"Sniffing a 90% dark chocolate odor added about 18 more repetitions to participants' leg extensions, while a 60% milk chocolate odor added about nine repetitions compared to the water control," said Nashrudin Naharudin.
How Smell Could Influence the Brain
The researchers think learned associations with food may help explain the results. From an early age, people repeatedly experience certain smells alongside eating. Over time, those aromas can become signals that lead the brain and body to anticipate what normally happens after food is consumed.
Those expectations may even shift a person's perception from hunger toward fullness before any food has actually been eaten.
"The dark chocolate scent serves as a learned cue for a rich, bitter, and highly satiating food, which essentially tricks the system into an anticipatory state of fullness," said Nashrudin Naharudin. "Conversely, the sweeter milk chocolate scent acts more like a hedonic reward cue, enhancing training volume by creating a highly pleasant sensory environment rather than by shifting basic metabolic hunger signals."
The findings raise the possibility that simply anticipating food could trigger some responses resembling those caused by actually eating it. That possibility is especially intriguing because the participants had been fasting when the effects were observed.
Food aromas may prepare the digestive system for an upcoming meal or produce psychological and physiological changes as the body anticipates eating. Some of these responses could resemble changes that normally happen after food consumption.
Important Limitations of the Study
The researchers caution that the biological explanation remains speculative. They did not measure blood hormones or neural activity, so the study cannot show exactly which biological pathways were responsible for the changes in appetite and exercise performance.
There were other limitations as well. The intensity of the dark and milk chocolate aromas may not have been perfectly identical. Because the control sample was odorless water, participants also may have realized when they were in the control condition.
The study was also small and included only healthy, moderately trained young men. Research involving larger and more diverse groups will be needed to determine how broadly the findings apply.
Could Other Food Smells Work Too?
Another unanswered question is whether chocolate has something special about it or whether other familiar foods could produce similar effects.
"We don't think chocolate is entirely unique, though it is a food cue with incredibly strong, universally recognized reward associations," Nashrudin Naharudin concluded.
Other foods strongly associated with feeling satisfied after eating might potentially produce comparable responses, although researchers have not yet tested that idea.
"A person likely needs to find the odor familiar and appealing - or at least not repulsive - to trigger the psychological shift in appetite that's needed to see a performance boost."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xiaohan Fan, Hengzhi Deng, Jia Yang Ng, Ahmad Amirul Hazim bin Ab Aziz, Mohamed Nashrudin bin Naharudin. Chocolate odor enhances resistance exercise performance through appetite suppression in the fasted state: an exploratory study. Frontiers in Physiology, 2026; 17 DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2026.1834757

Meet Swiftiephylus, an Australian bug named after Taylor Swift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Meet Swiftiephylus, an Australian bug named after Taylor Swift
The discovery fills a “Blank Space” in researchers’ knowledge of the bugs in Australia
If you’re down under and you give the right tree a rustle, you might encounter a record-breaking, globally recognized music icon. Or at least a bug named after her.
Meet Swiftiephylus, a newly described group of Australian insects. The big-eyed bugs — each smaller than a lentil — honor Taylor Swift in recognition of her “show-stopping talent, heart-wrenching lyrics, and the joy and comfort she has brought to many,” researchers report September 9 in Insect Systematics & Evolution.
There are some 10,000 species of herbivorous plant bugs found all over the world, but little was known about their diversity in Australia. In the early 2000s, a group of researchers including entomologist Christiane Weirauch at the University of California, Riverside, began to collect and describe these bugs. In 2022, when entomologist Sarah Schroeder began her PhD work with Weirauch, some of these mystery bugs became a part of her project.
“I was really excited,” Schroeder says. “It’s a dream thing for a scientist to get to describe new species.”
Schroeder and Weirauch studied the flower-eating plant bugs found in she-oak trees in Australia. By comparing their physical shapes, colors and genes to known species, the researchers found 12 new species. These were organized into five genera. One of these groups — Swiftiephylus — sports a name with special meaning to Schroeder.
“I’ve been a lifelong Swiftie,” Schroeder says. “Taylor’s music has underscored so many of the major milestones of my life, so it felt authentic to me to honor her by naming these species after her and giving her a gift back for all of her music.”
Schoeder picked the four species to bear Swift’s name because of their uniquely yellow colors punctuated with red accents.
“Taylor’s pretty well known for having her red lip,” Schroeder says. “And the fans affectionately call her Blondie.”
Beyond the more obviously named S. taylorae, Schroeder gave the other three species Latin translations of some of Swift’s album names. S. amator is for Lover, S. intrepidus is for Fearless and S. poetorum references The Tortured Poet’s Department.
For Schroeder, this song isn’t finished. Swiftiephylus barely scratches the surface of what’s left to find among insect life. She notes that species description is crucial for conservation, since you can’t protect what you don’t know is there. With potentially millions of undescribed insect species still out there, it’s a conservation vulnerability researchers know “All Too Well”.

There's one massive problem with Trump's Ukraine diesel price theory
U.S. President Donald Trump pauses to take questions from journalists while walking across the lawns of Aras an Uachtarain to his official vehicle on September 12, 2026, in Dublin, Ireland. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump has a very simple solution to the very real problem of rising diesel prices.
"(President Volodymyr) Zelensky has to do one thing — he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” he told reporters on Sept. 13. "Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel… that’s hurting the world."
Trump's implication was clear — halting Ukraine's long-running, long-range drone strike campaign against Russian oil refineries would significantly ease record-high diesel prices at American pumps, something an administration already under pressure from high gas prices ahead of midterm elections in November would welcome.
There's just one problem with Trump's theory.
"Of course this isn’t true," Alan Riley, senior fellow with the Atlantic Council Global Energy Center, told the Kyiv Independent.
read also
What's causing global diesel prices to spike?
The answer lies in the second part of Trump's statement to reporters, which he reiterated a few days later in a post on Truth Social.
"The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine war, not (the U.S. war with) Iran," he said, in a post in which he also falsely claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire.
There is little evidence to back up his claim, and "almost all" of the explosive rise in diesel prices has been due to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the disruption to refining capacity in the Gulf, Riley said.
The numbers are clear — at the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran at the end of February, diesel prices in the U.S. were averaging around $3.60 per gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). Prices at the pumps have now soared to $6.23 per gallon, the highest on record.
Diesel prices are surging across the world due to a confluence of factors, including higher crude oil prices and a lack of refining capacity. As a result, refineries in the U.S., the largest exporter of the fuel, are running at full tilt with the approach of peak winter demand and inventories depleted.
Crucially, in February 2026 when U.S. diesel prices began to surge, Ukraine’s deep-strike campaign was already in full swing and had been contributing to chronic fuel shortages in Russia since August 2025.
"The attacks are massive, coordinated, and repeated; they come in waves, and the refineries simply do not have time to repair the damage caused by the previous attack before the next one occurs," Boris Aronstein, an independent oil and gas analyst, told the Guardian that month.
Russia's Ryazan Oil Refinery, one of the largest such facilities in the country, was struck nine times in 2025 alone, forcing it to suspend operations on multiple occasions.
U.S. diesel prices in August 2025 averaged around $3.70, according to the EIA.
A study by Ukraine’s KSE Institute, shared with the Financial Times, assessed the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran had a far bigger impact on global diesel and gasoil supplies than Ukrainian drone strikes, estimating exports from the Persian Gulf fell by 152 million barrels between March and August, compared with a 68 million-barrel drop in Russian exports over the same period.
"The cumulative loss from the Persian Gulf was therefore around 2.2 times larger," the report said.
"Most refined fuel produced in Russian refineries is used in Russia," Riley said, adding: "That is why the strategy of the Ukrainian Armed Forces makes so much sense."
read also
What effect do Ukrainian strikes have on global prices?
None of this is to say that Ukrainian attacks have had no impact on global prices.
"(Russia's) ban on exports of diesel has had a significant effect globally as Russia has historically been, along with the U.S., one of the top exporters of diesel globally," refined product analyst Henok Gheotom of analytics firm Kpler told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian strikes against refineries intensified over the summer, leaving Russia struggling to keep up with repairs. Twelve major Russian oil refineries were hit in August alone, with a combined design capacity of some 100 million tons of petroleum products per year, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry. Refineries remain under fire in September.
"When export-oriented coastal or pipeline-linked refineries are hit, reduced diesel flows force global buyers to compete for replacement barrels from the U.S. Gulf Coast, India, and the Middle East, widening refining margins worldwide,” George Voloshin, an expert on Russian affairs and sanctions, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russia's seaborne product exports are down 21% between January and July, roughly twice the fall across the global seaborne market, but Russia still accounts for only about a fifth of that decline," Luke Wickenden of the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air told the Kyiv Independent.
This decline is largely driven by diesel, which accounts for the bulk of Russian exports of refined products. “Russian exports are down by a third and the drop is equivalent to around 4% of the world's seaborne diesel and gasoil trade,” Wickenden said.
"That matters because diesel is one of the fuels whose premium has kept climbing while crude has unwound," he added.
What does it all mean for Russia?
While the global energy situation remains tumultuous, it is particularly stark in Russia. The prospects for the Russian economy look bleak, as the enormous cost of the war strains the state budget while businesses are increasingly harried by Ukrainian strikes and Western sanctions.
"In its desperation, [Russia] has started importing fuel, which is genuinely new: between 2023 and 2025 it bought almost nothing by sea, with no cargo arriving at all in 13 of those 36 months," Wickenden said.
"In August 2026, it imported 172,000 tons, three times what it bought in the whole of 2025, and gasoline went from 6% of its product imports to 74%," he added.
"The volumes are trivial for the world market, but a country that was the world's second-largest oil product exporter last year is now paying to have its own crude refined abroad and shipped back.”
Since the beginning of 2026, Russian gasoline prices have risen 21.16% to an average of 78.25 rubles ($0.93) per liter, while the cost of diesel has increased 18.4% to an average of 88.44 rubles ($1) per liter, according to official statistics reported by Interfax.
And Russian public sentiment appears increasingly gloomy as weekly state polls suggest drone strikes and fuel shortages are stoking anxiety as the war mars everyday life — adding to the Kremlin's concerns ahead of the first parliamentary elections since the 2022 invasion.

Yemen’s latest escalation pushes millions deeper into crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:54:26 UTC
23:54:26 KST

Share & more
Some 125,000 people have been forced from their homes across Yemen in the past two weeks as a major new escalation linked to both the US-Iran conflict and Yemen’s own nearly 12-year war deepens hardship for millions already struggling to survive.
Hafedhaa Murshed had spent more than five years in a displacement site in western Taiz province before clashes broke out on 3 September near the site where she, her husband, and their seven children were staying.
As the fighting drew nearer, the family grabbed their most valuable and lightest possessions. “We walked nearly three kilometres on foot,” Murshed told The New Humanitarian, speaking from the makeshift camp elsewhere in Taiz where they are now staying. “There were no vehicles to transport our belongings, so we arrived here with only a few kitchen utensils and a blanket.”
Taiz has long been a flashpoint of Yemen’s war. Fighting, sieges, and restrictions on aid and trade access have been hallmarks of life in the southwestern province for years. Houthi rebels and a coalition of fighters allied with the internationally recognised government have been fighting since early 2015, and Taiz lies between territory currently controlled by the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government.
A 2022 truce had ushered in a period of relative calm, but the Houthis (officially called Ansar Allah) launched an offensive on multiple fronts in early September, part of their bid to control the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait. Saudi Arabia has hit back with airstrikes and the United States has reportedly sent advisers to aid the kingdom’s military efforts, raising fears of a return to all-out war.
Controlling the strait allows the Houthis – who have ties to Iran – to further block Saudi Arabia from exporting oil via the Red Sea (the kingdom has been using the strait to export oil since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz). It is also part of the longstanding stated goal of the Houthis to take the Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed fighters.
While the reasons behind the new offensive are murky and complex, the impact on Yemen’s most vulnerable civilians – among them more than 5.2 million who were already displaced before this uptick in fighting – have been clear and direct.
Like many others, Murshed was already dealing with extreme poverty before her latest displacement. But she had been staying with another displaced relative, who at least shared their mattresses and blankets.
The UN reports that 125,000 people have been newly displaced in just two weeks and the numbers are rising quickly – including tens of thousands in Taiz alone. Entire communities are being forced from their homes, and some are now fleeing the country altogether, with the UN’s migration agency reporting that 2,000 people have reached Djibouti's northern shores.
With the response to Yemen’s humanitarian crisis already chronically underfunded, and now compounded by the economic impacts of the US-Iran war, people like Murshed are finding themselves trapped in an endless cycle of displacement, with little to no assistance.
“Our life wasn’t perfect, but at least we had a safe camp,” Murshed said of life at the previous site, which was already her family’s second displacement. “The fighting has forced us to flee again, and to begin the suffering of displacement and starting from scratch again.”
Fuel prices and day wages
Long before Murshed and her family were forced to leave their camp, Yemen’s economic crisis was already battering people like her far from the front lines.
“Even before we fled last week, we lacked many of the basics because work opportunities were scarcer than before. Men would leave in the morning looking for work and return by midday empty-handed,” Murshed explained.
The growing regional fallout from the Iran-US conflict triggered a sharp surge in fuel prices across government-controlled areas in Yemen. A 20-litre container of diesel has jumped from 25,000 YER ($17) in May – several months after the war began – to 45,000 YER ($30) today.
A source at the Yemeni Petroleum Company in Aden told Reuters in May that the rise in fuel prices – even back then – was the result of a supply crisis and rising global fuel prices driven by the regional conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
That surge has had a cascading effect since, driving up the cost of goods and services that are dependent on fuel and transportation – including construction materials – hitting day labourers first. The only jobs that many displaced men like Murshed’s husband can get now are day-by-day jobs on construction sites or loading and unloading building supplies at local shops.
“I don’t remember a time in my life when we ate only bread and tea for breakfast and dinner like we do now. We buy just enough food to stay alive because our income doesn't allow for more, and we can't afford the food we actually want.”
Murad Thabet, a construction worker in his 50s who has worked in the industry across various parts of Yemen, described the current crisis as “the worst in his life”.
“I have been working for around 40 years, but these days are the worst,” he told The New Humanitarian. “The price of building materials is rising dramatically, so many contractors and property owners have halted work until things stabilise.”
Thabet, who is displaced from his village in the southwest of the province and rents a home in Taiz city for his wife and three children, said many day labourers are struggling to provide their families with basic necessities.
“I don’t remember a time in my life when we ate only bread and tea for breakfast and dinner like we do now,” he added. “We buy just enough food to stay alive because our income doesn't allow for more, and we can't afford the food we actually want.”
Thabet stressed that his main problem is the lack of job opportunities rather than the cost of food itself. This has long been the case in Yemen, where economic collapse as a result of their own 12-year war has been a major driver of hunger.
US-funded food insecurity monitor FEWS NET has consistently said that displaced people and those without income are of greatest concern across a country where 15-16 million people are expected to need food aid through September – not taking into account this month’s developments.
“If we have an income, we can buy food even if prices rise a bit,” said Thabet. “But when we have no work, as is the case now, we cannot afford food even if it is cheap.”
Competition and sacrifice
Thabet said he is among many men who wait at the same spot in Taiz every morning looking for work. Most leave disappointed. “When someone arrives looking for one labourer, around 10 people run after him and accept any wage because they desperately need work,” he said.
Abdullah Mohammed, a displaced father of three in his late 30s, recently lost his job as a construction worker and guard at a building site in Taiz. Before the building’s owner suspended construction in May and dismissed all the workers, it was enough for Mohammed to rent a home and take care of his family.
“The building owner told us he would resume construction when things calm down and prices drop, but it seems he won’t anytime soon because things are getting worse and prices keep going up,” Mohammed told The New Humanitarian.
He has now taken his oldest child out of school, bringing the 12-year-old boy along with him to collect empty plastic bottles they can sell for a small amount of money. “Education isn’t our priority right now – having enough food is,” Mohammed said. “Once we have enough food on the table and I have a steady source of income, I will send my children back to school and provide them with everything they need, even the toys I used to buy them every month.”
An August Save the Children survey found that nearly one in five cases of school dropouts in Yemen were due to child labour, with kids sent to work to help their families survive.
Taiz is the only government-controlled province in Yemen that completely lacks public electricity; the main power station was destroyed at the start of the war and has never been fixed. People buy electricity from private commercial generators, but the sharp surge in fuel prices has driven up costs from 1,100 YER ($0.70) per kWh in February to 1,500 YER ($1.00).
Sami Mohammed, a 47-year-old father of four, works as a government employee, earning a monthly salary of around $100. That’s just enough to feed his family, but electricity is now out of reach.
“I connected my home to electricity about three years ago when it cost around 400 Yemeni riyals ($0.25) per kWh, but at current prices I would have to spend half my salary on electricity alone,” Mohammed told The New Humanitarian.
“This recent increase was caused by the regional conflict and its impact on fuel supplies. We hope things improve, but until then I have disconnected my home from the grid because I simply can’t afford it.”
Sami is among many residents who now rely on small car batteries running off solar panels to provide some light in his house – this method is also used by displaced people in camps. While the batteries can provide a bit of light, they aren’t strong enough to run household appliances like refrigerators.
The hardest-hit groups
Fawzi al-Habashi, director of the Better Life Association, a Taiz-based aid group, told The New Humanitarian that vulnerable groups — such as displaced families and the Muhammasheen — are desperately in need of more assistance.
The Muhammasheen, which means “the marginalised ones”, are a minority group in Yemen who some believe are descended from African slaves or soldiers. They have long been discriminated against, and most live in slums and extreme poverty.
“In the recent escalation, we saw many displaced families fleeing their homes for the second or third time. As they fled and arrived at existing displacement camps, it placed immense pressure on the host communities,” al-Habashi said, noting that there was often not enough water for new arrivals.
“All Yemenis have been impacted by the recent increase in fuel and food prices, but vulnerable communities – such as displaced people and those who lost their jobs – are the most affected because they lack a source of income to help them survive the crisis.”
Aid groups are doing what they can under severe budget constraints, but shrinking funds are severely hindering the response, he said, adding that it was important to keep in mind that humanitarian needs didn’t just start with the recent wave of displacement or the US-Iran war.
“All Yemenis have been impacted by the recent increase in fuel and food prices, but vulnerable communities – such as displaced people and those who lost their jobs – are the most affected because they lack a source of income to help them survive the crisis,” al-Habashi said.
He called on the international community to increase support for Yemen so that groups like his can help more people: “Displaced families and other vulnerable people are being hit twice, first by the economic crisis, and now by the recent escalation, so the international community must not forget them.”
Murshed, newly displaced in Taiz, also appealed to international organisations for help, but she spoke too of the solidarity she has seen among other Yemenis who are sharing what little they have with those most in need.
“We sleep under the same small, overcrowded tent with another family because we have no alternative. Water is scarce, and food depends on whether others have enough to share with us,” she said. “The displaced families in this camp understand our suffering and do not hesitate to help us… but they are in dire need too, so we are all sharing the burden.”

US could hit Putin's Arctic gas empire by sanctioning 14 LNG tankers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:47:27 UTC
23:47:27 KST

The House of Representatives could vote this week on a bill that would allow the U.S. to sanction vessels transporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), including 14 specialized tankers serving the Yamal LNG project, sanctions-monitoring NGO Urgewald told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 15.
The bill, which targets Russian energy, could put the vessels that transport LNG from Russia's Yamal Peninsula under U.S. sanctions review. The measure comes as Europe prepares to fully ban Russian LNG imports and continues to account for the vast majority of Yamal LNG cargoes.
The Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed the Senate 86-11 in August and was advanced by the House Rules Committee on Sept. 14. Further consideration in the House is scheduled for this week.
The legislation would not automatically sanction all 14 Arc7 tankers serving Yamal LNG. Instead, it would require U.S. President Donald Trump to review vessels covered by the bill and determine which meet the criteria for designation.
Under the Senate-approved version, Trump would have 30 days after the bill's enactment to review the vessels and designate qualifying ships as blocked property.
The legislation would also allow sanctions against foreign port owners or operators that knowingly provide services to Russia's sanctioned vessels.
"Sanctions offer Washington a way to support Western security in the High North without putting American troops in harm's way," Alexander Kirk, a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald, said.
Yamal LNG is one of Russia's largest LNG projects and accounts for more than 60% of the country's LNG exports. Despite partial restrictions on Russian LNG, European countries remain the main destinations for the cargo.
European ports received 136 of the 140 Yamal LNG cargoes shipped in the first half of 2026, worth an estimated 5.96 billion euros ($6.82 billion), according to previous Urgewald analysis.
The EU is due to impose a full ban on Russian LNG imports in January 2027. Until then, European demand continues to provide an important market for Russia's Arctic LNG exports.
The 14 Arc7 tankers are specially designed to navigate the harsh winter conditions around Russia's Yamal Peninsula. Disrupting even part of their trade routes could have substantial consequences for Russia's ability to export LNG and generate revenue from the industry.

What will Luke Lindberg mean for WFP and humanitarians?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:45:31 UTC
23:45:31 KST

Share & more
The Trump administration dismantled aid and attacked the global system as wasteful. Now a Trump pick looks set to lead one of the world’s biggest humanitarian agencies.
US agriculture official Luke Lindberg will be named the new head of the World Food Programme, two aid officials familiar with the selection process told The New Humanitarian.
Officially, the UN secretary-general and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s director-general choose the WFP leader, in consultation with WFP’s executive board. A special session of WFP’s board is scheduled for 18 September.
A letter shared within humanitarian circles also confirms Lindberg as the pick. News of Lindberg’s pending appointment was first reported by Devex over the weekend.
Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader?
It follows months-long delays in choosing a new executive director at WFP – and for some, worry over what putting a Trump-aligned pick at the heart of the emergency aid system will mean.
WFP has been without an official executive director since Cindy McCain announced her departure earlier this year, citing health concerns.
Lindberg’s selection would continue a long history of opaque UN appointments and American dominance at the helm of WFP. The executive director role has been held by an American since 1992, under the UN’s practice of backroom horse-trading key roles.
It’s also another example of top leadership jobs going to the politically connected, whether at UN agencies or big NGOs. Lindberg is the son-in-law of US Senate majority leader John Thune, and currently undersecretary for trade and foreign agricultural affairs in the US Department of Agriculture.
Lindberg appears to have no experience in emergency response, but he will join a UN agency that is often seen as the lynchpin of the international humanitarian system.
His public record so far contrasts sharply with the neutrality and impartiality principles that the humanitarian sector often foregrounds. Lindberg has voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (who has an active arrest warrant for war crimes accusations), and touted weapons exports amid the Israeli military’s onslaught on Gaza.
Critics say the US is increasingly co-opting the humanitarian system along ideological lines – using funding and policy to align aid with geopolitical interests, and to sideline reproductive health and equity, for example.
Lindberg will lead a key agency at a time of deep budget cuts, severe hunger, and spiralling emergencies – in some cases in crises provoked by US military actions and US government policies. Some 151.6 million people face crisis levels of hunger or worse, according to famine analysts.
Crises are spiralling, deepened by conflict, climate change, and the flouting of international laws. At the same time, donor funding cuts have left the global emergency response system at a breaking point, triaging budgets to target only a fraction of the more than 239 million people said to need emergency aid. WFP’s projected funding this year sits at around $6.4 billion – less than half of what it was in 2022, and its lowest in about a decade. The US funds about 30% of the agency’s budget.
Here are four key questions:
Who does Lindberg answer to?
Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader?
The Trump administration has used foreign aid funding as a hammer: It steers its humanitarian and health money to align with geopolitical interests instead of needs; and sharpened its discriminatory global gag rule to sideline reproductive health and equity programmes funded by other donors.
This has put an extra spotlight on the delayed search for a new WFP chief. Will they be beholden to Washington, or to the organisation’s humanitarian mandate?
“We never really had to ask this question before for a UN appointee quite so explicitly,” said Sam Vigersky, a former US humanitarian adviser and now a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a New York-based think tank. “That to me in itself is a concerning development in our field.”
Before the Trump administration backed Lindberg for the UN role, other rumoured candidates had pushed to make US support to WFP conditional on aligning with foreign policy interests, Vigersky said. Lindberg hasn’t outlined such plans, and should be judged based on what he does when he starts at WFP, he said.
“Is Lindberg able to unlock sums of money from the Congress and the Trump administration that otherwise would be sidelined because there wasn’t an insider at the helm… or does this end up being an appointment to a multilateral agency that ends up running a political operation for the Trump administration to potentially be punitive towards NGOs they think are critical of the administration,” Vigersky said.
“A lot of the aid coming out of [the] State Department has directly framed how they are making decisions. So I’m going to be looking for the firewall between the two.”
Many of the issues at the heart of WFP’s work may contradict the current US administration’s interests – from climate change as a cause of crises, to famine declarations that are politically inconvenient for allies like Israel, to pushing back on aid cuts.
Still a US government official for now, Lindberg’s recent public comments have defended the cuts as a sort of “level-setting”.
”This idea that we’re retreating is an unfair characterisation of the pause that was taken to re-evaluate and re-design some of the structures and the way in which we do business,” Lindberg said during a CFR briefing this month. A study in The Lancet estimated that donor cuts could lead to 9.4 million deaths by 2030.
In his short time in the agriculture department, Lindberg has been open about using US aid for US interests.
The USDA-managed Food for Peace programme, which sends US commodities as food assistance, now targets only a handful of countries, after a restructuring overseen by Lindberg. It notably leaves out several countries facing severe levels of hunger – such as Mali, Somalia, Sudan, or Yemen – while including some that are not. These choices balanced hunger needs, the availability of distribution partners, and “the geopolitical interests of the United States”, Lindberg said.
How do other humanitarian agencies see Lindberg?
Lindberg is mostly unknown in humanitarian circles, but his social media feed has done most of the talking so far.
His personal accounts have been peppered with pro-Israel posts, pics of Lindberg grinning and gripping a rifle to be exported to the Israeli military, and plenty of cowboy hats.
A newer Twitter account created for his WFP bid presents a milder image, tinted with shades of UN blue, frequent retweets of WFP posts, and inoffensive statements about resilience and ending hunger.
Lindberg is “obviously MAGA” and the gun pics are concerning, but he appears to be less risky than other names floated for key positions, one aid official told The New Humanitarian.
“Basically, I think he’s someone we can work with,” said the official, who compared Lindberg’s potential to that of David Beasley, the former South Carolina governor appointed as WFP executive director during Trump’s first term. Beasley’s reputation is that of a prolific fundraiser; his time as WFP head overlapped with a years-long surge in donor government support for the humanitarian system as a whole.
How do staff see Lindberg, and how will people in crisis now see WFP?
But Lindberg’s politics are a deep concern for many, and an agency’s leader reflects on the entire organisation.
WFP’s staff of 20,000 stretches across the globe, from Central America to the Pacific Islands, or from Afghanistan to Sudan and Gaza. Like many humanitarian organisations, most are local staff, often from the communities they’re trying to help.
Some staff have expressed outrage about leadership positions on Gaza, or WFP’s choice of partners like Boston Consulting Group or Palantir. In conversations with The New Humanitarian, they have also expressed unease about US influence on the organisation, and about Lindberg.
Then there’s whether a WFP led by Lindberg changes how communities in crisis see a humanitarian organisation that often says it relies on its perceived neutrality to operate.
The agency’s likely new leader is an enthusiastic supporter of Netanyahu, whose government and military has inflicted harm in crises where WFP is asked to alleviate hunger.
“We are exporting freedom and prosperity to our friends,” Lindberg wrote in a social media post while clutching a South Dakota-made sniper rifle – one of several pics that have been widely shared among WFP staff and other humanitarians. At the time, Lindberg was a trade official for the US state.
The world’s leading genocide scholars say Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity against Palestinians.
Where does Lindberg push WFP on data, tech, and partnerships?
WFP faces growing criticism for its relationship with Palantir, the data analytics firm and military contractor.
Its private sector partnerships, and its ambitions around harnessing sensitive data of deeply vulnerable populations, are especially under the microscope as Big Tech and artificial intelligence corporations grow to dominate economies, culture, and power – and as WFP forms the backbone of international humanitarian logistics.
WFP’s envelope-pushing experimentation and data strategy have been encouraged by multiple leadership teams, and by several different donors.
Lindberg’s recent comments suggest the agency will continue full speed ahead on the same path.
“In a resource-constrained environment, you have to do more with less,” Lindberg said during the CFR briefing, mirroring existing WFP leadership talking points on tech partnerships and AI.
“I think there’s all kinds of tools out there in the world today that can make even the best organisations a little bit better,” he added.
The USDA signed a $300 million deal with Palantir earlier this year.
Edited by Andrew Gully.

This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:43:23 UTC
23:43:23 KST

This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
Burned grasses preserved in an Australian cave reveal ritual traditions that may stretch back an astonishing 25,000 years.
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Microscopic plant remains are revealing how GunaiKurnai ancestors used Cloggs Cave for ritual practices over thousands of years. People deliberately gathered whole grasses, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers, leaving behind traces that may span 25,000 years. A standing stone erected around 2,000 years ago and other ritual objects strengthen the evidence that the cave was a long-lived spiritual site.
- Share:
The GunaiKurnai, an Australian Aboriginal nation, are recognized as the traditional custodians of Gippsland and the southern Victorian Alps. Caves within their lands have long been linked to spiritual practices. Accounts recorded in the 19th century, together with oral traditions, describe them as places where powerful learned women and men known as 'mulla-mullung', along with other spiritual practitioners, carried out rituals involving magic, healing, and cursing.
Archaeological evidence now shows that one of these sites, Cloggs Cave, was used for such activities over an extraordinary span of roughly 25,000 years.
"Here we show that the Old Ancestors selected whole grasses from the wider landscape and carried them into Cloggs Cave to spread out in thin layers and burn. Over time, sediments covered these burnt layers, preserving each layer on top of another over thousands of years," said Dr Elle Grono, a postdoctoral researcher at the Australian National University and the corresponding author of a new study published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.
Microscopic Clues From Ancient Plants
Grono and researchers from Australia, France, and New Zealand examined phytoliths recovered from buried sediments inside Cloggs Cave. Phytoliths are microscopic silica structures that form within plant tissues and can survive long after the plants themselves have disappeared.
The research grew out of archaeological excavations carried out in 2019 and 2020. Those excavations were designed to determine how people collected and used plants inside the cave in the distant past. The work was requested by the GunaiKurnai Land and Waters Corporation, and GunaiKurnai representatives were involved in the research design, fieldwork, interpretation, and communication of the findings.
"Unlike pollen, which is dispersed by wind or insects, phytoliths mostly accumulate at the spot where a plant decays. No plants grow inside the cave due to a lack of light, so the phytoliths must have been carried in by people or by animals such as possums on their fur or through their scats," explained Grono. "We focused on half-burnt phytoliths from ashy layers, which can only have been brought in by people, as unburnt ones might have arrived through either means."
Because vegetation cannot grow naturally inside the dark cave, the burned plant remains offered especially strong evidence that people had intentionally carried grasses into the site.
Layers of Ash and a Standing Stone
Using microscopy, the researchers classified thousands of phytoliths collected from two excavation pits measuring 1.5 m and 2.3 m deep.
The upper sections of those pits contained 73 thin layers of ash deposited by people between approximately 4,400 and 1,600 years ago. Researchers established those ages using optically stimulated luminescence and carbon dating via accelerator mass spectrometry.
Hidden among the layers was another striking discovery: a standing stone measuring 28 cm high. Later analysis showed that Old Ancestors had intentionally placed the stone inside the cave for ritual purposes around 2,000 years ago.
Grasses Were Carefully Chosen
The team identified 29 different kinds of phytoliths representing grasses, herbs, and woody plants. Many were exceptionally well preserved, including delicate silica structures such as hair cells.
Grass phytoliths dominated the samples, accounting for as much as 97% of the total. They included members of the Pooideae subfamily, which favor temperate or cool conditions, as well as Panicoideae grasses, which generally thrive in warmer and more humid environments.
Phytoliths from Chloridoideae grasses, which tolerate drought and are adapted to warm, dry arid conditions, appeared less frequently. Remains from herbs and woody plants were also uncommon.
The pattern suggests that Old Ancestors did not simply gather whatever vegetation was nearby. Instead, they deliberately selected particular grasses.
Before European settlement, the landscape around Cloggs Cave included riparian forest and open woodland containing many different plant species. Yet those plants were largely absent from the archaeological deposits. The people using the cave instead chose grasses growing relatively close to its entrance.
"The phytoliths found at Cloggs Cave were from different parts of grass plants such as stems, leaves, flowers and roots, indicating that whole grasses were brought in, including the inedible parts," said Grono.
Evidence of Ritual Burning Across Millennia
As much as 18% of the phytoliths showed signs of burning or melting. Those altered plant remains occurred throughout the dated deposits, suggesting that people repeatedly carried vegetation into the cave and burned it there across the span of the past 25,000 years.
The finding fits with other archaeological evidence indicating that Cloggs Cave was a place of long-lasting ritual activity rather than an ordinary living site.
Professor Bruno David from Monash University, who co-led the excavations with GunaiKurnai Land and Waters Corporation, concludes that "their burning is consistent with GunaiKurnai traditional practices of using ash to perform magic and rituals, and also to track the footsteps of anyone coming in, including spirit-Beings. Other macro-botanical evidence, such as fat-smeared, trimmed wooden sticks from Casuarina trees, was also found in deeper and older deposits, indicating that other kinds of rituals using woody plants were also performed."
