Philosophy for an Ending World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

Samuel Scheffler’s well-known Death and Afterlife (2013) invites us to consider whether, knowing that human extinction is immanent due to wide-spread infertility, we can continue to find many of the projects and activities that animate our lives to still be meaningful. His answer is that we cannot: too many of our projects and activities make sense to us as worth pursuing because they aim at things that matter. But much of what we take to matter tacitly assumes that humanity will continue into the indefinite future. Scheffler’s conjecture is that knowledge of humanity’s immanent extinction would undermine our confidence that there are things that matter and we would collectively lapse into a state of anomie and despair.
The insight that animates Tim Mulgan’s exciting and carefully argued new book, Philosophy for an Ending World, is that a small change to Scheffler’s thought experiment brings into view a new series of challenging questions that reward philosophical exploration. What he proposes is that we consider the implications of knowing that, due to a cataclysmic event many light years from earth, human extinction (and the extinction of all life on earth) is certain but not immanent. Humanity can count on another two centuries before its story comes to an end. Despair and anomie might still be apt responses to the reality of this post-cataclysm world. But there are other plausible ways of responding to it that are live possibilities because there is time to adapt to the loss of future-dependent meaning.
Mulgan introduces the range of plausible ways of thinking about the significance of the cataclysm through a debate between the various positions. In these early chapters we meet, amongst others, the character of the Perennial Pessimist, who holds that life has always been meaningless and is inclined to embrace anti-natalism; the Presentist, who accepts that the cataclysm robs humanity of some ways of living that can give life meaning, but believes that there remain a sufficient number of goods available to be pursued in life that do not presuppose humanity’s continuing into the indefinite future to make life meaningful; the Post-Cataclysmic Pessimist, who holds that knowing that extinction is on the horizon, even if it is still a way off, undermines the possibility of leading a meaningful life, given our current conceptual repertoire for how one might lead a meaningful life; and finally, the multigenerationalist.
The core of the book is an extended argument for multigenerationalism. The view agrees with the Post-Cataclysmic Pessimist in holding, against the Presentist, that meaningful lives are not possible if the kinds of goals, projects, and activities that constitute leading a meaningful life are completely severed from any connection to future people. Not all goals and projects are, of course, multi-generational in character in the way that, say, curing cancer is a multi-generational project. But even present-focused activities get their point from intergenerational traditions in which they are embedded. Multigenerationalism insists, however, that we need not wallow is pessimism because the possibility of meaningful lives need not come to an end because we know extinction is on the horizon. For though leading meaningful lives requires intergenerational sources of meaning, it is both possible and feasible to reorient these sources in a way that frees them from the assumption that humanity will continue indefinitely. That is, meaningful lives are possible post-cataclysm if we develop intergenerational, time-limited projects of the kind that living meaningful lives requires.
Crucially, these new intergenerational projects must be able to sustain meaningful lives for even the last generation of humans. The multigenerationalist claim is that living meaningful lives requires participating, either directly or indirectly, in intergenerational projects and traditions. For this reason, one might think that, in fact, procreation is not permissible after the cataclysm. If procreation is allowed to continue, there will be a last generation that do not have the possibility of leading meaningful lives. Arguably, producing that generation is impermissible. But once this is granted, we quickly reach the conclusion that procreation is impermissible after the cataclysm, on pain of participating in an intergenerational Ponzi scheme. But if procreation is impermissible after the cataclysm, it follows that it also marks the end of people being able to lead meaningful lives.
Three of the book’s central chapters, on procreative ethics, argue that both consequentialist and non-consequentialist approaches to theorizing permissible procreation concur that we need not accept this conclusion. Procreation is permissible if multi-generational projects that support intergenerational meaning are feasible. To respect the constraints that Mulgan uncovers through his nuanced discussion of procreative ethics, suitable projects must involve intergenerational co-operation, allow future people the hope of a flourishing life that are hopefully better, and at the very least, not worse than that enjoyed by past generations, and allow the last generation to find meaning in the fact that they are contributing to a co-operative project of bringing the history of humanity to a fitting end.
A consequence of the constraints on permissible post-cataclysm procreation is the need for moral progress and transformation. The values and moral outlook we now have are poorly suited to enable humanity to cope with extinction because they presuppose humanity continuing into the indefinite future. Simply bequeathing them to the next generations is not, therefore, compatible with the constraint that we do our best to ensure their lives are at least as good, if not better, than the ones past generations have enjoyed. If the history of humanity is to be continued for the next two centuries before it comes to an end, different values will need to be taken up, values that are better adapted to navigating the changed circumstances of knowing that humanity will come to an end in the next two centuries. We cannot know what these values will look like from our current vantage point.
Uncovering these new or adapted values is an exercise in intergenerational moral creativity and imaginativeness. That a successful reimagining or moral transformation of this kind is in fact possible is illustrated, as Mulgan sees it, by the example of the Crow Indian Chief Plenty Coups, as portrayed by Jonathan Lear in his Radical Hope (2006). As Lear describes him, Plenty Coups was confronted with the task of leading the Crow through a period of cultural devastation in which the way of life presupposed by their values disappeared. Exercising a kind of imaginative courage, Plenty Coups drew on Crow teachings and traditions to transform Crow morality, reimagining what, for example, a good Crow life that exemplified the virtue of courage could be like under a radically changed circumstances in which the Crow no longer engaged in war. The permissible continuation of humanity after the cataclysm requires an intergenerational commitment to a similar imaginative moral transformation. Given the scale of what is involved, it cannot be successfully realized within a single generation.
What I have covered here are just some of the main ideas of Philosophy for an Ending World. There is a lot more in it. I have, for example, skipped over the very interesting discussions of religion, of whether the best way to ensure the flourishing of the last generations is for them to upload their consciousness into a virtual world, and of the kind of utopia towards whose realization by the last generation some multigenerational projects might aim. That Mulgan covers so much ground is both a strength and weakness of the book. It is a strength in that it exhibits the fecundity of the slowly ending world thought experiment.
But it is also a weakness, in two respects. First, because it covers so much ground and at times engages with recent work on, for, example, procreative ethics in great detail, it is likely to be off-putting for non-academic readers. Given the importance of its subject, that is to be regretted. As Mulgan points out at the end of the book, even if one doubts that humanity is on the precipice of extinction, it is easy to believe that the possible futures for our descendants will be radically different than anything humanity has experienced and that is all one need accept to find the questions Mulgan pursues in this book to be important. A much shorter version of it that just presented a broad overview of these questions and the complexity involved in thinking through them would certainly find a wider audience.
Second, the scope of coverage comes at the cost of certain key premises of the book’s overall argument being insufficiently defended. For example, the case for the importance of intergenerational meaning seemed to me to call for a more extended defense than it receives. Some of what I take to be meaningful in life, such as the exploration of philosophical ideas, is in part meaningful because I am participating in a venerable tradition that will continue after I am gone. But I don’t see why I should find it less meaningful if I knew the tradition would soon come to an end. Why isn’t it enough for me to feel that I am participating in a meaningful activity whose meaning transcends me that there are at least still some others who value philosophical inquiry as I do?
I would have also welcomed some discussion of the idea of ‘bringing the story of humanity to a fitting end.’ The idea that the cataclysm makes salient humanity and its history as something that enters our consciousness as an object of evaluative concern has a great deal of intuitive plausibility. But what it is that is of concern is ill-defined, in a way that invites skepticism that the appearance of plausibility can survive scrutiny. Some discussion of whether humanity and its history is in fact a defensible object of concern would have been welcome and is something hopefully we will hear more about from Mulgan and others working in this area.
REFERENCES
Lear, Jonathan (2006). Radical hope: ethics in the face of cultural devastation. Cambridge: Harvard University Press.
Scheffler, Samuel (2013). Death and the Afterlife. Edited by Niko Kolodny. New York, NY: Oxford University Press.

Ukraine has 'successfully tested' new interceptor against Russian jet-powered drones, Zelensky says
Ukraine has "successfully" trialed another interceptor drone designed to target Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskysaid Sept. 15 following a briefing by Ukrainian Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
As Russia expands its arsenal of Shahed-type jet-powered drones, including the Geran-3, Geran-4 and Geran-5, and the cruise missile-like Banderol loitering munition, Ukraine is facing mounting difficulties intercepting the weapons during prolonged attacks, with Kyiv and the surrounding region frequently targeted.
"A 'shahed' was hit successfully, but some aspects of controlling the interceptor still need to be refined. The work continues – it will take some more time," Zelensky wrote on X.
The jet-powered drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (nearly 370 miles per hour), making them more difficult to intercept than earlier, piston-powered Shahed variants. Their use also increased sharply this summer, rising roughly fivefold in July compared with June, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Aug. 31.
Russia launched nearly 800 jet-powered drones toward Ukraine over four days in late August, according to Zelensky.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Aug. 29 that Ukraine had field-tested four potential interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, without specifying which companies were developing them or how far along the projects were.
Anatolii Hrapchynskyi, deputy director of an electronic warfare company and a reserve Air Force officer, told the Kyiv Independent that the use of jet-powered drones was to be expected as Russian forces had been seeking ways to overwhelm Ukraine's anti-aircraft defenses.
Hrapchynskyi said that at the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russian troops had only expensive long-range weapons at their disposal, which could be launched from strategic aircraft, submarines, or the coast.
Russia most recently used jet-powered drones in a Sept. 15 attack on Kyiv that killed at least one person and injured 12 others. The daytime strikes damaged residential buildings, a data center, and two gas stations in the capital.

Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:28:38 UTC
23:28:38 KST

Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
Aging appears to trigger a major biological transformation in the human brain beginning around midlife.
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- New York Genome Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered sweeping changes in how the human brain controls and organizes its genome beginning in midlife, offering new clues to why aging sharply increases the risk of Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases. One of the biggest shifts occurred between about ages 50 and 75, when many of the brain’s original immune cells declined and were replaced by cells with more inflammatory characteristics. Researchers also found weakening of cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier, along with widespread deterioration in the genome’s three-dimensional organization.
- Share:
Researchers have found that the human brain begins undergoing broad changes in the way its genome is regulated starting in midlife. The findings may help explain why age is the strongest risk factor for neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
In a new study published in Science, scientists used advanced single-cell methods to examine gene regulation and three-dimensional genome organization in individual cells from the human hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. By analyzing samples from adults across a wide range of ages, the team created one of the most detailed pictures yet of how genome regulation shifts as the brain grows older.
Brain Immune Cells Undergo a Major Midlife Shift
One of the most notable changes appeared in microglia, the immune cells that help maintain and protect the brain. Between approximately ages 50 and 75, the researchers found a sharp decline in microglia that originate during embryonic development. At the same time, those cells were increasingly replaced by cells whose molecular features resembled immune cells found in the blood.
That result challenges a long-standing assumption that microglia established early in development remain in the brain for a person's entire life. The replacement microglia-like cells also showed stronger inflammatory signatures, raising the possibility that they could contribute to chronic inflammation in the aging brain.
The researchers also detected a substantial decline in cell populations that help maintain the blood-brain barrier. This protective barrier helps shield the brain from potentially harmful substances circulating in the bloodstream.
"Microglia are critical for maintaining brain homeostasis," said Bing Ren, PhD, a corresponding author of the study, Scientific Director and CEO of the New York Genome Center, Professor of Genetics and Development, Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics, and Systems Biology at Columbia University, and Associate Director in the Vagelos Institute for Basic Biomedical Science (Vagelos Institute) in VP&S, Columbia University, "When these cells fail to perform their housekeeping duties, toxic materials accumulate that can trigger inflammatory processes that may contribute to neurodegenerative diseases."
The Genome's 3D Structure Also Deteriorates With Age
The changes were not limited to immune cells. Across several types of brain cells, the researchers observed a broad erosion of three-dimensional genome architecture.
Inside a cell, DNA is not simply packed randomly into the nucleus. It is folded into a highly organized three-dimensional structure that helps control which genes are switched on or off. The researchers found that this organization became less orderly with age, suggesting that deterioration in genome structure could be a fundamental feature of brain aging.
"This work represents a major step forward in understanding how aging reshapes the human genome in brain cells," said Nathan Zemke, Director of Single-cell Genomics at the Center for Epigenomics at UC San Diego. "These findings demonstrate a critical need for studying gene regulation and genome organization to gain a mechanistic understanding of the aging process."
Aging May Involve Coordinated Remodeling
The findings suggest that brain aging is more complicated than a simple, steady decline. Instead, multiple systems appear to change together, including immune cells, blood vessels, neurons, and genome organization.
"Importantly, this study reveals that aging is not simply a gradual decline, but involves coordinated and dynamic remodeling of immune, vascular, and neuronal systems. These findings open the door to identifying new therapeutic targets aimed at preserving circuit integrity and brain function across the lifespan," said Xiangmin Xu, PhD, Chancellor's Professor and Director of the Center for Neural Circuit Mapping at the University of California, Irvine, and a co-corresponding author of the study.
Part of a Decade-Long Genome Mapping Effort
The research is one of six papers published in Science through the National Institutes of Health's 4D Nucleome (4DN) Common Fund program. The decade-long initiative was created to map how the genome is organized in space and how that organization changes over time.
From 2015 to 2025, the 4D Nucleome program brought together interdisciplinary research teams from across the United States to investigate how the genome's spatial arrangement influences biological processes. In addition to this study, Dr. Ren contributed as a co-corresponding author or co-author on three other Science papers examining genome architecture across different cell types and timescales.
Together, the studies create a major new resource for researchers and provide fresh opportunities to investigate how changes in genome organization contribute to development, aging, and disease, including neurodegenerative disorders.
Story Source:
Materials provided by New York Genome Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nathan R. Zemke, Seoyeon Lee, Sainath Mamde, Bing Yang, Nicole Berchtold, B. Maximiliano Garduño, Hannah S. Indralingam, Weronika M. Bartosik, Pik Ki Lau, Keyi Dong, Emily Hsu, Amanda Yang, Yasmine Tani, Chumo Chen, Qiurui Zeng, Varun Ajith, Liqi Tong, Chanrung Seng, Daofeng Li, Ting Wang, Jingtian Zhou, Joseph R. Ecker, Christopher K. Glass, Carl W. Cotman, Xiangmin Xu, Bing Ren. Epigenetic and 3D genome reprogramming during the aging of the human hippocampus. SNP accused of hostility towards Scotland’s defence sector
United Kingdom

23:26:34 KST

The Scottish Conservatives have accused the SNP government of being hostile to the defence industry and of undermining it through what they call grievance politics, responding to a Scottish Affairs Committee report warning that Scotland risks missing out on increased defence spending unless skills shortages are addressed.
Rachael Hamilton, deputy leader of the Scottish Conservatives and the party’s business spokesperson, said: “This stark report must be a wake-up call for John Swinney and the SNP government.
“Their grievance politics and narrow-mindedness have undermined Scotland’s defence sector, which is vital for jobs and Scotland’s economy, for far too long.”
She said: “In an increasingly uncertain world, the nationalists should be doing all they can to support investment and jobs in the industry, but instead they have been hostile to it.”
On the skills findings at the centre of the report, she said: “Their atrocious failures in education and funding apprenticeship places are directly behind this alarming skills shortage in Scotland’s workforce.”
She added: “Both of Scotland’s governments must urgently work together to boost defence spending, back the thousands of jobs the sector supports and prioritise protecting our national security.”
The report itself finds that demand for apprenticeships and technical training is high while provision is not keeping pace with future workforce needs, which the committee warns puts at risk both Scotland’s ability to deliver the United Kingdom’s defence strategy and its capacity to realise the benefits of rising investment.
Patricia Ferguson, chair of the committee, said: “Scotland has a world-leading defence sector and is well-placed to benefit from increased UK defence spending. However, unless long-standing skills shortages are addressed, this opportunity could be missed.”
Two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges are proposed for Scotland, and according to the committee the UK Government has said that without matched funding from the Scottish Government only one will proceed. The committee finds that progress on establishing the colleges in Scotland has fallen behind equivalent work in England, and that intergovernmental cooperation should not be a cause of delay.
Defence apprenticeships in Scotland run mainly through the Modern Apprenticeship and Graduate Apprenticeship systems, with Modern Apprenticeships administered by Skills Development Scotland and the programme supporting around 39,000 apprenticeships each year with £90 million of funding. The Scottish Government announced a review of publicly funded contribution rates in March 2026, intended to align them better with future economic needs.
The committee says it hopes to see the Scottish Government play its part in ensuring Scotland has the skills needed to meet demand in the sector, and that the two governments must work together with greater urgency to expand skills provision and improve long-term workforce planning.
On perceptions of the industry, the report records that some witnesses expressed a view that Scottish Government policies have contributed to detrimental perceptions of the sector, which the committee describes as one of the most persistent barriers to recruitment. The committee also concludes that the Defence Industrial Strategy called for a public conversation on the importance of defence but that sufficient progress has not been made, asking the government to set out how it plans to deliver that conversation in Scotland.
The report records that 6.78 per cent of Ministry of Defence spending with industry went to Scotland in 2024/25, worth £2,165 million, against £2,553 million and 10.19 per cent five years earlier.

agricultural waste forms complete building system in new york house by LTL architects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:15:42 UTC
23:15:42 KST

one straw system does it all in ltl architects’ residence
LTL Architects completes the All Straw House in New York, a prototype residence developed with Guy Nordenson and Associates and Princeton University that turns highly compacted straw boards into a structural building system. Prefabricated over two months at Princeton’s Architecture Lab, the house is assembled from 16 large straw units whose material properties determine the geometry of the walls and roof. At approximately 370 kilograms per cubic meter, the compressed straw reaches more than three times the density of conventional straw bales and performs simultaneously as structure, insulation, and interior finish.
Straw is a rapidly growing byproduct of grain agriculture and stores carbon as it grows, giving the material a different relationship to construction than mineral- or fossil-based assemblies. Here, however, the density of the material, its ability to be compressed and stacked, and its limits in forming the building all become design parameters. The research is developed through a learning-by-doing process involving a dedicated group of Princeton student researchers.
The construction of the house, designed by the team at LTL Architects, begins with the cutting, stacking, and compression of straw boards into large prefabricated elements. Inside, 111 layers of straw remain exposed as a smooth interior surface, while wood ring beams are introduced every 22 layers to provide lateral stability. The result avoids the sequence in which insulation disappears behind layers of drywall or other interior finishes. Instead, the material that performs the building’s thermal and structural work also becomes its visible interior surface.
The exterior follows the same logic. Thirty-three prefabricated thatch panels form a rainscreen, each overlapping the panel below by 21 inches. The panels are smoothed together into a continuous coat, while the elongated windowsills extend over the tapered thatch beneath them. Between six and eight inches thick, the thatch contains tens of thousands of linear reeds, producing a textured field across the exterior.
The combination of compressed straw and thatch makes the building read like a single material system. The walls and roof merge into one continuous assembly, with the structural straw continuing upward and the thatch responding to the requirements of drainage.
the All Straw House is wrapped in a continuous thatched rainscreen
material constraints determine form
The geometry of the All Straw House occurs from those material constraints, as the straw panels can only be corbeled to a certain degree, while the thatched roof requires a sufficient slope to shed water. Instead of concealing these limitations, LTL Architects uses them to establish the form of the building.
At the interior, the exposed straw makes this construction logic particularly legible. The repeating layers register the process of fabrication, while the timber ring beams mark the structural organization of the wall. Around the walnut sink, tadelakt plaster is applied directly to the straw to create a waterproof backsplash, extending the experiment into the smaller details of the domestic interior.
The All Straw House operates as a research project scaled to the size of a dwelling. Its significance lies less in the novelty of building with straw alone, a material with a long history in construction, than in the attempt to develop a contemporary tectonic system around its properties. Prefabrication allows the compressed panels to be assembled efficiently, while the exposed material reduces the number of separate layers normally required to complete a wall.
111 layers of compressed straw remain exposed inside the house
the interior brings together exposed straw panels, timber framing, and a compact living space
a walnut counter and tadelakt backsplash add contrasting materials
the thatched rainscreen meets a timber-framed window
the steeply tapered form follows the structural limits of the compressed straw panels

Poland Scrambles Jets as Russia Attacks Western Ukraine With Jet-Powered Drones
Poland scrambled fighter jets overnight on September 15 in response to renewed Russian attacks on western Ukraine involving jet-powered strike drones, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command reported.
At around 4 a.m., the Operational Command said Polish and allied aircraft had been deployed as Russian jet-powered drones carried out strikes against targets in Ukraine. Ground-based air defense and radar systems were also placed on heightened readiness.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The measures were taken as a precaution to protect Polish airspace and “aimed at securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions.”
At around 6:30 a.m., the Operational Command announced that the potential threat had passed and that the forces and systems activated during the alert were returning to standard operational status.

Earlier the same night, NATO aircraft intercepted and destroyed an unidentified drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, with preliminary information indicating that it had arrived from Belarus, according to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT.
The drone crossed into Lithuania shortly after midnight, triggering air alerts in several areas. About 30 minutes later, NATO fighter jets operating from the Šiauliai Air Base intercepted and shot down the aircraft over the Kaunas region.
Lithuania’s military said Italian fighter jets carried out the interception. The drone’s wreckage was subsequently found in a rural area, where police cordoned off and secured the site.
The incidents follow another recent airspace breach involving a NATO member. On September 8, Romania deployed two F-18 fighter jets after military radar detected an aerial object entering Romanian airspace at around 4:47 p.m., roughly 18 kilometers north of Roman.
The detection prompted air raid warnings in several nearby communities. Shortly beforehand, at approximately 4:20 p.m., neighboring Moldova reported that a drone, preliminarily identified as a Shahed, had entered its territory.

Ukraine Exposes 54 Russian Firms Behind Iskander and Zircon Missiles
Ukraine’s military intelligence has disclosed information on 54 Russian companies linked to the production of electronic warfare systems, military aircraft electronics, drones, and components for Iskander-M and Zircon missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) on September 15, the companies are part of or managed by Concern Radio-Electronic Technologies (KRET), a subsidiary of Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec. The information was published through HUR’s War&Sanctions database.
KRET companies primarily develop and manufacture electronic warfare equipment, identification friend-or-foe systems, and onboard electronics used by Russian fighter jets and helicopters, HUR said.
Their production also includes electric motors, navigation and control systems for drones, counter-drone equipment, and remotely operated machine-gun platforms.
HUR identified several KRET companies as participants in Russia’s missile supply chain. The Stavropol-based Signal plant manufactures and supplies S200A1 compact jamming stations for 9M723 ballistic missiles used by the Iskander-M system.
The Kaluga Scientific Research Radio Engineering Institute, another company within the KRET network, supplies components for the 3B228 electronic protection system installed on Russia’s 3M22 Zircon missiles, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
HUR also said KRET’s central organization provides financing to cover shortfalls in Russian state defense contracts carried out by companies within the concern.
Of the 54 companies disclosed by Ukrainian intelligence, 19 are currently not sanctioned by any country participating in the international sanctions coalition.
Among them is Inertial Technologies of Technocomplex, which HUR identified as a manufacturer of strapdown inertial navigation systems for Kh-59M2 and Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles and Orion unmanned aircraft systems.
The Tambov Elektropribor plant, also not covered by coalition sanctions, supplies gyroscopes for 9M727 cruise missiles used by the Iskander system. The Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association produces aircraft automation equipment, radio-navigation systems, and electric motors for drones, according to HUR.
KRET is the tenth Rostec holding whose corporate network has been published by Ukrainian intelligence through the War&Sanctions portal. The database now contains information on 764 companies associated with the Russian state corporation.
Earlier, on September 9, Ukraine’s military intelligence said it had breached the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology, a key Russian missile developer behind the Yars, Bulava, Iskander-M, and Oreshnik systems, obtaining data on the institute’s structure, projects, and 2,648 employees.

UV light reveals possible camouflage on a 125-million-year-old crocodile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:07:13 UTC
23:07:13 KST

UV light reveals possible camouflage on a 125-million-year-old crocodile
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo
- Summary:
- A 125-million-year-old crocodile fossil has revealed preserved skin, possible sensory organs, sophisticated respiratory structures, and an unexpected pattern on its tail. Ultraviolet light exposed alternating bands that may represent ancient camouflage, potentially preserving the oldest known coloration in a crocodylomorph.
- Share:
A remarkably preserved fossil from northeastern Spain is giving scientists a rare look at the skin, soft tissues, and possible coloration of an ancient crocodile relative that lived about 125 million years ago.
The new study, published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, provides the first detailed description of soft tissues preserved in Montsecosuchus depereti, a Lower Cretaceous crocodylomorph discovered at the Pedrera de Meià site in the province of Lleida (Catalonia, Spain). By examining the fossil under ultraviolet light, researchers uncovered new evidence about its skin, sensory structures, respiratory anatomy, and possible color pattern. The work was led by the Institut Català de Paleontologia Miquel Crusafont.
A Tiny Crocodile Preserved for 125 Million Years
Approximately 125 million years ago, a small crocodile died in a karstic lake close to the coast of what is now the Catalan Pre-Pyrenees. Its body settled into fine lake sediments, where unusually favorable conditions helped preserve it in exceptional detail. Over time, those sediments became the lithographic limestones of the Pedrera de Meià, now part of the UNESCO Orígens Global Geopark.
The fossil, cataloged as MGB-512, is about 50 centimeters long and is housed at the Museum of Natural Sciences of Barcelona. It was discovered more than a century ago and received some scientific attention in the 90s, but researchers have now extracted information that had remained hidden since its discovery, including the shape and distribution of its preserved soft tissues.
The breakthrough came while paleontologists Oscar Castillo and Jesús Serrano were building a database of fossils from the lithographic limestones of Montsec held in Catalan and European museums. When they examined the holotype of Montsecosuchus depereti under ultraviolet light, they noticed structures that appeared to be remnants of soft tissue.
Ultraviolet light can cause fossilized tissues and the surrounding rock to respond differently, making otherwise invisible structures stand out.
"UV light allows us to see details that would otherwise remain completely hidden in the rock," explains Oscar Castillo-Visa, first author of the work.
Ancient Skin Revealed Under UV Light
Using this technique, the team documented several kinds of soft tissue, including epidermal scales. Although Montsecosuchus depereti has been known to science since the early 20th century, the new analysis provides the first detailed picture of what its skin looked like.
The scales varied considerably in shape and size across different parts of the body. The researchers also found that the animal lacked the high caudal fin seen in modern crocodiles.
The fossil may also preserve evidence of sensory organs in the skin. The possible structures appear within some scales, particularly around the neck, limbs, and along the sides of the trunk and tail.
In living crocodiles, similar sensory organs can detect touch and changes in water pressure, while also responding to temperature and chemical signals. In Montsecosuchus, these possible sensory structures appear only in small scales located around the edges of the body. That distribution could suggest that such organs first evolved in specific localized areas before becoming more widespread across the skin in later crocodylomorph lineages.
Clues to an Advanced Respiratory System
The ultraviolet analysis also exposed cartilaginous structures in the chest. These features indicate that Montsecosuchus already possessed an efficient respiratory system that shared certain similarities with those of modern crocodiles.
The discovery suggests that sophisticated thoracic anatomy had evolved surprisingly early in crocodylomorph history.
"These traits indicate that, despite being a primitive animal, it was already very well adapted to a semi-aquatic lifestyle," concludes Castillo-Visa.
A Possible 125-Million-Year-Old Color Pattern
Perhaps the most striking discovery involves the animal's tail.
Under ultraviolet light, some scales in the caudal region show alternating light and dark bands running across the tail. Researchers interpret these bands as possible evidence of the animal's original coloration.
The pattern may have served as disruptive camouflage, visually breaking up the outline of the crocodile and making it more difficult to distinguish from its surroundings. If that interpretation is confirmed, Montsecosuchus would become the oldest known crocodylomorph with preserved evidence of coloration.
Scientists cannot yet determine the exact colors that produced the pattern.
"At the moment we cannot say for sure what color the crocodile's tail was, but it would be expected that it was not so different from current species, which also show different coloration patterns," explains Albert G. Sellés, co-author of the article.
The findings offer new clues about the early evolution of crocodylomorph skin, respiration, and external anatomy. They also highlight the scientific importance of the Catalan fossil record for reconstructing the evolutionary history of vertebrates.
In addition to Oscar Castillo-Visa and Albert G. Sellés, Àngel Galobart (Institut Català de Paleontologia Miquel Crusafont and director of the Conca-Dellà Museum) and Phil Bell from the University of New England participated in the research.
The research has been mainly funded by the VEBPI, PLEC2021-007903, and ARQ001SOL-173-2022 projects, with support from the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities, the NextGenerationEU/PRTR program, the Department of Culture of the Generalitat de Catalunya, and the CERCA program.
La Pedrera de Meià, an Exceptional Fossil Site
The Pedrera de Meià is considered a Konservat-Lagerstätte, a term used for fossil sites with extraordinary preservation. At such locations, fossils may retain not only bones and other hard tissues, but also delicate soft structures that are usually lost during fossilization.
That exceptional preservation has made Pedrera de Meià an important site for studying Lower Cretaceous fish, amphibians, reptiles, and plants. More than 8,000 fossil specimens have been recovered there so far.
Fossils from the site can be seen at the Montsec de Meià Interpretation Center in the town of Vilanova de Meià, where more than 100 exceptionally preserved specimens are on display. The Orígens Geopark has also created a website featuring many of the site's most representative fossils.
The fossil record includes spiders, flies, wasps or beetles, insect larvae, crustaceans, vertebrates such as fish and amphibians, and a remarkable diversity of plants. Among them is Montsechia, the first known angiosperm in the world. The center is also part of the "Dinosaurs of the Pyrenees" project, a network of museums and interpretation centers showcasing the rich paleontological record of the Catalan Pyrenees.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Oscar Castillo-Visa, Phil R Bell, Àngel Galobart, Albert Sellés. Soft tissue preservation in the Barremian Montsecosuchus depereti (Neosuchia: Atoposauridae). Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, 2026; 207 (2) DOI: 10.1093/zoolinnean/zlag076

‘NOT A PASSENGER’ INSIDE BERLIN’S ICONIC LUXURY DEPARTMENT STORE
Inside the OMA-renovated halls of KaDeWe in Berlin, a striking pink set up offers an unexpected pause. Marking the launch of the limited-edition ‘Passenger’ collection — co-created by fashion brand Namilia, Telekom Electronic Beats, and British indie rock band Wet Leg — Berlin-based design practice YONT Studio has crafted an immersive, analog sound installation open from September 15–27, 2026. Taking its creative cues from Iggy Pop’s 1977 track The Passenger, written during his West Berlin years with David Bowie, the project flips the original premise of passive observation into an empowering manifesto: Not a Passenger. Spanning a compact 35-square-meter footprint, the spatial installation asks visitors to take the driver’s seat, inviting them to sit in up-cycled car seats and select from 140 curated cassette tapes to build their own auditory.
‘We imagined an installation that feels like wandering around, observing or pausing, but always choosing what to look at, what to listen to next,’ explain Serdar Ayvaz and Coşan Karadeniz of YONT Studio in an exclusive interview with designboom. ‘Being a passenger means moving through the city while constantly being exposed to images, people, and sounds. Our installation places visitors at its center, creating a moment of pause or intimate interaction in a busy department store environment.’
‘Not a Passenger’ sound installation by Namilia, Telekom Electronic Beats, and YONT Studio | all images courtesy of Telekom Electronic Beats
BRIDGING TECHNO-QUEER SENSUALITY AND SOUND CULTURE
Not a Passenger combines the visual styles of Namilia, Telekom Electronic Beats, and YONT Studio into a shared design for a spatial pop-up installation, linking music, subculture, and fashion. The space hosts a limited-edition fashion collection co-created by Namilia and Telekom Electronic Beats. To give this collection a physical stage, YONT Studio translates a sense of road trip nostalgia into a sculptural intervention that bridges techno-queer sensuality with sound culture. Drawing on its signature scenography style with raw, monumental forms paired with custom stainless steel garment racks and up-cycled leather car seats, the Berlin-based practice creates an environment where visitors transition from passive onlookers to active participants.
‘Namilia’s techno-queer, kinky sensuality and Telekom Electronic Beats being an intersectional music platform were valuable ingredients for us,’ the designers tell designboom. ‘We took elements from analog music and fashion into architectural formal language; it’s fragmented but in a way connected. What came up feels something monumental but intimate. Human vs machine & vice versa.’
tapes demand manual handling, bringing tactile weight and deliberate patience back to the sound ritual
PINK FOAM, EXPOSED CABLES, AND THE NOSTAGIC RITUAL OF CASSETTES
At the heart of the installation sits a radial configuration anchored by a circular metal platform holding six up-cycled car seats. Around this central lounge are four monolithic volumes sculpturally crafted from styrofoam, treated with a mixed epoxy coating, and finished in a vivid, high-gloss pink car paint. Each unit serves a distinct purpose within the compact footprint: two units host integrated cassette players and headphones loaded with 140 curated tapes from artists like Madonna, Björk, Sade, and Kendrick Lamar; a third incorporates a full-length mirror, turning the niche into a private dressing room; and the fourth functions as a product shelf featuring custom hooks shaped like Namilia’s perfume bottle.
Rejecting slick digital interfaces and other high-tech systems often used in modern retail, the installation deliberately exposes technical infrastructure and leans into tactile friction. Tapes must be physically chosen, inserted, and rewound, reintroducing weight, texture, and patience to the listening process.
‘The analog elements make the installation feel active and slightly unpredictable,’ YONT Studio explains. ‘We also deliberately allowed cables and technical components to remain visible. Normally, retail design tries to conceal this infrastructure, but here it becomes part of the visual language. The cables give the objects a nervous, almost bodily quality, as if the installation has its own internal system.’
rather than concealing technical infrastructure, exposed cables and hardware are integrated directly into the visual language
Accompanying the spatial intervention is the exclusive fashion capsule co-created with British indie rock band Wet Leg, featuring three distinct garments: a cap, a fitted top, and a T-shirt. Together, the physical collection and spatial environment explore themes of individual self-expression, collective identity, and the fluid interplay between fashion and sound culture. Telekom Electronic Beats’ participation underscores its ongoing dedication to nurturing creative cross-sections between contemporary art, fashion, and electronic music. By inserting a tactile, slow-paced soundscape into a fast-paced luxury retail store, Not a Passenger ultimately offers a nostalgic yet futuristic disruption.
‘There is something powerful about a vision that doesn’t always fit into the given context, but sometimes contradicts or flips it,’ the studio adds. ‘So when visitors walk away, it should feel a little like waking up, stepping back into the real world. And a sense of road trip nostalgia.’
bridging object and space, the installation explores the fluid dialog between individual expression, shared identity, and fashion

New study challenges the core assumption behind the world’s most widely used implicit bias test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
14:00:02 UTC
23:00:02 KST

A new study suggests that the most widely used tool for measuring hidden prejudices might actually be capturing a person’s conscious effort to avoid making mistakes. By analyzing data from over a hundred thousand test sessions, researchers found that people’s tendency to slow down and be cautious is a stronger driver of their test scores than their underlying automatic associations. The research was published in Nature Human Behaviour.
Implicit biases are attitudes or stereotypes that can influence our understanding and decisions, often without our direct awareness. To detect these hidden attitudes, psychologists frequently use the Implicit Association Test, commonly known as the IAT. The test requires participants to quickly sort images and words into categories on a computer screen using two keyboard keys.
In a test examining racial bias, a person might first sort images of White faces and positive words using one key, and Black faces and negative words using another. The categories are later swapped, pairing White faces with negative words and Black faces with positive words. People usually take longer to respond during these swapped, or incompatible, pairings.
This delay in reaction time is typically calculated into a metric called a D-score, which researchers use to quantify the severity of a person’s implicit bias. The traditional interpretation of the IAT assumes that this delay happens because the swapped pairings conflict with a person’s automatic memory associations, a concept known as decision ease.
But the delay could also occur if participants simply adopt a more attentive strategy, slowing down to ensure they do not press the wrong key. This alternate mechanism is called response caution. While decision ease operates automatically based on memory, response caution is a conscious, strategic choice to prioritize accuracy over speed.
Pioneering mathematical modeling of the test concluded that bias is driven by how easily people process these associations rather than how cautiously they respond. For instance, a 2007 study broke the IAT into cognitive components and found that real bias lies in the ease of processing information, while response caution was treated as a background testing artifact. This assumption has shaped how bias interventions are evaluated.
Building on that idea, a 2020 study analyzed anti-bias programs by looking at how they altered decision ease versus caution, illustrating why understanding the true driver matters for real-world training.
The new study directly challenges this foundational view by investigating whether response caution is actually a more prominent factor in IAT results.
“The IAT is the most widely used tool for measuring implicit bias, and it’s usually interpreted as picking up on how easily a stereotype or attitude pops into someone’s mind,” lead author Kyle J. LaFollette, a postdoctoral principal researcher and statistical consultant at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business’s Roman Family Center for Decision Research, told PsyPost.
“But researchers have long wondered whether that’s the whole story,” LaFollette explained. “Some of what shows up in an IAT score might actually come from people being more careful or cautious in certain parts of the test, rather than from the strength of an automatic association. That distinction matters because caution is something people can control, while the automatic association process is supposed to be the part that’s harder to fake or consciously manage. We wanted to test how much of the IAT’s signal actually comes from each of these two things, using a large dataset and a modeling approach built for teasing them apart.”
To test their ideas, the researchers analyzed a massive dataset from the Ideology 2.0 Study, hosted on the Project Implicit website. The dataset included 109,417 unique test sessions spread across 39 different IAT topics. These topics ranged from race and sexuality to politics, age, and economic systems.
For each topic, participants completed the standard sorting tasks, and their choices and response times were recorded in milliseconds. Many participants also completed an explicit preference questionnaire. This allowed them to directly rate how much they liked or preferred one group or concept over another. The researchers then analyzed the data by focusing on the correct sorting choices, setting aside trials where participants made errors.
The research team applied a mathematical technique called a Racing Diffusion Model to the data. This model allowed them to separate the participants’ overall reaction times into three distinct cognitive mechanisms. The first mechanism is decision ease, which represents the automatic activation of mental associations.
The second mechanism is response caution, which captures how much mental evidence a person needs to gather before making a choice to ensure accuracy. The third is non-decision time, which accounts for the physical act of pressing a button or visually registering the stimulus.
The analysis indicated that all three mechanisms behaved differently depending on whether the participants were completing the compatible or incompatible sections of the test. However, the magnitude of these effects varied substantially. When looking at the final D-scores across the 39 topics, response caution emerged as a stronger predictor of a person’s score than decision ease or non-decision time.
Participants consistently slowed their responses down during the incompatible blocks to ensure they were categorizing the images and words correctly. This shift in strategy heavily influenced the final delay that the standard test calculates as bias. The standard D-score metric conflates all of these factors, meaning that the test may be grading people on how cautiously they completed the task rather than measuring their automatic prejudices.
“The role of caution was consistently greater than the role of automatic association, and that held true across almost every one of the 39 topics we looked at, using several different ways of scoring the test,” LaFollette said. “This wasn’t a small or one-off effect. It showed up again and again across very different kinds of topics, from race and age to more abstract ones like attitudes toward novelty.”
The researchers were particularly struck by the uniformity of the results. “We expected caution to matter, but seeing it come out on top across nearly every topic we tested, including some very different from one another, was more uniform than we expected going in,” LaFollette noted.
The team also examined how these cognitive mechanisms related to what people explicitly stated on the preference questionnaires. They found that a person’s stated preferences were reliably predicted by their level of response caution. In contrast, decision ease and non-decision time did not consistently predict these direct self-reports.
This suggests that the same conscious filtering that guides how people answer direct questions also dictates how cautiously they perform on the IAT. Rather than providing a pure window into automatic associations, the test seems to capture how individuals manage the conflict between speed and accuracy. By slowing down on tricky questions, test-takers are exerting conscious control over a measure that is supposed to bypass conscious thought.
“That cautious, more controllable behavior also lined up better with what people said they actually believed than the automatic process did,” LaFollette said. “It also did a better job predicting people’s stated attitudes, and it did so for about half the topics, compared to roughly 1 in 10 for the automatic process.”
“IAT scores aren’t as simple as they’re often made out to be,” he emphasized. “In short, an IAT score reflects a blend of factors, and part of that blend is more deliberate than the ‘implicit’ label suggests.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relies on mathematical models to infer cognitive processes from reaction times. While these models are well-established, they are still approximations of human thought and decision making.
“This isn’t a finding that implicit bias doesn’t exist or that the IAT is meaningless,” LaFollette clarified. “We absolutely find evidence for implicit bias on many topics. Rather, it’s a finding about what the score is actually made of.”
“Two people with the exact same underlying association could end up with different IAT scores just because one of them is being more careful on the harder parts of the test,” he explained. “So the score shouldn’t be treated as a pure window into someone’s unconscious mind. It’s a mix, and untangling that mix matters for how the test gets used and interpreted.”
Additionally, the dataset only recorded the final reaction time after a participant corrected a mistake, meaning the researchers could not model the reaction times of the initial errors. The data also comes from a platform where participants voluntarily choose to take bias tests online. This environment might attract a specific demographic that is highly motivated to monitor their own performance and avoid looking biased.
“At its broadest possible overview, I think this paper makes a serious attempt to grapple with a question that’s plagued us since the advent of the IAT: what are we really measuring?” Daniel J. Lee, an associate professor of entrepreneurship at the University of Delaware’s Book School of Innovation and Entrepreneurship who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “Indeed, this is something I (and many others) have tried to address in our own work as well.”
“So while I think in general this might be seen as challenging existing work, it actually fits very nicely within some open questions within the extant literature, for instance – how does previous knowledge of implicit bias influence scores on future IATs?” Lee added. “As a hypothetical, if I don’t want some psychologist’s test telling me I harbor ill will towards another race, I might very well be more ‘response cautious’ while taking the test!”
This motivation could elevate the levels of response caution observed in the study compared to how people might react in other settings. Future research might explore how different sets of instructions affect these results. Telling participants to prioritize speed over accuracy, for example, could potentially reduce the influence of conscious strategy and isolate automatic memory associations more effectively.
“We’d like to see future (and retroactive re-analysis of past) IAT research separate out caution from automatic association rather than lumping them into one score,” LaFollette said. “The automatic-association piece looks like a promising candidate for a cleaner measure of implicit bias going forward, but it still needs more validation before it could replace the traditional score.”
“We’re also interested in extending this kind of analysis to mistakes people make on the test, and to other tools used to measure implicit attitudes,” he added. “Future research should also carefully consider the caution component, as caution may be more predictive of people’s real-world behaviors and therefore critical for understanding how people act on or suppress their biases.”
To help advance this work, the researchers have made their computational methods accessible to others.
“For researchers or readers interested in trying this kind of modeling themselves, I’d also point them to FlexDDM, a tool my lab have developed that makes fitting these diffusion models much more approachable,” LaFollette noted. “It’s also great for instruction. FlexDDM is available for free on the Microsoft store.”
The study, “Challenging the Mechanism for the Implicit Association Test,” was authored by Kyle J. LaFollette, Doroteja Rubez, Heath A. Demaree, and Amit Goldenberg.

Danish government plans 20 tourist tax to help finance personal and business tax cuts
Unknown

22:55:46 KST

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

Danish stocks fall for eighth trading day as higher oil prices push up interest rates

Unknown Publisher

22:55:41 KST

Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.
According to a press release from the Danish Finance Ministry, Naalakkersuisut (the Government of Greenland) and the Danish government signed a partial agreement on Tuesday worth 1.2 billion DKK for investments in Greenland from 2026 to 2029.
“The agreement means, among other things, that there will be a relief package for the Greenlandic citizens who are the most vulnerable economically,” the ministry said.
The governments have also agreed to provide funding for Greenland’s utility sector. This includes water supply projects in Ilulissat and support for Nukissiorfiit, Greenland’s self-rule-owned utility company, to help develop the country’s energy infrastructure.
Funding will also go toward operating Greenland’s new international airports, with the agreement including money for feasibility studies in 2027 for a new regional airstrip in Ittoqqortoormiit and a new deep-water port in Qaqortoq.
“We are investing in initiatives that can be felt in the everyday lives of the Greenlandic people, and which at the same time support Naalakkersuisut’s work to develop a strong and sustainable Greenlandic society,” Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said.
The agreement follows another deal between Greenland and Denmark reached in February, which provided funding for Greenlandic patients to receive treatment in the Danish healthcare system.
Both agreements stem from a framework agreement reached in September last year between Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Under that framework, the two sides agreed on a package worth 1.6 billion DKK for Greenland’s healthcare system, the deep-water port and a new airstrip.
Around 100,000 AL Sydbank customers will no longer have to pay up to 600 DKK a year for an account, online banking access and a debit card.
The offer was previously available to customers of Arbejdernes Landsbank. Following the merger of Arbejdernes Landsbank, Vestjysk Bank and Sydbank, it will now be extended to all customers of the new bank, AL Sydbank.
“When we did the merger, we promised that you would be able to get an account, access to online banking, and a debit card without it costing anything,” said Svend Randers, AL Sydbank’s director responsible for private customers.
“That is the promise we are fulfilling now, and it applies both to our existing customers who do not yet have those terms, and then of course the new customers who hopefully will join,” he said.
Randers said the bank hopes the offer will attract new customers and encourage existing customers to stay.
“And then of course we hope that in the longer term, it means that those customers will want to do more business with us when they eventually buy a home or car or save up for retirement or something else entirely,” he said.
The change comes after AL Sydbank told customers this summer that several fees would change following the merger.
According to a Mybanker analysis for TV 2, fees increased for between 55 and 60 percent of the bank’s services, depending on which bank a person previously used. Between 25 and 35 percent of fees decreased.
Customers must have their NemKonto, the bank account used for payments from Danish public authorities, with AL Sydbank to qualify for the free account.

Nearly six in 10 Danish companies with more than 10 employees now use artificial intelligence, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark. That’s almost four times the share recorded three years ago.
In 2026, 59 percent of these companies use AI, up from 15 percent in 2023. The share was 42 percent in 2025.
The uses of AI include analyzing text, converting spoken language into machine-readable code, generating images and videos, and automating work processes.
Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said it has seen AI move from being mainly a topic of discussion to a tool used in daily business.
“Companies’ use of artificial intelligence is here to stay, and we can see that the large companies are the furthest ahead,” Frederikke Saabye, industry director at Dansk Erhverv, said.
According to the business organisation, companies see greater efficiency as the main benefit of using AI. A lack of employee skills, knowledge and time are the biggest barriers to making greater use of the technology.
IT-Branchen, an industry association representing technology companies in Denmark, said the wider use of AI also increases the need to consider issues such as quality, transparency and data security.
“The more the technology spreads, the more important issues of quality, transparency, data security, and not least human judgment become,” IT-Branchen’s CEO Natasha Friis Saxberg said, adding that the development makes broader AI knowledge and training more important, including upskilling and continuing education for employees.
The Danish government plans to charge tourists 20 DKK per overnight stay in Copenhagen and Aarhus and introduce a levy on cruise ships, according to government sources and a memo obtained by Børsen.
The previously undisclosed measures would help fund tax cuts that the minority government will seek support for this autumn. The plans require backing from other parties, expected to come from the center-right opposition.
The government wants to abolish the 7.5% intermediate tax on annual income between 641,200 DKK and 777,900 DKK. It also plans to remove the top-top tax on income exceeding 2,592,700 DKK.
Corporate tax would fall from 22% to 19% over three years. The ceiling for share savings accounts would rise to 500,000 DKK over the same period, and taxes on shares would be reduced.
Planned funding measures include keeping the duty on chocolate and sweets, reducing the research and development deduction for companies and raising taxes on dividends received by major shareholders.
The government also wants to limit interest deductions to 150,000 DKK for individuals and 300,000 DKK for couples. Estates worth more than 10 million DKK would face a tax rate 15 percentage points higher than today.
The tax cuts are not fully covered by higher taxes and duties. The government plans to use about 1.5 billion DKK from available public funds in 2027, rising to about 2 billion DKK in 2029.
Denmark’s government consists of the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Moderates and Social Liberals. It does not have a parliamentary majority.
Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.

The Danish government will require police to register all potential crimes as criminal cases and end the practice of shelving reports without a proper investigation.
The Justice Ministry announced Tuesday that it would implement all recommendations from the National Audit Office, Denmark’s independent public spending watchdog. The disputed police practice is known as “washing cases.”
“Citizens must naturally be able to have confidence that the police handle their case properly and correctly, regardless of where in the country you live,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said.
“In the future, all potential criminal cases must be registered as actual criminal cases,” he added.
The Public Accounts Committee, a parliamentary oversight body, strongly criticized police in May after receiving a National Audit Office report on the practice. Cases were reportedly shelved partly to save resources.
The new government reshuffled senior police leadership in June. Top positions in the National Police and PET, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, changed hands.
Several justice spokespersons in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, said they had no confidence in National Police Commissioner Thorkild Fogde after he said he did not know about the practice. Fogde was later removed from the position.
The ministry did not say whether police would receive additional funding. Wammen previously said he was open to providing more money and noted that a multiyear agreement had already increased funding and training.
The National Police and Director of Public Prosecutions must regularly report on future developments to the political parties behind that agreement.
Two earlier State Prosecutor reports were not used because the National Audit Office identified issues they had missed, Wammen said.

A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.

Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.
