Police arrived at a house on Dichtkunstlaan at around 17.00 following reports of what appeared to be an argument. The officers found one seriously injured woman and one armed woman who then jumped out of the window. Both died of their injuries.
Angèle, who was living with the armed woman, called the police. She told VRT her housemate had not been herself for several days. “When I came back from the shop, there was a large knife on the table. She was waving it about. I was scared.”

“I rang the police when I heard screaming. I was on the phone with them for about 10 minutes,” she says. She saw the emergency services arriving and tried to reason with her housemate. “I said to her, ‘Please, let’s find a solution’. But she panicked and jumped out of the window. It was terrible.”
The incident “appears to involve a woman with psychiatric issues and a friend who wanted to support her”, a spokesperson for the public prosecutor’s office said.

Probe Into Serbian Ruling Party’s Election Call Center Yields No Progress After Three Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:34:00 UTC
22:34:00 KST

Reported by
As Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic’s party gears up for elections at the end of October, suspicions of vote-buying in previous election cycles remain unresolved.
Serbian police have failed to question a single person in nearly three years of investigating an alleged vote-buying and illicit campaign finance scheme operated by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), opting instead to transfer the case between internal departments, the Center for Investigative Journalism of Serbia (CINS) reported.
The stalled investigation takes on renewed significance as Serbia gears up for snap parliamentary elections on October 25. The political stakes were elevated further Monday evening when President Aleksandar Vučić announced on Pink TV that he will officially resign on September 27. Vučić stated he will address the nation to thank them for their support before entering the campaign as an “ordinary citizen” representing the SNS.
“The only thing I can say is that I faithfully served the citizens of this country, faithfully, diligently, devotedly, and with determination,” Vučić said.
The First Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade confirmed to CINS that, as of late August, the Ministry of Interior (MUP) had not interviewed anyone regarding the SNS call center case.
Prosecutors initially instructed police to investigate in December 2023 and sent three subsequent reminders, which went unanswered. Instead, on July 8, the MUP transferred the case from its economic crime department to its anti-corruption department. The MUP told CINS it will submit a report to prosecutors once its checks are complete.
The investigation stems from a November 2023 CINS undercover exposé of an SNS call center. A reporter documented that employment was conditional on voting for the ruling party and photographing the ballot as proof. Workers were allegedly organized by the hostess agency M&J Lady and received undeclared cash payments at the offices of a youth non-governmental organization, the Center for Education and Youth Development of Belgrade (CEROB).
The SNS, M&J Lady, and CEROB have all officially denied involvement to Serbia’s Anti-Corruption Agency. Despite the denials, the CINS investigation was cited in the final election report by the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) as an example of voter pressure and illicit third-party campaign financing.
Following the exposé, former opposition Members of Parliament Jelena Jerinić and Đorđe Pavićević filed criminal complaints alleging voting bribery, tax offenses, and unauthorized personal data collection. The case was briefly elevated to the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade but was returned in early 2024 due to alleged insufficient evidence.
Experts have sharply criticized the prolonged delays. Nemanja Nenadić of Transparency Serbia called it one of the country's best-documented campaign finance violations, criticizing prosecutors for failing to direct the investigation or take action when police stalled. Retired police inspector Siniša Janković warned the police's inaction could constitute a criminal offense of abuse of office.
Vladimir Tupanjac, a lawyer and former deputy prosecutor, noted that prosecutors legally did not have to wait for the police and could have gathered the evidence themselves.
"Based on the conduct so far, one could conclude that the police and the prosecution are accomplices in covering up a crime," Tupanjac told CINS.

Von der Leyen’s failures on Israel must end, starting with a settlement trade ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:22:59 UTC
22:22:59 KST

On 16 September 2026, the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen will give her annual State of the European Union address. Here, Caroline Hansen, EU Foreign Policy Advocate at Amnesty International, and Claudio Francavilla, Associate Director for EU Advocacy, for Human Rights Watch, write that this year’s speech must be an opportunity to make good on past promises and finally present a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.
Last year’s “State of the European Union” speech made headlines when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen finally proposed suspending the trade part of the EU-Israel Association Agreement and sanctioning Israeli ministers and settlers. One year on, almost none of those measures have been adopted, and as more and more EU countries and allies adopt bans on trade with Israel’s illegal settlements, von der Leyen’s Europe is lagging behind.
These failures come with consequences: not only for her own credibility and that of the EU, but most of all for the lives of millions displaced, killed or wounded in Palestine and across the region.
Von der Leyen should use this year’s address to remedy that, by firstly making good on last year’s proposals, then by ensuring the EU joins the ranks of those banning trade with Israel’s illegal settlements.
Von der Leyen’s proposals last year came only after an official declaration of famine in the Gaza Strip, where Israeli authorities unlawfully blocked humanitarian aid as part of their genocidal campaign
Her proposals followed mass protests across Europe demanding an end to EU inaction and complicity, and calls by several EU member states and civil society groups to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement, whose essential human rights clause the EU found to have been breached by Israel.
“It truly pains me to say these words”, she confessed before announcing her proposals, which also included targeted sanctions against “extremist” Israeli ministers and settlers, and a suspension of a few million euros worth of EU funding to Israeli projects.
But there she stopped. As Germany and Italy obstructed the suspension of the Agreement and Hungary and Czechia vetoed sanctions against Israeli ministers, von der Leyen was reticent to speak out, in stark contrast to her approach on Hungary’s repeated vetoes on EU sanctions against Russia.
And while the EU repeated its condemnations of Israel’s illegal settlements, von der Leyen resisted growing calls to introduce a ban on the EU trade fueling the settlements’ economy and related abuses.
Von der Leyen also remained silent as Israel’s foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar lashed out at EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, nor did she comment when EU Commissioner Dubravka Šuica met him in Tel Aviv shortly after, exposing a growing division and lack of solidarity in her Commission mirroring those among EU states.
As Europe showed weakness, divisions and its inability to deliver more than a handful of sanctions against Israeli settlers, the situation in the region kept deteriorating.
Israel’s spiralling abuses
When von der Leyen’s delivered her 2025 speech, at least 64,000 Palestinians had been killed in the Gaza Strip. That number is now close to 74,000 despite a so-called “ceasefire” in force since October 2025. Israeli authorities continue to impose severe, arbitrary and unlawful aid restrictions as they have confined the population into approximately 30 percent of the territory, and are once again openly discussing plans to ethnically cleanse Gaza of its Palestinian population.
In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, despite protests by the EU and other close allies, Israeli authorities have turbocharged the expansion of illegal settlements. This resulted in expedited home demolitions, land seizure, fragmentation and dispossession of Palestinians – hallmarks of Israel’s ethnic cleansing and apartheid against Palestinians. At least 88 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed in the West Bank this year alone, bringing the total since October 2023 to nearly 1,100.
Israeli authorities also adopted a death penalty bill that de facto applies to Palestinians only and continue to detain thousands of Palestinians without charges or trial, including doctors like Hussam Abu Safiya, subjecting many to systematic torture.
In Lebanon, despite ceasefires that went into effect on April 17 and June 20, Israeli attacks have killed at least 4,383 people since the beginning of the March 2026 escalation, including 261 children, 399 women, and 135 medical workers, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. Israeli forces continue to cause widespread destruction and mass displacement, committing acts that Amnesty International has found to constitute war crimes.
Von der Leyen’s responsibilities
As President of the European Commission, von der Leyen has the duty to ensure that all EU policies – including its policies on trade and foreign affairs – comply with international law.
She can’t hide behind the EU’s humanitarian aid to Palestinians while doing nothing to address the reasons why such aid is so desperately needed. Nor can she blame member states for not approving her half-hearted proposals: she should actively and vocally engage with them and urge them to comply with the legal obligations under the UN Genocide Convention.
By the time of last year’s speech, Amnesty International, Al-Haq, B’Tselem, UN experts, and the International Association of Genocide Scholars were among those who had already concluded Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. Shortly after, a UN independent Commission of Inquiry confirmed those findings.
But whether von der Leyen agrees with the genocide qualification is irrelevant: under the Genocide Convention, awareness of a “serious risk” of genocide triggers the “duty to prevent”, compelling all states parties to that treaty – including all EU states – to “employ all means reasonably available to them, so as to prevent genocide so far as possible”. For the EU, that means suspending the Association Agreement and sanctioning Israeli officials.
Von der Leyen should also reaffirm the EU’s commitment to international justice and propose the use of the EU blocking statute to protect the International Criminal Court and those cooperating with it from crippling sanctions, adopted by the US as part of its campaign to dismantle the Court and shield its own and Israeli officials from accountability.
Von der Leyen should use this speech to propose an EU-wide ban of trade with Israel’s illegal settlements Much as she did with the Association Agreement, she doesn’t need preemptive support by the EU Council. No matter how much it might “pain” her, she should put the proposal on the table, and actively engage with member states, especially Germany and Italy, to ensure she has the necessary qualified majority to approve a measure that is required by international law.
Amid global turmoil and instability, Europe and the world desperately need principled, committed leaders determined to uphold the rules, especially those devised to prevent, punish and redress the worst atrocities, and adopt all necessary measures to that end.
For the EU, another year of failures, inaction and half-hearted proposals is blow to its credibility. For Palestinians and so many others in the region, it’s a matter of life and death.
What you can do to help
Suspend EU-Israel Trade Agreement
Send a message and demand the leaders of Germany and Italy support suspending the EU’s trade agreement with Israel.
There is no time to lose.

The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:14:55 UTC
22:14:55 KST

The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo
- Summary:
- A mathematical shape famous for covering a surface without ever repeating has revealed an unexpected ability to twist light into unusual chiral patterns. The discovery could lead to new ways of controlling light, polarization, and advanced optical devices.
- Share:
A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to new ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.
In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.
The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem
The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.
Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.
In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.
"What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," says lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena."
Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure
To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.
When laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.
Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.
"We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials."
Light Responds to Direction and Polarization
The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.
When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.
"These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity."
From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics
The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.
More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover new ways to control and study light.
Story Source:

Ukrainian Drone Threat Pushes Putin’s Valdai Forum From Sochi to Moscow Region
Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s annual Valdai Discussion Club meeting has been moved from the Black Sea resort city of Sochi to the Moscow region amid concerns that Ukrainian drones could pose a security threat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on September 15, four people familiar with the decision said Russia’s presidential security service pushed for the relocation because of concerns over possible Ukrainian drone attacks. Around 120 participants had initially been invited to Sochi before being informed in August that the venue had changed.
The Valdai Discussion Club confirmed on September 14 that its 23rd annual meeting will take place in the Moscow region from September 28 to October 1. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov and the forum’s organizers did not respond to the FT’s requests for comment on why the event was moved.
Putin traditionally uses the annual Valdai meeting to outline his views on Russian foreign policy and the international order. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, and presidential aide Maxim Oreshkin are also expected to attend this year’s gathering.
The decision comes as Putin has sharply reduced his visits to Sochi, where he maintains the Bocharov Ruchey presidential residence. According to the FT, Putin has not appeared in the city since the previous Valdai conference ended in October 2025.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin regularly traveled to Sochi. The FT reported that he visited the city 24 times during the final year before the invasion but made only two trips in each of 2024 and 2025.
The reduced travel and relocation of the Valdai forum come as Ukrainian forces expand long-range drone operations against military and strategic targets inside Russia, including in the Krasnodar region surrounding Sochi.
On August 9, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian S-400 air defense position near Gelendzhik, according to Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi.
On September 4, another reported Ukrainian drone attack targeted an oil depot and an S-300 or S-400 air defense unit near Sirius, southeast of central Sochi. Putin’s Bocharov Ruchey residence is located several dozen kilometers from the area.
The FT reported that security concerns linked to the growing reach of Ukrainian drones were behind the decision to move this year’s Valdai gathering away from Sochi.

Russian Military Losses Surpass 300,000 Killed and Wounded Since Beginning of 2026
Russia has lost 301,030 military personnel killed or wounded since the beginning of 2026, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on September 15.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
To illustrate the scale of the losses, the General Staff said the figure is equivalent to the personnel of nearly 150 motorized rifle regiments, assuming an average strength of around 2,000 troops per brigade.
Russia sustained its heaviest personnel losses during the three summer months, when 124,170 troops were reported killed or wounded. Of those, 39,290 were recorded in June, followed by 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August.
Losses have continued into September. As of the beginning of September 15, Russian forces had lost another 20,360 personnel since the start of the month, according to the General Staff.
The figures come amid broader assessments pointing to the scale of Russia’s personnel losses since the beginning of its full-scale invasion. British military intelligence estimates that around 500,000 Russian soldiers have been killed since February 2022.
Most of those deaths have occurred since January 2023, a period during which Russian forces captured only around 2% of Ukrainian territory, Air Chief Marshal Sir Rich Knighton, chief of the UK armed forces, told Sky News on September 11.
“I think these numbers illustrate clearly the senseless and futile waste of human life for such little progress, and against such an illegitimate aim of President Putin,” Knighton said in a prepared statement to journalists.
Ukraine’s General Staff, meanwhile, has reported that Russia’s overall military personnel losses, including both killed and wounded, have reached around 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion, describing the toll as the Russian military’s highest in a single war since World War II.
According to the General Staff, the figure exceeds the combined losses sustained by Soviet and Russian forces in all wars and armed conflicts during the second half of the 20th century and the early 21st century.
As Russian forces continue to suffer substantial battlefield losses, Moscow is moving to increase the size of its military. Russia could mobilize up to 600,000 additional personnel by the end of 2027 in an effort to replace losses and maintain sufficient manpower for continued offensive operations in Ukraine.

After all, most people give pralines as a gift to someone.”
For its 10th edition, Gault&Millau selected the 145 best chocolatiers in Belgium and Luxembourg. A jury assessed the flavour, texture, creativity, finish and presentation of their creations in a series of blind tastings.
It’s not just about chocolate or creating the best filling, but about the overall experience
Vandoninck’s pralines stood out because of their colourful exterior. The colours are always matched to the filling, and Vandoninck keeps his range limited to 12 flavours.
“I’m doing everything on my own and I want to be able to offer products that are as fresh as possible,” he says. “When I used to visit a chocolatier, I’d always get choice overload when I had to choose between 40 flavours. That’s why I keep it simple for the customer.”
Flavours range from a traditional hazelnut praline to salted caramel or calamansi – an Asian citrus fruit – with ginger.
“The aim was certainly to be included in Gault&Millau,” he says. “But to not only be featured in the guide within four months, but also to be named Discovery of the Year, is truly the reward for all the hard work.”
Gault&Millau also selected a Chocolatier of the Year for Flanders, Brussels and Wallonia: Chocolatier M in Knokke, Arthur Amblard in Brussels and Deremiens, Prouvy & Jamoigne in Chiny.
Amblard trained as a baker and pastry chef at Ceria in Anderlecht. The 28-year-old has a workshop in the Zavel district where he makes chocolate with no added sugar, inspired by his father, who has diabetes.
“Without compromising on pure taste, Arthur Amblard proves that innovation and craftsmanship can go hand in hand,” the Gault&Millau guide says.

‘Bogland’ explores beautifully strange ecosystems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Bogland explores beautifully strange ecosystems
These water-logged spaces are filled with decay and teeming with life
Bogland
Merritt R. Turetsky
W.W. Norton & Company, $29.99
Thank goodness Merritt Turetsky became captivated by boglands. The ecosystem ecologist evocatively describes the beauty, danger and vitality of these ecosystems in her book, Bogland.
“Buffering the space between forest and river, boglands refuse to be defined as either land or water,” writes Turetsky, of the University of Colorado Boulder. Their soggy, oxygen-starved conditions make it difficult for microbes to break down organic matter, allowing carbon-rich peat to form. It’s that peat that sets boglands apart from all other ecosystems, she writes.
Boglands primarily consist of bogs and fens (and sometimes marshes and swamps). Bogs derive their water from precipitation, are lacking in nutrients and are known for sphagnum moss and carnivorous plants such as sundew and pitcher plants. Fens, in contrast, get their water from streams and groundwater as well as rain. Because fens have access to more nutrients, they support more diverse plant communities.
Anytime Turetsky dove into her own adventures in boglands, I was transfixed. It’s in these moments — trying to stay calm amid insect swarms, reaching her arms deep into the murk and wading through muck with other devoted scientists — that the book shines.
Turetsky’s bug baptism occurred on a college trip to a Nova Scotia bog as hundreds of mosquitoes, black flies and other insects quickly descended around her netted head. The sounds “are seared deep into my memory,” she writes. “After a half an hour I knew I needed to conquer the noise or be driven insane.”
In Brunei, Turetsky meets up with a peatland restoration research team. The group enters the waist-deep water, moves through a rehabilitated area, then reaches a healthy peat swamp. This secret garden, Turetsky writes, “is pure pitcher plant heaven — unlike anything in my northern bogs, with layers of pitcher plants not only growing on the ground but dangling from the trees.” The colors and shapes she describes reminded me of something Dr. Suess would dream up.
But along with their beauty and wonder, boglands harbor potential danger. Turetsky recalls getting lost when she ventured out alone to check something in a study plot. “Even in familiar terrain, boglands are deceiving,” she writes. “I was disoriented even as I felt surrounded by what seemed well-known.” Luckily, it wasn’t too long before she found her team — otherwise, they would have had to commence a search-and-rescue mission.
Turetsky’s devotion to boglands celebrates the contradictions in these ecosystems: Filled with decay but teeming with life; places of refuge and risk; an ally in a changing climate as well as a potential foe.
Peatlands occupy just 3 percent of the world’s land area but store around 30 percent of Earth’s soil carbon, Turetsky writes. “This far exceeds the carbon stored in the world’s forest biomass, despite forests covering a much larger area.”
However, boglands are being drained for agriculture and damaged by wildfires, drought and changing climate conditions. As more are destroyed, there is a serious threat that they could release their carbon stores, adding to greenhouse gas emissions, Turetsky notes.
I have a general understanding of climate science, but I wish Turetsky would have provided more basic information on that topic. Just as she lost her way in the bog, I got turned around by mentions of different warming periods and ice ages. But the bigger message of how boglands formed over geologic time and their contribution to Earth’s climate system still comes through.
Overall, my time spent in Bogland felt expertly navigated by Turetsky. I emerged firmly on team boglands. For me, the book’s ultimate gift was igniting a reverence for these incredible ecosystems. And to my great delight, Turetsky closes with a list of bogs, some with boardwalks, that people can visit. I’m grabbing my bug spray now.
Buy Bogland from Bookshop.org. Science News is a Bookshop.org affiliate and will earn a commission on purchases made from links in this article.

The European Investment Bank (EIB) has approved a 100 million euro ($115 million) loan to make the Baltic Sea port of Klaipeda ready to accommodate NATO ships, it announced on Sept. 15.
The EIB is the lending arm of the European Union, and since 2025, its portfolio has expanded to help the continent beef up its defense capabilities and to continue supporting Ukraine.
The Lithuanian port of Klaipeda sits in a highly strategic location on the Baltic Sea coast, just over 50 kilometers (around 30 miles) north of Russia's Kaliningrad exclave and a three-and-a-half-hour drive from the EU and NATO's eastern border.
"Few projects illustrate Europe's priorities as clearly as the Port of Klaipeda," EIB Vice-President Karl Nehammer said.
The civilian cruise ship terminal is set to be revamped to allow NATO ships to dock, with a view to improving the logistics of defending the Eastern Flank.
Klaipeda's port is part of the EU's TEN-T transport network, comprising ten transcontinental routes identified as strategically important, accompanied by a roster of projects intended to improve civilian and military transport by 2030.
Not all of those projects are expected to be completed on time. For example, the Rail Baltica project to link the Baltic capitals of Tallinn, Estonia, and Vilnius is beset with delays.
In Brussels, the European Parliament and EU countries are haggling over a new law on military mobility, which aims to remove national-level obstacles to moving troops and equipment more quickly across the continent.
Some of the debates over that law revolve around how much to include Ukraine as both a country receiving military support from the EU and as a potential future member state.
The EIB funding for Klaipeda will cover nearly half of the project's 201 million euro ($232 million) price tag, with the remainder to come from EU and national contributions.

Train services across large parts of the Netherlands have been disrupted today, with the network operator suspecting sabotage. No group has claimed responsibility for the disruption, which was caused by placing objects on the tracks.
Sabotage suspected as Dutch railways suffer major disruption
ProRail received the first report of a disruption at 5.30 on Tuesday. Over the course of the morning, faults in the signalling system were detected at more than 20 locations, according to the Dutch broadcaster NOS.
As a result, trains were unable to run safely and it was not possible to monitor trains’ locations.
“Materials have been found at several points along the track that were deliberately placed there,” a spokesperson for ProRail said.
You cannot run a safe and reliable timetable under such circumstances
These include pipes that were secured to the track at 27 sites, causing the system to indicate that the track is occupied, even when it isn’t. “You cannot run a safe and reliable timetable under such circumstances,” ProRail said, adding that it appeared to be the result of sabotage.
Services were mainly disrupted on routes in central, northern and eastern parts of the country, but the disruption has had nationwide implications.
There was overcrowding on platforms at several stations as trains were unable to run. There were also consequences for road traffic, as the barriers at level crossings were out of order.
By midday, services were gradually being resumed, but national rail operator NS warned of continuing delays and cancellations.
The police and security service are investigating the incidents. Footage from NOS shows investigators removing the pipes and taking them away. Reports emerged later in the day that, in some places where material had been removed, objects had been replaced on the tracks.
Dutch media have speculated that the disruptions are the work of farmers angry about the government’s plans to regulate nitrogen emissions. Farmers’ organisations condemn the actions and say they are not behind them, but say they cannot rule out the possibility that individuals may have acted without the organisations’ knowledge or approval.
Meanwhile, fires were lit along provincial roads and motorways, according to the police and the government’s infrastructure agency. Footage showed hay bales on fire.
Extinction Rebellion, which frequently blocks roads, says it is not behind the sabotage. “We always take responsibility for our actions,” they said.
There is little to no impact on rail traffic in Belgium. “Train services are managed from our signal boxes via traffic control, and everything is being closely monitored,” said a spokesperson for network operator Infrabel.
“If there is a fault in the rail infrastructure, it is immediately detected by our systems and monitored in real time. Technical teams from Infrabel are then dispatched to the site to investigate further and resolve the issue.”

Supermassive black hole winds are 100 times more powerful than scientists thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:33:50 UTC
21:33:50 KST

Supermassive black hole winds are 100 times more powerful than scientists thought
Supermassive black holes may unleash winds 100 times more powerful than expected, spreading energy across hundreds of thousands of light-years.
- Date:
- September 15, 2026
- Source:
- Tohoku University
- Summary:
- Astronomers have discovered that winds from a supermassive black hole are about 100 times more powerful than previously thought. XRISM observations showed the resulting turbulence spreading roughly 300,000 light-years, extending far beyond the black hole’s host galaxy. The energy involved rivals several billion supernova explosions, revealing just how dramatically black holes can influence the space around them.
- Share:
Supermassive black holes may have a much larger influence on their surroundings than scientists previously realized. New observations suggest that winds driven by these enormous objects can carry energy across roughly 300,000 light-years, reaching far beyond the galaxies that host them.
Researchers found that the energy associated with these winds is about 100 times greater than earlier estimates, revealing that black holes can affect vast regions of space on a truly enormous scale.
"Black holes are largely known for sucking matter in, but they also eject gas in the form of powerful winds," says Satoshi Yamada, Assistant Professor at Tohoku University's Frontier Institute for Interdisciplinary Sciences (FRIS). "These winds were thought to be contained within the galaxy, but our study revealed that the force is immensely more powerful than previously understood."
XRISM Takes a Closer Look at a Distant Quasar
Yamada and his colleagues, including researchers from Kanazawa University and Tokyo Metropolitan University, among others, used the X ray astronomy satellite XRISM to study the quasar H1821+643. The object lies in the constellation Draco, about 3.4 billion light-years from Earth.
Quasars are exceptionally bright cosmic objects powered by supermassive black holes that are actively consuming gas. As material falls toward the black hole, tremendous amounts of energy can be released, making quasars visible across immense distances.
The rapidly growing black hole at the center of H1821+643 sits within a galaxy cluster. There, it stirs the surrounding hot gas, which gives off X-rays. To measure how that gas was moving, the researchers analyzed emission lines produced by iron ions.
Black Hole Turbulence Reaches Far Beyond the Galaxy
XRISM's high-precision measurements showed that the extremely hot gas around the black hole is far from motionless. Instead, turbulence causes it to spread violently across a broad region.
The team also found that this gas flow extends beyond the black hole's host galaxy, reaching distances of about 300,000 light-years. Even more striking, the energy contained in the turbulence was approximately 100 times greater than previous estimates.
That amount of energy is comparable to the output of several billion supernova explosions, the powerful blasts produced when certain stars reach the ends of their lives.
"For the first time, we have shown that black holes influence the broader cosmic environment through a shock wave of astonishing power," adds Yamada. "Black holes are key drivers of gas flows and motion in space, transporting vast amounts of energy to different regions of the cosmos."
A Bigger Role for Black Holes in the Cosmos
The findings suggest that supermassive black holes do more than consume nearby matter. They can also send energy and gas far into surrounding space, potentially helping shape the environments around galaxies and galaxy clusters.
Details of the research were published in the journal Nature Astronomy.
Future observations are expected to provide a clearer picture of how black holes affect their surroundings and how matter and elements move through different regions of the cosmos.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Tohoku University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Satoshi Yamada, Shutaro Ueda, Hirofumi Noda, Yutaka Fujita, Misaki Mizumoto, Kentaro Nagamine, Claudio Ricci, Shoji Ogawa, Taiki Kawamuro, Shinya Yamada, Yuichi Terashima, Yoshihiro Ueda. Vigorous turbulence driven by quasar-mode feedback in a cluster core. Nature Astronomy, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02939-x

The General Staff said nearly 300,000 losses were roughly equivalent to the personnel strength of 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an estimated 2,000 troops per regiment.
"The enemy's significant losses are the result of effective combat operations by all components of the Ukrainian Defense Forces," the General Staff said.

The largest losses were recorded during the three summer months, when Russia suffered 124,170 military casualties, the General Staff said. In September, Russia has already lost 20,360 troops as of the morning of Sept. 15, the General Staff said.
Russia's total military losses in Ukraine have reached 1,500,870, Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 9, marking another grim milestone in the war for the Kremlin.
It took roughly two years and three months for the Russian Armed Forces to incur their first 500,000 casualties. Moscow has now suffered roughly the same number in just the past 15 months, as technology increasingly shapes the battlefield and drones expand the kill zone almost daily.
The Kremlin's total personnel losses in Ukraine now exceed the combined toll suffered by Russian and Soviet forces in all wars and armed conflicts during the second half of the 20th century and the early 21st century, the General Staff said.

What to expect on Ukraine in the EU's big yearly roundup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15

21:08:26 KST

What to expect on Ukraine in the EU's big yearly roundup
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa walk with President Volodymyr Zelensky as he arrives at a European Union leaders summit in Brussels, Belgium, on June 18, 2026. (Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will deliver her annual State of the EU speech on Sept 16, usually a celebration of last year's wins and previewing the agenda for the next year, with Ukraine likely to feature strongly.
The speech itself is a closely guarded secret, and the subject of much speculation across Brussels in the weeks leading up to the event. However, there are hints of how Ukraine may and may not feature this time.
Last year, von der Leyen's speech led with Ukraine, discussing the country in several contexts: energy security, EU integration, defense collaboration — especially on drones, security guarantees, and the plan to use Russian assets to bankroll Kyiv.
One topic guaranteed to return: bringing back Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.
Von der Leyen posted on social media on Sept. 13 that she would "talk about a story that profoundly moved me," on how Ukrainian children are a "powerful example" of "courage and strength."
The Commission president identifies strongly with the topic, regularly commenting on it. Brussels also hosted a summit on the return of Ukrainian children in May, with a follow-up to take place in Canada on Sept. 28.
read also
Celebrating the wins
Other likely talking points can be found in the European Commission's recently published State of the Union report, and heard along the corridors of power in Brussels.
Having floated a drone alliance between EU and Ukrainian manufacturers in her previous speech, she will likely celebrate its Sept. 11 kick-off meeting.
EU diplomats suggested to the Kyiv Independent that von der Leyen will briefly mention the announcement facilitating Ukraine's ability to source Patriot interceptor missiles, as well as another disbursement of defense funding.
One senior EU official said they expect an amount smaller than the 4.7 billion euros ($5.4 billion) previously mentioned to be announced, due to delays in processing Ukrainian receipts for defense equipment.
Von der Leyen is also expected to comment on EU integration, revisiting how Ukraine opened two of the six so-called enlargement clusters this year, and perhaps reiterating her earlier calls to reopen the remaining four by year's end.
She will likely adopt the line recently and repeatedly deployed by Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos — that "2026 is a record year of progress" — while avoiding criticism of Ukraine's reform pace.
One EU official said they would be surprised if von der Leyen mentions making use of Russian assets, after her proposal last year failed to advance.
"We need the conversation to mature among the member states before the Commission will stick its neck out again," they told the Kyiv Independent.
She might reflect on how the EU passed the 90 billion euro ($104 billion) support loan in April, and use the podium and her Canadian guest of honor, Prime Minister Mark Carney, to call on third countries to fill the remaining third of Ukraine's expected budget shortfall.
read also
Teasing at the new
Predicting the future is not a science, but it would nonetheless be surprising if von der Leyen skipped the EU's discussions over its 22nd sanctions package, set to be the largest ever.
Even if watered down, the package will likely constrain Moscow's ability to wage war and target numerous third-country entities helping Russia evade sanctions.
In January, EU diplomats told the Kyiv Independent the bloc will review its visa rules — long considered a chance to restrict Russians' access, and to put protections for Ukrainian refugees on a longer-term footing. Von der Leyen could tease at how she would like that process to go.
She might also announce support for Ukraine's two main winter challenges: protecting energy infrastructure and reopening the Black Sea for agricultural exports.
EU officials said talks are ongoing to bolster the so-called "solidarity lanes," and increase food exports leaving Ukraine via Poland and Romania.
Kyiv asked the EU for financial support for its energy sector, but that is unlikely to be agreed to, given the ongoing disbursement of the 90 billion euro loan. In-kind contributions could be an option, though, with one notable gap last winter being the shortage of experts on the ground to install generators and other equipment.
For the EU this fall and winter, though, the biggest topic remains the need to unanimously agree on the bloc's budget for the years 2028-2034.
The Commission originally allocated 100 billion euros ($115 billion) specifically for Ukraine — a figure EU countries have since haggled down to 89 billion ($103 billion) — along with 131 billion euros ($151 billion) for defense and space.
In that context, von der Leyen could renew her case for spending big on both fronts, or equally, she may position herself less assertively, waiting to see which way the political winds blow.
The Canada question
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will be among those watching von der Leyen's speech from inside the European Parliament in Strasbourg, where he is expected to address Europe with a speech of his own.
That follows his recent pitch for "associate EU membership" for Canada — a concept that does not exist, and which he may therefore explain.
EU diplomats told the Kyiv Independent that Canada is negotiating to participate in the bloc's 90 billion loan to Ukraine on terms similar to the U.K., which could already be announced on Sept. 16.
However, there is mounting pressure on non-EU countries to make sizable pledges of their own, with President Volodymyr Zelensky claiming a $27 billion hole in Ukraine's 2026 budget.
Norway recently pledged $9 billion for Ukraine in 2027, and hopes are high in Brussels that Canada will make a separate announcement of its own.
The State of the EU speech will be broadcast on Sept.16 at 10:00 Kyiv time (09:00 CET).

Common antidepressants might help liver cells clear a dangerous type of cholesterol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:00:58 UTC
21:00:58 KST

Common antidepressants might help lower a stubborn, disease-causing type of cholesterol by helping liver cells absorb it from the bloodstream. This unintended side effect could eventually provide a dual-purpose treatment for patients facing both depression and an elevated risk of heart disease. The findings were published in the Journal of Lipid Research.
Lipoprotein(a) is a complex particle in the blood that carries fats and cholesterol throughout the body. It is structurally similar to low-density lipoprotein, commonly known as bad cholesterol. However, it contains an extra protein called apolipoprotein(a) that makes it particularly prone to causing blockages in arteries. High levels of this molecule are genetic and affect at least a fifth of the population of European descent.
Traditional cholesterol-lowering medications, such as statins, fail to reduce these specific particles in the blood. The lack of targeted clinical treatments leaves a major gap in preventing cardiovascular disease for many patients. Researchers are actively trying to understand exactly how the human body clears this molecule from circulation.
Cells absorb molecules from their environment through a process called endocytosis, which involves the cell membrane folding inward to swallow outside material. A specific type of endocytosis called macropinocytosis, or cellular drinking, handles the uptake of this particular cholesterol particle. During cellular drinking, the cell membrane extends outward to gulp large amounts of surrounding fluid and particles.
Researchers from the University of Otago and the University of New South Wales, led by Nikita Deo, Sally P. A. McCormick, and Gregory M. I. Redpath, wanted to map the mechanics of this cellular drinking. They sought to identify exactly what stimulates liver cells to absorb the particles.
The research team initially tested a drug called imipramine on human liver cells grown in a laboratory. Imipramine is an older tricyclic antidepressant that previous laboratory studies identified as a blocker of cellular drinking. The researchers treated the liver cells with the drug overnight and then introduced the cholesterol particles into the fluid bathing the cells.
After a short incubation period, the team measured how much of the substance the cells had absorbed. Instead of blocking the process, the drug caused the cells to absorb nearly three times as much of the cholesterol. The researchers confirmed this was an isolated effect by testing regular bad cholesterol, which the drug did not affect.
This unexpected outcome prompted the team to test newer, more frequently prescribed antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. These drugs treat depression by blocking a specific transport protein from pulling serotonin back into cells. This mechanism leaves more of the mood-regulating chemical active in the space outside the cells.
The researchers repeated the cell culture experiment using the common drugs citalopram, sertraline, and fluoxetine. Citalopram increased the cholesterol uptake in the liver cells to a degree similar to imipramine. Sertraline and fluoxetine did not alter the uptake levels. A later test with paroxetine showed it also boosted cellular absorption of the particles.
To figure out how imipramine and citalopram caused this effect, the researchers looked at the outer boundary of the liver cells. The cholesterol molecules must anchor to the cell surface before the cell can swallow them. The team cooled the cells to temporarily halt the swallowing process, added the cholesterol, and used fluorescent tags to measure how much stuck to the outside of the cells.
Both imipramine and citalopram roughly doubled the amount of cholesterol anchored to the cell surface. The drugs did not change the cells’ ability to bind to standard sugar molecules used as a control. This confirmed that the medications specifically enhanced the cell’s grip on this exact type of cholesterol.
Because these drugs increase the availability of serotonin outside the cells, the researchers hypothesized that serotonin itself might be driving the surface binding. They added pure serotonin to the liver cell cultures overnight and tracked the cholesterol particles. The serotonin treatment produced the same outcome as the medications.
The serotonin drastically increased both the amount of cholesterol sticking to the cell surface and the amount the cells eventually absorbed. This suggests the antidepressants enhance cholesterol absorption by increasing local serotonin levels. The serotonin then somehow alters the cell surface to make it more receptive to the passing cholesterol particles.
The team also explored why sertraline failed to enhance the absorption process despite being in the same class of drugs. Some forms of cellular drinking rely on a specific structural protein called dynamin. Dynamin acts like a lasso, pinching off the newly formed internal pouches so they can detach and drop into the cell interior.
Previous research shows sertraline can interfere with dynamin, preventing it from pinching off the pouches. The researchers tested this by tracking a different molecule known to require dynamin for absorption. Sertraline blocked this control molecule from entering the cells. Its interference with dynamin likely prevents it from enhancing cholesterol uptake.
To understand the mechanics of the surface binding, the researchers examined specific anchor proteins on the liver cells. They used fluorescent tags to measure the presence of a receptor known to grab the cholesterol particles. Treating the cells with imipramine or serotonin increased the amount of this receptor on the cell surface.
Citalopram did not increase this specific receptor. However, it did boost the presence of an accessory protein that helps orchestrate the swallowing process. The precise mechanism linking citalopram, serotonin, and this accessory protein requires further mapping.
Finally, the team tracked where the cholesterol went after the cells swallowed it. They used chemical markers to see if the cells sent the particles to internal compartments meant for degradation or compartments meant for recycling material back outside the cell. The cells treated with imipramine and citalopram routed the extra cholesterol into the recycling compartments.
The researchers suspect this recycling process strips the harmful lipid component from the particle before sending the harmless protein portion back into the bloodstream. If true, the overall impact would still be a reduction in cardiovascular risk.
This study relied exclusively on isolated cells in a laboratory. The behavior of these drugs and the cholesterol particles might differ inside a living human body. The liver interacts with many different tissues and chemical signals that a petri dish cannot replicate.
Additionally, the concentration of citalopram used in the main experiments was roughly twice the maximum dose prescribed to human patients. The serotonin levels tested were also much higher than typical biological conditions. While the paroxetine tests matched clinical doses, animal studies or human trials are needed to verify if these medications can safely lower this dangerous cholesterol in patients.
People suffering from depression often exhibit higher levels of this specific cholesterol, elevating their risk of heart attacks and strokes. Identifying an existing, affordable medication that manages both mood and cardiovascular risk could simplify treatment regimens for vulnerable patients.
The study, “Antidepressants stimulate lipoprotein(a) macropinocytosis via serotonin-enhanced cell surface binding,” was authored by Nikita Deo, Halima Siddiqui, Katie Peppercorn, Golnoush Madani, Alexandria Rutherford-Blyth, Malcolm Rutledge, Michael J. A. Williams, Sally P. A. McCormick, and Gregory M. I. Redpath.

Ebola responders grapple with widening outbreak in DR Congo
The deadly Ebola virus outbreak in DR Congo continues to spread across the vast country despite some success in containing it, aid officials said on Tuesday, in a renewed call for international support to help responders on the ground.
Key points
- 7,200 Ebola cases and nearly 3,500 deaths reported
- Outbreak spreading across an area covering two time zones
- Insecurity, poor roads and funding gaps are hampering response
- Weekly cases are doubling in parts of North Kivu
“If we don’t have the resources, the epidemic will come back…it remains a deadly and massive epidemic,” stressed Julien Harneis, UN Special Ebola Coordinator.
Latest data from 12 September indicates 7,200 reported cases of Ebola and close to 3,500 deaths across 62 health zones, according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO). The virus is now present in seven provinces “covering a very vast geographic area”, said Dr Olivier le Polain, Unit Head for Epidemiology and Analytics for Response at WHO.
“Although the response has been unprecedented in its scale, the epidemic continues to expand.”
In partnership with the authorities, UN agencies and partners have been assisting in tackling the Ebola Bundibugyo virus outbreak since the emergency was declared in mid-May.
But there are immense challenges involved in working in resource-rich regions where populations have experienced decades of violent insecurity and development setbacks.
Hard to reach
“[In] many areas, the roads are massive potholes – not even potholes – trucks disappear into the mud; [in] many areas, the access, even by small plane, is complicated. And then there’s violence against the response,” explained Mr. Harneis.
“We have cases in Bunia, in Ituri and in the far other end of the country in Sud-Ubangi, that is like a distance from Geneva to Dublin.”
The veteran aid coordinator warned that the $1.3 billion humanitarian response is only 49 per cent funded, while Ebola “makes things much worse for all Congolese, “from worsening hunger levels to falling attendance at health centres, increases in maternal mortality” and interrupted treatment for people living with HIV/AIDS.
“We’ve done a lot of positive work through the scaling up bed capacity, but unless we get more specialized medical care, we will eventually come to a plateau,” Mr. Harneis continued, stressing the need for countries to deploy international emergency medical teams immediately.
The ‘live enemy’
“If you don't provide the care, if you don’t finance the care, if you don't provide the technical resources, then Ebola is a live enemy and will come back at us,” he warned, adding that another $1 billion will be needed to sustain the response beyond the first six months.
“There’s been some indication from Member States that they might be prepared to send those teams, but we need a far greater support and dedication of those resources.”
The Ebola outbreak continues to unfold in areas of great humanitarian need and will take “many, many months to get this outbreak under control fully”, insisted WHO’s Dr le Polain.
The epidemiologist described how infections were beginning to decrease in some areas but rise “exponentially” in others, including North Kivu, where the number of weekly cases has now doubled, from about 100 to 200 cases. “We’re worried about particularly Butembo and Katwa”, a major axis in the northern part of North Kivu, the WHO official explained.

Gaza remains recovery points to possible war crimes, says UN rights chief

Gaza remains recovery points to possible war crimes, says UN rights chief
Bodies are still being pulled from the rubble of Gaza, three years after Israeli bombardment flattened entire neighbourhoods – most of them women and children.
The UN Human Rights High Commissioner said on Tuesday that this “painstaking” recovery effort raises serious questions about compliance with international law, and that war crimes may have been committed.
Volker Türk called for investigators to be given access to the territory. Palestinian authorities say thousands of bodies remain buried under rubble, but Israel is refusing entry to the heavy machinery needed to clear it.
“The remains of what appears to be entire families are now being unearthed at locations that were pulverized by Israeli attacks,” he said.
“It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst fears confirmed.”
Possible ‘tip of the iceberg’
The High Commissioner worried that remains recovered to date “may only be the tip of the iceberg” because “much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives.”
Furthermore, many areas where Israeli troops are deployed “continue to be levelled by bulldozers with no respect for the dead under the rubble.”
He stressed the critical need to preserve evidence of violations – including at destroyed sites – given ongoing legal proceedings regarding the conduct of hostilities in Gaza.
Allow investigators in
The rights chief called for international investigators to be allowed into all parts of Gaza to help gather evidence and noted that Israel refuses entry of heavy machinery for removing rubble.
He cited Palestinian civil defence authorities which reported more than 630 bodies and other human remains have been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025. They also estimated that over 8,000 are missing under the rubble.
“Every feasible effort must be taken to document and identify these victims, preserve forensic information and biological samples, record their burial locations and inform their families,” he said.
Recovery compounds suffering
Between 27 June and 27 August, local authorities reported recovering 233 of 407 bodies believed to be beneath 20 destroyed buildings, mostly in Gaza City. They included 74 children and 106 women.
This month, teams said they had recovered 96 bodies and human remains at one site in Az Zeitoun, a neighbourhood southeast of Gaza City which was allegedly struck in November 2023.
Most of the remains were recovered by hand, and among them were 58 children and 23 women.
“These painstaking recovery efforts are a stark reminder of the gravity and breadth of the destruction three years ago, compounded today by the prolonged suffering and misery brought by years of not knowing,” Mr. Türk said.
“The right of families to know the fate of their relatives does not end with identification and a dignified burial. They deserve to know the full truth.”
War crimes concerns
In a 2024 report, the High Commissioner’s Office, OHCHR, highlighted the use by Israel of heavy bombs of up to 2,000lbs from 9 October to 2 December 2023 against residential buildings, a school, refugee camps and a market, killing over 200 people.
The report concluded that the strikes may have violated fundamental principles of international humanitarian law, which requires warring parties to abide by the principles of distinction, proportionality and precautions in attack.
“On a number of occasions, I have expressed grave concerns that Israel’s choices of methods and means of conducting hostilities, including through the extensive use of explosive weapons with wide area effects in densely populated areas, failed to ensure that they effectively distinguish between civilians and fighters,” said Mr. Türk.
“The discovery of extensive remains under the rubble in Gaza City resurfaces these concerns of war crimes and other atrocity crimes.”

‘Super El Niño’ deepens hunger crisis in South Sudan – WFP

‘Super El Niño’ deepens hunger crisis in South Sudan – WFP
The already dire hunger crisis in South Sudan is becoming increasingly critical as violence, extreme weather and dwindling aid leave millions without enough food, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Tuesday.
Key points
- 7.8 million South Sudanese face high levels of acute food insecurity.
- El Niño is already threatening farming output.
- Sudan’s war is driving more refugees and returnees into South Sudan.
- Funding shortages and access constraints threaten life-saving food assistance.
“Conflict, displacement, economic hardship, climate shocks, and the situation in neighbouring Sudan are all converging to push millions of people deeper into vulnerability” just as humanitarian resources are starting to run out, said Matthew Hollingworth, WFP Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations.
Some 7.8 million people, or more than half of the country's population, struggle to find enough food each day, while 2.2 million children and 1.2 million pregnant and breastfeeding mothers require urgent nutrition support, he told reporters in Geneva.
October deadline
A further million vulnerable people could lose access to life-saving food and nutrition assistance by October without additional resources.
After returning from a visit to the country last week, Mr. Hollingworth insisted that the impact of the “super El Niño” is already immediately clear in South Sudan; even the most fertile agricultural areas have been affected, with crops failing and low yields due to drought.
Beyond South Sudan itself, the regional impact of extreme weather is also being felt in neighbouring Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Uganda and Kenya, causing a “bigger effect on food security in the entire area”, the WFP official warned.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern that typically occurs every two to seven years, when waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific become unusually warm, with impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns thousands of miles away. This year, El Niño is developing as the oceans are already exceptionally warm. Earlier this month UN chief António Guterres said that the phenomenon is “being supersized before our eyes”.
War in Sudan
Over the border in Sudan, the proximity of what UN humanitarians have called the world’s worst hunger and displacement crisis is making the dire situation even worse.
Each week, the country sees the influx of 3,000 refugees and South Sudanese who were formerly refugees in Sudan, “looking for safety, looking for food, looking for water, looking for shelter”, Mr. Hollingworth said.
The WFP official spoke of meeting women, children and older people in Renk, Upper Nile State, South Sudan, last week, who had “travelled for days, sometimes weeks on foot” to escape fighting between Government and opposition forces, arriving exhausted and hungry “into communities that are already struggling significantly to feed themselves and look after themselves”.
Access challenges continue to compound the crisis. Aid and commercial food transported along the River Nile “face illegal checkpoints and illegal taxation by soldiers across the entirety of the journeys that they take,” increasing operational costs and slowing down the delivery of assistance.
Illegal levies
In Upper Nile State’s capital Malakal, Mr. Hollingworth noted, “if a family is eating something other than tomatoes, okra, chilies and onions that are grown locally, anything else they are eating has been flown into Malakal” as it is too expensive to bring it in by road or by barge, including because of the illegal taxes that have to be paid along the way.
“This is starting not just to raise costs, it's starting to be a cost in terms of people's lives,” he concluded.

World fears major war more than any other global risk, UN survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

World fears major war more than any other global risk, UN survey finds
Two years ago, the idea of a large-scale war breaking out felt like a distant hypothetical to the experts who help chart the world’s dangers. Today it tops their list of fears, according to a new UN Global Risk Report.
The study draws on the views of 1,300 people from government, international organizations, civil society, the private sector and academia, spanning every region of the world.
They rated 28 political, economic, environmental, societal and technological threats on how likely they were, how damaging, and how ready the world was to cope.
Drumbeat of war
Large-scale war climbed 16 places up the rankings compared with 2024 – the steepest rise of any risk on the list. More than a third of those surveyed, 36 per cent, think its effects could touch a significant share of humanity within a year; 76 per cent expect that within seven years.
It is also a threat the world seems ill-equipped to face: large-scale war was the only risk to land in the top six across all four measures the survey tracked – importance, imminence, how interconnected it is with other dangers, and how unprepared institutions are to respond.
Two years ago, environmental threats, misinformation and pandemics dominated the picture. Now geopolitical tension, war and a weakening rule of law sit at its centre.
“The findings are sobering. Political risks have moved centre stage. The prospect of large-scale war is seen as far more important and far more immediate than it was two years ago,” Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in the report’s foreword. “At the same time, the institutions expected to respond are seen as less able to act.”
No region immune
The shift shows up everywhere. Large-scale war and geopolitical tension now rank among the top 10 threats in every one of the seven regions the survey covers, and in the top five in six of them.
Two years ago, these same risks made the top five in just one region.
Weapons of mass destruction also broke into the top 10 in Central and Southern Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and Oceania.
In Eastern and South-Eastern Asia, worries grew over a possible global financial crisis, the downsides of artificial intelligence, and the growing power of technology companies.
AI-related risks also entered the top 10 in Europe and North America.
Pandemics and biological threats, by contrast, fell out of the top 10 everywhere – a sharp reversal from two years ago, when they still ranked among the most pressing risks in Eastern and Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Sub-Saharan Africa.
Interconnected threats
No risk exists on its own, the report argues. Shortages of natural resources, economic fragmentation, misinformation and weakening multilateral institutions all raise the temperature on geopolitical tension – which in turn makes large-scale war more likely.
Of the 705 connections between risks that the survey identified, the link between geopolitical tension and war was the strongest.
AI alarm bell
Artificial intelligence draws particular attention in the report. Concerns about AI, other frontier technologies and the concentration of power they enable have grown sharply in two years – even as respondents say the multilateral system is the least prepared to handle technological threats.
Climate change, meanwhile, has not gone away: inaction on it remains the single risk rated most important overall, and it ranks high in every region, alongside worries about resource shortages.
The report’s authors caution that other environmental risks slipping down the list does not mean they have become less dangerous – only less visible. And visibility matters: issues that draw less attention often lose funding too.
Working together
So, what would help? Respondents pointed to weak governance and coordination, a lack of political consensus, and eroding trust and accountability as the biggest obstacles to managing risk – alongside poor prioritisation, resistance from the public, politicians or business, and gaps in data.
Separately, 86 per cent said funding for risk reduction simply was not enough, with the report singling out natural hazards and the risk of multilateral institutions collapsing as particularly underfunded.
No crystal ball
The UN is careful to frame the report as a snapshot of perceptions rather than a prediction. Respondents still see joint action between governments as by far the most effective means of prevention. No country, no company, no institution can face these risks alone.
“The 2026 Global Risk Report sets out the evidence that must inform our choices. We owe it to present and future generations to use this knowledge wisely, and to act while cooperation can still shape a safer course.
“The choice is ours,” the Secretary-General said.

Back to school in Haiti: ‘Madame, can you stop what the gangs are doing to us?’
When UNICEF’s Representative in Haiti Geetanjali Narayan stepped into a classroom in Port-au-Prince at the start of the new school year, she asked the children a simple question: What did they most need from the UN children’s agency?
“Madame, please, can you stop the armed groups? Can you stop what the gangs are doing to us?”
Her plea captured the reality confronting children across Haiti, where violence has disrupted schools, upended families, and made even the simple act of going to class an act of courage.
As children around the world head back to school, the start of the year in Haiti unfolds once again under the shadow of insecurity, displacement, and hardship. Children must cross gang-controlled zones to reach school, risking crossfire and forced recruitment.
Yet in a country battered by gang violence, school also remains a space of hope – where children can learn, reunite with their classmates and, despite everything, begin to imagine their future.
For Etzer, a father of four, internally displaced and an advocate for the rights of displaced people, returning to class means far more than simply going back to school.
After fleeing their neighborhood because of gang violence, many displaced children are reuniting with friends and rebuilding a social life brutally cut short by the crisis.
“Schooling is like therapy for these children,” he says. But in many areas, learning conditions remain extremely difficult.
Hope and fear
Jasmide, mother of seven-year-old Woodayline, is glad classes are reopening. But behind that hope lie the hardships facing many families: hunger, unemployment, insecurity, and the cost of schooling, which weighs particularly heavily on those who depend on private institutions.
“We Haitian parents are in favor of classes reopening – but not under the sub-human conditions being imposed on us,” she says.
Those concerns are widely shared among displaced families and communities scared by violence. Everywhere, Narayan says, she hears the same plea: to see children going to school safely.
“Above all, we want safety and continuity of education,” she adds.
Deadly insecurity
The scale of the crisis is staggering. UNICEF's latest figures, for the 2024–2025 school year, show that more than 1,600 schools were affected by insecurity – disrupting the schooling of over 240,000 children and the work of some 7,500 teachers.
Woodayline and Etzer's four children are among the many for whom a classroom is no longer a given.
In Port-au-Prince, where up to 90 per cent of the capital is under gang control, some schools have closed, become inaccessible, or been destroyed. Others now shelter families with nowhere else to go.
For many children, the danger begins before they even reach the classroom.
“Just yesterday, two young girls were kidnapped on their way to school. It was the day after the school year began,” Narayan recounts.
Such incidents cause “enormous fear and anxiety” among families, she explains – to the point that some parents now hesitate to let their children travel alone.
And the fear does not vanish once students are seated in class. A child who has been displaced or exposed to violence can hardly concentrate the way they used to. The teachers themselves may have fled their own neighborhoods or may no longer be able to reach their schools.
Keeping classrooms open
In response, UNICEF is helping more than 174,000 children this year across the country's West, Greater North, and Greater South regions.
The work ranges from distributing school supplies and helping children enroll to creating safe learning spaces, providing psychosocial support, training teachers to recognize and respond to signs of trauma, and rehabilitating damaged schools.
It also runs remedial classes and accelerated learning programs for children who have been out of school for months, or even years – a bridge back into the formal system. That support flows through the Ministry of National Education and targets the country's public schools.
‘They were so happy to be there’
At the launch of the school year, Narayan says she was struck by the students' enthusiasm. “They were so happy to be there.”
Parents want to be able to send them without fear. Teachers want to do their jobs under stable conditions. The children simply want to learn, and to feel normal again.
Despite everything, Haitian families and their children hold onto an aspiration that is as ordinary as it is defiant: to go to school, to learn, to find their friends again, and to imagine a future for themselves.

Ukraine: Attacks on education threaten an entire generation, UNICEF warns
In an underground classroom in Sumy, Ukraine, children sit quietly at their desks, busy with the day’s lessons. For the moment they are shielded from the horrors of nearly five years of war, but just barely.
It’s only 15 days into the new school year and already more than a thousand air raid alerts have sounded across the country, or more than 100 a day.
“Nobody hears them louder and deeper than children,” said Ricardo Pires, Deputy Spokesperson with the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), speaking from just outside the classroom door to journalists in Geneva.
“An air-raid siren means a maths lesson stops halfway through. Children leave their desks for shelter. They wait for the all-clear. They return. They try to concentrate again and then the siren sounds.”
Education under attack
Mr. Pires is sounding another type of alarm and this time for the international community.
“Nearly five years into the war in Ukraine, children’s right to education remains under attack, with consequences that will define an entire generation,” he warned.
As the full-scale Russian invasion grinds on, Sumy, located in eastern Ukraine, is among the hardest hit regions this year alongside Mykolaiv and Odesa.
One in two education facilities there has been damaged or destroyed in the fighting, but “across the country, the picture is just as stark.”
The Ukrainian Government estimates that between January and August of this year, hundreds more educational institutions were damaged, bringing the overall toll since the war began to over 4,200.
Learning losses, bleak futures
As Mr. Pires noted, “the cost to children is measured beyond broken walls, psychological scars and loud sirens.”
Educational assessments of 15-year-old Ukrainian students carried out by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) reveal that “a significant proportion” have not reached sufficient competency in subjects such as science, maths and reading.
“This narrows their options for further study, skilled work, and full participation in society as adults,” he noted.
Reading, writing and resilience
“Despite the war, Ukraine has demonstrated incredible resilience in sustaining the education system as verified by the stability of results between 2022 and 2025,” he said.
“However, as we continue to warn, children in Ukraine need peace to be able to learn properly.”
In Sumy, UNICEF has helped to establish 22 shelters-turned-schools, such as the one where he was speaking from which can accommodate some 300 students.
This month, nearly 4.2 million children across Ukraine – and more than 366,000 teachers - returned to school.
Yet a significant number continue to depend on blended or fully online learning, while nearly half of all pre-school aged children are missing out on regular education and care.
Winter threat and response
Mr. Pires said the approaching winter also poses another threat to education, as attacks on infrastructure will disrupt electricity and heating supply.
“Last year nearly two million children suffered in extreme winter conditions after being left without heat, electricity and water. Power cuts disrupted online lessons too, with the frontline areas like Sumy being hardest hit,” he said.
This winter, UNICEF aims to reach three million people in Ukraine, including 540,000 children.
The agency wants to ensure that 375,000 students can keep learning, including by repairing heating systems, providing back-up energy to schools, rehabilitating school shelters and supporting catch-up learning.
“We are doing everything we can to keep children learning, but no amount of support can shield their education from the consequences of continued attacks,” he said.

Escalating conflict drives new displacement in Yemen
The escalating conflict in Yemen is choking off aid shipments and driving fresh displacement, including to nearby Djibouti, with UN agencies reporting on Tuesday that nearly 100,000 people have been displaced since fighting intensified earlier this month.

- 93,864 individuals have been newly displaced across Yemen, said the International Organization for Migration (IOM)
- Rapidly escalating hostilities along Yemen’s western coast have forced thousands more to seek safety across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in Djibouti, said the UN refugee agency, UNHCR
