If the US Collapses Soon, Don’t Blame Emily St. John Mandel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

If the United States collapses in the near future, you’ll no doubt be tempted to point a few fingers. Just don’t blame Emily St. John Mandel.
As Covid tore across the planet, Mandel became something of a pandemic prophet for writing the hit 2014 novel, Station Eleven. Journalists and everyday Twitter users alike looked to her for guidance as they hunkered down at home, desperate for someone—anyone—to tell them what was happening, and what might come next. Now, Mandel is out with a new book, Exit Party, that documents the interwoven lives of people living in two different, near-future versions of the US: A violent, post-civil-war free-for-all, and a totalitarian state where surveillance runs roughshod over a paranoid populace. She started writing the book in 2022, when polarization and political extremism were already surging—but well before the era of Trump 2.0, widespread ICE raids, and tech-infused surveillance we’re living through today.
Exit Party is a tremendous, riveting, deeply human novel—one of the best I’ve read in years. And despite being strictly fictional, the two futures that Exit Party imagines also feel eerily, uncomfortably close to reality. But as Mandel reminded me when we sat down at WIRED’s New York studio, the book is also infused with plenty of hope, and forces readers to ask themselves important questions about what kind of person they’d be if it all went to hell. She was also, of course, quick to point out that “it doesn’t actually take any particular clairvoyance,” to see where this moment in US history might take us. So no, Mandel can’t help you much if the militias roll through—but Exit Party might offer a few lessons in how to show up for your neighbors. (And throw the best post-collapse party.)
You can read our full (light on spoilers) conversation below, or listen to Uncanny Valley anywhere you get your podcasts. Exit Party is out today, September 15, and I highly recommend you pick up a copy.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Emily, thank you so much for being here. I will get this out of the way at the top and acknowledge that we are both Brooklyn moms. And sometimes when you’re a Brooklyn mom, you become friends with another Brooklyn mom, and we are actually friends outside of work.
EMILY ST. JOHN MANDEL: Because you seek out the best mom you can find at the playground.
We met at the playground in the latter stages of the Covid-19 mask era. I’ve known you ever since. But regardless of that, and I’m saying this very, very genuinely, I read Exit Party—I was lucky enough to get a galley ahead of publication—in a single day. I highly recommend it.
Thank you so much. It’s such a pleasure to be here.
For those who didn’t get an advance copy, could you explain what it’s about?
God, the elevator pitch on this book has been so challenging.
I can understand why.
I suck at elevator pitches generally. But I think of this as a story about crime and resilience. It’s about trying to be a decent person when things are falling apart, and it’s about who you’re going to be at the end of the world. I don’t mean to imply that the collapse of a country is the end of the world, but what I do mean to imply is that it feels like it.
I do see this as a hopeful book. It’s about what comes next and trying to be a new person in a rapidly changing and difficult landscape.
It feels very timely, in troubling ways. When you think about what’s actually happening in the US right now and what’s happening in the US in the book, in what ways are those two places different?
The difference is that in the country that we live in, there’s still time. The United States that opens this story, that country ran out of time. That country fractured. I wish that it felt more fictional. You know, I started writing this book in the spring of 2022.
I was wondering about that.
We could already see the division that was coming because Trump was obviously so much on the horizon for a second term. But I wish it felt more speculative. I’m about to go out and do a 42-city tour where I talk about this absolutely fantastical speculative leap of imagination in which the United States falls apart.
Yeah, imagine if that happened. That would be wild.
Yeah, no one would’ve been able to see that coming. I don’t mean to be glib about it. It’s a terrifying prospect. A big part of the beginning of this book for me was working through my political anxieties.
In 2022?
Yes. I read the news. I’ve always read the news. It doesn’t actually take any particular clairvoyance to look ahead and see where the incredible division in this country could potentially lead. Of course I hope it won’t. But a way of thinking about that for me was, well, what might come next?
Suppose the worst were to happen. Suppose there were to be a second American Civil War. What might the aftermath be like? Which is not dissimilar to the project of Station Eleven. You know, imagining the aftermath of a very different kind of catastrophe and collapse.
This sounds ridiculous given everything I just said, but it’s actually a hopeful book. The book opens at the end of the world, but we’re going to a party. That’s kind of the spirit of it.
I have a memory, it was maybe about a year ago, we were having dinner with your wife. I knew that you had this book coming out. I didn’t know anything about it, and she was very stressed because she was like, “Book publishing is so slow. Look at everything happening in this country right now. This book that Emily has written is so timely right now. I can’t believe it’s not coming out for another year.”
Knowing that you started writing it in 2022 is interesting to me, because you have now watched Trump be reelected. You watched the ICE crackdowns happening at the top of the year. This encroachment of surveillance into different aspects of our lives, the ongoing fracturing of this country, the polarization. How has that felt in these last four years, and particularly once the book was finished and you knew what was in that book?
It’s funny, I remember that dinner. I remember my wife, Laura, her concern that the country might collapse before the book came out.
She’s like, “They’re going to ruin the book.”
Right. That is a spoiler. [Laughs] No. God, we have to laugh because otherwise it’s devastating.
Well, Donald Trump is going to ruin Emily’s book!
Yeah, stakes. Seriously.
No, it’s been a strange experience because, I don’t know if this is too big a spoiler, but the book envisions two different versions of the United States. There’s the vision we begin with where there has been a civil war, the country is fractured into somewhat contentious city states and small new republics and splinter groups. It’s a bit chaotic.
There’s another version of the country that is a totalitarian police state, and my experience of writing this book was that when I started writing it, I was just looking at the polarization, and I was thinking, “Well, obviously we’re in that first universe, the one where the country fractures into these little incompatible small new republics.” But by the time I finished the book, the ICE raids were happening, and my totalitarian vision of a country where citizens are disappeared by masked secret police wasn’t fictional anymore. So there was this feeling of struggling to stay ahead of the news cycle through the entire writing of this book.
Now, the protagonists in the book, Ibari and Ari, they’re the same person. But they also aren’t at all.
Right.
How did you think about the idea of identity in writing the book?
I’ve been fascinated for a really long time by the idea of the counter life. That’s the life you didn’t live, where you didn’t immigrate from Canada, or you went to a different school or took a different job or married a different person. These inflection points that would have made us, over the passage of time, into somewhat different people.
I think the reason I’m so interested in that idea is that the life I’m living feels a little bit improbable to me. I’m from Canada and I’m trained in contemporary dance, and I don’t have a high school diploma, so I do have moments of thinking, “This actually feels fairly implausible.”
I was thinking of identity in terms of the people we could have been. But then in this book, it was also interesting to me to think about, well, what is the counter life of the state? Because that’s a really interesting idea. I was going to say in any democratic country, but honestly in any country.
I was thinking about, well, if we take that idea of the counter life of the individual, these different people we could have been, how is that affected by the counter life of the state? Because we are so influenced by the environment we live in, the people that surround us. I think that I’m a different person having lived for 23 years in New York City than I would’ve been if I had stayed in, say, rural British Columbia where I grew up.
Oh, for sure. I think about that too all the time.
Yeah, you’re from Canada too.
I think a lot about, what if I had just stayed in Calgary?
Yeah. Canada is a little more chill.
It is a little more chill.
See, now here we are, both extremely un-chill people in New York City.
Yes, thriving.
Living our best lives. Extremely stressful lives, but here we are.
Ari and Ibari, they grow up in different versions of a country. They are so profoundly shaped by that country. I saw Ari as somebody who’s got this character flaw where she’s fundamentally drawn toward crime. Maybe that’s not even a flaw. Maybe it’s just an interest, because there’s a version of the world where she does the obvious thing and becomes a criminal, but there is another version of the world where she channels that into becoming the police. It was interesting to me to think about that, the way we might be drawn in one direction or another depending on the environment we’re raised in.
I almost hate to ask this, because both versions of the US that you portray in the book are really frightening in their own respects. But did you find yourself drawn towards preferring one over another? Is there one version of this that you would rather live in?
No, they’re both really hard. They’re both awful. The version I want to live in is Canada, candidly. It’s like, do you want to live in chaos, or do you wanna live in a totalitarian police state? Hard pass on both.
That’s an idea I’ve been thinking about a lot: no version of a country lasts forever, and there’s both terror and hope in that idea. The totalitarian police state version’s not going to last forever, and neither is the period of total chaos. What I wanted to suggest, and this is kind of a deep cut for people who have read a lot of my work, but in Sea of Tranquility there’s a futuristic section where an author’s on a book tour in the year 2300, and she’s traveling between the Republic of California, the Atlantic Republic, and the Kingdom of Deseret, and it’s chill enough to support a book tour, you know?
But yeah, I kind of wanted to suggest that this is the founding story of that space.
I wanted to ask you about your multiverse. You have a history that your diehards, your fans, really glom onto, which is you pull from previous works and you bring people and worlds into your new work, and that continues with Exit Party.
You’ve talked about it as a multiverse, a cinematic universe. The New Yorker called it, quote, “The Mandel Cinematic Universe,” which I think is pretty incredible. Is there a master plan here, or is it just ad hoc as inspiration strikes?
I wish I could say I had the kind of brain that could hold an entire multiverse. I should just say yes, but, uh, no. There is no plan. That’s the baseline for individual books when I start them, but also for The Mandel-verse, as some people have also called it. I don’t have any kind of master plan that I’m working towards. I just like the opportunities for connection. I guess I have some abstract longing for order in a chaotic universe, you know? I like finding the moments when books can be drawn together, or sometimes I just fall in love with a particular character, and I want to spend more time with that person.
Like Miranda in Station Eleven, I really liked her. It was really interesting to get to see a completely different facet of her life in The Glass Hotel, to see her as a shipping executive as opposed to an artist. Then I guess with Exit Party, I did lay the groundwork in Sea of Tranquility for a world where the United States no longer exists, so I guess you could make the argument that that implies the origin story.
One of the things I love about your books, several of them at least, is that they’re set in the future, but they don’t foreground the technology. They foreground the people and the human stories and the lived experience. Technology is often present, and it’s certainly present in Exit Party, but how do you think about introducing technology and science into your work? How much research goes into that, and how much commitment to factual accuracy as opposed to just letting your imagination run?
What I’m aiming for is plausibility in the context of a literary novel. Which is going to be a disappointingly low bar for your average WIRED podcast interviewee.
But I think that you’ve touched upon a really interesting choice that writers of speculative fiction need to make every time we embark on a new project, which is really just how deep into the weeds you want to go on your science fictional technology.
There are writers who go pretty deep. I loved Cixin Liu’s work, The Three-Body Problem, and the rest of that series. He will go so deep into these science fictional technologies, which to my totally untrained eye, feel totally plausible.
I did flirt with that a little bit when I was starting out on Sea of Tranquility, which has a time-traveling detective, because we were all deranged during the pandemic, but yeah, I was thinking about “Well, how would this actually work?”
I was reading about the quantum blockchain and trying to understand what the mechanics could be. But then at a certain point I realized, you know what? It’s just transport. Like, if I’m not explaining how your car works in the 2020 segment of the novel, then why do I care about the mechanics of the time machine?
There is a part in your book from Ibari’s perspective. She’s working as a detective in the secret police in one of these United States. She has this thought, and I’ll quote it, “I’ve spent a long time thinking about the nature of life in a surveillance state, which is perhaps obvious given my work, but there are observations I’ve made that I share with no one, and one of them has to do with the way in a place like this, reality splits into two.” That line, “reality splits into two,” is great. What does it mean to you?
In the context of that passage, she’s a secret agent with a cover story, basically. But the cover story is that she’s a professor, and she actually is teaching real classes. So it’s not false that she’s a professor, it’s just that she’s also secret police.
She has the most obvious kind of surface experience of that idea of living a double life. I don’t want to say it’s exactly modeled on East Germany, but the Stasi apparatus, where civilians were constantly reporting on each other, which everybody thought was overstated until the country collapsed, and it turned out to have been even bigger than anyone knew. Everybody really was reporting on each other. That does create this awful kind of doubleness where there’s the part of you that’s a friend, but then there’s a part of you that’s reporting on the friend to your handler, and both of those ideas are true.
But I think that also living that kind of doubleness would do a lot of damage to a person. It sounds so literary and pretentious to say damage to your soul, but I think that might be the situation.
In that surveillance state, there are some very stressful passages, at least for me, where you realize that none of these people can really fundamentally trust each other. And then in the other universe, there is this baseline notion of trust eroding because everybody is just looking out for themselves in the chaos. How were you thinking about that as you were writing the book? Did you have any revelations about trust in this country that we could all learn from?
It’s not specific to this country, but this actually leads us into AI for me. Do you remember when we were kids and a video was proof? It was like, “Oh, there is video evidence. Case closed.” How terrifying and damaging and ridiculous that our children are being raised in a world where a video means absolutely nothing. It’s incredibly hard to authenticate, and that’s what I find myself thinking about when I think about trust.
Sometimes I lurk on Threads, just recreationally. It is such a trash fire. It’s like Twitter in, I don’t know, 2012 or something. But something real that’s really struck me is the degree of betrayal that people feel when it emerges that an author has been using AI, and I share that sense of betrayal. It offends me in some incredibly deep way, and when I try to parse why that is, I think trust might be the answer.
I was going to ask you about AI. You write novels. You also work in Hollywood. And so you have exposure to what’s happening in the book world around AI, and also what is happening in the entertainment industry. Do you use it at all?
I don’t. Maybe this makes me an outlier at this point. I haven’t found it reliable in search, and so that made me distrust it completely.
Every now and again, I like to search and make sure that my daughter is not on the internet, basically. So I searched “Emily St. John Mandel daughter” I think about a year ago, and AI is so confidently wrong. It confidently introduced me to my son Leo, born in 2016, and said, “Emily St. John Mandel does not have a daughter.” And it’s so confident that you have a moment of just like, “Do I have a son?”
I do not have a son named Leo. I have no idea where that came from. I searched again a month later, and it had revised that, and my daughter remained unnamed, which is what I wanted to confirm.
But it made me distrust it fundamentally from a search perspective. I know that it can be used to streamline administrative tasks. I haven’t used it as such. I can write my own emails.
I was going to say, you’re still writing your own emails.
Yeah, exactly.
So am I.
I read your interview with Matthew Belloni talking about the use of AI. It was interesting to me because without refuting anything he’s saying, I’ve just had a different experience, and I haven’t heard of people using it in my writers’ rooms in Hollywood.
I suppose AI is an argument for the in-person writers’ room. You really can’t use it if you’re sitting around a table and there’s a chalkboard. Probably people are using it without my knowledge, but I haven’t personally encountered it.
When you look at the effect it’s having on book publishing—we have covered some of this—but it is chaos out there.
How does that look from where you sit? Do you worry about AI slop books becoming a mainstream commodity, taking up a bigger share of the fiction market? Or do you think people just don’t have the taste for that?
I’d like to think they don’t have the taste for it, but I think the slop will get less sloppish with time. What I really worry about, actually, is less the work, and I worry more about writers. Because for me, I started publishing in 2009, and I have a consistent voice across books.
My process is such that it would be very easy for me to produce iterative drafts of what I’ve been doing if I were ever forced to prove that it’s not AI, which it absolutely is not. But not all writers have that process. Some are just, you know, changing a Word doc over a period of time. Not all of us keep written notes. Something that’s emerging that alarms me is that it’s very hard to prove sometimes that your work wasn’t AI.
Oh, like to prove a negative.
Yeah, to prove a negative. The reputational risk is enormous. That’s the end of a career, or at the very least, the end of a book deal.
I had a weird experience a while ago where I was just curious, so I found some free AI detection thing online, which probably stole my work, and I pasted the first chapter of Exit Party in, and what it came back with was there’s a 20 percent chance that AI was used on this. At first I was completely beside myself. I was like, “How does it think that?” And then I realized, oh, because Anthropic stole five of my novels to train their LLMs.
But to your point, I mean, the idea of being a writer for a living right now, and you’re doing the work yourself, you’re doing it with integrity, you are painstaking in your process, and one accusation or one result … And these tools are extremely flawed …
Yeah. They’re very inaccurate.
… But that can end a career. The stakes of this are very, very high. I actually did the same thing. I think anyone who writes for a living right now has this paranoia. I fed some of my articles into one of these tools because I was like, “I just want to know what it’s going to say.” And I got back zero percent.
Congratulations.
Thank you, but it was such a relief because there is this sense, this cloud of someone can point a finger. And the people who are using AI, I would argue, in creative pursuits, are ruining it for everybody else.
I would agree with that, and I don’t have any respect for them. It’s like if you can’t write, then maybe do something different. There are a lot of better jobs.
I wanted to spend a bit of time talking about you and your career. You grew up in Canada, you were in Toronto. Objectively speaking, where you are now is improbable relative to where you were then. Tell us about those early years.
I’m going to digress for a second back to the book. So much of this book is about the condition of living one life after another. And this is so many lives ago that it’s like looking back at a stranger.
I grew up in rural British Columbia, Vancouver Island, and then Denman Island, which is, just for context, about the same size and shape as Manhattan, but with 1,000 people. It’s forest and deer and a general store. I was homeschooled. I did a couple semesters of community college without ever getting my GED. I auditioned successfully for a conservatory program in contemporary dance in Toronto, and I was a professional dancer after that for, like, five minutes.
I went pretty far, but I never really joined a company. I danced for a couple of independent choreographers. I loved that experience, but I never got into one of the big companies, I think in part because I’d realized by then that I no longer loved it. There’s this phenomenon, I think, where if you’ve been dead set on one thing your entire life, like since you were six, then you can fall out of love with it. People change.
In my early 20s, I realized that dance was feeling like more of a chore than anything else, and I kinda resented it, and I didn’t love it anymore. But this is kind of spectacularly poor planning on my part. I’d taken out student loans to go to the School of Toronto Dance Theatre, not a degree-granting program. So I had a mountain of student loan debt, no degree, no high school diploma. It would feel overwrought if you wrote that in a novel. My editor would probably do, like, question marks in the margin.
Right. Many poor choices.
I had a totally destroyed credit rating in Canada due to student loan debt. So I moved to the United States. That was the solution to that problem. I’d always written just as a hobby. It was just something I loved and something I did a little bit compulsively. Like, if I went for a long walk, I’d bring a notebook because otherwise I might start writing stories on Starbucks napkins.
I was starting to write in Toronto. I met a guy who lived in New York and we were dating, and I moved to New York to be with him. Moved back to Montreal, broke up, and then I was kinda stranded in Montreal working. In winter, working retail, trying to figure out what to do with the rest of my life.
And it’s a cold city.
It is a very cold city, which actually played into my writing process. My roommates and I were dead broke, so we kept the heat turned down pretty low. I would go to bed at 7:00 pm just because I was so cold. It was easier to be asleep. I would sleep until about 1:00 in the morning and then naturally wake up. I’d get up in the middle of the night. I would dress to write. I had this feeling that I was doing something formal and important.
I would put on, like, a sweater and a tie and my warmest coat and go out with my laptop to the 24-hour cafe two blocks away, and I would write until morning, and that was the book that ultimately became Last Night in Montreal.
I was able to find a way to move back to New York, with, I don’t know, $400 and a 10-day sublet in the West Village when I was 22 or so. I’ve been here ever since. I started writing Last Night in Montreal in Montreal. I finished it in New York, and then I just started cold querying agents, and the 13th or 14th one found me in her slush pile and took me on.
There was a lot of luck and also an incredible amount of hard work and literally cold nights in Montreal.
And you had a day job?
I did. I’m from a very working-class background. And what that came with for me was an absolute terror of quitting the day job, because there is no safety net. I was working retail in Toronto and Montreal. I became an assistant in New York. I had a really great job for a long time at The Rockefeller University. I was an admin in a cancer research lab, and I loved that. It was such a pleasure to be surrounded by such smart people doing interesting work, and the health insurance was incredible.
I kept that job until a year after Station Eleven came out.
That’s so wild.
It got so surreal, Katie, I can’t tell you. One of my jobs in that position, or one of my tasks, rather, was to book plane tickets for my boss. But I wasn’t booking my own plane tickets for the tour. I had three publicists doing that. Or, like, there was a day when I had to leave work early because I had a photo shoot at Time magazine.
Did someone tell you, “Emily, it’s time. You need to quit your job?”
You know, you know what it was? I did a podcast where the other guest was this comedian, Josh Gondelman. And at the time, I guess it was a few months after Station Eleven had come out, and I was really grappling with the day job question. Like, does it make sense to leave? Is leaving crazy? What if I never have another successful book? And he told me that a fellow comedian had once told him, “Keep your day job until you can’t afford to anymore.” I found that to be a really helpful way of framing it. I kept that job until I found out I was three months pregnant, and then that was too many things.
Station Eleven was successful right out of the gate, and then it had this second life during the pandemic. You became this pandemic prophet for people who were asking you on Twitter, like, “Help. What do we do in the pandemic?” Looking back on it now, what stands out to you from that experience? What was it like to write a fictional book and then be asked for guidance in a real-world pandemic?
It was so surreal, and the requests were so misplaced. Like, if you’re going to look to a writer for guidance, I want to be like, "Go talk to Ed Yong of The Atlantic." Or a scientist or something. There were so many people who were more qualified than I was to say what to do in a pandemic. It was very strange being … accused sounds too dramatic, but being accused of being a prophet in a weird way.
What a dark thing.
I was never able to quite convey at the time that there was always going to be another pandemic. I didn’t see myself as having foretold anything. The way I thought of it at the time was, well, if I’d written a novel with a fictional war, does that mean that I predicted whatever war came next after that in the real world?
What's funny is I was exactly as unprepared as everybody else. I’ve had this sideline for years of doing on-stage conversations and lectures, and I was doing that right up until March 2020. I had this long lecture that I developed about post-apocalyptic literature, about pandemics and Shakespeare and all themes that dovetailed with Station Eleven.
I was literally traveling the country delivering a lecture that contained the phrase, “There will always be another pandemic.” It is so embarrassing how shocked I was that there was, in fact, another pandemic. I was scrambling for toilet paper like everybody else.
Yeah, you’re like, “Guys, I don’t know if you should put Clorox all over your groceries.”
Yeah. And I did.
I definitely did that, for probably longer than I should have.
Same.
I’m curious about how you deal with celebrity. Just thinking about that social media onslaught during Covid. You don’t strike me as someone who’s particularly eager to post, you know what I mean?
You’ve discovered my secret. I’m not eager to post.
How do you deal with that part of the job? And do you feel pressure to do it differently than you’re inclined to do?
If I were on Instagram just to be on Instagram, I don’t know if you’d ever see my face, you know? Because I love posting weird, beautiful little videos. Like, I just posted one that’s spiderwebs on a hiking trail in the Adirondacks last week.
If I see something cool and beautiful and I think, “Oh, that’s kind of amazing,” in just a tiny little moment, and could I set it to music? That would be cool. I really like Reels. That’s how I probably naturally would use it. I do feel a certain pressure to post, I guess, to post my face for the algorithms. I do feel like I need to promote my books because it is literally how I pay my rent.
It just kind of feels like part of the job. I don’t want to get too negative here because I do genuinely love interacting with readers. So I guess I kind of want it both ways.
There is pressure there. I find social media generally terrifying. I’ve had a lot of very negative interactions over the years, and what’s funny is just the way the human brain is wired, the positive interactions outweigh the negative interactions 1,000-to-one. But I also remember the negative ones. The negative ones stand out.
What is it like to promote a book in the year 2026? How has it changed?
I think that I have a very atypical experience of book promotion, because I had these three novels published by a really small press, and then I jumped to Knopf in the US, HarperCollins Canada, and Pan Macmillan in the UK for Station Eleven, and I’ve been with those three publishers ever since.
Because Station Eleven was so successful, a lot of marketing resources have been poured into the subsequent books. I think that that gives me a really unusual experience, and I think that it’s not normal at all. So it makes me hesitant to draw any generalizations, because for me it’s fine, you know?
But that’s certainly not the case for the vast majority of novelists. I think there’s so much distraction and chatter and such short attention spans that I think it’s incredibly difficult to start out as a novelist now. It was never actually easy, but my sense is that it might be harder now in this more fractured and more chaotic media landscape. I think it becomes harder for a novelist to break through.
Do you have any advice for those people?
Stay off Threads, for real. I don’t really post, but I do read. I see the most deranged publishing advice on Threads.
Like what?
I don’t even know. Every time I read it, I’m like, “No, that makes no sense. Don’t do that.”
I want to end by coming back to Exit Party. [As you said], you were accused, for lack of a better word, of being a prophet when Station Eleven came out before the Covid-19 pandemic. You’ve now written a book that is close to what we are going through in the US. Are you bracing yourself for a similar reaction?
Yeah. But look, if the country collapses, it’s not my fault.
She said it here first.
I didn’t do it. I just read the news and got freaked out like everybody else.
Is there anything in the worlds you’ve created in the book that you hope turns out to be prophetic?
Absolutely. I don’t want to take credit for the parties after … but you know what? It’s hope itself. There is a lot of hope in this book. It opens at a moment when the country has collapsed, but something new is taking its place, and it’s a kind of chaotic in-between period, but I never meant to imply that would last forever.
I think that settles down into something more stable and potentially better. And then on the side of the book that deals with a totalitarian state, that totalitarianism is already crumbling toward the end. I think that we see that even now in our current incredibly dark political moment.
I mean, maybe what you’ll get credit for predicting is the dawn of an even better version of this country.
That would be lovely.

Convicted terrorist seeks €2m in damages over detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:59:34 UTC
18:59:34 KST

A Tunisian man convicted of terrorism offences in Belgium but later acquitted in the US is seeking damages from the Belgian state totalling more than €2 million.
Convicted terrorist seeks €2m in damages over detention
Nizar Trabelsi was arrested in Brussels in 2001 on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack on the Kleine Brogel airbase in Limburg on behalf of Al-Qaeda. He served 10 years in prison in Belgium. The US then requested that he be extradited, as American military personnel were stationed at the airbase.
According to Trabelsi’s lawyers, Belgium should not have complied with this demand. The European Court of Human Rights ruled that it violated the European Convention on Human Rights and ordered Belgium to pay €60,000 in damages.
Trabelsi spent 10 years in pre-trial detention in the US, before a jury acquitted him of all charges in 2023. He was then held in immigration detention for two years.
Following a protracted legal battle, Trabelsi was transferred to Brussels Airport in August last year by the US immigration service. He was immediately moved to a detention centre for undocumented migrants in Merksplas.
A new series of legal proceedings culminated in his release last October. Since then, he has been living in Brussels with the status of an undocumented foreign national who cannot be deported. He has no access to health insurance and cannot enter into a tenancy or employment contract.
A bailiff served the Belgian state with a claim for €950,000 in damages at the end of last year. The state disputes this and maintains that it has fulfilled its obligations.
Trabelsi’s lawyers have now recalculated the claim, arriving at a total of €2,075,000. This comprises €15,000 for each day he was detained at Merksplas between 8 August and 22 October, as well as damages on the grounds that the Belgian state failed to fulfil obligations imposed by the Court of Appeal.
They also want the state to cover costs, totalling €15,697, and have initiated legal proceedings. The court has one month to deliver a judgement.
Justice minister Annelies Verlinden of CD&V previously replied to a parliamentary question from Vlaams Belang MP Francesca Van Belleghem that the Belgian state has already paid a total of €552,096 in penalties and damages to Trabelsi or his lawyers.

Russian forces kill 11, injure 64 across Ukraine over past day, hit diesel locomotive close to Polish border

Russian forces kill 11, injure 64 across Ukraine over past day, hit diesel locomotive close to Polish border
At least 11 people were killed and 64 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as a diesel locomotive was hit in western Ukraine, close to the Polish border, local authorities said on Sept. 15.
According to the State Emergency Service, a diesel locomotive caught fire in western Volyn Oblast, which borders Poland, following a Russian strike overnight on Sept. 15.
Emergency services put out the fire, and no one was injured.
Previously, on Sept. 13, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw train near Ukraine's border with Poland, Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) reported. The train was about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
Alongside the attack near the Polish border, Russian forces launched 200 Shahed-type attack drones, including jet-powered versions, on Sept. 15, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 187 drones, while strikes were recorded at seven locations. Debris from downed drones fell at three locations, the Air Force said.
In northern Chernihiv Oblast, a Russian attack on the agricultural enterprise's warehouses in Pryluky killed three people and injured 15, governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed, and 12 were injured as Russian forces attacked settlements in the region 32 times over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed, and one was injured by Russian attacks, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Regional Defense Council, said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and the surrounding regions, killing one person and injuring 16 others, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region killed one person and injured 11 others, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.

Trains return to schedule after damaged overhead wires near Sorø are repaired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:54:51 UTC
18:54:51 KST

Train services between Fredericia, Odense and Copenhagen returned to their normal schedule at 10 a.m. Tuesday after damaged overhead wires near Sorø were repaired.
Trains between Copenhagen Airport and Slagelse also resumed normal operations, Banedanmark, which manages Denmark’s rail infrastructure, and passenger rail operator DSB said on X.
Banedanmark warned that some delays could occur while services restart. It advised passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public journey-planning service, before traveling.
The damage had caused cancellations and delays since noon Monday. Repair work covered the section between Ringsted and Slagelse.
Banedanmark described the repairs as “extensive” and “very complex.” A support cable had fallen, and the equipment holding it had also been damaged.
“These are just some of the damages we see on our traction power system,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Sigsgaard said Monday.
Banedanmark received the first report of the problem at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train traffic was then stopped completely while workers identified the cause.
DSB and Banedanmark said passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes could use DSB’s travel time guarantee.
DSB paid 67 million DKK in passenger compensation during the first six months of 2026, more than twice as much as during the same period in 2025.
A delay of at least 30 minutes provides a new ticket for the same route or a refund of 50 percent of the ticket price. Passengers delayed by an hour can receive 75 percent and claim up to 75 DKK for food and drinks.
Delays exceeding 90 minutes qualify for a full ticket refund.
According to a press release from the Danish Finance Ministry, Naalakkersuisut (the Government of Greenland) and the Danish government signed a partial agreement on Tuesday worth 1.2 billion DKK for investments in Greenland from 2026 to 2029.
“The agreement means, among other things, that there will be a relief package for the Greenlandic citizens who are the most vulnerable economically,” the ministry said.
The governments have also agreed to provide funding for Greenland’s utility sector. This includes water supply projects in Ilulissat and support for Nukissiorfiit, Greenland’s self-rule-owned utility company, to help develop the country’s energy infrastructure.
Funding will also go toward operating Greenland’s new international airports, with the agreement including money for feasibility studies in 2027 for a new regional airstrip in Ittoqqortoormiit and a new deep-water port in Qaqortoq.
“We are investing in initiatives that can be felt in the everyday lives of the Greenlandic people, and which at the same time support Naalakkersuisut’s work to develop a strong and sustainable Greenlandic society,” Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said.
The agreement follows another deal between Greenland and Denmark reached in February, which provided funding for Greenlandic patients to receive treatment in the Danish healthcare system.
Both agreements stem from a framework agreement reached in September last year between Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Under that framework, the two sides agreed on a package worth 1.6 billion DKK for Greenland’s healthcare system, the deep-water port and a new airstrip.
Around 100,000 AL Sydbank customers will no longer have to pay up to 600 DKK a year for an account, online banking access and a debit card.
The offer was previously available to customers of Arbejdernes Landsbank. Following the merger of Arbejdernes Landsbank, Vestjysk Bank and Sydbank, it will now be extended to all customers of the new bank, AL Sydbank.
“When we did the merger, we promised that you would be able to get an account, access to online banking, and a debit card without it costing anything,” said Svend Randers, AL Sydbank’s director responsible for private customers.
“That is the promise we are fulfilling now, and it applies both to our existing customers who do not yet have those terms, and then of course the new customers who hopefully will join,” he said.
Randers said the bank hopes the offer will attract new customers and encourage existing customers to stay.
“And then of course we hope that in the longer term, it means that those customers will want to do more business with us when they eventually buy a home or car or save up for retirement or something else entirely,” he said.
The change comes after AL Sydbank told customers this summer that several fees would change following the merger.
According to a Mybanker analysis for TV 2, fees increased for between 55 and 60 percent of the bank’s services, depending on which bank a person previously used. Between 25 and 35 percent of fees decreased.
Customers must have their NemKonto, the bank account used for payments from Danish public authorities, with AL Sydbank to qualify for the free account.
The bank has not yet decided which debit card will be included.

Nearly six in 10 Danish companies with more than 10 employees now use artificial intelligence, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark. That’s almost four times the share recorded three years ago.
In 2026, 59 percent of these companies use AI, up from 15 percent in 2023. The share was 42 percent in 2025.
The uses of AI include analyzing text, converting spoken language into machine-readable code, generating images and videos, and automating work processes.
Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said it has seen AI move from being mainly a topic of discussion to a tool used in daily business.
“Companies’ use of artificial intelligence is here to stay, and we can see that the large companies are the furthest ahead,” Frederikke Saabye, industry director at Dansk Erhverv, said.
According to the business organisation, companies see greater efficiency as the main benefit of using AI. A lack of employee skills, knowledge and time are the biggest barriers to making greater use of the technology.
IT-Branchen, an industry association representing technology companies in Denmark, said the wider use of AI also increases the need to consider issues such as quality, transparency and data security.
“The more the technology spreads, the more important issues of quality, transparency, data security, and not least human judgment become,” IT-Branchen’s CEO Natasha Friis Saxberg said, adding that the development makes broader AI knowledge and training more important, including upskilling and continuing education for employees.
The Danish government plans to charge tourists 20 DKK per overnight stay in Copenhagen and Aarhus and introduce a levy on cruise ships, according to government sources and a memo obtained by Børsen.
The previously undisclosed measures would help fund tax cuts that the minority government will seek support for this autumn. The plans require backing from other parties, expected to come from the center-right opposition.
The government wants to abolish the 7.5% intermediate tax on annual income between 641,200 DKK and 777,900 DKK. It also plans to remove the top-top tax on income exceeding 2,592,700 DKK.
Corporate tax would fall from 22% to 19% over three years. The ceiling for share savings accounts would rise to 500,000 DKK over the same period, and taxes on shares would be reduced.
Planned funding measures include keeping the duty on chocolate and sweets, reducing the research and development deduction for companies and raising taxes on dividends received by major shareholders.
The government also wants to limit interest deductions to 150,000 DKK for individuals and 300,000 DKK for couples. Estates worth more than 10 million DKK would face a tax rate 15 percentage points higher than today.
The tax cuts are not fully covered by higher taxes and duties. The government plans to use about 1.5 billion DKK from available public funds in 2027, rising to about 2 billion DKK in 2029.
Denmark’s government consists of the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Moderates and Social Liberals. It does not have a parliamentary majority.
Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.
Denmark has rejected Russia’s claim that a Danish military helicopter acted “provocatively” before a Russian frigate fired two flares toward it Monday.
Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Danish helicopters had repeatedly performed “dangerous maneuvers” near Russian warships.
“The latest incident shows that the communication problems are not on the Russian navy’s side, but on the Danish side,” Barbin wrote to the Danish news agency Ritzau.
Denmark’s Armed Forces said the frigate fired two signal or distress flares toward an Air Force Fennec helicopter in international waters off Gedser. The helicopter was conducting routine photographic monitoring of the ship.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates called Barbin’s account “a Russian excuse” and denied that Denmark had provoked the frigate.
“What we do to monitor our own immediate area is completely legal, and it does not give the Russians any alibi whatsoever to start firing at us, even if it is only with flares,” Rasmussen told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats also said the helicopter had a legitimate reason to be there and was following normal practice.
Barbin said Russia would investigate the incident. He also cited an alleged encounter on August 27, 2025, when a Danish helicopter flew low over the Russian warship Viceadmiral Kulakov near the German island of Fehmarn.
The ambassador said that helicopter created a collision risk and failed to answer radio calls or warnings. Ritzau has asked the Danish Defense Ministry for comment on that allegation.
Denmark has summoned Barbin to the Foreign Ministry for talks about Monday’s incident.
The Danish government will require police to register all potential crimes as criminal cases and end the practice of shelving reports without a proper investigation.
The Justice Ministry announced Tuesday that it would implement all recommendations from the National Audit Office, Denmark’s independent public spending watchdog. The disputed police practice is known as “washing cases.”
“Citizens must naturally be able to have confidence that the police handle their case properly and correctly, regardless of where in the country you live,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said.
“In the future, all potential criminal cases must be registered as actual criminal cases,” he added.
The Public Accounts Committee, a parliamentary oversight body, strongly criticized police in May after receiving a National Audit Office report on the practice. Cases were reportedly shelved partly to save resources.
The new government reshuffled senior police leadership in June. Top positions in the National Police and PET, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, changed hands.
Several justice spokespersons in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, said they had no confidence in National Police Commissioner Thorkild Fogde after he said he did not know about the practice. Fogde was later removed from the position.
The ministry did not say whether police would receive additional funding. Wammen previously said he was open to providing more money and noted that a multiyear agreement had already increased funding and training.
The National Police and Director of Public Prosecutions must regularly report on future developments to the political parties behind that agreement.
Two earlier State Prosecutor reports were not used because the National Audit Office identified issues they had missed, Wammen said.

The hearing will begin at 1 p.m. at Copenhagen City Court, the Copenhagen Police prosecution service said Tuesday. A formal indictment has not yet been filed.

The incident happened June 30 during a public screening at Islands Brygge of the World Cup match between Norway and Ivory Coast.
The Swedish man fell after being struck, hit his head and later died from his injuries. He worked for the Swedish police but attended the event as a private citizen.

The 24-year-old Danish citizen is suspected of stomping on the Swedish man while he was lying down and hitting another Swedish citizen.
The 29-year-old, a Somali citizen, is suspected of kicking the second Swedish man. Police have notified him of the charge by telephone and through his defense lawyer because they have not located him.
Police have said the three cases will be handled separately because there is no evidence that the men acted together. Court dates for the other two men have not been announced.

The frigate fired two flares, which are normally used as attention signals at sea. One passed close to the helicopter.
“It is obviously an escalation from the Russian side,” said Thomas Danielsen, defense spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Alex Ahrendtsen, defense spokesperson for the Danish People’s Party, urged calm.
“Of course, we should not go to war with the Russians because of some signal lights that have been sent up,” he said.

A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.
Russian frigate fires flares near Danish military helicopter in international waters
A Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, Denmark’s Armed Forces said.
The Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the ship when the flares were fired. One passed close to the aircraft, according to a military statement.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea. No personnel were injured, and the helicopter was not damaged.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats called the incident serious and described Russia’s actions as “very unprofessional seamanship.”
“It is serious. It is an expression of the boundaries having been moved regarding the willingness to take risks from the Russian side,” Bruus said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen will summon the Russian ambassador to discuss the incident, though the date of the meeting has not been announced. Bruus said he did not expect further action beyond that meeting.
The defense minister said the incident would not change Denmark’s monitoring operations.
“We view it seriously, but it is not the case that we will change our behavior, understood in the sense that we have a completely legitimate task in monitoring what is going on,” Bruus said.
Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party, said the incident showed that Russian provocations had reached Denmark.
She called for NATO unity and continued support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
“It is therefore crucial that NATO stands united, and that we continue to support Ukraine,” Støjberg said. She added that she expected a briefing from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.
CPH Half will expand to 45,000 runners for its race on September 19, 2027, because of high demand, organizer Sparta Atletik og Løb, a Danish athletics and running organization, said in a news release.
Around 35,000 people are taking part in this year’s half marathon, up from about 32,000 in 2025.
Tickets for the 2027 race will be sold through a lottery instead of on a first-come, first-served basis.
Registration for the lottery opens September 16 and remains open for two weeks. People can register alone or in groups of up to three. Each group will either be selected together or not selected at all.
Selected runners will have 48 hours to buy a ticket. The price is DKK 795 plus a small administration fee.
“When demand is so high, access to the bib numbers must also function in a way where everyone has a fair and equal chance of getting a bib number,” Dorte Vibjerg, CEO of Sparta Atletik og Løb, said in the release.
The organizers also used a lottery to sell tickets for this year’s CPH Half, which is part of the World Athletics Road Running Championships. Similar systems are used for major marathons in Berlin and London.
This year’s race starts Sunday. Elite international runners will begin first, followed by the other participants.
Danish police brought 79 new charges linked to possible crime-for-hire cases from January through the end of July, the Ministry of Justice said Monday.
In total, police brought 316 charges from April 2024 through the end of July this year that may involve crime-for-hire, a practice also known as “Violence as a Service.”
The figures come from NSK, a Danish police unit that handles serious and organized crime. In January, authorities had recorded 237 charges, according to figures released by the ministry in February.
The government disclosed the latest figures as it sent a bill proposing stricter penalties and other measures against gangs and crime-for-hire for consultation. That process allows judges, lawyers, police and other groups to submit concerns or objections before the proposal moves forward.
The bill would increase penalties for crime-for-hire and treat criminal families in the same way as gangs.
“We will not tolerate children and young people being recruited into a life of crime, and residential areas being marked by fear, control, and parallel power structures,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said in a statement.
The proposal would also add a provision to the penal code intended to make it easier to convict people who provide minor services to gang leaders.
Other measures include allowing background checks for dockworkers and increasing the penalty for violating a stay ban. Police have recorded a large increase in such violations.
A stay ban can be imposed on a person who has committed a crime connected to a gang. It prevents that person from entering a specific area, such as part of a town or municipality, for a set period.
Violating a stay ban currently carries a fine of 10,000 DKK. Under the proposed law, a violation would result in 30 days in prison.
Power and diesel prices heading for nearly two-year high
The electricity price on Monday evening is the highest level in almost two years, when the price exceeds seven kroner per kilowatt-hour. The energy company OK writes this in a press release Monday morning.
According to Troels Skipper, commercial director at OK, the high electricity price is due to a combination of rising gas prices and a lack of wind and solar energy.
“Right now, we are in the unfortunate situation where the high gas price pushes the electricity price up along with it. And unfortunately, we do not get enough electricity production from wind turbines and solar cells to push the price the other way,” he said.
The last time the hourly price was at around seven DKK per kilowatt-hour was in December 2024.
Also, Diesel prices in Denmark rose to a record high on Monday, reaching 19.19 kroner per litre after an increase of 20 øre, according to FDM, the Danish motorists’ association. Denmark is set for a week of changing autumn weather, with periods of rain, sunshine and mild temperatures, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI.
Monday began cool, particularly in central Jutland, where temperatures fell to between 6 and 8 degrees.
“The temperature is down to 6-8 degrees, so if you are going out cycling, you can clearly feel that autumn has arrived,” DMI duty meteorologist Jesper Eriksen told Ritzau.
The rest of Monday is expected to remain dry, with a mix of sunshine and clouds. Temperatures will reach between 15 and 18 degrees, with light to moderate winds from the west.
### Tuesday to be warmest day
Tuesday is expected to be the warmest day of the week.
Winds will turn to the south, bringing slightly warmer air over Denmark and pushing temperatures to between 17 and 21 degrees.
There will be periods of sunshine, although some rain is possible, particularly in Jutland.
More rain is expected to reach Jutland later Tuesday afternoon before moving east during the evening and overnight.
Wednesday will bring some sunshine but also showers.
Temperatures are expected to fall back to between 15 and 18 degrees, while winds will turn west again.
Thursday and Friday are expected to bring periods of rain and showers, with temperatures remaining between 15 and 18 degrees.
Winds from the west and southwest are also expected to strengthen gradually toward the end of the week.
Eriksen said the week would not be particularly cold despite the unsettled weather.
“In the week as a whole, you will not need the really warm clothes, but in periods you will need rainwear and rubber boots,” he said.
It remains unclear whether September will bring another spell of warmer weather later in the month.
“We will have to see what happens, whether the last spasms with some warmth arrive. It is not decided yet,” Eriksen said.
More than half of the Danish schools that were selected for the latest Pisa survey declined to participate. In total, 398 schools were drawn for the survey. Of those, 215 chose not to participate, writes Kristeligt Dagblad.
When a selected school chooses to decline, a reserve school could step in. In advance, two reserve schools had been designated for each of the drawn schools.
Therefore, a total of 283 schools ended up participating in the survey. However, this is significantly fewer than in 2022, when 347 schools participated.
According to Kristeligt Dagblad, the number also remains below the OECD’s “technical minimum requirement”.
According to Monika Klingsbjerg-Besrechel, chief consultant at Statistics Denmark, which was responsible for the practical part of the survey, the many declines have not affected the quality of the survey.
“Fortunately, we reached a higher response rate, but despite that, we were unfortunately still below the minimum requirement from the OECD. If we had not had the reserve schools, we really would have been in serious trouble,” she says to Kristeligt Dagblad.
She points out that it was subsequently investigated whether the many declines had affected the result.

Danish man faces October court hearing over fatal assault at Copenhagen World Cup event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:54:44 UTC
18:54:44 KST

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

Danish parties support government response after Russian frigate fires flares near helicopter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:54:38 UTC
18:54:38 KST

Danish political parties broadly support the government’s response after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a military helicopter Monday, according to Denmark’s Armed Forces.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats briefed party representatives Tuesday. The Foreign Ministry has summoned Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, to discuss the incident.
“It is completely the right thing to do,” said Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party.
The Armed Forces reported the incident in a statement at 11:02 p.m. Monday. It said an Air Force Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser.
The frigate fired two flares, which are normally used as attention signals at sea. One passed close to the helicopter.
“It is obviously an escalation from the Russian side,” said Thomas Danielsen, defense spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Alex Ahrendtsen, defense spokesperson for the Danish People’s Party, urged calm.
“Of course, we should not go to war with the Russians because of some signal lights that have been sent up,” he said.
Bruus said both the frigate and helicopter had a right to operate in international waters and called the helicopter’s work normal.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats described the incident as serious but unsurprising.
She said it was part of a pattern involving “an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia” that is testing NATO and conducting hybrid warfare against Europe.
“Russia wants to intimidate and sow discord. Our response is to stand closer together and strengthen the defence of Denmark and Europe,” Frederiksen said.
According to a press release from the Danish Finance Ministry, Naalakkersuisut (the Government of Greenland) and the Danish government signed a partial agreement on Tuesday worth 1.2 billion DKK for investments in Greenland from 2026 to 2029.
“The agreement means, among other things, that there will be a relief package for the Greenlandic citizens who are the most vulnerable economically,” the ministry said.
The governments have also agreed to provide funding for Greenland’s utility sector. This includes water supply projects in Ilulissat and support for Nukissiorfiit, Greenland’s self-rule-owned utility company, to help develop the country’s energy infrastructure.
Funding will also go toward operating Greenland’s new international airports, with the agreement including money for feasibility studies in 2027 for a new regional airstrip in Ittoqqortoormiit and a new deep-water port in Qaqortoq.
“We are investing in initiatives that can be felt in the everyday lives of the Greenlandic people, and which at the same time support Naalakkersuisut’s work to develop a strong and sustainable Greenlandic society,” Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard said.
The agreement follows another deal between Greenland and Denmark reached in February, which provided funding for Greenlandic patients to receive treatment in the Danish healthcare system.
Both agreements stem from a framework agreement reached in September last year between Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Under that framework, the two sides agreed on a package worth 1.6 billion DKK for Greenland’s healthcare system, the deep-water port and a new airstrip.
Around 100,000 AL Sydbank customers will no longer have to pay up to 600 DKK a year for an account, online banking access and a debit card.
The offer was previously available to customers of Arbejdernes Landsbank. Following the merger of Arbejdernes Landsbank, Vestjysk Bank and Sydbank, it will now be extended to all customers of the new bank, AL Sydbank.
“When we did the merger, we promised that you would be able to get an account, access to online banking, and a debit card without it costing anything,” said Svend Randers, AL Sydbank’s director responsible for private customers.
“That is the promise we are fulfilling now, and it applies both to our existing customers who do not yet have those terms, and then of course the new customers who hopefully will join,” he said.
Randers said the bank hopes the offer will attract new customers and encourage existing customers to stay.
“And then of course we hope that in the longer term, it means that those customers will want to do more business with us when they eventually buy a home or car or save up for retirement or something else entirely,” he said.
The change comes after AL Sydbank told customers this summer that several fees would change following the merger.
According to a Mybanker analysis for TV 2, fees increased for between 55 and 60 percent of the bank’s services, depending on which bank a person previously used. Between 25 and 35 percent of fees decreased.
Customers must have their NemKonto, the bank account used for payments from Danish public authorities, with AL Sydbank to qualify for the free account.
The bank has not yet decided which debit card will be included.
