Expert insights: I came for my partner’s job. Now what?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

The author: Chiara Marmugi is an Italian communications professional based in Copenhagen since 2014. She works in corporate communications and runs a communication consultancy on the side, with a background in literary translation and academic work in Italy, Spain and Germany. She runs INTERCOM, a network for intercultural and DEI communicators, and is co-editor-in-chief of Sette giorni in Danimarca, the Italian-language newsletter of the Last Week in Denmark circuit. She writes about international careers and the work-related questions faced by accompanying spouses in Denmark.
I arrived in Denmark in my forties. Before that, I’d been a copywriter, an editorial translator, a university lecturer, a researcher, a public speaker. Years spent building a professional identity, moving between different worlds.
Then I landed in Denmark and, almost overnight, became an accompanying spouse. Just that.
My professional identity hadn’t disappeared. But I was hundreds of kilometres away, in another language, inside a network I could no longer reach easily. The experience was still mine. Its value had simply become harder to see.
Denmark is very good at attracting international employees. It’s much less good at recognising the professional capital that arrives alongside them. And this matters for a practical reason: retaining talent isn’t only about the employee. If the partner can’t build a life here, the whole family eventually leaves.
There are programmes for this already. Many, and all useful. But at some point another CV workshop isn’t what an accompanying spouse actually needs.
Sometimes the problem isn’t the CV. It’s how we see ourselves, and how we let ourselves be seen by the Danes around us.
Stop looking for your old job
One of the first mistakes international spouses make is trying to recreate the career they had before moving. It’s understandable. Marketing manager in Brazil, you search for marketing manager jobs here. Lawyer in Germany, you look for lawyer positions.
But your old job title might be one of the least useful things you have. Start with a harder question instead: What did I actually do? Manage people? Negotiate with clients? Build partnerships? Solve problems nobody had given you a manual for? Those are transferable skills. Your previous employer may mean nothing here. Your skills still do.
Sometimes the fastest way in isn’t through the door you expected. That doesn’t mean taking any job and hoping for the best, it means being open to a sideways move. A project. Consulting. Freelancing. Volunteering in a professional capacity. Something that gives you a Danish reference, and a Danish professional context.
The point isn’t to collect something called “Danish experience” for its own sake. It’s to give employers a reason to place you. Once you’re inside a professional environment, the conversation shifts. You stop being an unknown CV from somewhere else. People have actually seen you work.
Be visible
This sounds obvious until you try to do it. Most accompanying spouses spend the first year or two keeping a low profile, waiting to feel ready before they put themselves forward. Nobody ever feels fully ready.
Being visible doesn’t mean self-promotion, it means existing in the rooms where your field talks to itself. Show up to the event even if you don’t know anyone. Comment on the LinkedIn post instead of just reading it. Say the thing in the meeting instead of rehearsing it afterwards in your head.
And don’t sand down what makes you different to fit in faster. An accent, a different way of structuring an argument, a habit of asking the question nobody else asks: these read as foreign at first, and as an asset once someone actually needs what they produce. Danish workplaces value people who bring something the room doesn’t already have. That only works if you let them see it.
Network differently
“Network” gets repeated to international jobseekers constantly, and it’s rarely explained. If you’ve just arrived, you probably already have one: other international spouses, parents at school, people from your language community, your partner’s colleagues. Keep them.
But don’t stop there. Want Danish finance? Find finance people. Communications? Find communications people. And skip the question “Can you help me find a job?”. Ask instead: How does this industry actually work here? What would someone with my background need to understand? Which part of my experience is actually useful in this room?
Take the first step yourself. Danes rarely go out of their way to invite the new person in, not out of unfriendliness, more a cultural habit of assuming people will ask if they want something. So ask. Write the message, request the coffee, follow up on the introduction someone half-offered you three weeks ago.
Those questions and that initiative are easier for people to respond to. They also let the other person see a professional, not someone’s unemployed partner. Networking isn’t about racking up connections. It’s about becoming recognisable in the community you’re trying to enter.
Don’t hide the spouse story, but don’t let it define you
Don’t avoid mentioning that you moved here because your partner got a job. It explains why you’re here, why your career shifted direction. Nothing embarrassing about it.
But it belongs in your story, not at the centre of your professional identity. You are not “the wife of a researcher at DTU looking for something to do”. You’re a professional who moved for a family decision, and is now figuring out how your experience fits a new labour market.
The move itself probably taught you things you never needed before. Functioning without your usual reference points. Navigating systems you didn’t understand. Building relationships from zero. Don’t put “I survived Danish bureaucracy” on your CV. Do ask what’s underneath that experience: adaptability, independence, the ability to live across cultures, plain persistence.
Find your Danish angle
Take everything you know how to do and ask where it’s actually useful here. Maybe you know the Balkan market and a company here needs exactly that. Maybe you’ve worked across extra-European markets and can bridge teams that don’t naturally talk to each other. Maybe the languages you speak matter to a company trying to expand.
None of that is automatically an advantage. Nobody owes you a job for speaking six languages or having lived in four countries. It becomes one once you connect it to something a business actually needs. “I’m internationally minded” gets you nowhere. “I can help you understand this market” gets you a meeting.
Stay curious about the language, and about the culture underneath it
Learn Danish. But treat it as one part of a bigger curiosity, not the whole task. Don’t wait until your Danish is perfect to start participating professionally. Some jobs genuinely require fluency. Plenty don’t, and in a lot of international companies English already runs the place. Learn the language while you build a life here, not as a locked door you have to get through first.
The same goes for the culture: you don’t understand it and then integrate, you understand it by trying, getting it wrong sometimes, and staying curious enough to keep adjusting.
Danish work culture runs on things nobody writes down. Flat hierarchies that are flatter in theory than in practice. Meetings where consensus matters more than the loudest argument. A discomfort with visible ambition that can read as coldness until you understand it’s actually a norm about not standing above the group, fredagsbar as a genuine extension of the workday, not an optional extra.
None of that is in a textbook. You learn it by paying attention: asking people, treating every confusing moment as information instead of an insult.
I spent my first year in Denmark waiting to feel ready. Ready enough, fluent enough, connected enough. I’ve since learned that readiness isn’t something that arrives. You build it by being visible before you feel like it, by asking the question you’re not sure you’re allowed to ask, by staying curious long after the first frustration wears off.

Britain flies new turbojet drone engine in seven months
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
10:43:20 BST
18:43:20 KST

Britain has developed a new family of domestically produced turbojet engines, with one design taken from the drawing board to the air in less than seven months and a smaller engine already entering serial production, the Government has announced.
The programme is being run by the Ministry of Defence’s Strategic Capabilities Office with UK start-up Alloyed, combining government investment with matched funding from the company to establish a sovereign British propulsion capability for future weapons and aircraft.
The family spans engines producing between 30N and 2,000N of thrust, covering potential applications ranging from relatively small uncrewed aircraft to larger systems.
Two engines have already moved beyond the initial development stage. A 300N-class engine has completed flight testing and is now in serial production in the UK, while a larger 1,100N-class design progressed from its initial concept to flight-ready status in less than seven months.
The Government said the work had established the ability to design, manufacture, test and support this class of engine domestically, reducing reliance on overseas propulsion supply chains.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said: “Taking a jet engine from concept to flight-ready in just a matter of months shows how defence and industry can work together to deliver capabilities at the speed required by today’s world.”
He added: “The threats we face demand the ability to produce cutting-edge technology on demand and at scale – this programme delivers that, combining sovereign manufacturing, digital engineering and industrial innovation to ensure our Armed Forces retain an operational advantage, while delivering good jobs for working people here in the UK.”
Digital design and production
The engines have been developed using a digitally led engineering and manufacturing process intended to reduce the time between design, testing and production.
Alongside the engines themselves, the programme has established a UK-based digital design and modelling capability which the Government says can be used to develop new propulsion systems and variants in months rather than years.
The approach combines digital engineering with modular design, allowing elements of an engine to be changed or improved without requiring a complete redesign of the propulsion system.
Alloyed chief executive Michael Holmes said: “Working alongside the Ministry of Defence has enabled Alloyed to bring to bear its world-leading metals technologies to mature and demonstrate advanced propulsion systems at remarkable pace while building a lasting capability in the UK.”
He added: “This programme shows the power of combining defence expertise, digital engineering and industrial innovation.”
The 30N to 2,000N thrust range would allow the underlying technology to be applied across systems of markedly different sizes, while the modular architecture is intended to make later adaptations easier as operational requirements change.
Production expanding in Britain
More than 60 engineering and advanced manufacturing jobs have already been created through the programme, according to the Government, with a further 45 positions expected during the next 12 months as production increases.
The work also involves more than 40 suppliers across the UK, most of them small and medium-sized businesses.
The co-development model differs from a conventional procurement in which Defence specifies a finished system and then purchases it from industry. Instead, the Strategic Capabilities Office and Alloyed have jointly funded and developed the technology, with the aim of shortening development cycles and retaining the resulting industrial capability in Britain.
The Government said the programme supports commitments in the Strategic Defence Review to strengthen the domestic defence industrial base and increase the speed at which new technology can be developed and fielded.
There is also an export ambition, as Ministers said the propulsion technology could eventually be offered to allies seeking domestically supportable or resilient engine solutions, although no export customers or specific overseas programmes have yet been announced.
For now, the most concrete result is the move into production of the 300N-class engine and the rapid development of the larger 1,100N design, giving Britain a new domestically based turbojet development and manufacturing capability spanning a much wider family of future systems.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,400 Troops, 41 Artillery Systems and 1,839 UAVs in One Day
Ukraine’s General Staff estimated that Russian forces lost around 1,400 personnel during the latest 24-hour reporting period, as well as 41 artillery systems and 1,839 operational-tactical UAVs.
As of September 15, Russia’s total personnel losses since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, had risen to approximately 1,510,000.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest figures also showed the loss of three armored combat vehicles, raising the cumulative total to 25,334. The number of Russian tanks recorded as lost remained unchanged at 12,345.
Russian forces also lost an estimated 41 artillery systems, four multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), and one air defense system over the past day. These losses brought the overall figures to 49,793 artillery systems, 2,131 MLRS, and 1,638 air defense systems.
The estimated number of Russian aircraft and helicopters lost since the beginning of the full-scale invasion remained at 442 and 356, respectively.
Drone losses continued to account for a substantial share of the daily tally. The General Staff recorded another 1,839 operational-tactical UAVs, increasing the cumulative figure to 518,280. Eleven unmanned ground vehicles were also reported lost, bringing their total to 2,626, while cruise missile losses remained unchanged at 5,111.
In addition, Russia lost an estimated 376 vehicles and fuel tankers and seven pieces of special equipment during the latest reporting period. Their cumulative losses now stand at 149,183 and 4,690, respectively. Naval losses remained unchanged at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Meanwhile, combat operations remained intense across the frontline, with Ukrainian forces reporting 262 clashes during the latest reporting period.
The latest figures come amid continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian military equipment. In one recent operation, a Ukrainian drone crew destroyed two Russian BM-21 Grad multiple rocket launchers and damaged two others, with one of the drones traveling 45 kilometers before striking its target.

Russian Wildberries Orders 478,000 m² of Mesh Netting to Protect Warehouses From Ukrainian Drones
Major Russian online marketplace Wildberries is rushing to secure its logistics infrastructure following sustained aerial strikes, launching a tender for 478,000 square meters of galvanized metal wire mesh across eight regions in Russia, The Bell reports on September 14.
By August 17, damage to the company’s facilities reached approximately 2.4 million square meters, which represents nearly 43% of its total storage space.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Bell, the procurement terms published in early August specify that the wire diameter must not exceed 2.5 mm, with delivery required within seven days. While public tender documentation omits the purpose of the order, an industrial source confirmed that the materials are intended for protection against unmanned aerial vehicles.
The procurement effort comes after targeted long-range strikes began on July 18. Over the following month, at least 22 facilities were hit across multiple regions, including Leningrad, Ryazan, Samara, Penza, Tula, Vladimir, and Tver regions, as well as Yekaterinburg.
One of the largest incidents occurred in Samara region in early August, where a fire destroyed a warehouse measuring approximately 160,000 square meters.
Perimeter metal netting set several meters away from structures is increasingly used across Russia to intercept incoming aerial impacts.
Manufacturers describe these modular steel lattice towers as reaching heights of up to 100 meters, capable of absorbing impacts from units weighing up to 400 kg at speeds of up to 200 km/h.
Similar protective structures are now deployed around oil storage sites, thermal power plants, and electrical substations.
The current Wildberries tender remains under evaluation, with bids submitted for three of the eight available lots. Offered prices range from 154 to 474 rubles ($1.80 to $5.60) per square meter, placing the potential total cost between 73.6 million and 226.5 million rubles ($871,000 to $2.68 million).
The company has also opened a separate tender for silica fabric across 14 sites to act as a fire barrier against operational disruption.
Ukrainian drone attacks on Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, have destroyed around one-third of the company’s total warehouse capacity.
The retailer generates roughly 6 trillion rubles ($74 billion) in annual sales through nearly 100,000 pickup locations.

Ukrainian parliament dismisses prosecutor general amid corruption scandal, anti-graft war and bizarre Paris trip
Ukraine's parliament dismissed Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko on Sept. 15, a week after he resigned and a day after he announced that he had approved charges against the head of the country's anti-corruption bureau.
The dismissal, which passed without a single vote against it, comes amid a confrontation between Ukraine's anti-corruption agencies and the Prosecutor General's Office, which is facing a National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) investigation into an alleged criminal group that protected scam call centers and helped launder millions of hryvnias.
NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) said Kravchenko's announcement about the charges against NABU chief Semen Kryvonos was part of a broader effort to undermine the independence of the anti-corruption agencies.
Late on Sept. 14, the Prosecutor General's Office posted a statement that seemed to signal division between the agency and its outgoing boss. The statement claimed the reported charges were "not true" but also "canceled" — by whose authority, it remains unclear.
Just before the vote, Kravchenko urged lawmakers not to vote under "pressure," while stressing that he "has not signed any politically motivated procedural decision" against them.
"I did not sign a single politically motivated procedural decision, neither regarding representatives of the opposition nor members of the ruling political party," he said.
Ukraine's Prosecutor General is required to sign notices of suspicion against lawmakers before they can be formally charged with a crime.
Kravchenko, who was long seen as a staunch loyalist of President Volodymyr Zelensky, resigned Sept. 7 following a meeting with the president and amid the corruption controversy.
The NABU investigation has raised questions about Kravchenko's alleged ties to a group that provided protection to scam call centers. In recordings obtained by the bureau, investigators refer to a "boss" who allegedly protected the group. The person's patronymic, Andriiovych, and former position as head of the State Tax Service match Kravchenko's details.
An earlier Telegram post by the Prosecutor General's Office indicated that investigators understood the "boss" mentioned in the recordings to be Kravchenko.
Kravchenko has not been formally charged in the case.
His announcement on Sept. 14 that he had approved charges against Kryvonos further escalated the confrontation between the Prosecutor General's Office and the anti-corruption agencies.
The dispute also unfolded as Kravchenko prepared to leave Ukraine. He requested permission to attend a Sept. 16 European conference on Ukrainian children in Paris, and the Kyiv Independent saw a signed and approved document authorizing his departure.
The conference on international accountability for Ukrainian children was organized by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). The authorization was signed on Sept. 13, just hours before Kravchenko left the country and announced the charges against Kryvonos.
However, Kravchenko's name does not appear on the event's program, and PACE confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that he would not attend.
"Neither Ukraine's Prosecutor General - nor any member of his office - will take part in this meeting," a PACE spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent.
The Ukrainian president called on the parliament to swiftly dismiss Kravchenko.
"This prosecutor general has only one path: dismissal from office. That is exactly what I told him," Zelensky said on social media. "Ukraine has seen all the reasons."

A New Headset to Help With Depression Is Now Available in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

An at-home wearable for the treatment of depression is now available by prescription in the US.
With roughly one in six American adults taking an antidepressant medication, Swedish firm Flow Neuroscience is positioning its device as an alternative to traditional drugs. But at the current four-figure price tag, it might take a while for the futuristic-looking headset to catch on with patients.
Worn on the forehead for 30 minutes a day and operated with an app, the device provides low-intensity electrical stimulation to the left frontal lobe of the brain, an area involved in regulating mood and emotions. People with depression tend to have lower activity and weaker neural connections in that part of the brain.
Flow received approval from the Food and Drug Administration last December, and its device is among a new breed of wearables that monitor, record from, or stimulate the brain. California-based Cognixion, for instance, has modified the Apple Vision Pro to build a communication system for paralyzed people that doesn’t depend on speech or motor control. A headband by Muse promises to improve meditation, and a device by Elemind is meant to help people fall asleep faster.
The Flow device targets the same part of the brain as transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, an approved treatment for depression that uses magnetic fields to activate neurons. With TMS, patients have to go to a clinic, and a full dosing series typically requires treatment sessions administered five days a week over several weeks. The whole course of treatment can cost up to $15,000 without insurance.
Flow CEO Daniel Månsson, a clinical psychologist before he cofounded the company, says he set out to make a more convenient option for patients. “In order to have a real impact on the problem, you need to create something that has the effect on the brain needed, but that can be used in a home environment in a safe and effective way,” he says.
In a trial of 174 people with major depressive disorder, 45 percent of participants who received Flow’s device experienced a remission in symptoms at 10 weeks compared to 22 percent of those in a control group who received a sham version. The trial included people who were taking antidepressants and those who weren’t—evidence that the device can, under medical supervision, be used in addition to medication, Månsson says.
Reported side effects were mild: Some people experienced skin irritation, headaches, and trouble concentrating. Antidepressants, meanwhile, can cause nausea, weight gain, drowsiness, dry mouth, and sexual problems, but these can go away a few weeks after beginning medication.
In Europe, where the device has been approved since 2019, more than 65,000 people have used the Flow device, says Månsson. The UK’s National Health Service is also piloting the headset.
In the US, patients will be able to get a prescription for the Flow device from a clinician in person or via telehealth. But at least for now, they’ll have to pay out of pocket to use it: $2,200 for 10 weeks and then $325 per month after. That’s a lot more than standard antidepressants, which are usually covered by insurance. Månsson says the company is working to get reimbursement from insurers.
Vinod Khosla, a billionaire venture capitalist and an early investor in Flow, thinks a nonchemical approach to treating depression is the way of the future. “My bet is, if you ask any person who's on depression drugs, they'd prefer not to be on them,” he says. “They'd like a nondrug, nonchemical treatment for it.”

safety curtain series puts contemporary art center stage at vienna state opera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:25:49 UTC
18:25:49 KST

For nearly three decades, museum in progress and the Vienna State Opera have brought contemporary art into the theater with their Safety Curtain series. In traditional theaters, the safety curtain is the heavy barrier that separates the stage from the audience in the case of an emergency. Looking at the four borders of the curtain conjures the idea of a picture frame or a typical quadrilateral canvas that contains works of visual art. Seeing this as a site of opportunity, Safety Curtain has welcomed the likes of Anselm Kiefer, Joan Jonas, and Kara Walker, facilitating an annual encounter between the performing and visual arts.
The inaugural project in the Safety Curtain series came in the 1998/1999 season with Kara Walker’s installation. The American artist’s work often confronts the country’s violent history with slavery, most notably leveraging silhouetted figures that reflect on narratives of Blackness in the antebellum South. Typically, the Safety Curtains are accompanied by texts and interviews that contextualize the work within the Opera and the artist’s greater practice. In 1998, curator Nancy Spector wrote on Walker’s work, explaining its relationship to minstrel shows, the American Civil War, and Blackness in America. She writes, ‘Walker’s approach to her subject matter operates on the level of “entertainment” – it is raucously humorous and bitterly sarcastic. Her commission to design a curtain for the Vienna State Opera brings her own sources in early American theater tantalizingly to the surface.’
Cao Fei, The New Angel, 2022, Safety Curtain, museum in progress, Vienna State Opera, 2022/2023, large-scale picture
Creating Visual Work in a Space for Performance
In highlighting how Walker leveraged the theatrical setting in her piece, Spector foreshadows what will be a defining element of the Safety Curtain series: artists making use of the scale and dramatics of the operatic setting. In 2017, curator and critic Bice Curiger, in anotheressaywritten in conjunction with the project, maps the terrain the Curtains exist within, discussing artists that have made use of this peculiar, yet ripe, visual space. She identifies the Safety Curtain as occupying the same terrain as the ‘fourth wall,’ the metaphorical and physical barrier between spectator and stage. Additionally, the expectant audience and the preparation ahead of a show can be a landscape of distractions.
Given this, Curiger acknowledges that, ‘The conditions for confronting the work are nevertheless excellent: at the very least, the viewer is dealing with non-authoritative, unconventional monumentality. In spite of this power, however, the pictorial message has to come through, not least because of the potential for distraction and the heterogeneous audience.’
In 2026, Herbert Brandl joins the ranks of the Safety Curtain’s lineup of contemporary artists. This year’s jury—Daniel Birnbaum, Bice Curiger, and Hans-Ulrich Obrist—selected the late Austrian painter, who contributed a massive blue-and-white work for the Opera’s stage. The curtains remain throughout the entire season, starting from the fall and continuing into the summer of the following year. It’s visible before the performance, during intermission, and after the curtains close, giving audiences three opportunities within the span of the show to view the work.
In her analysis of Brandl’s curtain, curator Cathérine Hug identifies within the duochromatic painting its origins in space exploration and the depiction of the Blue Marble, or the capturing of Earth from the perspective of space. ‘It is this change in perspective achieved by leaving the Earth and flying above it, the so-called “overview effect”, that so fascinated Herbert Brandl and enables us to reflect collectively on the fragility of life,’ she writes, decoding the swirling whites that appear upon the stage.
In the decade since its inception, Safety Curtain works have played with, subverted, and reinvented the frame upon which the Vienna State Opera’s performances take place. There’s Rirkrit Tiravanija’s 2006/2007 work Fear Eats the Soul, which makes use of the rainbow television test card, invoking the Rainer Werner Fassbinder film Ali: Fear Eats the Soul, or in its original German, ‘Angst essen Seele auf,’ which appears on the curtain itself. Similarly calling on the language of media, David Hockney’s 2012/2013 piece, created on an iPad, depicts a theater within a theater, loose curtains depicted in curving lines open up to reveal a stage with the words ‘Wien Musik’ dancing across a pile of colorful geometries. In each iteration, these art-world actors stage an exhibition that continues to advance the conversation on art, spectacle, and performance.
David Hockney, 2012, Safety Curtain, museum in progress, Vienna State Opera, 2012/2013, large-scale picture
Cy Twombly, Bacchus, 2010, Safety Curtain, museum in progress, Vienna State Opera, 2010/2011, large-scale picture
Cerith Wyn Evans, 2011, Safety Curtain, museum in progress, Vienna State Opera, 2011/2012, large-scale picture
Tauba Auerbach, A Flexible Fabric of Inflexible Parts III, 2016, Safety Curtain, museum in progress, Vienna State Opera, 2016/2017, large scale picture
29th safety curtain jury: Daniel Birnbaum, Bice Curiger and Hans-Ulrich Obrist

How a 100-year-old population estimate may have got Australia wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:12:05 UTC
18:12:05 KST

In brief
- Estimates of Australia's pre-colonisation population may have missed the mark by millions, new research suggests.
- Its authors say the findings illustrate the magnitude of colonisation's devastating impacts on the Indigenous population.
How many people lived in Australia before colonisation? For nearly a century, many answers to that question have been influenced by a figure developed by anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown, who estimated the population at 250,000.
But new research from a national team of academics suggests there could have been about 2.2 million Indigenous Australians living on the continent before the British colonisation in 1788.
Based on the revised population figure and comparisons with early Census records, researchers estimate the Indigenous population declined by more than two million people between 1788 and 1861.
Corey Bradshaw, a professor of global ecology at Flinders University who co-led the research, told SBS News the findings illustrate the magnitude of the demographic collapse experienced by Indigenous Australians.
Researchers believe the decline was likely driven by a combination of introduced diseases, frontier violence, malnutrition, dispossession and other impacts of colonisation.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We're now starting to look at things like the massacres and try to de-bias a lot of that as well, because of course that's only the tip of the iceberg in terms of what was recorded," Bradshaw said.
The team relied on three independent approaches — archaeological, genetic and environmental modelling — rather than relying primarily on historical accounts.
Bradshaw said the approach is less vulnerable to the biases and gaps in historical records, and each of the three methods produced a relatively congruent set of estimates.
The 1930 estimate of roughly 250,000, Bradshaw said, was developed at a time when researchers lacked access to modern tools.
He said its creator acknowledged it was likely an underestimate, but the figure became widely accepted despite its limitations.
Other historical estimates suggested the population of Indigenous Australians may have been up to one million people, still under half of what the new research suggests.
'It's something we have to acknowledge'
Bradshaw said understanding the size of Indigenous populations before colonisation was essential to truth-telling and reconciliation.
"It's something that we have to acknowledge in our history and not sweep under the carpet," he said.
"It's part of understanding why the gap still exists in many aspects of society, and how to address it, and how long we might expect things to take to realign. I mean, these are huge demographic catastrophes that affected people for generations and generations."
The Indigenous population in Australia has grown since the 1950s, and represented 3.2 per cent of the overall population at the time of the 2021 Census at just under 813,000 people.
At current growth rates, the study estimates the Indigenous population will not return to its estimated pre-colonial size until around 2047.
Lynette Russell is a professor of Indigenous studies at Monash University's Indigenous Studies Centre and a co-author of the report.
She said the findings bring a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma that can inform future policy that helps Indigenous people.
"In addition to recognising this intergenerational trauma and disadvantage, it is also time to recognise intergenerational privilege," she said.
Bradshaw said the work also illustrates the resilience of Indigenous communities.
"It is remarkable that we have the variation and diversity of Indigenous cultures and languages and approaches to managing country that survived that catastrophe," he said.
More than 100 First Nations languages are still spoken across Australia, though some are in serious danger of being lost.
"We should celebrate the fact that these people were very resilient, and in face of all of that persecution, managed to persist."

System 76 Pangolin Pro Review (2026): Powerhouse Linux Laptop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

I have similar feelings about the very large glass trackpad. For things like photo editing, the trackpad's size is great, but I found my palms occasionally clicked the buttons at the bottom of the trackpad when I took a break from typing. It didn't happen often, but I learned to be careful about where I put my palms.
The 2-MP 1080p webcam is fine for casual use, chatting with family and friends, but if you do a lot of Zoom meetings in a professional context, you may want an external webcam. Also, open-source purists should note that Coreboot still does not support AMD Ryzen chips (or AMD does not support Coreboot, depending on how you want to look at it), so the Pangolin Pro does not use open firmware.
Finally, the Pangolin Pro is easy to open up to replace or repair components. There are nine screws on the bottom of the chassis, and none of them are hidden under the rubber feet or other shenanigans. Unscrew them all, and the bottom lifts off, giving you access to the SSD slots, RAM, WiFi card, and the rest of the internals. You'll have no trouble upgrading components down the road if you decide to, say, upgrade your memory when RAM prices come back down. (Is that actually going to happen? Who knows.)
Pop!_OS Linux Integration
System76's Pop!_OS Linux has long provided what I consider one of the best Linux experiences out there. The Cosmic Desktop and the custom apps System76 ships with it provide that "just works" stability you need to use Linux daily without even noticing you're using Linux.
As a long-time Linux user, I'm probably biased, but I find Linux to offer a better user experience than MacOS or Windows. I never feel like I'm fighting the operating system to get things the way I want them. I mainly run a terminal for writing, email, reading RSS feeds, etc, and a web browser. When I need to edit photos, I open Darktable; videos in DaVinci Resolve. None of that should require much from an operating system, but for some reason it's all easier for me in Linux.
Pop!_OS is particularly good in this regard, as it manages to feel familiar enough for Linux newcomers to find their way around, while still offering a good amount of power-user features. For instance, if you don't know what tiling windows are, you never need to be bothered about them, but if you want them, you can enable them with a toggle switch in the settings app. There are loads of (customizable) keyboard shortcuts for developers who eschew the mouse, and there are plenty of trackpad gestures to control workspaces, window focus, and more.
Should You Buy It?
At the beginning, I said the Pangolin Pro is overkill for most peoples needs, which is true. Although the Pangolin is actually cheaper than the smaller System76 Lemur Pro (review coming soon), the more portable Lemur Pro might be a better fit for many. However, if you're doing highly intensive things with your laptop, building local AI models or training custom agents, compiling software, or just want a powerful, future-proof machine, Pangolin is one of the best Linux laptops I've tested.
If you're a Linux user looking for a 16-inch laptop with all the bells and whistles, and one that isn't crazy expensive or crazy heavy, this is the machine I would get.

luca battaglia captures the ghostly glow of disappearing carousels with long-exposure photography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:20:57 UTC
17:20:57 KST

luca battaglia uses long exposure to turn carousels into light
Luca Battaglia takes the familiar carousel and transforms it into a luminous, almost architectural apparition in Ticket non remboursable, an ongoing photographic series rooted in memories of his childhood in Milan. Using long exposures of 20 to 30 seconds, the Italian photographer captures carousels as they rotate through public squares and city streets, allowing horses, decorations, and individual figures to dissolve into bands of light.
Growing up in Milan, Battaglia regularly passed a carousel that has since disappeared. The attraction remained with him as an image connected to childhood, waiting, movement, and the peculiar way memories become attached to particular places. In Ticket non remboursable, that absent carousel persists indirectly, resurfacing through other structures encountered in different cities.
Deauville 2024 | all images courtesy of Luca Battaglia
long exposure turns rotation into architecture
Battaglia’s photographic process removes the carousel from its immediately recognizable form. Working with an ND256 or ND1000 neutral-density filter, he exposes each image for between 20 and 30 seconds. During that time, the rotating structure traces continuous lines of light across the photograph. Horses and decorative figures gradually vanish. In their place, illuminated rings, vertical structures, and glowing volumes appear. The resulting forms can resemble floating architecture or, as the Italian photographer suggests, objects that have briefly landed in the city.
Long exposure records the carousel over several seconds rather than freezing a single moment. As it turns, its horses, decorations, and individual figures begin to disappear, leaving behind lines and bands of light. This changes the way the structure is seen. A carousel is solid and recognizable when still, but Battaglia’s photographs make its form increasingly difficult to identify. The movement remains visible, while the object itself begins to dissolve.
Dijon, France
a circular journey that returns to where it began
The title, Ticket non remboursable, or non-refundable ticket, introduces another layer to the series. A carousel ride promises a journey while remaining fundamentally circular. It moves continuously without taking the rider anywhere else, eventually returning to the point of departure.
That circularity mirrors the movement of memory itself. Battaglia returns repeatedly to the image of the lost carousel from his childhood, but never encounters it directly again. Instead, he finds versions of it elsewhere. Landscapes change, contexts shift, and individual carousels take on different forms, yet something of the original memory remains.
The series now comprises more than 50 photographs and continues to grow as Battaglia encounters new carousels in different cities. The images form what the photographer describes as an imaginary constellation, connecting places through recurring structures, light, and movement.
Battaglia positions his photographic apparatus at a child’s height, allowing the long exposure to reveal a suspended temporality. The photograph, he suggests, strips the attraction of its familiar appearance and fixes fleeting sensations on paper.
Brooklin 202″
when a temporary attraction becomes a permanent image
The carousel is temporary by nature. It appears in a square or park, turns for a while, and eventually disappears. Photography would seem to do the opposite, holding on to something that has passed. But Battaglia’s long exposures do not preserve the carousel as it looks. The longer the camera records its movement, the more the horses, decorations, and individual details disappear. Ticket non remboursable becomes closely tied to memory. Battaglia does not try to reconstruct the carousel he remembers from his childhood in Milan, accepting that it’s now gone. He encounters others in different cities, each with its own colors, structure, and surroundings. Across the series, these different carousels begin to echo one another. The photographs retain traces of their structures, but the movement transforms them into something less familiar. Battaglia describes this as a kind of visual memory: blurred, altered, and slightly unreal.
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

Australian fashion brand Cue Clothing falls into receivership
Sydney-based fashion business Cue Clothing Co entered receivership on Tuesday afternoon.
In a statement, FTI Consulting, appointed as receivers and managers for Cue, said increased sales and other improvements across the group were not enough to offset the overhead costs.
The company, which was founded in 1968 and operates Cue and its sister brand Veronika Maine, will continue trading while the receivers assess the business and restructuring options.
Cue has 69 stores across Australia, including concessions in Myer and David Jones department stores.
A sale process seeking offers for the business would "commence immediately" to secure the future of the brands, according to FTI Consulting.
Duncan Clubb and Shaun McKinnon of BDO were appointed as voluntary administrators on the same day.
It is unclear at this stage whether there will be any job losses due to the company's receivership.

BEIJING, September 16. /TASS/. Russian-Chinese relations are at an unprecedentedly high level and serve the fundamental interests of the peoples of both countries, Russian State Secretary and Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilyova said during the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum.
At the beginning of her speech, Tsivilyova welcomed all forum participants and expressed her gratitude to the People's Liberation Army Academy of Military Sciences for organizing this important and large-scale event. "Today, this authoritative discussion platform has taken on special significance. The forum has become a key platform for those seeking an objective perspective on global developments and striving for dialogue," she said.
Tsivilyova noted that Russia and China are marking two significant anniversaries this year: the 30th anniversary of their strategic partnership and the 25th anniversary of the Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation. "Our countries' relations, which are at an unprecedentedly high level, represent a conscious historical choice that serves the fundamental interests of the Russian and Chinese peoples. The tone for this cooperation is set by the regular and fruitful personal contacts between [Russian] President Vladimir Putin and [Chinese] President Xi Jinping. On May 19-20, Russian President Putin paid an official visit to China, during which crucial agreements were reached, a significant joint statement by the leaders was signed, and a Joint Declaration on the Formation of a Multipolar World and a New Type of International Relations was adopted. Our leaders met just two weeks ago in Bishkek on the sidelines of the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting," Tsivilyova emphasized.
